en: The First Chapter of the Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā:
Homage to Vāsudeva, the witness, the abode of the world.
To the one devoid of qualities, the supreme ether, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace— formerly, certain great sages, desiring to know Brahman,
were wandering the earth while [observing] the *agnihotra* sacrifices of other great sages.
Having gone to all the hermitages together with their sons and wives,
and having first paid homage to those staying there in due order,
they asked: "By which scripture will the knowledge of Brahman be attained?"
"By which scripture may the propitiation of the Blessed One be performed?
By which scripture should that action beloved by the Blessed One be carried out?
O sages, tell me all of that for those sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra. (1.4–1.5)
When they had been asked this, one sage named Kahola said: "As for us, we are sages who know Brahman alone as the ritual action prescribed in the Karma-kāṇḍa. (1.6) The Sages—
We worship Viṣṇu alone, who indeed takes the form of the Agnihotra and other rites;
for who knows his lore, and where does that great sage dwell?
1.7 Kahola said:
Having heard the words of Kahola, he spoke thus to those sages with a serene inner self:
"O best of sages, listen to the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman."
On the northern side of Meru, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
there is a hermitage of the Siddhas where a sage named Ekata, the son of Brahmā, dwells;
we have heard that he obtained this scripture from the Lord of Śrī.

Having heard these words of his and having paid their respects, they set out; reaching the northern side of Mount Meru, they bowed down to that great sage. Seeing them gathered there from one direction, he honored them immediately thereafter.

[With greetings and inquiries after their welfare, and with roots, tubers, fruits, and the like, he satisfied those ascetics; then, gathering them together, he spoke these words: "O sages, you have come here for my benefit; of this there is no doubt. (1.12–1.13)
"Furthermore, O great seers, tell me what business you have here.
Having heard these words of his, the sages, with joyful minds,
all stood with palms joined in reverence and paid homage according to the prescribed rite.

"O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, we have wandered over the entire earth to learn the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), yet no one who knows it is to be found. O bull among sages, it is because of Kahola’s words that we have come to Meru."
"You are a knower of Brahman, a son of Brahman, and one who knows the essence of the meaning of all the scriptures;
through austerity, you have beheld the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī.
Therefore, O Great Sage, teach that scripture which has been studied by you."
"For us who are afflicted and have attained fear of saṃsāra, you are our refuge.
Having heard these words of theirs, with a serene inner soul, he spoke these sweet words, pleasing them all at once: || 1.18–1.19 ||
Welcome to you, O great sages who dwell upon the Vindhya mountains!
O lords of munis, listen as I speak the truth concerning an event of old.
[Desiring the sight of you all, I made my dwelling on Mount Meru.]
"By my good fortune, the eternal Lord Vāsudeva has today entered your minds and sent [this message] himself. Therefore,
this birth of yours has become fruitful through the gift of knowledge."
"I shall attain the state that is the abode of Śrī and is served by the suns among devotees, just as in the first age I obtained the knowledge of Brahman from the Lord of Śrī.
I shall speak of that in its proper sequence; listen, O best of sages."
"We were created by Brahmā as Ekata, Dvita, and Trita.
Among them, O bulls among sages, I am the first by name, Ekata;
having realized the worthlessness of saṃsāra, I have come from the north of Meru."
"Having dedicated myself to Hari, the Lord of Śrī, I perform penance day and night.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees, revealed himself;
I beheld him, the abode of Śrī."
Having seen the Lord, and thereafter the Goddess and Śrī with uplifted minds, I was submerged in an ocean of bliss; then I praised Hari and Śrī:
"Homage to the lotus-eyed one! Homage to You who are clothed in yellow!"
Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to you whose feet are lotuses;
salutations to the formless one, to the one of beautiful form, to the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Salutations to the creator of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, whose nature is Brahman.
Salutation to the one who is accompanied by Padmā, whose form is the protection of devotees;
to the wearer of the forest garland, the sustainer of the various incarnations,
who arose from the churning of the milk ocean and is consecrated for the protection of the world.
"Salutations to her who wears a garland of lotuses; salutations to you, the source of immortality!
O Mother of the three worlds, I have come to you for refuge.
Having thus bowed down, as I stood up, he who is the protector and is kind to his devotees [spoke].
Then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, together with Śrī, was pleased. "I am well-pleased, O son of Vidhi; what boon do you desire from me?
he said then, "Choose a boon from me, the giver of boons. (1.33–1.34)
Having heard these words of Hari, I spoke with my palms joined in reverence:
"O Hari, indeed thousands of millions of births have been attained by me.
Therefore, O Blessed One, having crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, I—"
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu has been proclaimed by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and other scriptures;
indeed, for the devotees stationed there, there is no returning [to this world]. O Lord, lead me, who am terrified of the ocean of saṃsāra, to that state.
"May this boon be mine, O Hari; I choose nothing else," thus did I pray, and the Blessed One replied to me:
"O Sage, I grant you a world characterized by the absence of rebirth."
Nevertheless, O Mahāmati, I shall say something; do that.
This Śrī [Goddess of Wisdom], out of a desire for the welfare of the world, has learned a single treatise from my own mouth and wishes to teach it to you. (1.39–1.40)
"You alone are his worthy recipient; learn it from the mouth of Śrī.
Furthermore, after some time, great sages born of lineages such as Vasiṣṭha will arrive, for they have been initiated by me."

"Even while still in the womb, you taught them this scripture; then, having come to my world, may they rejoice like the eternal sages. Having spoken thus, you looked upon Śrī and taught [it] to the sage.
O eminent sages, having heard that which issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa,
Śrī taught the Pāñcarātra known as the *Śrīpraśna*.
O eminent sages, I performed the worship of those two according to the prescribed rules.
Then the Blessed One spoke to him who stood with his palms joined in reverence:
"Having performed worship and standing before me, Hari,
this purifying scripture that accomplishes liberation has been taught."
"You ought not to instruct one who is not a devotee, nor one who is full of desire, nor one who hates me, nor a woman, nor a thief, nor one who is not upright.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the World vanished along with Śrī.
"In which lineages were you born? Tell me, O great sages. Vedaśiras replied:
"Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viśvāmitra as the third."
And Kauṇḍinya—these sages are indeed the founders of our lineage. I am named Vedaśiras, as well as Kavaṣa and Aruṇi; Bharadvāja and these four are vessels of the Blessed One’s affection.
"Since they have received initiation even while in the womb, may you therefore favor us— these disciples who have come for the sake of accomplishing liberation.
This scripture called the *Śrīpraśna*, which was heard by you from the mouth of Śrī..."

"O Brahmin, tell us for our benefit that which bestows liberation, the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, beginning with the method of propitiation, which was obtained by you from the mouth of Śrī. Having performed the propitiation of the Blessed One, may we attain liberation. [1.52-1.53]
Thus entreated, the learned sage bowed to the Lord of Śrī from one side;
having meditated upon Him in his mind, he began to speak.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Scripture," in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
The second chapter.
Śrī said:
O lotus-eyed one, cause of the universe, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace!
Worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
O you who are without beginning, middle, or end, compassionate toward devotees, and devoid of qualities—I ask a certain doubt; please deign to explain it to me.

O Lord of All, actions never abandon living beings; and living beings, having attained their nature, are likewise never free from actions. O Lord of the World, that which is called *prakṛti* is indeed *māyā*, created by You.
Having encountered the divine illusion (māyā), which possesses manifold destinies, all living beings from Brahmā downwards indeed regard many afflictions as happiness;
for their knowledge has been stolen away by illusion regarding the distinction between pleasure and pain.
They do not know you, O Lord of the World; for such indeed is your māyā,
which cannot be overcome by knowledge, nor by austerity, nor even by the study of the Vedas (2.6),
nor by the recitation of the Dharmaśāstras and the like, nor by the reading of the Purāṇas.
O Hari, beloved of many ages, even after conquering Your Māyā through sacrifices and other rites, or through daily obligatory duties, no one shall attain liberation. (2.7–2.8)
"Indeed, some living being has arrived here through illusion among those who are deluded;
you have recognized the cause of that, O Blessed One, but I do not know it.
Without you, O Puruṣa, I shall not depart elsewhere even for a moment."

Nevertheless, I did not know that Vedic scripture which bestows liberation; nor was the task prescribed by you revealed to me. O affectionate one, if it were not a secret, [please tell it] to me, your devotee.
"For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, O ocean of compassion, Lord of the universe! Teach us, O Master of the world, so that these may attain liberation.
The Blessed One said:

"O Padmā, O beloved of the three worlds, there is nothing in the three realms that must be hidden from you by me; for you, O lady of holy vows, abide with me even during my incarnations and other such states.
This being so, O Sovereign of the Universe, what is there left for me to hide?"
"O Goddess, you are indeed all-knowing, yet to me, my beloved, you appear as if ignorant. O fair-faced one, desiring the welfare of the world, you question me;
for this inquiry of yours is appropriate for one who is afflicted by the world."

"O Goddess, I shall first relate how, in the past, I did not teach the scripture of liberation to Brahmā and the others for the sake of the world's welfare, O Rame. When the ancient Brahma-kalpa had arrived, everything was enveloped in water."

Indeed, you are hidden within the Śrīvatsa mark in the form of the very essence of the fortune of Yoga. When all the worlds, including everything mobile and immobile, were pervaded by darkness, you remained within my belly, together with Brahmā, having reached that world.
Then, assuming the form of a child even within the ocean,
I spent that time in delight, reclining upon a banyan leaf.
When the Brahma-night had passed, O beloved, by my own volition—
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was born from the navel-lotus;
remaining for some time within the pericarp of that lotus which was submerged in the waters,
he stayed there for a while, reflecting in thought as he did not yet know [his surroundings].
Then the thought occurred to him: "I am standing upon a lotus;
there can be no standing without some support for the lotus.
To what is this lotus bound? I shall find that out," he resolved.
Hurrying within through the hollow of the lotus stalk, I was searching for a path;
indeed, as I sought that path, I heard sounds.
Then, having fallen into reflection, he [the sage] undertook imperishable asceticism.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, having assumed the form of a swan and remaining in the sky,
I taught Brahmā in ancient times the auspicious Veda consisting of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa),
which is the primary root of the creation of the world.
Then, his heart satisfied, Brahmā, having obtained the triple Veda which sets action in motion, worshipped me with mental flowers;
and by my permission, the Creator departed for Satyaloka.
Having first created Marīci and the others, he taught the Vedas to them; they too, having received the triple Veda (trayī), likewise created many living beings,
O lovely one, including all stationary things, trees, shrubs, and creepers.
Having thus created the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), those who constantly study it,
perform its various rites, and find satisfaction therein— the deities—
set forth the ritual sections in manifold ways upon the world of mortals.
"O slender-waisted one, because of your instruction regarding the goals of life— dharma, artha, and kāma— human beings have gained confidence in them;
[so too] in the other scripture of renunciation or the Veda which has that same purpose."

Those who speak of the sacred rules did not question me, nor did I speak [of them], for I find delight [in this]. According to the scriptures, that which is to be taught to a worthy disciple must follow after a year or half a year of service to the teacher.
Having transcended that ritual procedure, O Padmamālinī, I did not speak of this supreme secret scripture, nor of that Veda which reveals it. (2.34) Śrī—
I bow to you, O Lotus-eyed One, the primordial source of the universe, the ocean of compassion;
for your power, deluded by the *guṇas* and *māyā*, is indeed manifold.
How, then, can they proceed to understand it, or the scripture that has that as its purpose?
These people have fallen into this most noble cycle of worldly existence;
if you have affection for me, O Hari, then out of a desire to favor the world, teach this entire Veda and that scripture from the very beginning.
The Blessed One said:
"This is the Veda named Ekāyana, which stands at the head of all Vedas;
the Pāñcarātra has that as its purpose and bestows liberation upon those who perform its rites. (2.38)
In that [Veda] where the single, eternal path to liberation is proclaimed in the form of my own worship, therefore it shall be the Ekāyana.
Night is said to be ignorance; thus, the Pañcarātra is the destroyer of ignorance.

That scripture shall be called Pañcarātra, in accordance with its literal meaning. It consists of one and a half crores of verses in the Anuṣṭubh meter; like the Vedas, it is eternal, and in my world, there are eternal sages who know it.
They always honor it with devotion and worship it with their minds;
yet this knowledge of the Vedas and Shastras does not by itself bestow liberation. [That is not so] in which [knowledge] is accompanied by wisdom and especially by yoga.
The manifestation of abodes and the manifestation of images—
these characteristics have also been explained in detail, along with the consecration,
the fire-ritual, and the expiation in its entirety. (2.43–2.44)
The initiation of worshippers and the established doctrines have been proclaimed;
various types of wine-offerings and festivals with many divisions have been described.
Indeed, many tasks such as the extraction of mantras are contained within this [tantra].
Śrī said:
O God of gods, how do people fallen into this great ocean of worldly existence proceed within it, and how might knowledge arise?
Or how could there even be faith in those who are sinking into the cycles of worldly existence?

Some, overcome by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), declare the world to be without a Lord; others say that the body is eternal, and that there is no happiness to be found within this cycle of transmigration.
Thus, there are many various kinds of differences in the inclinations of living beings; they wander in other ways. O Lord of the World, how might their cessation come about?
For there are no great teachers upon the face of the earth.
People deluded by desire do not accept what has been taught.
Nevertheless, out of compassion for me today, having condensed the essence of the scripture and taking its sattvic portion, please teach the Pañcarātra.
The Blessed One said:
"O Queen, it is as you have said: even the deities such as Vidhi and the others wander through the cycle of existence; how much more so, then, for humans on earth? (2.52)

"O Goddess, as I was requested by you—just as the nectar [was extracted] from the ocean—I have drawn forth the *sāttvika* portion for the sake of the world's welfare. O Lotus-born One, benefactress of the world, listen as I speak to you. (2.53)
And in the Upaniṣads, they speak of five kinds of my forms,
distinguished as the Supreme Manifestation (paravyūha), the Heart-form (hārda), the Expansive (vibhava),
and the Worshipful (arca). Among these, the wise always behold the Supreme Manifestation within this Vaikuṇṭha.

O Goddess, because sages always perceive me within the center of the heart as the object of their meditation through the reality of yoga, I am called "Hārda" (the Heart-abiding). Even ordinary people on earth, when they behold me during my incarnations at those times, [perceive me thus].
"The sages disregard it; the wise know it; I rejoice in it. Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Third Chapter:
Śrī said: "O Blessed One, please explain to me the reality of yoga, preceded by knowledge."
The Blessed One said:
"All gods, great seers, humans, and likewise animals—they are all bound by my *māyā*; therefore, its severance is a marvel."
I shall proclaim the essence of yoga, endowed with the reality of knowledge;
it is the destroyer of birth, death, old age, and disease, the savior from death,
and the supreme state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) that is difficult to attain through various other paths.
That which is inexpressible, inaccessible, all-pervading, and the witness of all;
partless, stainless, peaceful, transcending everything, and untainted—
that which is called the Supreme Brahman is reached only by means of yoga.
Through attachment to the qualities (guṇas), the enemies such as desire, anger, and the like,
constantly bind the liberated soul with fetters in the form of saṃsāra. Therefore, I shall tell you the means for liberation from those fetters.
O fair-faced one, how could knowledge devoid of yoga grant liberation?
And yoga devoid of knowledge would likewise not be capable of being demonstrated.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should maintain the wondrous yoga through knowledge.
From ignorance alone comes saṃsāra; indeed, from knowledge alone one is liberated.
What is the purpose of knowledge? It is the manifestation of the object to be known—possessing all forms yet formless, resembling pure crystal. (3.8–3.9)
Four-armed Vāsudeva, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
the ocean of bliss, pure, beyond qualities (nirguṇa), clad in yellow garments,
and the supreme cause of the origin of all gods beginning with Brahmā.
[He should meditate on] the Lord with a slightly smiling face and eyes as long as lotus petals.
By means of the yoga learned from the mouth of the Guru,
a wise man, contemplating the form of the Blessed One, should practice yoga according to the path.
This is declared to be knowledge; now the essence of yoga is being stated:
mantra-yoga, laya-yoga, as well as paricaya-yoga, niṣpatti-yoga, and the stages (avasthā) are proclaimed among the yogas.
I shall describe their characteristics; listen, O lotus-eyed one!
One who is pure should recite the mantra joined with the Mātṛkā and so forth for twelve years;
in due course, he attains knowledge endowed with the powers such as aṇimā.

The lowest of practitioners, possessing little intelligence, practices this yoga; it is proclaimed that the yoga of dissolution (*layayoga*) consists of the dissolution of the mind in millions of ways.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, or meditating, one should contemplate the partless Lord.
That indeed is what is called layayoga; now hear about haṭhayoga:

restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), both of these, posture (āsana), control of breath (prāṇasaṃyama), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna) upon Hari between the eyebrows.
Samādhi is the state of equanimity; it is called the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga), as well as Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, Khecarī, Jālandhara, Uḍḍiyāṇa, and likewise Mūlabandha. (3.19)
The prolonged retention of the *praṇava* and likewise the hearing of the *siddhānta*;
*vajrolī*, *amarolī*, and *sahajolī* are considered the threefold [yogas].
O Goddess, hear now their characteristics individually according to reality.
"O Lotus-born One, in truth, moderation in food is the foremost among the *yamas*,
and non-violence is the foremost among the *niyamas*. Furthermore, there is a fourfold [posture] consisting of the *siddha*, *padma*, *siṃha*, and *bhadraka*."
But at the time of the first practice, O Rame, obstacles may arise in many ways:

laziness, boastfulness, the pursuit of the counsel of rogue assemblies, and the means of [worldly] accomplishment; as well as greed for wealth, women, and the like—all of which are indeed like the water of a mirage. (3.23–24)
Having understood this, the wise one should abandon all obstacles through the power of merit;
then, seated himself in the lotus posture, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
He should construct a very beautiful hut with a narrow door and free from cracks.
It should be carefully smeared with cow dung or with lime;
it should be swept every day, especially with a broom,
and scented with fragrant perfumes and incensed with guggulu and other aromatics.
Having sat there, the wise man, established in the lotus posture (padmāsana),
with body straight and palms joined in reverence, should bow to his chosen deity. Then, with the thumb of his right hand, [he should touch] Piṅgalā...
Having restrained [the breath], one should fill the air through the *iḍā* very slowly and gradually.
Then, according to one's capacity, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention).
One should release it again through the *piṅgalā* very slowly indeed, not with force.
Again, having filled [the nostril] with the *piṅgalā*, one should slowly fill the abdomen;
having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale slowly through the *iḍā*.
Whichever [nostril] one should release [the breath] from, having filled [with that same one], one should retain it without contradiction.

Having circumambulated the knees neither too quickly nor too slowly, one should perform a finger-snap; that is proclaimed as one *mātrā*. Having filled the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] gradually with sixteen *mātrās*, || 3.32–33 ||
After filling [the breath], one should retain it for sixty-four measures;
then, one should exhale through the piṅgalā nāḍī for thirty-two measures.
Again, having filled [the breath] through the piṅgalā as before, one should remain well-composed.
One should practice the kumbhakas four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually up to eighty repetitions each time.
Through such practice for three months, the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) will occur.
But when the purification of the channels has occurred, then signs arise externally upon the body of the yogi; I shall describe them in their entirety:
lightness of the body, radiance, and the increase of the digestive fire. (3.37)
And at that time, the body will become steadily emaciated.
The best of yogis should avoid food that creates obstacles to yoga:
salt, mustard, sour, hot, pungent, and dry.
One should avoid leafy vegetables such as asafoetida and the like, sexual intercourse with women, and physical hardships such as morning baths and fasting;
at the beginning of the period of practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended.
They know that wheat, mung beans, and rice increase the power of yoga.
After that, one becomes capable of retaining the breath for as long as desired;
from such voluntary retention of the breath, the *kevalakumbhaka* (absolute breath-retention) is perfected.
When kevala kumbhaka, devoid of both exhalation and inhalation, is mastered, there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain.
First, perspiration arises; one should therefore perform a massage with it.
Then, from the excessive retention of the breath, phlegm arises in the body of the yogi seated in posture, gradually and very slowly. From even more intense practice, a violent sweat will arise.
And at that time, the frog-like state moves by leaping again and again;
the yogi, seated in the lotus posture, then moves across the surface of the earth.
Through even greater practice than that, the abandonment of the earth occurs.
Remaining in the lotus posture, he exists having transcended the earth. At that time, superhuman feats and such powers will arise;
yet he should not display his power, for if he were to do so, there would be a depletion of his ascetic merit.
When neither pleasure nor pain, once encountered, causes him distress,
then his urine and feces become scant, his sleep becomes minimal,
and there is a foul odor of sweat in his mouth, along with nasal mucus, eye-secretion, saliva, and perspiration. (3.49)
These [faults] do not arise for him in any way thereafter.

From even more intense practice than that, great power is produced, by which one becomes a perfected being who moves on earth and is capable of moving through water like those who move on land. 3.50–3.51
The knower of yoga slays tigers, lions, and śarabhas with his two arms;
he should practice the protracted *oṃkāra*, by which sin is destroyed.
The *praṇava* is the mantra that removes all obstacles and eliminates all defects.

Thus, through the practice of yoga, the stage of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā) arises. When prāṇa, apāna, mind, and intellect function without mutual conflict between the individual self and the supreme self, wondrous knowledge is accomplished.
That is called the "state of the jar" (ghaṭāvasthā); I shall describe its signs to you.
One should abandon a fourth part of the practice previously mentioned;
whether by day or at night, one should perform it for only a single watch (yāma).
One should perform the *kevala-kumbhaka* alone once every day.
That which is clearly the withdrawal of the senses from the objects of the senses,
performed by the yogi while established in *kumbhaka*, is called *pratyāhāra*.
Whatever one sees with the two eyes, one should contemplate that as the Self;
whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that as the Self; whatever one perceives with the nose, one should contemplate that as the Self. (3.58)
Whatever taste the tongue consumes, he should contemplate that as the Self;
whatever the yogi touches with the skin, he should contemplate that as the Self.
For one who contemplates in this way, there arises a power that transcends the human.
There shall arise hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and likewise traveling a great distance in an instant;
there shall be perfection of speech, the ability to assume any form at will, and invisibility.
By anointing with excrement and urine, iron and other metals shall turn into gold.
Through the practice of the five states, his movement will arise in the sky.
At that time, the wise one should remain focused for the sake of the yogin’s perfection of yoga;
these are obstacles to great accomplishment, and the wise one should not take delight in them.
The king of yogis should not display his own power to anyone whatsoever;
he should conduct himself among people as if he were dull-witted, foolish, or even deaf,
for the sake of concealing his own power.
And disciples undoubtedly request [instruction] for their respective tasks.
One should be intent on those various tasks, yet practice must not be forgotten;
without forgetting the Guru’s word, one should practice day and night. (3.65–3.66)
In this way, the state of the jar [of the mind] occurs through the yoga of continuous practice;
for one who lacks such practice, it is not accomplished by idle conversation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice yoga alone.
Then, through the practice of yoga, the state of familiarity arises.
Having diligently cultivated the *kuṇḍalinī*, the vital air (*vāyu*), once familiarized,
enters the *suṣumnā* along with the fire without obstruction.
The mind, together with the vital breath, shall enter the Great Abode;
for him whose mind and his own breath enter the *suṣumnā* here in this world.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—this is the pentad.
Among these five, the support of the bodies is said to be fivefold.
From the feet up to the knees is called the station of Earth;
the Earth is square, yellow in color, and has the syllable *la*.
Having mounted the wind upon the earth-element and joined it with the letter *la*,
one should meditate on it as having the form of the four-faced [Brahmā], four-faced and golden;
by holding [the breath] for five *ghaṭikās*, one attains victory over the earth.
Through union with the earth, death shall not come to that yogin.
From the knees down to the anus, the locus of the waters is declared;
the waters are described as the half-moon, white, and having the seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
Having placed Vāyu within the syllable *vā* and conjoined it with the syllable *va*,
one should remember the god Nārāyaṇa— four-armed, wearing a diadem,
resembling a dark blue cloud, peaceful, clad in yellow garments, and infallible. (3.76)
If one holds [the breath] for five *ghaṭikās*, one is liberated from all sins.
Then there is no fear of water, nor is death in water found.
From the anus to the end of the heart, this is proclaimed as the seat of fire (*vahnisthāna*).
One should meditate upon Fire as a red triangle, endowed with the syllable *ra*,
and as Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has four arms, is possessed of the qualities of strength and knowledge,
holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and is exceedingly gracious.
If one holds [the breath] for five ghaṭikās, one is not burned by fire.
For one who has entered that maṇḍala, fire indeed does not burn the body.
From the heart up to the middle of the eyebrows, it is proclaimed as the station of Vāyu.
One should meditate on the wind as a black hexagon, radiant with the syllable *ya*, in the location of the wind;
there one should hold the form of Brahmā, Aniruddha, four-armed, for five *ghaṭikās*. One will then move through the sky like the wind.
O Rame, for the yogin there shall be no fear of wind nor likewise of death.
From the middle of the eyebrows up to the top of the head, the station of space (ākāśa) is said to be;
it is the sphere of the sky, smoky in color, and radiant with the syllable *ha*.

Having placed Vāsudeva, the four-armed Lord of Ramā, who resembles pure crystal and bears the conch, discus, and mace, upon the wind in the sky— him who is equipped with the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya)— [one should meditate]. 3.85.
By holding [the breath] in space, one will certainly attain the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva). Wherever one may be situated, one enjoys ultimate happiness.
Thus, the wise yogi should perform these five dhāraṇās.
Thereupon his body shall become firm; for him, death does not exist.
Even at the dissolution of Brahmā, that king of yogis does not perish. Thus, one should practice yoga for sixty *ghaṭikās*.
"Having restrained the vital air in space, [one should meditate on] the deity who grants desired boons.
(3.89) "Performing this every day, free from desire and anger, the best of yogis shall please the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. (3.90)
If one desires the body of a god or other such being out of a longing for pleasure,
one obtains that very body and rejoices therein.
If there is a desire for qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, it arises merely through recollection.
In this way, these various yogic practices are the means for the yogin to achieve his desired goal.
For one engaged in yoga, physical afflictions arise as well as mental afflictions in many ways; of this there is no doubt. (3.92–3.93)

When he desires liberation, then, remembering me with his mind and placing his vital breath in the crown of his head, he remains established in yogic concentration; having crossed the Virajā river, he should cause [the self] to issue forth through the aperture of Brahmā.
Having reached My world, he attains My own form. The wise one shall rejoice eternally with the seers through the vision of Me.
Thus ends the third chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Fourth Chapter: Śrī said:
"The essence of Yoga, which accomplishes that which is difficult to attain, has been proclaimed by you."
Nevertheless, remove the many kinds of obstacles from these yogas.
Who indeed would apply himself to those [practices] that must be accomplished over a long period of time?
For generally, living beings in this world are devoted to desire and anger.
Therefore, having abandoned this path which indeed brings success very swiftly for the welfare of the world and is not shaken even by obstacles—
O Lord of Gods, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, tell me that path.
The Blessed One said:
"O you who dwell upon a lotus and hold a lotus in your hand, here is an answer corresponding to your question:
for the vision of which indeed bestows all accomplishments upon living beings."
Until this time, O fair-faced one, neither the wise nor even the yogis—
nor others— have recognized your form as an image of worship,
whether they be gods or humans, among all four goals of human existence.

Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, O fair-faced one, you may ask me for one or even four boons; having previously performed [this] in a sacred field together with you, O slender-waisted one, [you shall attain] a residence comparable to Vaikuṇṭha.

Having first performed the initiation prescribed in that scripture, the most excellent of teachers should install Hari within the temple in the form of the deity according to the Pāñcarātra rite— the form which grants all desires— and as the very embodiment of the mantra.
If one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences should worship my image,
or having installed it in his home, should worship it constantly,
I shall enter that image and become the fulfiller of the desires of those devotees.
"I shall be with you; let there be no doubt in this matter.
Śrī said: "O Blessed One, in which lands or by what means [shall I be present]?"
"What should the patron be like? With what qualities should the teacher be endowed?
What kind of characteristics should your beloved temple possess?
The Blessed One said:
He is a believer (*āstika*), intent on the performance of the rites prescribed in the *Karmakāṇḍa*;
he is full of faith, free from malice, a donor, and endowed with grain and wealth;
he is my devotee, taking delight in the worship of the gods and other such virtues. (4.13–4.14)
O Rame, whether he be a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or even a Śūdra, or even one born of a natural (anuloma) lineage, let him be the sacrificer;
provided he is skilled in all branches of knowledge, peaceful, and a preeminent among Brahmins.
One who has conquered his senses and subdued his anger, who is diligent in action and established in austerity;
who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, proficient in the science of architecture, and the most excellent among those skilled in the arts;
and who has been initiated according to the rules prescribed in the Pāñcarātra by the most eminent initiates.
Such is the Guru, my own portion, who knows the true essence of the meaning of the Pāñcarātra;
having recognized such a Guru, the wise man should go to his home.
Having first bowed to him with his head, he should request him for the work of building the temple.
"I am intent on building a temple for the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.
You, who are an expert in characteristics, ought to have this palace constructed by craftsmen.
Having thus entreated the lord of brahmins, he then [offered] a coconut fruit.

The Guru, being requested by the patron for the attainment of its fruit, should entrust the entire burden of the ritual work to him and place it upon him. On an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and at a propitious moment (lagna), the Guru himself—
One should perform the acquisition of land and other preliminary rites together with astrologers.
At the commencement of all undertakings beginning with the acquisition of land,
the Lord of All Mantras was formerly [worshipped] with all mantras preceded by the twelve syllables.
The Blessed One is to be propitiated with devotion upon the lotus of the disc, the pitcher, and the fire;
having gratified him with devotion through offerings such as the *arghya* and with mantras and rites prescribed in the Vedas,
one [should worship] the Blessed One Adhokṣaja in the form of Viśvakarman.
With various services, such as incense, lamps, and ointments,
and having offered milk-rice oblations, the preceptor should perform the sacrifice for the assembly.
When the dismissal has been performed for Viṣṇu, who is seated upon the lotus along with the fire, [the rite is complete].
At an auspicious moment, the wise man, accompanied by the patron,
having obtained permission from the brahmins along with the groups of artisans,
as well as from the brahmin practitioners and the most excellent chariot-makers, [departed] from the house. (4.27)
While the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" was being chanted by those who had mastered the Vedas,
the preceptor, the most eminent among the knowers of mantras, took up a full water-pot accompanied by banners,
parasols, flags, and various musical instruments.
Betel leaves, areca nuts, flowers, and fruits,

as well as sandalwood in a golden vessel— these indeed are the offerings for the bali, O Rame. Having placed these upon the heads of the bathed and purified attendants, the preceptor [should proceed].
For the purpose of securing the ground for the construction of Hari’s abode,
one should go toward the east or the north after meditating upon Hari, the bestower of all goals,
while observing the omens of beasts, birds, and humans.
In a meritorious field, favorable and pleasing, frequented by sages, filled with fruit-bearing trees and endowed with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass;
blessed with cattle, grain, and rice, and free from small creatures. (4.33)
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, on the shores of the ocean, and so forth;
in the midst of a village, in a city, or in places of exile—having first examined the omens, one should then purify the ground. (4.34–4.35)
Having reached the designated ground and meditated mentally upon the imperishable Hari,
one should first prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the northeast corner.
Then, having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with water consecrated by the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula.
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the embodiment of the waters, filled with rivers and sacred fords,
within a golden pitcher, and having likewise meditated upon Hetīśa in a nearby jar,
one should then worship the Lord and Hetīśa with offerings such as the *arghya* and other enjoyments.
The preceptor should offer oblations to Vāsudeva into the fire established upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Then,
when the deity has been dismissed along with the fire,
those born of the lineage of Viśvakarman and experts in the science of architecture (*vāstu-śāstra*) [should proceed].
And those who are the best of chariot-makers— let them also worship Hari.
With sandalwood paste and the like, with garlands, garments, and bracelets, the patron,
applying diligent effort, should satisfy both the artisans and the chariot-makers.

The preceptor should place in their hands a very firm cotton thread, empowered with the mantra of the thousand-spoked wheel, together with many small sticks. Both the patron and the preceptor, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, [should proceed].
Starting from the station of Indra, while the Brahmins who recite the Vedas and the practitioners most skilled in mantras were chanting the Bhūsūkta,
he proceeded by way of circumambulation, [warding off] even the spirits and demons.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the piśācas, the grahas, the nāgas, and the enemies of the gods,
up to the station of Īśāna, the Guru then proceeds to the center of the ground while reciting this verse:
May the bhūtas, piśācas, yakṣas, asuras, rākṣasas, and grahas— may they all depart from this place to their respective abodes,
before the divine Vāsudeva, the soul of all beings.
"I wish to establish the abode of the Lord of Śrī upon this ground.
Having recited this mantra, one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
The Guru should scatter white mustard seeds in all directions with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Having thus offered the bali according to the scriptures, one should cast the threads.
One should mark stakes made from milky trees in the eight directions;
its head is in the northeast corner, O Rame, while [the other] is in the west.
With both hands facing downward and the feet extended,
one should first draw the deity of the site (vāstudaivata) upon the scattered sesame seeds;
then, having invoked Indra and the other deities into its limbs, one should worship them.
Having established the sacrificial fire on its right side, one should offer clarified butter—
either a thousand, a hundred, or twenty-eight oblations— with the five Upaniṣads for the sake of pacifying the site.
One should offer sixteen oblations of food with the Puruṣasūkta for the sake of the Yakṣas,
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Nāgas, and Dānavas,
using Apāmārga, Śamī, and Khadira wood respectively.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial fuel-sticks for each [deity].
With the mantra of the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), one should offer a hundred oblations of *caru* rice;
then, having offered the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should cast the sacrificial offering (*bali*) for Indra and the other deities.
O Goddess, such is the sequence for the eight directions, and likewise the sequence for villages and so forth.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the venerable *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
The fifth chapter.
Śrī said:
In matters concerning the acquisition of land, the patron himself [should consult] the preceptor.
"You have indeed said that one should choose a knower of the Pañcarātra;
(1.5) O Dhara, I respectfully entreat you among the divine worlds beginning with Brahmā: who might be the master-artisan there? (5.2)
"O Lord, what kind of object does a deity employ for a magical creation?
The Blessed One replied:
"O gods, great seers, perfected beings, and humans, I delight in being honored. (5.3)

"O Goddess, the gods and the perfected ones (siddhas) in regions of pure virtue and upon the mountain peaks will seek me out in my wondrous form as a reflected image (bimba), and for my sake, they will build dwellings appropriate for each. 5.4.106–107a.

In the celestial worlds of the gods, Viśvakarman fashions palaces with gold and other precious materials; he likewise constructs the abodes of the Siddhas. But the great seers, through their ascetic power, create dwellings of stone within the forests.
O Goddess, humans construct houses in villages and towns;
they build them with baked bricks and stones by means of artisans.
I shall explain that method to you; listen, O Lotus-born One!
Then, on the following day at an auspicious moment, the supreme guru,
having bathed two oxen and adorned them with garlands and other ornaments,
placed those two bulls in front and was joined by the patron.

Having reached the previously described ground at the site of Brahmā according to the rules, the wise preceptor, together with the assembly of all musicians and with Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, should worship the earth with a boar [image]. 5.10-5.11ab.
One should worship the Earth-goddess with the mantra "uddhṛtāsi" and Hari with the *puruṣasūkta*.
One should worship Varāha with the *puruṣasūkta* and the Earth with the *bhūsūkta*.
Having offered oblations of sesame, clarified butter, fuel-sticks, and cooked food, one should perform the final *pūrṇāhuti* offering.
Having circumambulated the ground clockwise, one should utter this mantra:
"May all those nāgas, piśācas, and yakṣas who dwell here upon this earth depart; together with the rākṣasas, they shall leave, for I am constructing a palace for Hari."
Then, one should scatter white mustard seeds consecrated by the Astra-mantra in all directions.
As before, one should perform the Vāstu-homa and likewise offer the Vāstu-bali.
Thereafter, the Bhāgavata preceptor should plow the ground with a plough.
A plough and yoke made of *pālāśa* wood are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
those of a Kṣatriya should be made of *nyagrodha*, and those of a Vaiśya and Śūdra of *plakṣa*.
For all [castes], the pair of yoke-pins and the ploughshare should be made of *nyagrodha* and *pippala* wood respectively.
For all castes alike, the sacrificial cord (yoktra) should be made of gold;
or else it may be made of silver or copper, according to their respective order.
The bowstring should be made of kuśa grass, vīriṇa grass, or kāśa grass, each being fashioned from its own material.
One should have the sacrificial post and the threshing floor made from a single species of wood.
Having bathed, wearing new garments, with a turban, pure, self-possessed,
adorned with garlands and ointments, and provided with an upper robe and attendants— || 5.19 ||

Adorned with the five ornaments, he should then wash his feet; having sipped water (ācamana), restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma), and performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) according to the rules,
he should be authorized by Brāhmaṇas who are Vaiṣṇavas and most proficient in the mantras.

First, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; by that, he should sprinkle the ground. Then, at a favorable moment and a favorable conjunction (*sulagna*), the best of preceptors, while uttering the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*), [should place] the pair [of images] upon the shoulders of two bulls.
And one should yoke the plow with its yoke by means of that very vidyā.
One should cause kettledrums, tabors, conchs, and other instruments to resound in every direction.
O brahmins, the learned should recite the Śākunika-sūkta, which bestows peace upon all.
Meditating upon me in the lotus of the heart with the eye of the form of the Vidyā,
one should fashion a staff and a vehicle from trees such as the *palāśa* and others.
First, facing eastward, one should draw [the forms] using the Root-Vidyā.
The second plowing on earth is performed with the Puruṣasūkta;
the third with the Viṣṇusūkta, and the fourth with its Gāyatrī.
The fifth plowing should be performed with the Nārāyaṇānuvāka.
The sixth [rite], the plowing of the ground, should be performed with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads;
the seventh, one should plow upon the lotus-seat with the Bhūmisūkta.
One should perform the plowing on the earth precisely by way of circumambulation.
In this manner, beginning from the south, one should draw [the thread] up to the north.
(5.29) Likewise, when the bed of an ox is disturbed, when the yoke-poles and so forth are broken, when there is confusion due to transposition, and when ill omens arise; (5.30)
And by repairing the pegs of the thread, the prosperity of the patron becomes certain;
all those defects are pacified, and the instigator shall not meet with misfortune.
One should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣads.
The preceptor and the patron should satisfy the Brahmins with wealth.
Then, they should feed the earth, level it,
and subsequently construct irrigation basins provided with many channels.
One should sow seeds such as rice, mung beans, and barley there;
the field should be watered with abundant water every day. One must also take great care to provide protection until the completion of the harvest.
One should reap the ripened rice and other grains from that field and lead them to the cow-pen;
when the fruit is great, that abode shall endure for a long time.
There, one should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins. (5.35–5.36)
One should give wealth, such as cows and other gifts, to the Brāhmaṇas who have eaten;
one should sprinkle the ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the five Upaniṣads.
Or, one should dig the earth with spades or pickaxes until water is reached.
The extent [of the site] is desired to be equal to the first enclosure.
(5.38) But if, while digging into the ground, the most excellent guru should see ashes, charcoal, husks, and so forth, or snakes, scorpions, and other creatures, (5.39)
For their pacification, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sacrificial wood;
O Goddess, with the five Upaniṣads, the Sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta.
One should give gold and other wealth to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability.
Upon seeing jewels and such, the abode shall always be prosperous.
Then the Guru should fill the area of the pit with water from a jar;
he should cast flowers into that water as an omen of auspiciousness.
If the auspicious [mark] spirals clockwise for the Lord and the temple, it bestows prosperity;
however, if it should be otherwise, one should perform a *śānti-homa*.
One should perform the *khāta-homa* outside the excavation on a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having established and ignited the fire, the preceptor should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) with clarified butter and the *Puruṣasūkta* while reciting the root mantra;
he should likewise offer guggulu resin, sesame seeds, and wild rice (*nīvāra*) with the root vidyā-mantra.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should then cast rice into the pit.
The jars should be well-wrapped with threads and cloths over the rice;
the jars are said to be made of iron, or in its absence, of clay.
One should place the golden *ādhāra-śakti* (supporting power) into the central jar.
Into the eastern jar of that [central one], one should fill it with seeds;
into the southeastern [jar] with all metals, and into the southern [jar] with all minerals.
One should place earth from a sacred bathing site (puṇyatīrtha) in the pitcher in the southwest;
furthermore, one should fill the pitcher in the west with honey, and the one in the northwest with clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
One should place jewels in the pitcher in the north, and mountain soil in the northeast.
One should likewise cast soil from a rice field,
earth produced from a lake that never dries up, and clay originating from an anthill into the central jar;
standing facing the east, one should also place the bulbs of lotuses and other such plants.
Likewise, he should place iron ornaments and a bundle of *darbha* grass;
having filled [the vessel] with these and with earth, he should have it covered with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*).
Upon the jar placed over the central jar, [he should place] one made of gold or other metals.
Having placed the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] upon Kālāgni, who is formless in his third aspect,
one should then place the support of the earth (*vasudhādhāra*) into the jar above;
thereafter, one should fill those jars with scented water and worship them.
One should bring the earth, sand, and water to a state of equilibrium;
then, one should construct the foundation of the temple for the pacification of all defects.
When the temple is being commenced, many obstacles arise.
"O Goddess, once the abode for the Child has been made, those [obstacles] will perish of their own accord.
Or else, O fair-faced one, having entered that image of the Child, I shall destroy all defects; therefore, one should install him first. (5.56–57)
In a location as desired, for the temple that has been commenced,
the site for the child-temple (bālālaya) should be auspiciously five cubits in length;
O Beloved, the door of the primary sanctuary should be situated in that very place.
For one who dwells as a child, an image should be fashioned,
either from metal or again from stone or wood; it should hold the conch, discus, and mace,
have four arms or four hands, and be endowed with all the auspicious marks.
The height of that image shall be twenty-four finger-breadths;
in cases of reduction, it should be made five finger-breadths less, for there is nothing smaller than that. This is how the primary image should be for the temple being constructed.
One should have an image made in that manner from materials such as clay or metal.
Having consecrated that image in water, one should then consecrate it within a pavilion,
in the center of the temple of the Child (Bāla), provided with three tiers of enclosures (mekhalā).

At dawn, during an auspicious moment, having installed the image of the Child in the center of the altar raised to the height of the hands, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other rites. There, one should pray to Hari for His presence within the form of the Child.
"O Lord Hari, from the beginning of the foundation of the root-abode until its completion, O Blessed One, accept worship in this house for the child;
pacifying the host of Daityas who create obstacles for the primary sanctuary. (5.65–66)
Having thus prayed and bowed to him, one should arrange his retinue:
at the gate, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, Kṣetrapāla, and Khageśvara;
and one should arrange Indra and the other world-protectors in their respective directions.
One should worship Vighneśa in the northeast corner and Gaṇeśa in the southwest.
The Guru should worship the bodiless deities upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila),
and he should worship all the groups beginning with Kumuda upon its pedestal.
Having done this, the wise man should also hold a festival;
when the temple has been completed, O Rame,
he should then place the Śakti residing in the *bālabimba* into the primary image (*mūlabera*) at the conclusion of the consecration.
Having appointed her at the root of the pedestal, one should contemplate that Śakti there.
(5.71) Thus, when Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one, is worshipped in the child’s chamber, all those who cause obstacles will perish; of this there is no doubt. (5.72)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Image of a Child," in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Sixth Chapter:
On an auspicious month, on an auspicious day, conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion,
when the ascendant is stable and possesses a stable degree, and while Vāsudeva is worshipped— 6.1.
For the sake of increasing the prosperity of the patron’s abode, one who is most learned in the scriptures should cause it to be commenced by architects, chariot-makers, and artisans.
A house made primarily of stone is the best; one made of brick is middling.
One should know that [an image] made of wood is inferior, while one made of clay is the lowest of the low.
(6.3) That abode of Hari which is constructed with stone or brick should be known as the best when it is built up; [an image] made of two materials is considered unconstructed. (6.4)
O Rame, that temple made of clay or wood would be middling;
that which is called "accumulated" (upasaṃcitaga) would be the inferior abode.
One should avoid using stone or wood containing a hollow interior for the construction of a deity's abode.
If he should do so, the patron would undoubtedly fall ill.
One should not take stones or other materials from the abode of another deity;
if one were to build a temple by taking [materials] from a ruined shrine, [the patron would suffer]. (6.6–6.7)
His lineage shall perish and he will fall into hell.
Two kinds of bricks are taught: stone and baked brick, O Rame.
When produced from stone, it is the first kind of brick.
The temple (vimāna) may be constructed of baked bricks; that same [material] should serve as the foundation bricks (mūleṣṭakā).
Alternatively, it may be made of stone or baked bricks, but its foundation should be of stone.
In a location where stones are available, one should perform the preliminary rites such as the consecration (adhivāsa).
One should undertake the collection of stones only after examining their gender;

one should perform the first brick-rite using a stone with female characteristics (*strīliṅga*). From the sandals up to the stupa, [the construction] should be done with a stone having male characteristics (*puṃliṅga*).
The preceptor should cover the head [of the altar] with a stone from a neuter rock.
Now, the procedure for the collection of baked bricks is being described;
having gone to the site indicated by the chariot-maker, the guide [should proceed].

Having generated a blazing fire with the root mantra, O Rame, one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter; then, with the Puruṣasūkta, one should again offer the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having offered sixteen types of oblations, one should indeed offer a hundred with the root mantra.

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with fuel-sticks to Viṣṇu and his attendants; likewise, O Rame, he should offer oblations to the Lord of the Site, the Lord of the Field, and the spirits,
as well as to the deities, the sages, and the guardians of the directions, in their proper order.

One should perform the fire-oblation with the mantra according to its specific characteristic, ending with "svāhā," as well as with the *bhūḥ* and other *vyāhṛtis*, and likewise with the great *vyāhṛtis*. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should proceed in due order toward the east and the other directions.
Having recited this mantra, the most excellent teacher should offer the *bali* oblation to the attendants of Viṣṇu and to all beings;
having also offered the *bali* to the lords of the site and the field, he should dismiss the fire.
Facing east, the potter should fashion there a brick of earth;
it is best when twenty-four finger-breadths in length,
while the middling one is eighteen finger-breadths long, and the smallest should be sixteen.
Its width is half its length, and its thickness is desired to be half of that.
Furthermore, the distinction between male and other genders should be known by means of a line;
indeed, a stone of the masculine gender will have straight lines there that are odd in number.
Or if there be a pair of lines slanting across [the forehead], that woman is a source of delight;
if there be no line, or if there be lines on both ears, she is a eunuch.
This very same characteristic is proclaimed for stones as well.
One should construct the pedestal for the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* using bricks of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*),
and those up to the topmost brick using bricks of the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*).
O fair-complexioned lady, the length of the covering bricks should be equal.
Having the luster of a well-baked or slightly underbaked bimba fruit, possessing a good sound, very firm, even,
uniform in color, and praised— such is the first brick, which is beneficial. One that is joined with a dark circle, or broken, or split, or crooked [should be rejected].
O Goddess, one should avoid bricks that are cracked when beginning the construction of a temple (prāsāda).
Four [intact] bricks should first be placed in an auspicious abode of the gods;
for the residence of mortals, one should arrange five such initial bricks.
One should first offer sprouts during the rite of consecration (adhivāsana),
in whichever direction the site to be commenced may be located. Then,
one should prepare a grain-altar (dhānyapīṭhikā) upon a water-shed (prapā) in the center of the sacrificial ground.
Having likewise placed nine water-pots to the north,
one should prepare an altar for the consecration of the stones;
and having properly arranged a pedestal of grain and other materials upon it.
And in the jars placed for the purpose of bathing, in due order:
clarified butter should be in the central jar; in the eastern [jar], milk; then curd;
[clarified butter] should be poured into the south-eastern jar, and sugarcane juice into the southern jar.

In the southwest (Nairṛta) there should be the five products of the cow; in the west (Vāruṇa), however, that which arises from fruits. In the northwest (Vāyavya) there should be fragrant water; in the north (Saumya), there should be iron-water.
In the northeast (Īśāna), one should indeed arrange a jar filled with honey; thus one should prepare the jars.
Having wrapped [the jars] with cloth threads, one should place tufts of *darbha* grass,
along with coconuts and mango sprouts, [into them].
One should install Nārāyaṇa in the central jar, and Vāsudeva and the others in sequence.
One should worship with substances such as perfumes and offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should worship the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) in the jar established for the sake of protection.
Once the bricks have been placed on the pedestal, one should bathe them in turn with the ritual jars.
One should first bathe [the image] with milk using the *sāman* chant beginning with "payo-ghṛta";
then one should bathe it with sugarcane juice using the mantra beginning with "madhu-vāta".
One should bathe it with water infused with fruit using the *anuvāka* beginning with "phalinī".
One should bathe [the image] with water containing iron filings while reciting the Hiraṇyagarbha mantra;
one should arrange a bath with curd using the Yajus verse beginning with "Dadhikrāvṇo";
and one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the five Varuṇa mantras.
One should bathe [the stone] with fragrant water using the mantra "gandhadvārā";
one should perform the honey-bath using the mantra "madhu vātā";
and one should indeed bathe the stones with ghee using the Sāman chant "ghṛtasāma."
Having gathered all the bricks and decorated them according to the prescribed rule,
the most excellent of preceptors should place her upon a bed covered with the skins of tigers and other such animals, and he should cover her with a brand-new cloth.
One should worship the arches, the door-pitchers, and the banners in due order.
One should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in either the eastern or the northern direction.
Alternatively, one should offer oblations into the fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) while seated on a lotus seat.

The preceptor should touch all the bricks with clarified butter using the root mantra and likewise with the *sūkta* and the *caru* offering; he should indeed sprinkle them with the residual drops of the clarified butter. He should offer oblations of ghee one hundred times with the mantra of the Lord of Dreams (*svapnādhipati*).
For the sake of the dream, the patron should lie down together with the preceptor.
If a bad dream is seen, one should abandon the construction of that house.
But when a good dream has been observed, on the following day, the preceptor—
And one should cause those well-consecrated bricks to be placed within the palace,
in the excavated ground on the right side of the prepared doorway,
beneath the base of the pillar, until the end of the moon, amidst the sounding of musical instruments.
One should place [the deity] with the root mantra and the Śrīsūkta in the house of the head;
one should contemplate the manifestation of the fourfold emanation (vyūha) of the four forms within the square [mandala].
One should meditate upon the divine [deity] known as Vidyāgama within the long square.
When the wheel has ceased and arisen in tranquility, one should remember it with its parts fully withdrawn.
One should meditate upon the Lord reclining on Ananta within that auspicious, circular expanse;
he who bears the body of the *kālapuṣkara* is the stainless *puryaṣṭaka*.
Born from the navel-cavity of Viṣṇu, abiding in the form of the eight directions within the temple of the gods,
one should meditate upon the eight-cornered dwelling of the earth.
All-pervading, with the face of Brahman, illuminating, and possessing the prowess of truth.
And thus the powers that sustain the universe are said to be complete.
Know that which is the stone supporting the jar to be the all-pervading consciousness;
it is the power of capacity, the universal, partless, and supreme power of the Lord.
Having satisfied [the deity] with the root mantra and the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*), O Lotus-born One,
the preceptor should, with the mantra "ekam ajanābhe adhi," have the other stones established by artisans using the *ekāyana* rites.
O Goddess, until the placement of the womb (the foundation stone), the previously mentioned Śaktis should be worshipped in all directions at the joints;
having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should perform the placement of the womb.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Seventh Chapter.
I shall describe the procedure for the deposition of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*); listen to it from me regarding the lotus.
First, having prepared the earthen materials, [place them] in ten locations in due order. 7.1
Clay produced from these— on a mountain, in a lake, at a sacred ford, from an anthill, from the lair of a crab,
on the tip of a bull’s horn, on an elephant’s tusk, in the ocean, and on a plow—
is therefore recommended.

One should likewise collect these five tubers: of the kumuda, the aravinda, the kaśeru, the utpala, and the blue lotus (nīlotpala). [One should also collect] realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, and black lead.
One should collect saurāṣṭra, yellow orpiment, red ochre, and mercury,
as well as diamonds, lapis lazuli, pearls, crystal, topaz, and conch shells; likewise, rubies, moonstones, and sapphires.
He should bring śālī rice, nīvāra rice, and kaṅku rice, as well as priyaṅgu, sesame, and māṣa beans; (7.6) mung beans, barley, and bamboo seeds—these nine kinds of grain he should procure.
He should also bring gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead. (7.7)
Having consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) a golden tortoise, a golden conch and discus,
and a casket provided with nine cavities and a lid,
the knower of the scriptures [places them] within its cavities.
Having set aside all the ritual items, the most excellent of gurus should cover [the casket].
O Abode of Lakṣmī, he should wrap the casket with a pair of cloths;
then the preceptor should place it upon a heap of grain while reciting the root mantra.
Having meditated upon the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) there, one should worship them with nine perfumes and other offerings.
Having kindled the fire according to the scriptural injunctions, one should first remember Lord Hari there.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra and sixteen with the Nṛsūkta.
To Indra and the other world-protectors, and likewise to the worlds;
to the mountains and the oceans, and to the Ādityas, O Rāma;
and then to the Vasus, the Maruts, and the sages.
From the Vedas, from all the scriptures, and beyond that from the Purāṇas;
likewise from Pātāla and the other regions, from the quarters, and from the Nāgas;
from the Gaṇas, from all beings, and beyond that from the lords of men.
And from all the houses as well as from the constellations, according to the prescribed rite,
the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sacrificial wood, ending each with "svāhā.
Having taken the residue from those offerings, he should sprinkle it upon the vessel containing the embryo.
Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the preceptor, having fasted,
wearing a bright upper garment and adorned with ornaments,
his body decorated with perfumes and garlands, [performs the rite] at night during an auspicious conjunction.
Taking that vessel accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and auspicious hymns,
as well as the sounds of musical instruments, he circumambulated the abode and entered the inner chamber on the right side of that door.
Having filled the pit with the five products of the cow and sprinkled it on all sides,

and having worshipped it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), fragrances, flowers, and so forth, the Guru [then] [visualizes her] as standing upon the heads of the serpent-king Śeṣa, who bears the foremost elephants of the quarters.

Having mentally entered the auspicious, dark-complexioned Earth, who is two cubits in height, and having meditated upon her as one who has bathed after her menses, while remembering himself as Hari, he should address her:
"O beloved supporter of all beings, adorned with mountains for breasts! (7.21–7.22)
"O Goddess who are clothed by the ocean, bear the embryo, bear it!
Having thus prayed and placed the casket within that womb,
one should make it firm with lime and then fill up the pit.
One should perform protection day and night for three, four, or five nights.
O Goddess, this deposition of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*) brings prosperity to the temple;
if the deposition of the embryo is not performed, a great transgression will occur.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Eighth Chapter:
Now, O lotus-eyed one, I shall describe the construction of a palace, [measured] from the base neither less nor more, by means of appropriate cubits and finger-breadths. 8.1
Up to twelve cubits, or even more by the span of the palm,
for the sake of auspiciousness, accomplishment, and the increase of the inner sanctum, O Rame;
having first calculated the cubic volume of either the field-measures (kṣetra-aṅgula) or the cubits (kara).
One should properly abandon that which is entirely unfavorable, and having reflected upon what remains, [one should accept it].
(8.3) The single, the double, the eighth, and the endless; the banner, smoke, the lord of beasts, and the dog; the cow, the donkey, the elephant—these four; and the crow: these are auspicious. (8.4)
The proportions known as one, three, five, and seven are prescribed everywhere;
likewise, together with the count of the walls, there is the internal circumambulation path.
And the area for the temple of the deity is twice the width of the inner sanctum.
In a temple with a single wall, this measurement of the site is prescribed.
It is stated that the inner sanctum (garbha) should be one-third of that, whether by a suitable or unsuitable path.
In that case as well, one should consider the purification of the dimensions through decrease or increase.

In this way, understand that the portion which is without a surrounding wall (*nirjagatīka*) and devoid of a pedestal (*pīṭha*), as well as the measurement of the temple site (*prāsādakṣetra*), is joined with that [measurement].
It is [divided] by a sixth part, a quarter, a third part, or by both [parts].
Then, the work [of the projection] in the four directions is done with three-fifths of that;
indeed, the projection in the middle is prescribed with one-third.
From corner to corner, however, one should cause the remaining portion to enter into each respective part.

The pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be high and equal to the womb; by means of that pedestal or its petals, one should conceive the beginning, middle, and end of the characteristics of the pedestal as described for the temple-pedestal. Indeed, in the four directions, it should be arranged in many ways, beginning with Ananta.
Then, one should indeed determine the height of the temple from the site as a triangle;
it should be made one and a half times, or twice, or according to one's desire.
One should first divide that [height] equally into eleven parts.
The base (vidheya) should be like a pedestal, and then the cushion (masūraka) by one part;
the shank (jaṅghā) fashioned above that should be raised according to the measurement of the womb (garbha).
It is marked with auspicious characteristics by the gods who are the attendants of Bhava.

On the *jaṅghā* (the shaft), the *śikhara-pīṭha* (the pedestal of the spire) should indeed be made with a pair of shoulders that are either increased or decreased [in proportion], as characterized by the previous definitions;
however, in that case, the entrance and exit [of the spire] are measured at half a part (*ardhāṃśa*).
And here, a pinnacle (śikhara) is prescribed, endowed with nine storeys (bhūmikā).
Having contracted that previous thread (sūtra), one should take it up to the height [of the structure].
Then, spreading it out from just one corner (karṇa) along the thigh and the earth [of the base], [the pinnacle is formed].
One should touch the pinnacle and the pedestal directly, having fixed them;
O lotus-eyed one,
one should lead the cord from the corner upwards on the outermost part of the ground, marking it in due order.
O fair-faced one, it should indeed wander in this very manner toward the high peaks in the four directions, being marked from ear to ear,
until that cluster of peaks becomes like the petals of a white water-lily.
Thus, having completed it by means of the visualized drawing through the casting of threads,
for the sake of establishing the ground-section, the thread should again be divided tenfold;
moreover, the upper portion should be like *āmalasāra* wood.
The stages (bhūmis) are indeed the proportions; therefore, one should perform [the construction] upon that [ground].
According to the rule of decrease and increase, that [measurement] is equal to sixteen parts (dviraṣṭāṃśa).
The arrangement of distinct pedestals (pīṭha) should be made among them according to the established order.
With various petals accompanied by wheels, and with all manifestations whatsoever;
or with new marks in embodied form, established in the aesthetic sentiments of dance and song;
determined by one's own foot from the upper portion by means of its ninth part.
The *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) of the upper level should indeed be fashioned with its proper arrangement;
having prepared one's own pedestal (*pīṭha*) as before by means of the [first] circle,
then the ear by the second, and by the third, which is directed upwards.

One should make it perfectly level and endowed with beauty, its end resembling the rounded surface of a *dhātrī* fruit. Having fashioned a nine-fold *uṣṇīṣa*, one should rotate the four altars (*vedikā*) by a portion equal to three parts; then, the pillars may indeed be either with [the base] or alone.
Elevated by half the height of the pinnacle and resembling the petal of a blue lotus,
it should be fashioned above the pedestal of the pinnacle, adorned with divine craftsmanship.
Then, one should construct an even more auspicious pavilion, commensurate in size with the pillars.

It should be adorned with the lord of birds (Garuḍa) and with a circle for the sacrificial offerings (bali). Likewise, three pavilions (maṇḍapa) should be constructed at the four gates and in the cardinal directions; within the main pavilion, there should be a pavilion provided with three entrances.
One should construct a pavilion as previously described, or with an exit according to one's preference;
however, the construction of the chariot and its sub-chariots is prescribed from their inner sanctum (garbha).
The projection (niryāsa) shall be one-tenth or one-twelfth of the width in the case of the Rame [temple].
Alternatively, they should again be made with a sixteenth part, like a rim;
smeared on the sides in the four directions and adorned with the work of pedestals,
one should fashion an equal set of doors in the four directions of the spire.
Then, from the center, it is prescribed to be divided into three, four, five, or six parts;
its height is double [the width], and it has three, five, or nine branches.
It is provided with two door-keepers, or alternatively, with jars and elephant tusks.
Having thus constructed the celestial mansion (vimāna), one should then perform the consecration ceremony (pratiṣṭhā).
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Ninth Chapter:
Śrī said: "O Blessed One, O lotus-eyed one, O supreme knower of the meaning of all scriptures!"
"Now you ought to tell me the classification of palaces.
The Blessed One said: "Now I shall explain the classification of celestial mansions (*vimāna*) along with their defining characteristics."
Since it is impossible to describe all the varieties, only a few are set forth:
"Upon that foundation, I sport in many kinds of celestial palaces (vimānas),
which are square, circular, as well as octagonal and hexagonal."
Due to the distinctions between square, elongated, circular,
and oval shapes, they declare that which is circular at the head and neck to be the *vaijayanta* [type].
If it is thick at the base and fine at the tip, it is so at each successive level.
On the front portion, it has a large nose, while in the three directions [the sides], the nose is small. There are four stūpīs on the nose, and both types of vimānas— circular and oblong—
are honored as the abodes of the chariot.

With the tips of its peak-ridges and ears, and with a *bhadra* of the same kind in the middle, it is called the *Śrīviśāla*; it is octagonal and provides security. The *Śrīkara* is square, while the *Puṣpaka* is sixteen-sided.
Together with the *bhadra*, it has a head-binding at the center;
the *koṣṭhaka* has limbs like the nose of a *bhadra*, and its neck and head are well-rounded.
This temple, named *kesara*, is adorned with every ornament.
In every opening there was a face, while the head possessed two or three eyes;
it had a pleasant countenance, was shaped like a water-jar, and was provided with a circular inner chamber.
At its mouth was a great nose, and such was the case for both [the temple and the vimāna].
The pair of stupas may be either even or odd in number, with small spires in the three directions;
it may be circular, oblong, or perfectly round, and by name this is called Sudarśana.
Its base is square, and likewise its corners and its summit.

It was joined with four peaks and provided with four courtyards; its great spire was adorned in all directions with large nose-ornaments (nāsās). It was embellished with various wonderful paintings, as well as with archways and auspicious altars.

This is called the Svastika; it is remembered as the most excellent among celestial palaces (vimānas). That same [structure] is called Sauṣṭhika if its compartments are low and high, and it is joined with an internal terrace; this is vast and beautiful.
One part, two parts, one and three-quarter parts, one and a quarter parts,
two parts with a quarter added—
these are the proportions for the neck and head of the *prastara* (the middle story) when the rise of the base is divided into nine parts in a two-storey temple or similar structure.
Equipped with inner galleries and provided with peaked halls,
adorned with various ornaments and embellished with diverse bases—
such a mountain-shaped celestial mansion (vimāna) is said to be highly honored among all mansions. || 9.17–9.18 ||
That very circular structure, with its altar-cavity and pinnacle, is shaped like a jar;
it has eight peaks, is provided with four halls, and possesses seven or eight nostrils.
In the center is a stainless chamber, adorned with two or three pillars and eight [ornaments].
Equipped with a complete neck and head, provided with a pinnacle-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha),
joined with various foundations, adorned with various bases,
