either square or perfectly circular, and endowed with many naves. || 9.20–9.21 ||
O Abode of Kamalā, this celestial chariot is called Mandara;
its summit consists of four [sections], each with a half-corner,
and it is provided with a square top and endowed with four pinnacles.
Joined with many *tāla* measures, with various foundations, and marvelous;
accompanied by a thousand *nāsī*s, or half of that, or even a quarter; adorned with many limbs, this is known by the name *svastibandha*. 9.23–24.
That very same [structure], when provided with internal partitions for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), with a small central courtyard,
beautiful, slightly depressed, having nine or fewer [rooms], and possessing a small nose (front porch),
and being adorned with various paintings— this is known as the *kalyāṇaka* [type].
A quadrangular temple site,
provided with a circular inner sanctum and adorned with all ornaments, is this "Beloved of Kubera.
That same quadrangular form may also have a non-rectangular (asūkara) inner sanctum.
If it is circular from the base to the pinnacle, it is a "Round Mansion" (vṛttaharmyaka); if the foundation is elongated,
the neck hexagonal, and the head [circular],
it is adorned with various ornaments and is called the "Charming" (manohara).
It was joined with various foundations and adorned with various bases;
it was beautified by the svastika posture of those seated upon its pedestals,
possessed many stories, and was endowed with diverse ornaments.

This [structure], joined with many heads and endowed with numerous *stūpis*, is named Bhadrakoṣṭha; it is elongated and square. That same [structure] may be circular, as well as having *karṇakūṭas* and *karṇaśiras* [projections].
This [structure] should have four corners and be circular at the summit (vṛttakūṭa). That same [shape], when extended by one-eighth more, becomes square.
Likewise, the corner-summit (karṇakūṭa) and the corner-extension (karṇamāyata) are circular at their tops.

The remainder is designated as before by the name Śrībhoga; it is circular and appears circular, endowed with many turrets, and adorned with various wonderful paintings. It is joined with many stories and resplendent with diverse marvels.
This Puṣkara is held to be provided with supports for the celestial chariots (vimāna).
Abandoning the water and land [sections], it extends upwards, being square in shape, possessing a corner and a pinnacle, and likewise endowed with four nostrils (niches). || 9.35–9.36 ||
That which is endowed with various beauties is called the *lambapañjara*;
it is furnished with various *masūraka* pillars, altars, and so forth.
That which is joined with variegated pedestals is designated as the *jayākhya*.
That very neck and head were four-cornered like the Vedas, adorned with various other ornaments such as pillars and pedestals made of *masūraka* stones;
and having thus had these celestial palaces constructed by craftsmen... [9.38–9.39]
Then the best of preceptors should perform the laying of the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*);
the procedure for the crown-brick should also be the same as that for the foundation-brick (*mūleṣṭaka*).
Having performed the worship of the water-jars (*kumbha*) and other items, the preceptor [should act] with the patron (*yajamāna*).
One should pass that very night in vigil, remembering Hari.
In the morning, having performed the daily rites and meditating upon Nārāyaṇa Hari,
one should proceed accompanied by the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the chanting of the Vedas.
Taking the stones with the officiating priests, he should cause them all to be placed by circumambulation upon the upper surface of the temple; then,
having ascended the top of the temple, facing the east, [he should sprinkle] it with meritorious water.
Having sprinkled it with water and meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, one should install that stone, O Rame.
Then the artisans should construct a firm base for the stūpa, equal in size to the egg;
if there are many stūpas, they should be made in the shape of blue lotus petals.
Having fashioned [the base] as long or narrow, or even sixteen-sided, or square, circular, or octagonal,
one should arrange the petals of the lotus in the region of the pitcher-base (kumbhādhāra).
One should establish the *stūpikās* upon that according to one's desire:
either one, two, three, four, O fair-faced one, or eight, twelve, sixteen, or even twenty. (9.47–9.48)
Having established a pinnacle made of metal or wood, equal in height to the neck of the *vimāna*, whether it be a single peg or many, O Rame;
and whether the *vimāna* be circular, oblong, or even square.
For those desiring non-rebirth, there should be a pair of stūpikā-kīlas;
for others, however, the arrangement of the stūpikā should indeed be odd.
A pair consists of twenty in number, while an odd number is one less than that.
In a square, hexagonal, or octagonal [mandala], there shall be a single kila;
the pinnacle-kila (stūpikā) shall be one kila that bestows the fruit of all desires.
Having thus fashioned [the structure] up to the end of the kila on all sides of the celestial mansion (vimāna),
The wise man should have images installed by those skilled in the science of sculpture:
Indra in the eastern direction of the temple, or Kumāra, or Agni;
Vāsudeva or Śrīdhara in the southern direction, and Umāpati [in the north].
Or Dakṣiṇāmūrti, or Saṃkarṣaṇa,
or Satya, or Varāha, or Acyuta in the west;
or Pradyumna, or Nṛsiṃha, and likewise Dhanādhipa in the north.
One may likewise conceive of Brahmā, Aniruddha, or Ananta. However, if the space exceeds one square palm, one should arrange the aforementioned deities in their proper sequence.
These [deities] should be equal in size to the principal image (dhruvabera) in the case of reclining images and the like.

But Indra and the other deities of the directions always remain seated, whether in a square abode or one that is rectangular; or they may occupy a circular residence, assuming a circular form as well. They are the upholders of the sacred dwellings.
Vīrasena, Suṣeṇa, Vīranātha, Subhadraka, Pūrṇa, Puṣkarākṣa, Ānanda, and likewise Nandana—
these attendants of Viṣṇu, endowed with terrifying countenances, should be installed.
Likewise, gods and Vidyādharas will dance in various ways upon my celestial chariot, bearing flutes, lutes, and drums. My incarnations and their deeds must be fashioned everywhere.
Likewise, the Bhūtamālas should be fashioned with distorted faces as they dance;
on every step, Garuḍa should be depicted with the marks of the conch, discus, and so forth.
Having thus first fashioned these forms, one should then apply the coloring and plastering.
Those learned in the scriptures know that there must necessarily be an application of colors:
white, yellow, red, green, and black.
These five colors belong to earth and the other elements, and they are the presiding deities of the colors.
O Rame, there shall be a difference in the colors of the forms according to the distinction of the Yugas:
in the Kṛta age he is white; in the Tretā, he is ruddy; and again in the Dvāpara, he is yellow; but in the Kali age, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, is dark as a rain-cloud.
The god Saṃkarṣaṇa is red; Pradyumna has the luster of gold; Aniruddha is declared to be dark-blue; Keśava has the luster of gold;
Nārāyaṇa is white in color; and Mādhava is dark-blue in color.

Govinda should be like crystal; Viṣṇu resembles the filaments of a lotus. Madhuhā is red in color; Trivikrama has the hue of a peacock. Vāmana has the luster of the rising sun; Śrīdhara has the brilliance of a white lotus.
Hṛṣīkeśa is the color of lightning, while Padmanābha is blue;
Dāmodara is said to have the color of the bandhūka flower.
Puruṣottama is the color of crystal, whereas Adhokṣaja is dark-complexioned.
Nṛsiṃha is golden-colored; Acyuta is yellow-colored. Janārdana is red, while Upendra is remembered as dark-blue.
Hari is yellow-colored, whereas Kṛṣṇa has the luster of a black cloud.
Śrī is like gold; Bhūmi is dark or pale-white;
Sarasvatī is white in color; Prīti would be whitish-red;
Kīrti is red and the color of crystal; while Śānti and Tuṣṭi are yellow.
The Guru should have the eight [images] made: Puṣṭi is dark-complexioned, while the other eight are of eight different colors.
The Fish is like crystal; the Tortoise possesses a golden hue;
the Boar is dark in color; and Nṛsiṃha has the color of the moon.
The son of Jamadagni, Rāma, is golden-hued; Bharata possesses a dark complexion, while Lakṣmaṇa has the luster of gold. Śatrughna should be red in color, and Sītā should resemble gold.
Māṇḍavī shall be red in color, and Ūrmilā shall have a dark complexion;
Śrutakīrti shall have a white body, and Dhanumān shall have the luster of gold. Aṅgada shall be red in color, and Sugrīva shall be golden-tawny.
Guha and Vibhīṣaṇa likewise; Nīla, with a luster like that of a blue gem;
and Jāmbavān, who is golden-hued—this is the group of attendants who have taken refuge in Rāma.
Rāma has a dark body and a blue complexion, while he possesses a pale-white hue.
Rukmiṇī shall have the luster of gold; Satyā shall be dark-complexioned.
Revatī shall be red in color, and Sātyakī shall possess a blue hue.
Yaśodā shall be golden-colored, and Devakī shall have the radiance of refined gold.
Arjuna shall be white in complexion; these [others] are devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa.
Kalkī shall be white in complexion, and Brahmā shall have a golden form. Ananta shall be the color of milk, and Garuḍa shall have the luster of gold.
Rudra is blood-red in color; Hayagrīva has the luster of a red horse. Senānī is said to be dark-complexioned, and Vināyaka is white in color.
Brāhmī is blue, while Maheśvarī is red, as is Aparā.
Kaumārī is Vaiṣṇavī and Śyāmā; Vārāhī has a dark-blue luster.
Indrāṇī is said to be Śyāmalā, while Cāmuṇḍā is red in color. Indra is Śyāma, Agni is Aruṇa, and Yama is likewise Kāla.

Nirṛti shall be blue in color, and Varuṇa dark-complexioned; Vāyu is smoky, Soma white, and Rudra red—these are situated in the eight directions. Vijaya shall be dark-colored, and Padmī should be like a lotus.

Gadādhara is golden-colored; Kṛṣṇa is black and holds a sword; another is the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, resembling gold; [another] holds a thunderbolt and a mace, both being white in color. Kanaka holds a noose and is black in color; Aṅkuśin is black in color.

Caṇḍa is red, and Pracaṇḍa is white; Jayas is likewise yellow. Dhātṛ resembles red and yellow, while Vidhātṛ is white in color. Subhadra, Bhadra, and Varuṇa are [also present], and Kṛtānta has a dark-blue luster.
Asuradhvaṃsana is red, while Kuberākṣa is yellow;
Kubera is of red complexion, and Durjaya is black in color.
Prabala is white in color, and Viśvabhāvana is red.
Puṣkara shall be white in color; Saṃbhava will have a dark-complexioned form. Suśobhana is dark-colored, while Prabhava possesses a red complexion.
Subhadra, Kumuda, and Śveta are [white], and Kumudākṣa has the brilliance of fire.
Puṇḍarīka is said to be white; Vāmana has a dark-complexioned form; Śaṅkukarṇa is red in color; Sarvanetra has a black luster;
Sumukha is dark in color; and Supratiṣṭhita has a reddish glow.

Having thus caused the application of color to the celestial palaces (*vimāna*), the forms [of the deities], the gatekeepers, and the attendants (*pārṣada*), one should then have pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) constructed.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the venerable *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.

The Tenth Chapter: Immediately after the construction of the sanctum (garbha-mandira) is completed, the measurement of that inner chamber [should be] one and a half times its own measure at the front. 10.1
The wise one should construct the half-maṇḍapa according to the path prescribed in the scriptures;
he should make it level with the ground of the chamber that is half the size of the main hall.
In front of the half-maṇḍapa, one should construct the structure named the dance-maṇḍapa.
In front of the half-dance pavilion, one should construct an assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa), O fair-faced one;
or, for the sake of exit on both sides, the skillful artisan should construct stairs in front, O auspicious lady. || 10.3–10.4 ||
Within the constructed pavilions,

one should fashion enclosures for the purpose of housing the retinue and for the beauty of the temple; this first enclosure, known as the inner circle (*antarmaṇḍala*), is understood by the wise to be the primary wall (*sāla*).
The second would be Antarhāra, and immediately following that, Madhyahāra;
the fourth would be Pāribhadra, and the fifth is called Parvata.
One should know the sixth as Vaidyādhara, and the seventh as Sarvaveṣṭana.
The height of the halls with four, five, or eight pillars should be such that their width is seen in the first enclosure and those following it.
In the southeast, there should be a kitchen provided with a long hearth.
In the middle, between Agni and Yama, one should prepare a sacrificial pit for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
For the purpose of seating Marīci and the others, there should be a space between Vāyu and Soma;
on the outer enclosure, one should construct a house for storing grain.

The stationing of vehicles and the like should be in the eastern quarter; water should be provided in the western quarter. During a festival, the sacrificial rite for the deity should take place between the Soma and Īśa [cups]. One should construct one well at the kitchen site and two outside, O Rame.
Having thus had various locations— flower gardens as well as lakes—
constructed by artisans within the enclosures,
[he likewise had them built] on all the upper levels of every wall.
One should have figures of Garuḍas, conchs and discs, or even lions fashioned [therein].
For each individual sāla, one should provide four gates. At the gates, there should indeed be gate-towers (gopuras) that are square and elongated.
There should be entrances and exits at each gate-tower (gopura).
The best of gurus should place the foundation (garbha) of the pavilions and other structures in the southeast corner; for the gate-towers, the placement of the foundation should be in the south.
O Rame, for all the gate-towers (gopuras) and for the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
there should be two very firm and smooth door-panels (kavāṭa) on each, provided with bolts (tāla) and wedges (ghana).
One should fasten them on all sides with bolts (kīla) made of gold and other materials, as well as with bands (paṭṭa).

And one should attach small bells made of gold and other metals with no gaps between them. Having thus caused the inner sanctum, the vimāna, and the pavilions provided with porticos to be constructed, the best of preceptors should then [construct] the gate-towers.

O Goddess, one should undertake the consecration; its ritual procedure is now described here. One should construct a pavilion for the installation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of the temple, equipped with all necessary implements and conforming to all the prescribed characteristics.
One should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the pavilion in every direction.
In their absence, however, one should place four; and in their absence, the most excellent teacher should establish a single fire within the pavilion as previously described.

A stūpa may be made of gold, silver, copper, wood, or even stone; it should be properly installed, provided it is not lacking its pinnacle (*mūrdhan*). Therefore, one should install that temple with great care so that it is complete.
The measure of that second *goḷa* is the supreme image.
First, the wise one should prepare the consecration (*adhivāsa*) in another secret pavilion together with the *stūpikas*, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (10.24–25)
One should perform the entire ritual of bathing and so forth for the image and the stupas;
having adorned them well with garments, ornaments, and flowers, and having worshipped them thoroughly,
one should place the image into that jar which is filled with jewels and other substances.
Slowly, together with the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ), he should ascend the palace terrace.
There, he should have the preliminary striking, washing, and other rites performed;
then that practitioner should raise the image and its stūpa-like pedestal upward.
The preceptor himself, standing upon a lotus and facing either east or north, should then establish [the vessel] in the location of the central jar with white lime.
The most excellent preceptor should then make it firm with the mantra: "Pratiṣṭhāsi" (You are established).
One should perform the placement of mantras (*mantravinyāsa*) upon the jar containing the image;

the instructor [should do so] with the *aniruddha* [mantra] for the heart and other [limbs], and with the root mantra. Having first focused thereon, one should indeed make it one, joined with the supreme.
Having worshipped it, one should indeed establish two stūpas at its sides, O Rame;
then, having smeared them with lime, one should also install the mantras.
On the frieze of the temple, however, [one should use] twenty-five threads.
Having first tied the *parisara* cord and then having tied the *kautuka* cord oneself,
one should first offer the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) in sequence according to the rules for installation (*pratiṣṭhā-vidhi*).
O Rame, one should indeed perform the consecration of the shadow (*chāyādhivasana*) within the cauldrons (*kaṭāha*) and other vessels.
The best of those who know mantras should perform the ritual bathing of the images upon a mirror;
he should then perform the opening of their eyes according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Having meditated upon the radiant celestial chariot, the preceptor [should place it] in its respective locations.
One should contemplate the path of the worlds, beginning from the feet up to the *kumbha*.
O fair-faced one, the worship of the deities in their respective locations, as well as in the jars and in the mandala, should be performed in due order. 10.36–10.37

Having consecrated the fire according to the rules in the sacrificial pits prepared around the palace, he should satisfy Vāsudeva and the other deities, in accordance with the scriptures, by means of their origin and dissolution; or else, he may do so while standing before that city.
The preceptor himself should perform the entire fire-oblation in the sacrificial pit;

the learned and wise one should cause the mantras to be recited and bring the installation to completion. Having performed everything up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to that very procedure once again—‖ 10.39–10.40 ‖
O Rame, one should have the chanters of the Sāman hymns recite the mantra "kṣuro hara" while placing a disc made of *āmalasāra* wood in the center,
according to the desired form, with its faces directed toward the cardinal directions and its mouth facing upward.

One should place the mantra of the wheel— residing upon its own power, its syllables, and its staff, and radiant like the fierce sun— therein; and one should deposit the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) previously described,
characterized by the knower of objects of knowledge, through the practice of going and returning.
Having previously understood that the Lord resides within the form of the mantra, one should establish him in the position above; not otherwise, O fair-faced one.
And thus is the desired wheel, which pacifies all obstacles.
Having installed and worshipped that [image], immediately thereafter, one should consecrate the flagpole with the weapon-mantra (astra) and,
taking a third part from the region of the head, which is adorned by the King of Birds (Garuḍa),
one should apply the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra). || 10.45–10.46 ||
Having first established the presence of the weapon (astra) upon that cloth bearing the emblem, O Rame,
one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings, having placed it at the tip of the flagstaff. If there is a single stūpika on the chariot, Vāsudeva indeed resides there.

If there are two of them, Vāsudeva and the other, Saṃkarṣaṇa—the two best of gods—should be established in three [images]. Or, one should request the four beginning with Vāsudeva for the three [images] in sequence. (10.48–49)
One should worship the six [deities] beginning with Keśava in the group of six jars;
one should pray to Rame (Lakṣmī) there in the group of eight jars beginning with Keśava.
One should assign the [twelve deities] beginning with Keśava to the twelve pitchers.
The installation of the water-pots (*kumbha*) for those desiring liberation is performed in pairs;
for others who desire fruits such as heaven, they should be odd in number.
Having thus prepared the central pot with water, the self-possessed Guru—
And having ascended to the top of the temple, O Rame, one should sprinkle all around with sudhā (mortar) or even with large stones upon the images that have been fashioned,
as well as upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā), O Rame, from the very beginning.
Then, the preceptor should have artisans fashion the arrangement of jewels, metals, and other materials;
having strengthened it with medicinal herbs, he should perform the consecration of the primary image and the other images along with the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Thus, the consecration of a temple has been briefly described by me, as well as that of pavilions, halls, and gate-towers (gopuras). Now,
the ritual procedure for the consecration of the rafters and the door-panels is being stated.
In the same manner, one should first cleanse the pavilion, beginning with the initial structures and ending with the assembly hall;
then, O delightful one, one should wash the ramparts, the five Nāga-halls, the fire-sanctuaries, and so forth,
and subsequently prepare all the ritual sprouts (aṅkura).
Having performed the circumambulation with fire, one should fumigate it in every direction;
having purified it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should sprinkle it with auspicious water.
Then, having adorned it with lime powder, one should scatter white mustard seeds.
Having performed the worship of the site and its lord, the best of preceptors should perform the installation of the jars; having invoked Hari into them, he should sacrifice.
Now, a certain specific detail regarding the door-posts and the door-panels is being told.

The Guru should wash the branches and door-panels with water and the five Upaniṣads, and he should adorn them with perfumes, garlands, and clothing. Then, during the auspicious moment known as Vijaya, he should perform the installation of the branches.
And one should perform the placement of jewels and other items within the openings of the branches while reciting mantras (10.63).
One should cause door-panels to be set in the openings near the branches;
Brahmā is to be placed on the southern branch, and Bhava on the northern (10.64).
The most excellent of gurus should pray to Mahālakṣmī at the Udumbara tree;
he should have my ten forms painted above the door-panels,
and the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, as well as the sages, painted below.
Viśvanātha is established upon the door-panel;
Viśvabhāvana is to be installed in the key of the door.
Having worshipped these in the water of the ritual jar, I indeed take delight in those respective locations.
And having invoked [the deities] upon the door-panels, one should sprinkle them with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Thus, having caused the palace of Lord Viṣṇu, complete with its gate-towers,
to be constructed by groups of artisans and having consecrated it according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
One should fashion the root-amulet according to the patron's desire.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The eleventh chapter:
Standing, mounted on a vehicle, seated, striding through the world, reclining, and the universal form—this is said to be the sixfold image. 11.1
O Goddess, in my various incarnations, [the form] is divided manifoldly according to the requirements of each specific task and in accordance with the needs of the sacrificer.
One should install the Lord in a square, a circle, or a hexagon.

Having beheld the single one who possesses universal form—whether standing, mounted on a vehicle, seated, or striding through the world; whether circular, oblong, reclining, or likewise square and oblong; or even in an octagonal form—one should contemplate him.
In the fashioning of the form for worship, there are six kinds of materials:
gems, crystal, metals, stone, wood, and clay.
(11.5) If the image is fashioned such that it is not deficient from front to back, [it is successful].
They call that a "complete image" (*bimba*) where the front portion indeed contains the face and other features; that which is half-painted is called an "image" (*ardhacitra*);
and that which is merely painted on cloth or similar materials is called an "inferior painting" (*hīnacitra*).
An image fashioned from *raṅta* bestows the fruits of all desires;
an image of gold bestows prosperity; silver shall be the giver of knowledge;
and copper bestows good fortune—thus it is said to be of three kinds.

That which arises from the White Mountain bestows fame, wealth, and knowledge; it is to be propitiated by a Brahmin. Other [forms] grant all desires and are to be propitiated by Kṣatriyas and others for the attainment of their own desired goals.
Where perfected great seers and even twice-born ones perform austerities— accessible to mortals yet frequented by gods, composed of well-refined stone— there,
O Rāma, the Teacher first went to find a stone suitable for the image.
Having examined [the site] thoroughly and returned, he should inform the patron.
The patron and the preceptor should first feed the Brahmins;
having received their favor, [the preceptor], equal in status to the patron, [should proceed].
Accompanied by the chariot-maker and others, he should go there and construct a water-shed;

having first performed the rite of sowing the sprouts, he should place the jars upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) while reciting the mantra known as Parameṣṭhin and using tufts of grass and young shoots.
Having adorned and covered it, one should worship it along with its periphery;
having sprinkled it with water from the *puṇyāha* rite and scattered white mustard seeds with the *cakra-vidyā*, the Guru should then display the *cakramudrā*. || 11.15–11.16 ||
One should worship the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the center, Sudarśana in the water-pot (karaka),
and Indra and the other deities in the secondary pots (upakumbha), performing the rites up to the final offering (prāpaṇa).
Then, with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, flowers, fruits, and even leaves, one should proceed with the fivefold oblations.
One should offer oblations separately one hundred and eight times with the root mantra.
One should also offer sixteen oblations with the *caru* using the *Nṛsūkta*,
[dedicating them] to the forest deities, the mountains, the boulders, and the riverbanks as well.
He saw peaks, waterfalls, oceans, trees,

and even medicinal herbs; forest giants (or trees), as well as those born from a womb, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts— all living beings, and even the three sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*).
Having offered oblations with the *namas-tayā* invocation, he should collect the remnants.
Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should place the remnants upon that stone with the *sparśavidyā* mantra and perform the offering of the sacrificial fee (*balidāna*).

The preceptor should offer an oblation (bali) to all beings, consisting of curd-rice mixed with turmeric powder, parched grain, cakes, milk, curd, ghee, plantains, and tender coconuts, together with sacrificial porridge (caru).

Having observed the stone for a short while with the Cakra-vidyā, O lotus-eyed one, one should offer an oblation to the spirits in every direction. Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited and having sprinkled [the site] with the Puruṣa-vidyā; || 11.24–25 ||
Then, having touched the stone with the root mantra and offered the *arghya* in the Temple of Delight (*prītimandira*),
the most excellent guru should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
He should then perform the laying of the foundation lines upon the ground of the stone in accordance with the proportions of the image.
One should fashion the image with a cool stone, never with a hot one.
(11.27) If one fashions the image with a cool stone so that it is endowed with the auspicious marks, then, in the presence of the deity, prosperity will certainly be perpetually full. (11.28)
One should always fashion Hari with a masculine stone that possesses resonance;
the footstool should be made of a feminine stone, and the placement of gems should be done upon a neuter one.
Having thus examined the stone, one should then have it carved by craftsmen.
That stone might fall to the ground and fail to serve as the *bimba*;
or, even if it remains in the center, the Guru should lift that stone up,
sprinkle it with water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*), and then with water from the ritual vessel (*karaka*).
Having sprinkled [the site], the preceptor should have an image fashioned by artisans;
for the construction of goddesses such as Śrī and others, a female stone is best,
while a male stone should be used for the footstool, and a neuter stone for the placement of gems.
One should perform the collection of stones for the goddesses using the Śrīsūkta itself.
In the central pitcher, one should worship the goddess Śrī, and in the surrounding pitchers,
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Sṛṣṭi thereafter.
Then one should worship Prahvī, Satyā, and Brāhmī, as well as Sudarśana in the water-pot;
the others [the weapons] as before, and Śrī in the fire.
Having invoked the other deities as well, beginning with Vāgīśā, in their proper order.

O Goddess, in the rite of installing the jar during the conceptualization of Brahmā and the other deities, the wise man should worship Brahmā and the others situated in the central jar, and Indra and the others in the directions starting from the east in due order; he should also worship Sudarśana in the water-vessel (karaka). || 11.36–11.37 ||
Then the preceptor should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and touch the stone with the residual ghee upon its various limbs using the root mantra.
He should have the images of the Goddess, Brahmā, and the others fashioned by a group of artisans.
If one intends to fashion images for the accomplishment of one's own purpose,
one should procure wood during the three months beginning with Scorpio;
or else, from the eighth month of Scorpio onwards, one may use agarwood or sandalwood.
The *kāśmarya*, *devadāru*, *madhūka*, and *haricandana* trees;
the *khadira*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, and likewise the *panasa*;
the *bilva*, and those previously mentioned trees that are full of heartwood and free of hollows.
One should select those lords of trees that are free from hollows and the like;
O Rame, one should avoid those that are burnt, crooked, knotted, or possessed of branches.
All the fire-offerings should be performed according to the rules, just as in the collection of stones.
The limbs of the wild trees, such as the young shoots and so forth, are as described before;
the most excellent Guru should offer clarified butter and other substances into the eastern pit.
O Rame, he should wash the base of the tree and cover it with a cloth.
Recalling the root mantra with a garland of flowers, the supreme guru, moving clockwise,
should then worship the tree in succession with the twelve forms beginning with Matsya and the *vyāhṛtis*. (11.45–46)

"O tree, having attained the state of an immobile being through previously performed karma, I choose you as the image of Viṣṇu for the sake of your own liberation. From this state of immobility, go forth to a divine and unsurpassed form."
"Having obtained abundant enjoyments through the grace of Vāsudeva,
and having experienced them, you shall then attain liberation frequented by the Sun.
Having thus performed the ritual service with the mantra, one should bind the protection cord.
Other matters not yet mentioned should be performed at night, like the collection of stones. At dawn, having bathed and become pure during an auspicious moment, the preceptor,
facing east with the nature of a man, should cut down the tree with an axe.
Then, with the permission of his preceptor, the chariot-maker should cut down a tree.
A tree that has fallen toward the east or the north brings prosperity;
he should fashion the image from its trunk or from a suitable branch.
Having meditated upon Hari situated there, one should sprinkle him with water from the pitcher;
one should sprinkle him all around with water from the ritual vessel while reciting the root mantra.
Having led him to the temple or to a tree, according to the measurement of the sanctuary...
Having established the residence and so forth in the Ālaya, one should place a tree upon the ground; or else, one should perform everything outside in the forest according to the prescribed rule,
including an image of most wondrous form made of stone or wood.
One should have it performed in the refined language (Sanskrit) alone; otherwise, one would incur misfortune.
One should perform it according to the prescribed rule, for when so done, it leads indeed to liberation.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Twelfth Chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"O lotus-eyed one, I shall now describe the manifestation of the image."
Or the measurement of the interior of the womb, or the length of the door,
or the measurement of the base of the palace, or by the measurement of a cubit— O Rama, one should fashion the primary image which bestows success in all goals at birth.
O lotus-born one, the best image should have a height equal to its internal width;
the medium-sized image should be one-ninth less than that.
There is no doubt that the smallest image should be one-fifth less.
It may have four arms or two arms, according to the desire of the patron.
One should fashion it as seated, reclining, standing, or mounted on a vehicle; or as Trivikrama or Viśvarūpa, in accordance with the prescribed rule.

Now I shall describe the measurement for one born from the lotus while lying down. O Rame, having first divided the length of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into eighteen parts, one should discard one part at the foot and at the head-end.
One part shall be for the remainder, and two parts for the crown (kirīṭa).
(7) One should set aside one part between the crown and the remainder; with the remaining portion, one should fashion the primary image (mūlamūrti). (8)

This shall be the most excellent of the excellent; now the "excellent" [type] is described. Having first divided the internal width of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) into sixteen parts, one should discard four parts at the position of the head and two at the position of the base.
The best method for constructing a bed is with ten equal parts.
If one omits five parts from the head and three from the feet,
the remaining parts are declared to be the middling method for the bed.
If one omits four parts from the six [parts] at the head and likewise at the feet,
the image fashioned with the remaining six parts is the smallest (kanīyasī). Now hear the measurement for the standing primary image when it is reflected in water.
The image that is equal in size to the door is considered the most excellent of the excellent (uttamottama). O Rame, the excellent (uttama) is indeed one part less than the door;
the middling (madhya) shall be three parts less, while the inferior (adhama) is half the measure. || 12.13–12.14 ||
Now, regarding the seated image on a lotus-seat, I shall explain:
having divided the womb-gate into four parts, one should increase it by one part;
the excellent primary form of the image is joined with three such parts.
For the medium [size], two parts are for the larger [image] and one part is for the smaller.

(12.16) The height of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is the measure; half of that is said to be the vehicle (*yāna*). Half the height of the door of the inner sanctum is the image (*bimba*), which is placed above the neck of the vehicle. (12.17)
The height mounted on the vehicle (yāna) is full; the middle [height] is one-third of that, and the inferior should be half of that. Now hear the procedure for the Viśvarūpa [temple].
Having divided the height of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into twelve parts above...
Having set aside one part, two parts are likewise on the pedestal;
this is called the "excellent" form of Viśvarūpa, characterized by a middle elevation.
Having set aside two parts above, three parts are likewise below.
The height of Viśvarūpa was established by seven parts;
having set aside three parts from both the top and the bottom,
the smallest image was fashioned with the remaining six parts.
In this manner, the height of the image intended for the world-conquest is prescribed.
When the god stands, the goddesses likewise stand; when he sits, they likewise sit.
[When the god stands, the goddesses sit; when he sits, they may also stand.]
While the gods were lying down, she remained either seated or standing;
thus has this creation been described, wherein she is dependent upon Śrī and the others.
If she is positioned on the lap of the best of gods while he is mounted upon his vehicle, [she likewise remains dependent].
No other goddess should be placed at the side of that central image (bimba).
However, those goddesses who are dependent (paratantra)— having gentle faces and two arms—
should be fashioned in a state of dependence, elevated upon the shoulders of the god.
O auspicious lady, such is the exaltation of the celestial women in their independence:
whether mounted upon the shoulder of a vehicle, or lying down, or likewise standing;
in their freedom, one may imagine them as having four arms or two.
The reclining posture of the primary image of the Recliner is remembered as being fivefold:
Udyoga (Exertion), Yoga (Union), Bhoga (Enjoyment), Sṛṣṭi (Emanation), and Saṃhāra (Withdrawal).
These are performed upon the couch of Ananta’s body, which is fashioned with soft coverings.
With his right hand placed upon his cheek and pillow,
and distinguished by his left knee resting upon his left arm;
adorned with a crown, necklaces, bracelets, and a forest garland.
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, with a serene face, and with his neck slightly raised—
having thus fashioned the bed, one should previously take thirteen parts of that measure and divide them by eight.
In the case of the Lotus-born [Viṣṇu], one should fashion the images of Śrī and Bhūmi;
[placing them] on either side of the head of the worship-stand, with palms joined in reverence and seated in the svastika posture—
[one should depict] the goddess Śrī with two arms, and Dharā likewise upon the footstool.

On the wall situated at the side of the god’s crown, Sanaka and the others should be depicted. On the back wall of the god, however, one should likewise depict the weapons such as the discus and so forth, in human form with two arms, endowed with their own characteristic heads.
One should visualize the gods, beginning with Vidhātṛ, with joined palms upon the feet and the wall;
where the bed is thus arranged, the wise know that to be the most excellent of the excellent.
On a bed of Ananta’s coils, [the deity] may be two-armed or four-armed.
Bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, with a serene countenance, he alone is established in yoga;
reclining upon Śeṣa, he may have either two arms or four. Lakṣmī, whose limbs are like those of the goddess Śrī, is on both sides of the pedestal for worship.

With palms joined in reverence, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), Brahmā and the others, and those whose wealth is austerity, indeed serve him on all sides; they know him as the Aparayoga. Lying upon Śeṣa, he may have two arms or four hands.
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, his face serene, he either rests happily with the feet of Śrī and Dharaṇī placed upon his two laps, or else that Śrī,
whose limbs are like those of the Earth, has taken refuge at the base of his arms.
On either side of the worship altar for the god’s foot-rest,
or on the surface of the wall, Brahmā and the others, as well as Gandharvas and celestial women, are [depicted];
they indeed constantly attend upon the god’s pleasure bed.
O Rame, I shall describe the bed known as "Creation" for Vāsudeva:
he should lie upon Śeṣa or on a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha), adorned with childhood ornaments; with locks of hair, his face serene, a child possessing the luster of a blue lotus.

Brahmā rests happily within the ocean of nectar, taking refuge in the navel-lotus of that Lord of the World; he stands there with his palms joined in reverence. This is the "bed of creation"; now hear about the dissolution, O Lotus-born One.
Upon a couch of infinite enjoyments, adorned with a thousand hoods,
he is four or eight cubits tall, his face contorted with a frown,
his mouth terrifying with fangs, and adorned with weapons such as the discus.
He alone lies upon his bed, most terrifying;
by the side of the pedestal for worship may be Śrī, Lakṣmī, or the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa). Then, with palms joined in reverence, listen to [the description of] Trivikrama.

Having two arms, or four arms, or even endowed with eight arms, he should place his right foot upon the ground and toss the other one into the sky, saying to the Dānava: "Give me a place for the placement of a third step! (12.49–12.50)
One who is being entreated with the hand and one who is fashioned by craftsmen—
know that very Lord Hari upon the shoulder of Vainateya is the manifestation of prowess; now hear of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa).
Two cubits in height and with a single neck, [the faces] in the directions starting from the east should be arranged in due order;
the face of Vāsudeva and the others are adorned with forest garlands.
Above the face of Vāsudeva, there are also the faces of the gods.
The faces of the ṛṣis should be above the mouth of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
above the face of Pradyumna are also the faces of the Daityas and Rākṣasas; and from the mouth of Aniruddha come the faces of the Nāgas and Gandharvas.
Above each of those faces, various other faces should also be fashioned:
faces of piśācas, pythons, tigers, humans, and birds;
these should be arranged one after another, repeatedly, above each respective face.
The throat, starting from the lower region down to the ends of the feet, has the form of a person;
one should thus conceive the form of the Blessed One, whose body is the universe.
To perform worship after having fashioned [the deity] in the *ālaya* and other locations would be an act of extreme rashness.
Therefore, one who desires the welfare of the world should not entertain [such] conceptions in any matter.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
The thirteenth chapter begins.
The Blessed One said:
"One should diligently fashion the primary image out of stone, or metal, or wood, or with lime, or even with clay. (13.1)

"O Rāmā, if one wishes to fashion the primary image out of clay, it may take as long as a year to complete; such images would remain eternal, there is no doubt of this, and their craftsmanship would be of that nature. (13.2)
O Abode of Kamalā, listen as I describe the method for the application of materials to the forms, which must be performed in sequence:
first is the assembly of the wooden structure, and second is the binding with ropes.
The third is a clay coating, while the fourth is the binding with a tube.
The fifth would be a wrapping with rope, and again, the sixth is clay mixed with coconut husk. The seventh is a wrapping with rope.
The eighth is the application of sugar; know the ninth to be the joining of the cloth. The tenth is the ornamentation; beyond that is the white coating.
The twelfth is the coloring coating, according to the specific form [of the deity].

The procedure for applying color-paste, however, should be performed without the primary image [though the primary image may be anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, oil, and so forth]. The measurements for the primary images previously mentioned are now stated. (13.8)
First, the artisan should carve a single straight form upon the ground; having then taken all the measurements and so forth therein,
he should subsequently fashion the supreme image using either wood or stone.
That which is one hundred and eightieth part of the depression (unnati) shall be one *aṅgula*.
Two *aṅgulas* constitute a *kalā*, as do a *netra*, a *golaka*, and a *bhāva*.
That which is one-eighth part of an *aṅgula* is proclaimed to be a *yava*.
And one should fully understand that the *tāla* measure consists of six units for the work of the *bimba* [image] and so forth;
likewise, the face, the navel, the genitals, and the earth [the feet] are measured by one *tāla*, as is the pair of thighs.
The two shanks, the ankles, the knees, and the neck are each two *tālas*.

It should be known that [the measurement] is three finger-breadths each; thus the measurement has been declared. However, for the images of those who wear matted locks, according to the requirement of length or reduction, one should add a measurement of four or three finger-breadths outside the standard measure.
The crown has three, five, or seven peaks and rises eight digits high;
above the forehead of those without matted locks, there should be a very beautiful diadem.
Here, the increase or decrease [of its size] should be determined by the digit (kala) according to the requirements of the work.

According to the proportions as stated, one should divide the portion of the face into three parts, each measuring one finger-breadth, for the sake of the mouth, the nose, and the forehead. Then, the nose at the front should be one *kalā* in measurement, shaped like a sesame flower.

The width of the two nostril-pits is half a *kalā*, and their depression is likewise; they are free from any protrusion at the tip of the nose and measure four *yavas* in breadth. That [depression] at the tip of the nose, separated by a space of four *yavas*, is the measurement for the nostrils.
The upper lip is half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula), while the lower lip is one full finger-breadth (sāṅgula).
Know that the chin (golaka) is [one finger-breadth], and the two corners of the mouth (sṛkviṇī) are four finger-breadths [in length],
situated at the middle portion of the first part of the nose.
One should fashion two eye-holes there, separated by a space of one *kalā*;
they should be equal to a *kalā* in length and half a *kalā* in width.
That which has the shape of an *utpala* petal should be increased by two *yavas*.

One should fashion the shape of a lotus petal, with half a netra for the pupil and a circular iris. The length of the pupil should be one-third [of the total]; for the first [eye], it is increased by one yava, and for the other, by half a yava; that light [of the pupil] is one-fifth of that [iris].
That lotus-petal eye is prescribed as being one-third [of the face];
the socket of the eye is sixteen barley-corns in width, with an additional barley-corn.
It is known to be two and a half finger-breadths in length; the two eyebrow-crests are said to be two kalās.

In the middle, at the distance of two *yava*s, there are two auspicious marks resembling the crescent moon; the space between them is half a *kalā*, and their tips are aligned on the same suture-line. The two ears are two finger-breadths wide and twice the size of a *golaka* in length.
The two joints of the neck-circumference are each two *yavas* long;

know that the middle part between them is likewise [two *yavas*], while the *droṇī* is indeed one and a half *aṅgulas*. The hole for it should be half a *kalā*, and the size of the loop should be according to one's preference.
Wherever there is even a discrepancy of less than a finger-breadth (aṅgula),
that interval should be known as four barley-corns (yava) and free from gaps;
thus the two ears are said to be adorned with ornaments.
The forehead is four digits wide, with two peaks each measuring two globes;
it is three digits in height and one digit in width at the front.
Arising from the hairline, it is situated above the forehead.
One should fashion the face supported by the brows with a measurement of half a *kalā*;
one should make the circumference of the cheeks equal from ear to ear.
In the middle of that, the two rounded cheeks are defined by the proportions previously mentioned.
Know that the circumference of the head is thirty-six finger-breadths;
it is the distance from the two tips of the ears to the back of the skull. His neck resembles a beautiful conch shell, being well-proportioned at its base, middle, and top.
The circumference [of the base] is twelve parts, with twenty-one finger-breadths at the tip;
it is eighteen finger-breadths from its own base and expanded by one-third of that.
The two shoulders are at the expansion of their roots, elevated, circular and elongated, and symmetrical.
Its thickness is six *aṅgulas*; now the measurement of the arm is described. From the shoulder to the top of the head is three *kalās*, and up to the end of the joint it is recorded as six *kalās*.
Indeed, the measurement from the joint to the wrist is recorded as nine *kalās*.

The middle finger of a Maṇi is considered to be seven aṅgulas long, ending at the tip of the middle phalanx. That measurement for the middle finger should be understood as reduced by one kalā; and that same [measurement] for the left forefinger (pradeśinī) is further reduced by four yavas. || 13.37–13.38 ||
The little finger together with the thumb should be known as two *kalās*;

the thumb is traditionally held to be two joints long; all the fingers are spread out [in this manner], and from the base to the tip of each, one should diminish them by a barley-corn (*yava*) at each successive joint.

The nails should be made to resemble the phalanges, measured by half the length of the tip of the thumb. That measurement which is the circumference at the base of the thumb, and that which is the measure of the three fingers, should be known as reduced by four barleycorns.
When the circumference is less by one finger-breadth, the reduction is one and a half *kalās* as before;
from the tip, it is known to be one thumb-joint (*aṅguṣṭha*) or one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), or else three or six barley-corns (*yava*).
Know that when it is reduced by half a finger-breadth from the tip, the middle sequence is impaired.
The hand is not equal to a *lakṣa* in length from the tip; it is two finger-breadths (*dvitala*) wide, including the fingers. Its palm is slightly depressed and adorned with the lines of a *lakṣma*.
From the base of the fingers to the wrist, the breadth of the hand is two barley-corns per finger-breadth (*yava*).
From the limit of the wrist, O Rame, it should extend four *yava*s further;
its thickness at the middle should be equal to half a *kalā*.
The arm-encircling [measurement] from the limit of the wrist is traditionally held to be six *kalās*.
Know that the joint is seven units [in length], traditionally recorded as being three barley-corns and one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The nine globes at the base are indeed reduced by half a finger-breadth;
likewise, the width above the joint is here as previously described.
Here too, as before, having observed that the earth itself is situated within the work,
one should leave a space of one *tāla* from the limit of the neck and, having made the interior [of the chest] according to that measure,
one should fashion the two breasts equally, and their supporting base should be well-fleshed.

The lower half of the heart-sphere is depressed, while the upper half is adorned with the finest jewels. (13.49) The outer portions of the two breasts are three *kala*s less [than the heart-sphere], and the breast-circle is three *yava*s [in diameter]. The nipple is elevated by one *yava* from its base and is as wide as that [elevation]. (13.50)
The eye is said to be three *yavas* and a half; the measurement of the armpit, excluding the measurement of the shoulder, is the sixth [measurement] for the Lord of Śālīs,
which is fleshy and resembles a mass of grain-stores (*droṇī*).
Know that the girth-measurement around the waist is five *tārās* with the eyes included;
twice two *tālas* minus two finger-breadths, and joined with three barley-corns—know that to be the measurement for encircling the belly. (13.52–13.53)
The measure of the navel-maṇḍala should be known as three *yavas* less than one *kalā*.
That same measure, reduced by three *yavas*, is prescribed for its depth.
The circumference at the center of the navel is three *tālas*, O Three-eyed One.

The measurement of that [buttock] is six *golakas*, and it is recorded as being half the circumference of the waist. The two fleshy buttocks (*sphijau*), resembling the frontal globes of an elephant, are five *golakas* in circumference; they are recorded as being two finger-breadths wide at their base, like the seam of a loincloth.
The penis should be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in circumference and three parts (kalam) in length;
its sheath should be four barley-corns (yavas) wide, and its circumference six finger-breadths.
The testicles should be two finger-breadths in length, with their width equal at both the base and the tip.
Know that the anal aperture is perfectly circular and measures two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) all around.
The measurement of the thighs should be understood as nine finger-breadths for the middle portion;
from the base, it is six units (kalās), and it is recorded as being three units at the tip.

The kneecap is one finger-breadth less than the [thigh] and measures two *kalās* in both width and height; it is equal to four barley-corns. At the base of the shank, the circumference should be known as nine *golakas*.
In the middle, it should be twelve finger-breadths [in height] and five and a half kalās;
know that here too the circumference is expanded by one-third.
From the middle, the base, and the top, the expansion follows the appropriate proportion.
The state of having two elephant trunks is to be obtained through the two arms, the middle part of the body, the collection of fingers, and the pair of thighs along with the shanks;
and the length measured by seven tālas is indeed remembered as the characteristic of a Cāraṇa.
In the middle of that [foot], which is extended by two *golaka*s at the heels, there is a space of one *aṅgula* and two *kala*s;
and the width [of the foot] is known by the wise to be two *kala*s, equal to one *kalā*, less three *yava*s from near the big toe.
The circumference at the region of the ankles is generally one-sixteenth [of the body] plus one finger-breadth;
from the base of the little toe to the end of the ankle, the girth of the instep is one finger-breadth.
From the lower limit of the shank, the circumference is seven eyes (twelve fingers).
In the same way, the circumference is determined by subtracting one-sixteenth from the top;
by that rule, the sole becomes like the back of a tortoise. Its length is three finger-breadths, as is the length of the big toe.
The rim there should indeed be known as five fingers wide;
the forefinger (pradeśinī) should be made two barley-corns longer than its length. Furthermore, it should be equal in height to the thumb and positioned in the middle of the footprint.
The middle finger is reduced by two-eighths [of its length]; then that which follows it is likewise,
and those which follow it have three joints as before,
joined with a network of nails resembling the back of a tortoise.
The girth of the two front legs is two *kalan*s less half a *yava*;
for the remaining [legs], it is proclaimed to be four *yavas* less at each [successive joint].
All [limbs] should be fleshy, gentle, and symmetrical; such parts are auspicious.
The ten [teeth] situated outside the wrinkles [of the lips] are the fangs, elevated by seven barley-corns (*yava*).
The measurement for the four middle teeth is two barley-corns;
know that the measurement for all those belonging to the sides of those [middle teeth] is four barley-corns.
Two *yavas* in height and two *yavas* in width from the tip to the root; with that same measure of one and a half *yavas* at the middle part, all his teeth were without gaps.
His hair curled to the right, a sign arising from a birth not shared by common folk.
This is well-ascertained as beneficial and unfailing pride:
know that the quality of being captivating in one instance is always adorned by both beauty and charm, and that these two exist in a state of mutual dependence.

Exquisite beauty sometimes exists by encroaching upon pride; sometimes gracefulness remains by completely covering over pride. Just as in this world a handsome man who is poor attains a state of being honored.

Even one who is ugly may be exceedingly wealthy, yet he is neither truly beautiful nor truly poor. Likewise, O Mahāmati, an image endowed with both [qualities] becomes unacceptable, whereas that which is joined with only one is always acceptable. (13.79–13.80)
When there is correct measurement and beauty, the power of the mantra’s presence indeed remains fruitful through the desire to bestow grace upon devotees;
it becomes manifest to the vision of one who has correctly approached the image situated before them.
Knowing this, one should practice that which brings immediate joy to the formless [mind]. Now, for the perfection of beauty regarding measures, weights, and proportions:
the distance between the feet of one who is upright and has well-even feet should be three finger-breadths.
That [space] at the tip of the uneven foot is known to be equal to a palm;
however, from the middle of its two heels, it should be understood as being two *golaka*s [in measure].
This is for the sake of the stability of the *brahmanāḍī* and likewise of the two pathways.
One should make it perfectly level with a thread on the body, extending from south to north.

Having stretched a thread from the forehead to the top of the penis of the image standing with feet even, and having covered [the distance] with that, [one measures] the interval between the navel and the heart.
The perfection of the nose-tip and the *malaka* belongs to him whose *tilaka* is situated above;
likewise, for one with uneven feet, one should lead [the breath] to the tip of the right big toe.
Having achieved symmetry of the limbs by means of moving from field to field, [one attains success].
By means of the cord, the irregularity of all images is eliminated.
(13.88) Beautiful and pure in length, with four, three, or two corners all around; but when it is impure and not clean, the constructed image is the reverse. (13.89)

The forehead of the horse-faced one is twelve finger-breadths in width; it has eight eyes, and its extent from the front is four finger-breadths. The nostrils have apertures at the tips of their parts, with the intervening space between them divided into portions.
The two jawbones (hanuka) are eight finger-breadths (aṣṭāṅgula) long, and the two temples (sṛgviṇī) are equal to that.
In the middle, the two ear-conchs (śrotraśukti) are two finger-breadths wide and two units (kala) high.
The nasal bridge (ghrāṇavaṃśa) is two finger-breadths [in width], and above that, it is known to be two units high.
Know that the expansion of the mouth should be two *yavas* in width, increasing gradually from the front;
indeed, one should bring that very [expansion] to a thinness at the edge of the jaw by a fraction of a *yava*.
The two sides of the nasal bridge should be depressed in the middle and joined together.

With two and a half *yavas* between the eyes and the nostrils; the lower petal is curved inward by a measure of one *yava*. The forehead, along with the *sālaka*, is as before; the middle of the eye is one *kalā* and one finger-breadth.
Know that the face of Nṛsiṃha has eight eyes all around;
from the region of his lips, one should fashion two ears arising therefrom.
Again, using the measurement of those two ears, one should extend [the line] to the edge of the forehead.
Prior to the measurement and from the previously described exertion, the characteristic of the nose should be such that it is moistened,
with its openings expanded, and provided with a nasal bridge.
In those openings, the measurement should be three *yavas* more than one's own previous measure.
The temple (sagola) should be placed among the upper limbs, and the eye should possess all its parts.
The lower lip is to be known as one finger-breadth (aṅgula) with four barley-corns (yava).
The face is four kalās and a half; the remaining length is recorded as that of the jaw.

Its expansion should be known as one *netra* measure plus one *yava*; it diminishes toward the front by one *aṅgula* up to the corners of the mouth. The entire circumference of the pair of eyes, including the whites, is half of that [measure], and they appear full of wonder.
The ear is extended as before; its height is half a *kalā*.
The eyebrow, equal in measure to the union of two lunar digits (*kalā*), consists of three globes (*golaka*). Its measurement is one *kalā*, large and resembling a conch-shell spiral.
The measurement of the portion should be clearly executed upon its head.
The length of the Boar’s face is prescribed as one and a half *tālas*;
in width, from the forehead, it is that same measure increased by two *aṅgulas*.
The width of the forehead region of the Lord, who is of gentle form and radiant with his [divine] portions,
is one-fourth of that measure;
its thickness above is equal to that, while below it is one finger-breadth.
The measurement of the two jaws is traditionally held to be seven and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The remaining measurement, including the cavity, is the distance between the two corners of the mouth;
its expansion at the front part is one and a half kalās and a half-finger-breadth.

That very [measurement] should be understood in finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the two nostrils; the nasal aperture and the mouth are as previously stated, while the fangs are raised by half a kalā. The bridge of the nose is as before, like the back of a plantain leaf-base.
When the ears are as described for a horse's face, they should be at a distance of seven kalās from the tip [of the nose];
the eyes should be equal to those [ears], yet their outer corners are sharp and elevated by one barley-corn (yava).
Their necks, however, are prescribed to be two finger-breadths [in width].
That radiance which arises from each individual part, joined together and manifesting in a gentle form—
that radiance of whichever limb of Nṛhari exists without [excessive] height—
becomes greater by half a digit (kalā) through the light of its surrounding halo.
His chest, waist, belly, and hips exceed the standard proportions by one part;
likewise, his fingernails and toes are so, and his body is well-fleshed,
with hair that is complete, curling to the right, and very curly.
For a face with three, four, or five mouths,
one should effect a reduction of two *golakas* by means of the right and left faces,
excluding the upward-facing one; therein, the expansion is said to be that of the lion-face, which faces north.
However, for the sake of accomplishing liberation, the alignment of the gaze of the four [faces] should be equal.
But for the attainment of health, enjoyment, and isolation (*kaivalya*), one should perform the alignment of the gaze by half a finger-breadth to the left and to the right.

The face turned toward the west possesses equality with that very one facing the east, provided its height, breadth, and the proportions of the nose, eyes, eyebrows, and ears are identical. Then, the auspicious right face has its gaze cast slightly askance toward the earth.
And likewise, the ear, eye, and mouth [of the deity] grant all accomplishments in the subsequent [state].
Because they indicate their own function, there is indeed the presence of that mantra;
otherwise, the King of Mantras remains in a state of quiescence.
And because of its constant presence, spirits, vetālas, and rākṣasas flee at the mere sight of it; O Rame, they dissolve upon being seen.
Taking my command upon their heads, those mantra-wielders depart.
Therefore, one should practice with diligence so that there may be the presence of the Image (bimba).
Indeed, because of its presence, no one undertakes anything auspicious—
[the Image] which has the tusks of a boar, the eyes of a lion, and likewise a flat nose.
The western face of the all-pervading Lord, who possesses five faces, is to be fashioned;
its equality with the upper and lower lips [of the central face] shall be by half a finger-breadth less than those two,
and clearly situated between them.
The row of teeth should indeed be made equal from root to middle to tip.
Then, the two cheeks should be rounded and prominent by half a *kalā*.
The beard at the front should be two *kalās*, with the hair gradually decreasing by one *kalā* and then half a *kalā*.
The connecting veins (saṃbandhaveṇī) should extend in all directions according to the previously stated measurement.
One should bring gentleness to the primary faces, like those of a lion or a boar;
indeed, the measurement is determined from the visible mark (lakṣya) for the sake of practical application.
And there is the expansion [of power] through the speech of Aśvavaktra and the gentle-natured Bhūbhṛt;
likewise, one who practices according to what was previously taught by Nṛhari and others, as well as in the manifestation of the faces and limbs of the Lord Śaktīśvara. (13.127–13.128)
Adorned with necklaces, anklets, garments, garlands, bracelets, and armlets,
and graced by flower wreaths, sacred threads, upper-armlets, crowns, and other ornaments—
an image fashioned in this way becomes a bestower of success for those who embody the mantras.
That which was previously described as the fivefold vehicle, the deity of the vital breath—
its facial circle is measured by the *tāla* derived from its image;
the forehead is said to be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the matted locks are bound above the two eyes.
The ears are elevated by two finger-breadths; the chest is known to be five kalās;
that belly is eight finger-breadths [in width], and the hips are elevated by five finger-breadths.
The thighs are elevated by nine finger-breadths, and the knees are known to be two finger-breadths [thick].

The shanks are eight finger-breadths in height, and the two masses of the feet are two finger-breadths. The circumference of the neck is one unit less than that [of the head], and the total extent of all the limbs should always be understood as equal to the [circumference of the] face.
Know that the circumference of her abdomen is greater than that by one-sixteenth;
the girth of her waist is indeed four times the measure of an eye (two units) more.
Know that the circumference at the base of her thighs is equal to a *bimboka* fruit.
Thus, the middle of the calf and its end are indeed the same.
The foot is five kalās in length and four aṅgulas in width;
it is three aṅgulas from the region of the heel, and the two big toes are equal at two kalās each.
The measurements from the region of the feet should be understood as follows: the successive steps are [measured] in finger-breadths less one barley-corn (*yava*).
The navel cavity is very extensive, measuring two and a half eyes (*locana*) in width.
From the wrist (*maṇibandha*) to the tip of the middle finger is nine finger-breadths.
The circumference of its [the head’s] base is three *kalās*, and its nails are sharp and prominent.
Know that its arm is two *kalās* in height, measuring two eyes (*dvilocana*).
That which is joined by the upper arm and forearm is known to be equal to two *tālas*.
The circumference of her arms is greater than half a *kalā* more than the diameter of her face;
for thus was the rule declared by the Lotus-born regarding her lips and shoulders.
Her eyes, in their circular breadth, are like lotus petals.
The pair of eyebrows is described as being like those of Narasiṃha; the tip of the nose is like the beak of a parrot.
The bridge of the nose is half a kalā in measure and long, shaped like the back of an elephant.
From the region of the belly, the pair of flanks is neither too short nor too long in its own span.
In that same manner, it is spread out to half its length, like the wing of a swan;
its tail, measuring twice the size of its own wings, has a hundred branches.
This entire extent, including the wings, is truly endowed with its constituent parts.
Know that this applies generally to all; now hear the specific details.
One should reduce the height of the two thighs by three finger-breadths, while increasing the height of the shank-sections; and here, one should provide a binding with the shanks.
From the root of the wrist-joint known as the *bimba*, where the channels arise,
the webbed membrane (*jāla*) at the base of the foot should be understood to extend for half of that [root] plus half a finger-breadth; in width, it is six finger-breadths.
Know that everything else spoken by Satya applies to all at all times.
However, the two wings are provided with feet and their breadth is equal to their length;
this is the measurement of wing-span for those who fly.
And for the five who abide, their characteristic is half a *lakṣa*;
taking this as the measure, yet devoid of the five eyebrows and eyelashes—
know this, O lotus-born one, to be the characteristic of the dwarf form.
Having taken three finger-breadths from the forehead, the nose, and the mouth,
one should fashion the binding of matted locks (jaṭābandha) above the head;
the length of the binding of the matted locks should be five tālas.
Thus has this measurement of the primary images been declared.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
[Now begins] the fourteenth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lotus-born One, the distinction in terminology and the characteristics of the various forms of ritual action, worship, and so forth, as well as their application, shall now be explained."

The worship of the ritual action (*karmārcā*), the festival worship (*utsavārcā*), the offering worship (*balyarcā*), as well as the other two which consist of both bathing and pilgrimage sites (*snānatīrthobhaya*), and the final one intended for the purpose of the deity’s rest (*śayanārthikā*)—
where these six forms are worshipped, that worship is known as the most excellent.

In the intermediate [rite], there are three images; however, in the final [rite], there is worship of a single image. This procedure applies when there are many images; but when there is only one image, it is described as follows:
in the case of the primary image (mūlārcā), there should always be both worship and ritual bathing.
Therefore, the two *kautuka* [images] are not intended for the purpose of bathing and worship.
O lovely-faced one, when the height of the *dhruvabera* is divided into ten parts,
the *karmārcā* [should be made] with two parts, while the *autsava* [image] is likewise.
The image [of the deity] shall be eleven parts, and the bed shall consist of ten parts.
The image for the offering (balibimba) shall be nine parts, and the image for the sacred ford (tīrthabimba) shall be eight parts.
The bathing image (snapanaberam) shall be six parts; such is the arrangement of the heights.
Or, having first taken the root-body as one *aṅgula*,
O auspicious lady, the height of the action-body (*karmabera*) should be twenty-six *aṅgulas*;
or one may make it twenty-four *aṅgulas* or eighteen *aṅgulas*.
Or it may be sixteen finger-breadths in measure, or twelve, or eight;
or six finger-breadths, O auspicious one, or even four.
Among the previously mentioned measures of finger-breadths, the supreme image should be fashioned.
This procedure has been taught for [an image with] many limbs by the Lotus-Seated One;
this very same procedure should be devised by the wise even for a single-limbed [image],
whether it be seated, reclining, or mounted on a vehicle, including its primary and secondary auspicious ornaments.
One should make them equal, or they may remain as one pleases.
The image for the perpetual festival should be present everywhere.
Having divided the measurement of the worship-image into three parts, one should fashion a lotus with one part.
The pavilion should be circular and pleasing to the mind, provided with five parts such as sandals and so forth;
or it may be square, with its width equal to its length,
its radiance measured by a third [of its size], and equipped with two stakes.
Having divided the height of the pedestal into three parts, one should fashion a lotus with one part.
O Rame, it should be endowed with twelve petals or eight;
likewise, it should be provided with upper petals and a broad pericarp in the center.
Adorned with a pedestal and shaped like a slightly blossomed lotus,
it may be the size of a foot, or as wide as a petal, or simply a full lotus;
or it may be a pedestal according to one's desire, but one must never make it hollow.
This construction of the pedestal for a standing *kautuka* has been described.
For one who is seated, it should be long, circular, or rectangular;
one should fashion it with a height equal to half that of the image, like a lotus.

One should visualize the left foot of that god as contracted and the other [right foot] as resting upon a lotus; the foot of Hari should be depicted as hanging down. One should imagine Śrī at the right side of the god and Dharā at the left.

The Karmārcā, however, must always be inseparable from those two [Śaktis] at their sides. For other images, however, the two wives or the Prabhās may be present together or absent; they may be on the same seat or even separately.
When the god is standing, the two goddesses should likewise be seated;
but when he is mounted upon a vehicle, the radiance of the archway (toraṇa) should be fashioned.
Having melted beeswax, one should fashion the image with it.
Having consecrated a pedestal made of grain and other materials, and having drawn a lotus with a wheel (cakra) upon it,
one should prepare a bed of *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward. Then,
the Guru should lay a new cloth and the image upon it.
One should offer oblations into the blazing fire with its head facing eastward,
using flowers, sacrificial wood, parched grain, and clarified butter— one hundred and eight times—
with the root mantra, the hymns, and the *caru* offering. Then again:
One should sprinkle the image, which is the sequence of the principles (tattva-paddhati), with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter.
One should meditate upon it during an auspicious moment and worship it with the root-mantra (*mūla-vidyā*).
Then, the patron should honor the most excellent guru with wealth, cows, and grain.
One should satisfy other excellent Brahmins as well as the artisans;

the master craftsman (sthapati) shall fashion the image with the authorization of the chariot-maker (rathakāra). One should construct that auspicious image according to the correct measures of weight, height, and proportion.
Then one should apply a coating of clay according to the rules of the craft treatises (śilpa-śāstra).
Having taken gold, silver, copper, or pure, high-quality iron,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon a seat of grain as previously described.
One should offer oblations as before, according to the path seen in the scriptures; then,
having melted pure metal acquired by righteous means,
the master craftsman, learned in the treatises on sculpture, should fashion the image with it.

Having thus had the images of the deities, beginning with the Mūla-pratimā, as well as the sanctum and other structures constructed in sequence by groups of artisans according to the path prescribed in the treatises on architecture (śilpa-śāstra),
one should have the retinue deities fashioned and install them in their respective places.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The fifteenth chapter:
The Blessed One said—
For the sake of worshipping the retinue and for the beauty of the temple, they should be especially visualized in the first enclosure and other such areas;
at the door of the half-pavilion, there are the two [deities] who have the conch and the discus as their crowning ornaments.
With fangs bared and terrifying eyes, wearing crowns of skulls,
they stand on the right and left sides, dressed as ascetics and bearing maces;
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa should be fashioned either from metal or even from stone.
O fair-faced one, Jaya and Vijaya are to be installed on the two sides of the door of the Sāla tree, which is designated as the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala).
At the eastern door of the inner enclosure (antarhāra), there are those who hold a lotus and a mace.
The Guru should place those bearing the sword and the bow at the southern gate;
he should station those holding the thunderbolt and the mace at the western gate;
and in the north, O Rame, they should be those holding the noose and the goad.
In the eastern and other directions of the central Hārasāla hall, respectively, are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, then Bhadra and Subhadra,
Kṛtānta and Asuravidhvaṃsa, and Kubera and Akṣakubera.
In this very way, it is desired that there be gate-towers (*gopura*) for the others in the four directions;
likewise, in the directions starting from the east, there is the boundary-marking *sāla* gate-tower.
Durjaya and Prabala shall be the two [guardians] at Viśvabhāvana and Puṣkara.
One should arrange Saṃbhava, Prabhava, Suśobhana,
and Subhadraka at the lower gate and in the directions starting from the east.
[Likewise] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—
eight [deities], two by two, should be arranged at each door according to the prescribed rite;
these are the attendants of Viṣṇu, surrounded by armies numbering in the tens of millions.
O Rāmā, one should place those with staffs in hand, who are three-eyed and endowed with four arms,
either in the first courtyard or in the second pavilion,
at the front location facing the primary image.

One should install Vainateya, the hero with two arms, palms joined in reverence, and adorned with a basket-shaped crown, either in copper or in stone. One should place Vīralakṣmī in the southwest, or in the other directions in due order.
Having conceptualized the *ālaya* therein according to the division of moving and stationary [elements],
the preceptor should worship each one during the time of Hari’s worship. One should visualize the deity Viṣvaksena between Someśa and Īśāna.

The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭhaka) may be located either inside or outside the gopura. For a temple possessing many enclosures, the attendants have been described previously; now hear these attendants for a temple possessing a single enclosure. || 15.17–15.18 ||
On the two sides of the inner sanctum, one should arrange Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka;
in front, Vainateya; and in the southwest (nairṛta), Vīralakṣmī. In the northeast (īśāna), one should likewise place Senanātha upon a lotus seat.
The supreme guru should also install these in the form of physical images.
Then, he should have the implements for worship prepared according to the prescribed characteristics;
the bell, consisting of the *śabdabrahman*, should be one cubit in height.
