Shaped like the sphere of the universe, fashioned from the components of Saurāṣṭra, it is downward-facing, one *tāla* in width, and of beautiful form. The handle of the bell is one *tāla* in length; above that is the Lord of Birds.
One should fashion a discus, a conch, or a lotus on the birth-mark of a lotus;
for it is always useful in all rites such as worship,
and for the placement of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings of the Enemy of Madhu.
One should install for the God of gods a pedestal provided with four legs,
made either of gold or other metals, or even of wood;
it should be equipped with an outlet for water and possess the characteristics of being one cubit in height and so forth.
O fair-faced one, for the purpose of placing the vessels for the sacred waters such as the Arghya and others,
there should be five vessels shaped like lotuses and capable of being filled with a *prastha* of water; within these, one should fashion wheels.
One should prepare either five or one of these for the purpose of receiving [the offerings].
Because it draws forth the *arghya* and other substances, it is celebrated as the "Extrator" (*uddharaṇī*).
At the end, one should place a wheel, one span in length, shaped like a conch shell.
At the rear, one should have a water reservoir made of gold or other precious materials. There should be a vessel for holding the water for washing the feet of the Lord of Ramā,
shaped like a *unmatta* flower and provided with a footrest.
The incense burner, resembling a lotus and provided with two feet,
is adorned with a corner, a stalk, and two petals, and is fashioned from gold.
Its stalk is one cubit in length, and it may have either three or two legs.
Of the arranged lamp-vessels, shining in the form of a circle—
there should be seven, five, or three, though they may indeed be in descending order.
And in the first lamp-vessel, there should be a hundred wick-holders.
In the second and subsequent [levels], it should be smaller, ending with a water-lily bud;
this is declared to be the lamp-vessel. Now hear about the bath-seat:
it should be one cubit long and three cubits wide, square in shape.
At the edge, it should have a height of two finger-breadths and be joined with a water-channel;
its base should be two cubits high, and it may have the form of a lion or a tiger,
while the central lotus should be fashioned from gold or other metals.
O Rame, all the bathing vessels should be made of metals such as gold;
two vessels in the shape of a conch and a discus should have a hundred openings in their centers,
while another vessel, circular and fashioned from gold, should have a thousand openings.

One should fashion [a vessel] one *aratni* in width, with a lotus in the center; there shall be a thousand perforations upon the petals and the pericarp. Listen now to the description of the worship, the seat, and the Lakṣmī-vessel, which is one cubit in height.
It should be one *aratni* in width, fashioned with gold and other materials;
it is square, centrally designed, and adorned with a lotus.
It is provided with four legs equal in size to those of a tiger.

Thus, O fair-browed one, the seat for the meal should be provided, though it may be without a footstool. One should arrange vessels made of gold or silver for the offerings of food, shaped like bowls and proportionate to the quantity of the sacrificial materials.
One should fashion a golden vessel from the leaves of the *nāgalatikā* creeper,
circular like the stem of a lotus and measuring one *aratni* in width;
its pedestal should be half that width and beautifully adorned with various designs.

The wise man should fashion a vessel for the bali offering four tālas in height, made of gold or other precious materials; it should be circular and provided with a lid as desired. The vessel for the nīrājana rite should likewise be made of gold or other such materials.
The central lotus should be two or one *tāla* in circumference; its height should be equal to that of the principal image (*mūlabimba*), which is either lying down or standing in front of it,
and it should be fashioned from gold or silver.
Alternatively, they may be made of copper, but one should not have them made of iron. There should be four principal lamps, or two according to one's means;
there should be three or five vessels for holding the ghee.
In front, however, one should place the conch or the discus belonging to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),
with its white parasol removed, adorned with gold and other precious materials;
or one may fashion it from pure gold or silver, O Beloved.

One should fashion a parasol of this kind, with a handle made of gold or silver and adorned with a lattice of jewels; and one should likewise prepare four chowries, O Rame, with handles fashioned from gold and other precious materials. || 15.50–15.51 ||
One should prepare four diverse fans made of *uśīra* grass and peacock feathers, adorned with jewels and other ornaments;
likewise, one should provide a comb made of gold or silver, measuring eight finger-breadths in length.
It should be six finger-breadths in width and provided with twenty teeth;
or else, O fair-faced one, it may be fashioned with sixteen teeth.
It is made of gold and shaped like a scorpion, serving as a container for powdered collyrium.
O Rame, whether it has the form of a lion, a swan, or a deer,
one should fashion a cavity in its belly or its head;
it should be as beautiful as a mirror, measuring either the full height of the image or half of it.
It may be circular or square, made of bell-metal and adorned with jewels.
The drinking vessel should be made of gold, filled with water from a water-jar (āṭhakāmbu),
one tāla in height, and its circular circumference should be five aṅgulas in width.
Its two parts should be fashioned at two finger-breadths each, and its foot should be one finger-breadth.
The traveling seat should be wide, with a length and breadth of two cubits;
its width should be double that, and one should fashion its foot at one *tāla*.
The young [image] should be elevated all around, measuring one tāla in height,
depicted with the ten incarnations, and adorned with various jewels;
the seats should be as prescribed, or fashioned from gold.
One should fashion the sandals of the God of gods from wood, according to availability and with an extent suitable for the image, using gold and other precious materials.
Their pedestal should be made of gold, shaped like a blossoming lotus.
One should place those two sandals upon the pericarp of the lotus.
One should fashion a palanquin, a chariot, an elephant, a horse, or Gaṇeśa,
or any other beautiful vehicle, out of gold.
One should provide a palanquin fashioned from jewels, equipped with a canopy,
and adorned with banners made of white, black, red, and variegated silk,
featuring staffs of gold placed here and there.

One should prepare a water trough and a basin made of materials such as gold for the purpose of the Lord’s consecration; these should be deep and accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments, including trumpets and conchs.
The maddala, kāhala, kāṃsya, bherī, and paṭaha [drums]. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The sixteenth chapter.
The Blessed One said:

"In this manner, the patron of Hari should perform the examination of the ground and so forth, together with the primary forms and other requirements, characterized by all the auspicious marks. (16.1)
Having surveyed that site (ālaya), one who is intent on performing the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should first choose a preceptor (ācārya) possessing the characteristics described in the Pāñcarātra.
I shall now declare those characteristics in this [text] adorned with garlands of lotuses.
They say that Brahmins who know the four Vedas are designated as *śrotriyas*.
However, those officiating priests (*arcakas*) who know the *Pāñcarātra* are equal to ten *śrotriyas*.
One who knows both the *Pāñcarātra* and the Vedas is designated as "complete" (*pūrṇa*).
That twice-born man who studies the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Pāñcarātra,
and who teaches disciples the Pāñcarātra as well as the Śrutis—
he is said to be a consecrated guru equal to ten full [gurus].

Born into a family of consecrated ones (dīkṣita) and himself consecrated by a Bhaṭṭācārya, he who has received from the mouth of his guru the triple Vedic knowledge (trayī-vidyā) as well as the Pāñcarātra according to its true meaning,
and who is endowed with tranquility and self-control, shall indeed become a Bhaṭṭāraka. (16.6–16.7)
Equal to ten Bhaṭṭārakas, he had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;

he was proficient in the meaning of Vedānta and a knower of the essential truth of the Pāñcarātra. Born into a family initiated through traditional lineage, he was possessed of meditative concentration.
Having received initiation in both ways, he was devoted to the fivefold daily ritual;
he was proficient in the Yoga scriptures, possessed of knowledge, and contemplative of liberation.
[He performed] all the rites beginning with the acquisition of land and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
A man who is not afflicted by disease, who is independent, devoted to the elders, handsome, and a believer, is capable of performing that [rite] even without assistance;
likewise one who is irreproachable by others, renowned, and has conquered his senses. (16.11)
Skilled in the propitiation of the mind and expert in the science of mantras,
he who has mastered the mantras and possesses all-seeing vision is called a Bhaṭṭācārya.
Śrī said:
The Guru indeed performed initiation for him in the mandala of the wheel and lotus;

he was consecrated and endowed with the previously mentioned qualities, [including] everything from the plowing of the site up to the final consecration, as well as the special worship and other rites.
He alone should perform [the rite], while the other should be intent on its accomplishment.
If one who is devoid of another's initiation were to perform [rites such as] plowing and so forth, that performed action would be fruitless;
he should have it performed again by another.
"O Lord, such as this has been declared by you; what kind of initiation (dīkṣā) is that considered to be?
Is it the mandala of the lotus-wheel, or rather the consecration (abhiṣeka)?
Tell me, O Supreme Person, for I am desirous of knowledge. (16.16–16.17)
The Blessed One said:
O lotus-dweller, I shall first describe the true nature of initiation—that rite by which one beholds that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 16.18
Because it tears asunder the entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), it is called *dīkṣā*.
This *dīkṣā* should be performed by one who is dispassionate, and not by those devoted to ritual action (*karmin*).
Just as *dīkṣā* is prescribed in the ritual sections (*karmakāṇḍa*) for the successful accomplishment of sacrifice, so too is this [spiritual] initiation intended.
Likewise, in the Kāthaka Veda, for the sake of accomplishing worship, sacrifice, and so forth,
and in order to establish the preeminence of initiation (dīkṣā), the Lotus-born [Brahmā] divided himself:
first into the form of sound, and thereafter into the form of activity.
Having entered in due order the third form, which is that of the object (*artharūpa*), likewise the form of the teacher (*ācāryarūpin*), and the fifth form, which is that of initiation (*dīkṣārūpa*),
he for whom initiation has been performed by me is none other than I myself; of this there is no doubt.
That initiation is said to be threefold: gross, subtle, and likewise supreme.
Furthermore, by means of its divisions, it is also threefold and fourfold;
the initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), and the third is known as the practitioner (sādhaka).
The preceptor (ācārya) is also to be known; thus, all four are likewise initiated.
Performing the duties prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras, which are dear to Hari, I shall perform daily worship, having been consecrated by the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra).
O Rame, for one who, having thus resolved, performs worship every day,
that initiation of his is proclaimed as "mental" (mānasī).
Indeed, it is suitable for all Vaiṣṇavas for the purpose of domestic worship.
This is to be known as "gross" (sthūlā), as proclaimed in the scriptures:
[he who], out of pride, initiates one born of another lineage;
he whose knowledge regarding the consecration and other rites of the Pañcarātra is not found.

The initiation that is performed for both of these by the most excellent initiates is proclaimed as the "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) and the "intermediate" (*madhyamā*) by those best versed in the Vedas. O Rame, for these two there shall be no consecration (*abhiṣeka*); there should be only the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The teacher and the practitioner should be dear [to one another] during festivals and other such occasions.
Initiation by a teacher is of two kinds: seedless (*nirbījā*) and with seed (*sabījakā*).
This is stated in another *tantra*, in the *āgama*, and in the work known as the *siddhāntatantra*.
For those engaged in worship among them, initiation is known as "seedless" (nirbīja).
For others, there is no authority to perform initiation for them;
therefore, O lotus-eyed one, it is called "seedless" by the wise. (16.32–33)
The procedure for initiation according to the *Mantrasiddhānta*, which possesses seeds (*sabīja*), is now proclaimed;
it is performed with mantras declared in the four Vedas and with mantras established in the *Ekāyana*,
according to the method of the *Mantrasiddhānta* as spoken by me and according to one's lineage (*gotrin*).

That initiation which was previously conferred upon me by the elder in the form of an Ācārya— that initiation is indeed remembered as the supreme initiation (parā-dīkṣā). Having truly attained the supreme initiation, one should indeed perform worship in the temples.
O Goddess, the preceptor should first be one who is intent upon the performance of ritual acts,
endowed with devotion to the Lord, detached, and possessed of faith;
one whose wisdom is cultivated in the three Vedas and other sciences, and who has been purified by expiatory rites.
Having observed a disciple who is endowed with all virtues and deemed worthy,
the preceptor should first prepare a sacrificial pavilion for the completion of the initiation; there,
he should construct a central altar measuring two palm-lengths toward the west.

The sacrificial pit for Brāhmaṇas should be square, while that of a king (Kṣatriya) should be circular; for a Vaiśya it should be bow-shaped, and for the Śūdra caste, triangular. Having also gathered the ritual materials previously prepared for the initiation ceremony, [he should proceed].

O Rame, one should first cleanse all the pavilions and other structures. Then, having purified them according to the rules with auspicious-day waters and the five products of the cow accompanied by mantras, one should first offer the ritual germination (aṅkura).
When the eleventh lunar day has arrived, one should perform the consecration of the jars; then,
having wrapped the jars on all sides with threads,
adorned them with garlands, sandalwood paste, and unbroken grains of rice, and clothed them in garments.

Adorned with mango sprouts, coconut fruits, and *kūrca* grass, one should recite the mantra over the water held in the ritual vessel (*karaka*) one hundred times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). With that water, one should sprinkle the sacrificial materials as well as the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
Having sprinkled himself and the circle of disciples with the waters of an auspicious day,
he should then construct an altar that is two cubits in height and width,
square in shape, and having first sprinkled that as well.
Upon that [surface], one should draw a mandala of a wheel and lotus, adorned with twelve petals,
provided with a pericarp in the center, and embellished with various colors; having drawn it,
one should then prepare an altar on its northeastern side.
Upon that [altar], one should arrange a pedestal for grain and other materials in the shape of a wheel.
Having drawn a mandala of a lotus within that wheel, complete with petals,
one should place the principal pitcher in the pericarp and twelve pitchers around it.
Having placed the *karaka* vessel in the north, the Guru should fill the jars with fragrant water.
Within those jars, he should deposit images engraved with their respective forms;
furthermore, the Guru should place eight auspicious objects all around them.
One should worship the door-arches and the water-pots in due order; one should worship Vāsudeva in the center of the wheel and Keśava and the others all around it (verse 16.52).
Likewise, O lotus-eyed one, having invoked them into the pots, one should worship them.
Having churned the fire with the eight-syllable mantra, one should place it within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru) therein, one should first divide it into four parts;
then, with three portions, one should worship those situated at the jar, the mandala, and the fire.
The most excellent preceptor, O Goddess, should himself consume one portion,
having recited the root mantra over one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*),
as many oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), and sixteen with the *Nṛsūkta*.

Having offered oblations with the *caru* rice-porridge, one should then perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, [one should initiate] the disciple who has bathed and become pure, who is clean and adorned with garments—
either accompanied by his wife, or a maiden, or a celibate student (*brahmacārin*).
Having summoned them, I delighted their eyes with new garments;
while reciting the Netramantra, I bound them and seated them at my own right side.
And the supreme Guru was touched by those Darbha-grass bundles placed there by them.
Having offered twelve oblations each with clarified butter, fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridge, flowers, and sesame seeds, using the Puṇḍarīkākṣa mantra,
and then with the root mantra, I delight in the ashes of the fire-pit.
Having touched the head of the disciple, he should then bind the *pratisara* upon his arms;

having recited the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) one hundred times, he should tie it on with a cord made from milk-plant fibers. He should then cause him to consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), in due order.
[The disciple, having drunk the five products of the cow with the *praṇava*, should then, by the permission of the guru, clean his teeth with a tooth-stick.
If the tooth-stick thrown upon the ground by the disciple [falls] toward me, O Rame, [it is auspicious]. 16.63–64.
If it falls facing south or even facing west,
one should know that to be inauspicious; for the pacification of that fault,
one should offer a hundred oblations of ghee with the Nārasiṃha mantra.
Having first caused the disciple— who has rinsed his mouth— to sip water for purification, he should lead him into the presence of the deity and pray to the Lord while reciting this verse:
"For the liberation of these human-beasts bound by the snares of saṃsāra..."
O God, you alone are our refuge; no other goal exists.
For the cause of liberation from the bonds is that which consists of your propitiation.
Having performed these rites, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), they indeed become entitled to worship.
"I purify [it], O Lord of Gods; you should grant permission for that.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should bind [the site] with threads of illusion—threads that are white, red, and black, triple-stranded and consisting of three qualities.
The Guru himself, having placed upon the body of the disciple— from the forehead down to the feet— the twenty-six knots corresponding to the number of the *tattvas*,
according to the previous procedure, positions them on a spot to his own right.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
Then, reciting this verse at the gates while offering black gram and boiled rice:
"Those beings who follow Viṣṇu, and those who follow them..."
"May they accept this offering and bestow auspiciousness upon me.
Having thus given the offering to them, he should wash his feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then, from the bodies of the disciples, [he removes] the thread of illusion from their eyes.
Then, having performed the ritual removal of the cloth, the preceptor places those illusory threads into a shallow bowl,
covers it with another bowl,
sets this aside by the side of the water-pot, and performs the evening rites.
Having propitiated the Blessed One in the pavilion upon a bed of *darbha* grass,
the Guru should lay those disciples down for the sake of obtaining auspicious dreams.
O Rame, having touched their eyes with the fire-mantra, he should offer oblations into the fire.
With the mantra of Svapnādhipati, he should offer sixteen oblations of clarified butter.
Keeping that night awake, the preceptor, along with other initiated disciples,
should engage in Vaiṣṇava discourses, mindful of the welfare of the disciple.
Having bathed at dawn and performed the obligatory rites according to the rules,
the supreme guru, having approached the pavilion, should ask the disciples— who have also bathed—
about their dreams from the previous night, and then initiate them in the proper sequence.
If there is a bad dream, one should indeed perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*) and then undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*).
One should worship the banners, arches, and water-pots, as well as the mandala.
Having fully worshipped the Blessed One, one should offer food with jaggery and other such items.
Having performed the daily rites, the preceptor should again bind the eyes of the disciples;
having seated them in order on the right side as before,
the instructor [should proceed] with the root mantra using sacrificial wood, food, and other offerings, just as previously.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] to Padmamālinī.
Then, having severed the thread of illusion while recollecting the true nature of the disciple,
[one should dissolve it] from the earth up to Īśvara by way of reabsorption as before.

Then, having meditated upon the supreme, stainless Nārāyaṇa within one's own mind, one should offer oblations either one hundred and eight times for each [deity] with the eight-syllable mantra accompanied by clarified butter, or twenty-eight times, or even eight times. (16.85)
In that [state], the self-possessed guru should withdraw the life-force (*jīva*) of the disciple.
Then he should perform the purification of the disciple's body through processes such as drying (*śoṣaṇa*).
Thereafter, he should contemplate the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) within that body and emanate it through the sequence beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Meditating on the Lord in the forehead as the form of consciousness, facing in all directions, one should offer oblations with his own seed-syllable, the deity being established there, according to the number of the principles (tattvas).
Below that, between the forehead and the eyebrows, [one should meditate on the deity] with the radiance of the sun.
Meditating on that which is situated within its own seed-syllable, one should perform the oblation known as *jīva*.
Recollecting *prakṛti*, resembling a drop of vermilion, between the two eyebrows, and *buddhi*, situated at the root of the palate, with a radiance like the full moon. (16.89–16.90)
Meditating on the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) in the middle of the palate as resembling a red flower,
one should contemplate the mind (*manas*) between the palate and the ears, possessing the luster of a royal gem.
Within the heart-lotus and the throat-lotus, divided into five parts, O Beloved, [one should meditate].
Meditating on the five [senses], beginning with hearing, as having the form of shimmering stars;

remembering speech and the others fivefold in the middle between the heart and the navel, I rejoice. Remembering the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest from the navel, the bladder, and the middle of the anus, I rejoice.
Recalling the gross elements from the pair of feet up to the thighs,
and having fashioned the gross body, one should contemplate the breaking open of that egg.
Then, the Guru should transfer the individual soul (jīva) from his own mind into that [body].

Having sprinkled the disciples with water from the auspicious day (puṇyāha), he should release their eye-bindings; having made them put on other garments, he should wash their feet. Then, having had them sip water (ācamana), he should again apply the eye-bindings.
As before, having established the disciples on the right side,
the teacher [explains]: "The path of time (kālādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and likewise the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan),
the path of principles (tattvādhvan), and the path of phonemes and mantras (varṇamantrādhvan)— these are proclaimed as the six paths."
Having offered these four times in sequence, the best of instructors should,
at the conclusion of the homa, place the residual ghee (saṃpātājya) upon the head of the disciple;
he should then offer oblations with clarified butter while reciting the Mahāvyāhṛti mantra.
First, one should perform the oblation with sesame and clarified butter using the previously mentioned mantra.
Beginning from the feet and ending at the thighs, the Guru should touch [the disciple] with the remnants of the offering.
Then, he should again touch the navel; O Rame, he should offer oblations with the *padma* mantra.
One should offer oblations with ghee while touching the chest, and then the head.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with ghee and indeed touch [the body] with the residual ghee; then, having offered separately one hundred and eight oblations with the root-mantra.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, having taken the disciple by his right hand and led him clockwise around the water-pot and the fire-mandala,
[the teacher] should place jewels or heaps of flowers into the joined palms of the disciples.
Having thus filled [the vessels], he should then lead the disciples to the mandala of the lotus-wheel.
He should command them, "Scatter a handful of flowers in this mandala.
Meditating upon Hari, the disciples should scatter a handful of flowers in the mandala of Rāma.
On whichever petal the very high heap falls from whose hand, one should indicate the name of the lord of that petal and of his disciple.
Having removed the eye-cloth, which corresponds to Vāsudeva and the others, [one should proceed].
Then, having shown the maṇḍala, he should lead [the disciple] near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having drawn a wheel and a conch upon the hand, the best of gurus should touch [the body] from the feet up to the crown of the head with that very mantra.
Then one should perform the five purificatory rites for the disciple in their proper order:
branding, the sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), the naming, the mantra, and the sacrifice as the fifth.
Among these, O lotus-eyed one, listen to the procedure for branding.
The preceptor, together with his disciple and with the permission of the Vaiṣṇavas,
sits facing east on the western side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, the discus and the conch are consecrated with their respective mantras.
On the occasion of my own initiation, my own guru bestowed upon me [the name] Rama by means of the eight-syllable mantra and the Gāyatrī preceded by Viṣṇu;
and with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," he offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter.
Then the preceptor, having conceived the sacred seat (pīṭha) within the fire, should offer oblations;
having meditated upon the discus and the conch therein, he should worship them in sequence with the arghya and other offerings,
using the two mantras for the conch and the discus, and with the mantra "pavitraṃ te."
O Rame, one should offer oblations with clarified butter into you, O Viṣṇu, with the Ṛgveda hymn either one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times; or likewise,
sixteen oblations with the Pauruṣa Sūkta and with sacrificial porridge (caru).
Then, having heated the discus and the conch in due order,
and having first meditated upon the Blessed One and then upon the lineage of gurus,
one should heat the discus and the conch with their respective mantras.
Taking up the discus while reciting this first mantra:
"O Sudarśana, of great radiance, remover of all sins!
O Blessed One, purify this [discus] which is prepared for the worship of Hari."
Having thus made this prayer with the mantra, the most excellent guru should mark the right hand of the disciple with the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) on its upper part;
then, while reciting the mantra, he should also mark the left hand with the conch (śaṅkha).
"O Pañcajanya, burner of fuel, crusher of Daityas and Rākṣasas!
By your sound, you ought to make him free from sin.
Then one should also consecrate the discus and the conch with water.
One should present edible foods such as jaggery-rice and other delicacies.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra,
the preceptor should apply vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) upon the disciple using white clay.
The knower of mantras should apply [the clay] to twelve parts of the body, beginning with the forehead;
first, he should place water in his left hand with the *praṇava*,
and then rub the excellent clay with the mantra "gandhadvārā."

Having stirred that [mud] with water, one should then perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana). Having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should write the Nārasiṃha mantra with a finger that is not bent, which bestows the desired object.
Or else, one should apply the upright and beautiful *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* on the forehead and other parts with the fingers; it should have the shape of the two feet of Hari,
with a gap between [the lines], well-proportioned on the sides, and measuring either two or three finger-breadths.
Then, one should first apply [the ash] on the forehead, four finger-breadths in width and length; on the belly, it should be eight finger-breadths long;
likewise, one should apply it on the chest, and four finger-breadths on the neck.
O Rame, one should apply a *puṇḍra* eight finger-breadths in length on the right side of the abdomen, as well as on the right arm; on the left side of the abdomen, however,
it should be four finger-breadths in length, while that on the neck is eight [finger-breadths].
On the left arm, a long *puṇḍra* is declared to be eight finger-breadths in length;
on the left neck and its back, it should be four finger-breadths.
As before, one should apply them on the back, in the middle position among the *puṇḍras*.
One should apply the excellent powder of *rajanī*, previously consecrated by Hari,
in a straight and long line upon the central part of the *puṇḍra*s;
or it may be in the shape of a circle or the shape of a bamboo leaf.

Having applied the marks (*puṇḍra*) upon those [spots], he should instruct the disciples— beginning with the forehead— to meditate upon Keśava and the other deities together with their Śaktis for the sake of attaining success in meditation.
This is according to what was previously established regarding Keśava and the others within the circle of the discus and lotus.
One should first assign a name for the learned Brāhmaṇa ending in "Bhaṭṭāraka" or indeed in "Bhāgavata. One should make the Kṣatriya's name end in "Devā" and the Vaiśya's end in "Vardhana."
The supreme guru should address a person of the Śūdra caste by a name ending with the word "dāsa.
Furthermore, he should instruct the Śūdra in the ritual of the five times (pañcakāla-vidhi) without [the use of] the seed-syllable;
for those beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, however, it should include the seed-syllable, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
To a Śūdra who is devoid of those two [qualities], one should teach the mantra for women;
it may be the *mūla-mantra*, or the twelve-syllable mantra, or even the six-syllable mantra.
Alternatively, the supreme guru, having carefully considered the capacity of the disciple, [should act accordingly].
One should instruct all the mantras along with their meanings, the ornaments and their presiding deities,
as well as the sequence of propitiation, excluding the Śūdra.
Therefore, one should perform one hundred and eight repetitions with the mantra of the five Upaniṣads.

Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, O Goddess, one should conclude the ritual service of the fire (*vahnikārya*). One should then cause the deity residing within the fire-mandala and the water-pot (*kumbha*) to ascend into one's own heart.
Having thus conferred the common initiation (*sāmānyadīkṣā*) according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
Having placed the disciples upon vehicles, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas and accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, the Guru should lead them to a river or a pond;
and he should cause the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the conclusion of the initiation to be performed according to the prescribed sequence.
Having gratified their teacher with wealth, cattle, land, ornaments, and other gifts, and having paid him homage, they then, by his permission,
[proceeded] with the sounds of Vedic recitation, the sounds of musical instruments, and with their kinsmen and others as well.
O Daughter of the Lotus, let them go to their own homes with great joy.
Listen attentively, O Goddess, to the secret enjoined by the scriptures regarding the initiation for the sake of others' worship, preceded by the office of an Ācārya.
Those born of my lineage, those who have entered into discipleship under them,
among whom the wisdom of the scriptures has been cultivated and who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta—
being free from disease and in the prime of their youth— they [proceed] preceded by their teachers.
One should first perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) for that very purpose during the worship of the temple;
the Guru should perform it for others when conferring initiation, and not otherwise.
Now, for the sake of the Master-consecration (ācāryābhiṣeka), [one should select] a disciple endowed with all virtues.
Having placed upon a vehicle one born into a family consecrated through lineage, free from disease, and accompanied by umbrellas, chowries, fans, and the like;
with the chanting of the Vedas, the sounding of musical instruments, and likewise by consecrated ascetics—
The practitioners and others should circumambulate the abode of the deity;
then, together with all the ritual implements, they should go to the bank of a river or the bank of a lotus pond. Having gone there, the best of teachers— || 16.152–16.153 ||
On that ground, one should smear a square area with cow dung;
having adorned it with lime powder, one should then arrange a seat.
Then, the supreme guru, having placed the disciple upon it facing eastward, [proceeds].
O Rame, formerly for the sake of those initiated and for the Vaiṣṇava ascetics,
having obtained permission from him for the consecration of the teacher on this earth,
one should prepare a seat with grain in front of the disciple.
Upon that [surface], one should draw a twelve-petaled lotus together with a pericarp;
within the pericarp, one should place four jars, and likewise twelve around it.
[These should contain] clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, fragrance, flowers, and fruits.
One should fill those jars with jewels, grains, barley, mung beans, *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice, and water; and [the five products of the cow], the *pañcagavya*, as well as *kataka* nut water.
Alternatively, one may fill the pitchers in sequence with fragrant water.
Having tied the protective cord (pratisara) on the right hand of the disciple,
the Guru should then purify the disciple and the vases with the waters of the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having conceived the ritual seat (pīṭha) within the vases, [one should do so] in the four central vases.
One should meditate upon the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva around [the central deity],
and likewise the twelve-syllable [mantra] within the circle of the discus and lotus;
one should worship Keśava and the others all around with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites.
Then, having generated the fire and prepared a seat therein,
one should invoke and worship the emanations beginning with Vāsudeva into the fire.
[The Guru, having tied a protective cord on the right hand of the disciple...]
Having pronounced their names, the mantra-practitioner should offer twelve oblations for each with clarified butter, and present offerings such as rice mixed with molasses.
For the bathing of the disciple, one should place a wooden plank upon the ground.
Having adorned that [seat] and sprinkled it with water, and having indeed consecrated the *pīṭha* there,

he should seat the disciple upon the *pīṭha*, preceded by the worship of the *pīṭha* and other rites; [he should offer] the *arghya*, the *pādya*, as well as the *ācamana*, along with fragrance, flowers, and incense.
One should present a lamp, a coconut fruit, and betel leaf to the pitcher, the maṇḍala, the fire, and the disciple.
[One should also worship] the pitchers with their respective substances and mantras, and with the Puruṣasūkta.
While musical instruments resound, he should consecrate that disciple with the root mantra, the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, and the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Then, accompanied by the disciple, the most excellent of gurus [should proceed] with the Vaiṣṇavas.
O Rame, preceded by this resolve, one should perform the avabhṛtha bath in a river or similar body of water;
adorned with two unwashed garments, anointed with collyrium,
marked with the vertical *puṇḍra*, and further decorated with garlands and ornaments.
Then, having placed [the image] upon chariots and other vehicles, preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
accompanied by parasols, fly-whisks, and female attendants, and mingled with the chanting of the Vedas, [he performed] the circumambulation of Devadhama along with his kinsmen and others.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], accompanied by his disciples, he should go to the door of the temple and perform the washing of the feet and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) together with his disciples. Then,
having entered the inner sanctum of the temple preceded by a prostration—
He should seat that disciple on the right side of the deity (16.174).
Having caused all the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) to be performed in due order,
up to the end of the incense, lamps, and food offerings, and ending with the fire sacrifice (*homa*), in accordance with the ritual for the *bali* offering (16.175).
For it is traditionally taught that the inner sanctum of the deity is indeed his body;
therefore, having come outside, the disciple should perform a prostration.
He should pray to Vāsudeva, the eternal God of gods.
"O God, having received initiation, this man is devoted to the propitiation of you;
whatever he worships here, even if there is some lapse due to negligence, you ought to forgive it as my own, O Lord of Gods, O observer of noble vows. (16.177–16.178)
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods and partaken of the holy water and other offerings of Hari,
the disciple should then go outside after bowing repeatedly to the Guru;
and having gratified him with jewels and other gifts, he should then receive the Guru’s permission.
And one should go to one's own home, O Goddess, and honor kinsmen and friends.
Then, one should feed all one's relatives and partake of a meal.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The seventeenth chapter:
Śrī—
The Guru should first instruct the disciple in the ritual procedure for the five periods of the day.
"O Govinda, you have spoken thus; let that be explained in detail.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The first action is approaching [the teacher], and after that is receiving instruction."
Sacrifice comes first, then the study of sacred texts, and after that yoga; such is the sequence.
Having thus divided his time, a person should always perform the appropriate virtuous deeds at their respective times according to the rules, for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One. (17.2–17.3)
I shall now describe that sequence here; listen, O lotus-born one!
In the scripture, it is declared that the time of dawn consists of five times five [muhūrtas]. That indeed is the Brāhma-muhūrta; at that time, one should abandon sleep.
Having washed his hands and feet, he should remember Hari, the remover of sins.
Through the grace of the guru, one attains knowledge, supreme Vaiṣṇava-hood,
and the relationship of the servant and the served between the individual self (jīvātman) and the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Knowing this to be the eternal yoga, preceded by the service of a true teacher and others, a man, carrying the requisites for bathing and pure clay,
should go to a lake or a river while chanting the praises of the imperishable Hari.
The wise man should cast all of that upon a pure bank of a river or similar place.
He should wrap the sacrificial thread around his right ear and place his upper garment on his head;
then, alert and unwearied, he should go toward the ground in the direction of Nirṛti.
There, having covered the ground with grass and leaves,
the wise twice-born man, facing north during the day and at the two twilights,
and facing south at night, should void his excrement and urine.

Then, having gone to a body of water for purification, one should take earth sufficient for oneself to the depth of a cubit and place it on dry ground. For the sake of purification, twelve applications of earth are required for the anus, while three are required for the penis.
O Rame, the best of the twice-born should perform hand-cleansing at intervals;

he should cleanse each of the two hands seven times with clay, and then, having joined them together, seven more times. He should then gradually cleanse his feet with the same number of applications of clay as before.
He should perform twelve mouthfuls of rinsing and then wear the sacred thread.
Having sipped water, the twice-born man should clean his teeth with a tooth-stick or leaves;
then, having performed the rinsing and other preliminary acts, he should sip water again for the purpose of bathing.
Having performed three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule with the Vyahṛtis,
for the sake of accomplishing service to Viṣṇu and the other teachers, and for the purification of Hari,
I shall perform this bath according to the prescribed rite with his permission.
The ring is said to be two finger-breadths wide, and the knot is considered to be one finger-breadth.
The tip should be four finger-breadths; such is the pavitra with its proper characteristics.
O best of the twice-born, the pavitra may be made of kuśa grass or of gold.
One should always wear [the clay] in the middle of the ring finger for the sake of purification—
either the clay from the abode of Tulasī, or other clay belonging to Viṣṇu.
O Rame, having brought that clay, one should divide it into three parts in due order.
Having performed the binding of the directions with one part and, O twice-born, having fashioned a seat in the water with the second part, he should contemplate the sacred bathing-places of Viṣṇu;
then, with the third part, he should smear his own limbs.
Recalling Hari while reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta and the Puṃsūkta,
the wise man should perform his bath with the root mantra and the jewel-mantra.
[He should bathe in] the Virajā river, which ends at the Gaṅgā, where the Gaṅgā itself ends at the feet of Viṣṇu.
Having remembered the Kāverī, the best of rivers, and the lotus-feet of his preceptor,
he should then offer libations in the water while standing therein, intending for his initiating preceptor, the gods, the sages, the hosts of ancestors, and their wives.
Having reached the riverbank, he should recite, "They bring [the waters]," and then put on two clean garments as well as a loincloth. Then,
having washed his feet and hands, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
A twice-born man should indeed wear the *puṇḍra* marks on twelve places beginning with the forehead;
or else, O Rame, he should wear six *puṇḍra*s, or even just one on the forehead.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).

"Before sunrise itself, for the sake of accomplishing service to the Blessed One, one should perform the twilight worship according to the path prescribed in one's own Sūtra. Having thus resolved mentally with a disposition of pure renunciation, [one should proceed].
In the morning and evening, while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, one should offer arghya;
having drawn up water to the height of a cow's horn, one should pour it back into the midst of the water—
one portion for the destruction of weapons and missiles, and one for the destruction of vehicles.
For the sake of slaying the asuras, the twice-born man should indeed remember one Hari;
and for the purpose of expiation, as well as for the perfection of that mantra,
he should always remain pure and perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) accompanied by the *praṇava*.
To pacify that fault, one should perform a single circumambulation while recollecting Sūryanārāyaṇa, thinking, "This Āditya is Brahman. Furthermore,
one should offer libations to the presiding deities of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
One should recite [the mantra] either one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times,
or twenty-eight times, until sunrise,
while meditating on Nārāyaṇa in the heart and upon Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas.
Then, having performed the drying and other rites both externally and internally, one should place the Mātṛkā [syllables] at the base,
or indeed Keśava and the others according to the path of the scriptures; likewise, one should perform meditation with the five Upaniṣads and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Puruṣasūkta.

Or, having performed the installation of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) preceded by the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) twenty-four times, one should perform the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*.
This applies at the commencement of worship, in situations of fear, and likewise during daily and occasional rites.
In life-threatening situations or during calamities, one should perform the six-limbed nyāsa (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Among the mudrās, the Cakra-mudrā grants the attainment of union with Viṣṇu (viṣṇusāyujya),
while the Agniprākāra-mudrā always bestows all supernatural powers (sarvasiddhi).
Seated in the center of the solar disc, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
adorned with ornaments such as a crown and a forest garland,
he sits upon a lotus throne and is saluted by all the gods.
Then, remembering the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī and Bhūmi,
he should worship Him with the sixteen mental offerings,
reciting either the Gāyatrī mantra accompanied by the root-mantra or without it.
Then one should perform the service according to the path prescribed in one's own sūtra;
at home, one should worship the Blessed One in the form of fire by means of the *aupāsana* rite.
Then one should perform the approach (*abhigamana*) and the worship dear to the Blessed One.
Having done so, the twice-born man should then go outside to gather materials;
having collected pure and sattvic flowers and other offerings for the sake of propitiating Hari, he should then go to his own home. (17.44–17.45)
When the time for sacrifice has arrived, having bathed and become self-restrained and pure,
one should perform the midday rites according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra.
But that Guru who performs worship for the sake of others shall enter the Abode.
One should worship [the deity] preceded by the ritual worship of Vāsudeva and concluding with the festival.
[17.47] Those who lack the initiation of others should not eat in the same row.
However, one who worships in his own home according to the Pāñcarātra system may perform the worship. [17.48]
I delight in the food offered to Viṣṇu and in the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
Having performed the daily śrāddha and other rites, as well as the Vaiśvadeva offering,
[I eat] together with kinsmen worthy of purifying the company and likewise with my ancestors.
He should eat in silence together with elderly Vaiṣṇava guests; furthermore,
he should feed even the children in their respective appropriate places,
and he should give them the remnants of Viṣṇu’s meal, betel, and sandalwood paste.
At the appropriate time, one should partake of the consumption of Viṣṇu’s *naivedya*.
Women or those who have not been initiated should not eat in the same row.
If a Brahmin eats while standing, he must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
O Goddess, if a Brahmin places food and other items in vessels made of tin, bell-metal, or the like, or even in his left hand,
and then eats with his right hand,
he certainly goes to hell.
One should recite the *svādhyāya* for the sake of the *brahmayajña*, aloud and with proper intonation;
when the evening time has arrived, one should study the Veda or the meaning of the Veda,
as well as the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the teachings of the Pāñcarātra.
One should listen to the Vedānta, the Itihāsas and other works composed by the wise, or else one should personally recite them; at that time,
one should be intent on the service of Viṣṇu through action, mind, and speech.
But one who is lacking in capacity among these should meditate on either the two [mantras], the eight-syllabled, the twelve-syllabled, or the six-syllabled; he should not think of anything else.
Then, as the sun is setting, following the sequence prescribed in his own *sūtra*, [he should perform the rite].
Then, having performed the twilight rites (saṃdhyākarma), he should perform the domestic fire-ritual (aupāsana).
He should worship Viṣṇu as before, bowing with devotion in due order;
having performed the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga) and all other rites, the most excellent of teachers [should proceed].
But on his own pure bed, meditating upon the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa,
he may lie down if he should consort with his own virtuous wife.
Then the preceptor, having bathed and wearing clean garments and so forth, [should enter the bedchamber].
A Vaiṣṇava man, however, should resort to another bed as before.
Having risen during the great night at the time for yoga with a tranquil mind,
he should perform the purification of the feet and so forth, and sip water according to the rules.
Seated upon a seat such as a grass mat, he ascended the yogic posture;
by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), [he beheld] the Supreme Person bearing the conch,
discus, and mace, clad in yellow garments, white in complexion, and adorned with a forest garland and other ornaments.
Meditating upon Vāsudeva as the Supreme, the wise one, having established himself in yoga,
should dissolve the principles (tattvas) into his own self by resorting to the process of withdrawal;
when Vāsudeva is stationed in the heart, he should likewise unite his own self [with Him].
Having meditated in that manner for some time, the tireless Guru should create that [form] from his own body; then, gradually relinquishing even the yogic posture,
O Goddess, he should resort to his own pure bed, which removes all afflictions.
Thus, O Goddess, the fifth [topic], the time for yoga, has been described.
(17.68) [By practicing in this way for as long as one lives, one attains union with Hari;
however, for those who have received only the general initiation, there is the ritual action of the *karmakāṇḍa* and so forth. (17.69)

O you who dwell in the lotus, this procedure for the five times has been declared for those born of my own portion during the three junctions of the day, provided it does not conflict with the sacrifice to Viṣṇu;
as well as for those consecrated by the initiation of others, following the path described in the section on ritual action (Karmakāṇḍa).
One should worship Keśava and the other [deities] situated in the solar mind of their respective months.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Eighteen.
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of my own pervasive form as an image,
for the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of human beings and, furthermore, for the purpose of bringing about [the deity's] presence.
This is due to the majesty of the mantra, O Goddess, and the ascetic power of the preceptor.
Requested by him, I am the bestower of desired success upon the image [of the deity].
Śrī said:
"I shall become so; I will indeed explain the ritual for that purpose in due order."
Having fashioned an image on the ground— whether made of metal, stone, or composed of clay and other materials—
or one produced from metal and jewels, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
mortals should have it moved about or kept in their homes, provided they have accumulated the necessary wealth.
"Having performed the consecration, the virtuous carry out rites such as worship;
and you have stated that their fruit becomes incomparable.
Yet, at times, [the image] has gone beyond the range of the gods' vision."
If you have the intention to worship them in the form of an image,
or if you, O one who pervades the universe, would abide in many ways within those worlds in the form of substances such as metal, [then do so] by means of direct perception. (18.6–18.7)
The Blessed One said:
"The gods, beginning with Parameṣṭhin, having beheld my form manifested as a dwelling upon the earth, [revealed] this most essential scripture."

Like a treasure obtained by mortals but difficult for the immortals to attain, the denizens of heaven were overcome with anxiety to acquire it for themselves. Having resolved this in their minds, they reached the island of Śveta, free from all possessiveness.
They shall perform fierce austerities for a thousand human years.
Knowing their desire for a city equipped with walls and other features,
I will manifest my own auspicious form within a celestial chariot to show them.
O Rame, they shall praise with various hymns the imperishable one in the form of an image, who is endowed with the conch, the discus, and other [attributes], such as Jitantā and others;
and through their praise and prostration, I shall become pleased with them.
"I shall speak; let them speak now, and I shall carry out your word.
Having heard these words of mine, Brahmā and the other deities then said:
"If you have affection for us, O Lord Janārdana."
O Teacher of the World, in the worlds granted by you which belong to me,
you must remain forever in this very manner within a celestial chariot in the form of a cosmic orb;
we shall always worship you, especially with distinction.
"The scripture must also be taught so that we may remain attentive during rites such as worship. Thus they will pray;
therefore, I, who cause the hearts of devotees to tremble with joy, shall awaken Brahmā and the other gods.
"For your delight, I shall indeed assume the form of a *bimba* and dwell here and there; you should worship me constantly.
I shall grant you the fulfillment of your desires; of this there is no doubt. (18.18)
"I shall indeed teach this scripture in detail to Vidhi.
"The Four-faced One will teach this scripture to you.
While being addressed thus, I [beheld] myself together with my celestial chariot.
Having paid homage to him, we, filled with wonder, shall show it to you in many ways—
whatever celestial vehicle (vimāna) each of you desires, which grants the fulfillment of your wishes.
Thus spoke Brahmā and the other foremost gods amidst the sounds of all kinds of musical instruments.
They shall lead each to his own world and worship it constantly. O Rāma, I shall teach this scripture to Brahmā and to others as well, both in detail and in summary from every perspective.
They shall spread [this teaching] beginning with truth, according to the path declared in this scripture;
they shall worship me,
who am manifested of my own accord, as well as others, beginning with truth, among those worlds, O gods.

That which is divine occurs in other worlds; that which is accomplished is [the domain] of the siddhas; but that which is of the ṛṣis is human. Therefore, one should never perform the consecration of those [images], whether they are fashioned on the ground from ordinary materials by craftsmen, [or otherwise].

For the purification of the substance, for the purification of the site, and indeed for my own presence, the Guru must perform the installation according to the rules; that I shall now describe to you. Furthermore, the characteristics [to be observed] at the time of seizing the ground and in the chapter on initiation [are as follows].
One who possesses the characteristics and qualities mentioned by Bhaṭṭācārya,

and is endowed with the previously described initiation, should be chosen for the tasks such as the plowing of the site; the patron should request that very person to serve as the preceptor for the consecration ceremony.
Without the formal selection of a preceptor, one may go to a temple or a consecrated image.
Even if he was initially chosen, should he be incapable, one should approach his son who is endowed with those same qualities.
If even he is lacking in mantras and other such requirements, one should seek another who is possessed of all excellent qualities.

The patron himself should go to the house of the preeminent teacher—one who belongs to the lineage mentioned by me, who is pure, initiated, and honored by all; who knows the true meaning of the Pāñcarātra, and is proficient in mantras and tantras. || 18.31-32 ||
Having first paid obeisance and placed a coconut fruit in his hand, O Goddess, one should pray to the all-pervading Vāsudeva:
"O Guru, you ought indeed to perform the consecration of the temple."
Thus entreated, the learned preceptor, who is most skilled in discerning the proper time,
should thoroughly determine the auspicious moment together with the astrologer;
he should avoid the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), Mārgaśīrṣa, and the month of Māgha.
In other months, on the first day of the bright fortnight,
as well as on the second, third, fifth, and seventh lunar days;
and on the tenth and eleventh, as well as the twelfth and thirteenth.

Among these lunar days (tithis), it should be performed only as long as the full moon and the fifth day of the dark fortnight persist, and not beyond that. Among the weekdays, the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter are declared to be auspicious.
Venus and the lords of the days, and the lunar mansions—listen to them from me:
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Punarvasu, and then the three Uttarās;
the two Uttarās, Hasta, Śravaṇa, and likewise Revatī.

And among these, having avoided those lunar days associated with the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, as well as the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the period of Venus’s retrogression (*śukramauḍhya*), and likewise Jupiter’s retrogression (*gurormauḍhya*),
one should [perform the rite] when the ascendant is Taurus.
Or, O Rāma, when the ascendant is Gemini, Leo, Pisces, or Sagittarius,
or in Libra, the lord of the ascendant is strong, or it is Jupiter;
or Venus aspects the ascendant while situated in the eleventh house.
Having determined that the auspicious moment which bestows prosperity upon the abode of the deity for the patron occurs ten days hence,
the most excellent preceptor then proceeds to the temple of the deity at an auspicious hour.
Whether inside or outside, wherever there is indeed a space free from obstruction,
one should construct the pavilions and other structures using this very measurement. Measurement, alternative measurement, the fist, the measure, and likewise the body [are the units].
Listen also to their characteristics, O lotus-eyed one:
the rays of the sun that reach the path of the window pass through them,
and within those rays move the most subtle particles, the atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Those eight, called *leśas*, are designated as one *aṇu*;
those eight [aṇus] are a *mahān*, and those eight [mahāntas] are designated as one *yava*.
Eight *yavas* constitute an *aṅgula*, and that [aṅgula] is considered the medium measure.
Eight barley grains (*yava*) make one *aṅgula*, which is the smallest *aṅgula*.
This is what is called the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger-breadth) as proclaimed by artisans; it may also be defined as eight horizontal barley grains or three straight barley grains.
Wherever one should lay out [the proportions] according to a measurement, another measurement is taught for that.
By this, the construction of the altar, the pedestal, the chariot, and so forth is also determined.
One should divide the fist-measure of the Guru into four parts in sequence, starting from the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
The implements for the fire sacrifice, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, as well as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), should be measured in finger-breadths (*muṣṭyaṅgula*).
That which is the middle joint of the middle finger of the Guru’s right hand is called a "measure-finger" (*mātrāṅgula*).
The measurements for the ritual implements should be made using those *mātrā-aṅgula*s.
Having divided the image (*arcā*) into nine parts, one part among them is successively divided into twelve;
having thus divided it into twelve, one [such] part is declared to be a *mānāṅgula*.
A master of the arts should construct the entire palace, the gate-tower, and various images using this aforementioned finger-measure;
or [the structures may be] twenty-four cubits, ten, or eight cubits in size.

It may be made with sixteen or even twelve *karas*, corresponding in its width and length, and provided with four gates. A single girdle for the pavilion is considered to be as high as a *tāla* from the ground.
If there is no obstruction by pillars for the altars or the sacrificial pits,
then the best of preceptors should arrange the pillars in that pavilion;
having first leveled the ground, he should then construct the altars.
If at any time there is a consecration ceremony for the temple of the deity,
then two altars (vedī) should be prepared for the rite of installing the water-pot (ghaṭa).
Their height should be one cubit, and they should be square with four sides.
At the beginning and at the end, there is a single girdle (mekhalā) adorned on all sides by sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
Likewise, for the rite of releasing the gaze, there is [a pit] to its north for the purpose of lying down;
and in the northeast, for the rite of establishing the child, there is a pitcher (pālikā).
In the ritual procedure for the mandala of the wheel and lotus,
the wise one should arrange the altars on both sides of each respective altar;
he should then sequentially leave open pathways for the purpose of entry and exit.

The length and breadth of the altars (vedīs), however, shall be according to the specific ritual requirements, or in accordance with the dimensions of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and the sacrificial materials. Thus has the construction of the altars been described by me; now the preparation of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is being stated.

Having understood the number of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the ritual procedure, the varieties of pits, and their design, one must certainly perform the rite; otherwise, it leads to fault. [The shapes are] triangular, quadrangular, pentagonal, and hexagonal.

O Daughter of the Lotus, the best of gurus have declared that there are fourteen types of fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*): those with seven, eight, or nine corners; those with ten or eleven corners; the twelve-sided, the bow-shaped, the circular, the lotus-shaped, and the womb-shaped (*yonikuṇḍa*). || 18.67–18.68 ||
I shall now explain the purpose; listen, O lotus-eyed one!
One should perform all rites for worldly prosperity within a square [mandala];
nourishing rites in a lotus-shaped pit, and peace-bringing rites in a circular one.
The rite for subjugating yakṣa maidens is performed on a five-cornered [yantra], and for the purpose of paralyzing, on a six-cornered one;
one should perform the rite of deluding on a seven-cornered [yantra],
the rite of killing on an eight-cornered one, and the rite of creating enmity on a nine-cornered one.
In a ten-cornered kuṇḍa, it is indeed for the gratification of the ancestors, beginning with the Vasus;
in an eleven-cornered one, for the accomplishment of rites pertaining to the deities, beginning with Brahmā;
in a twelve-cornered one, for the vision of Hari; and in a triangular one, for the sake of obtaining a daughter.
In the trine [Aries and Libra] there is the rite of killing, while in Sagittarius there shall be eradication.
In the trine or in Sagittarius, there is the attainment of treasure, and victory over enemies shall occur.
O dweller in the lotus, I shall now describe the emanation of each of these individually.

One should mark from the center toward each of the four corners in sequence with a cord measured by the number of fingers [of the practitioner], using the mantra *manvagni* (32). From corner to corner, this forms a single-sided [triangle].
If it thus becomes a square, I shall now describe to you the method for a triangle.
One should mark the corners with a cord numbering thirty-two finger-breadths.
In the five-sided [mandala], from the region of the navel, one should drop a cord numbering sixteen finger-breadths, provided with four barley-corns, onto the corners.
One should perform the laying out of the lines for the seven-sun [diagram] from corner to corner.
In the hexagon, there are sixteen [lines] from the central peg and from corner to corner;
and in the heptagon, from the navel peg, there are six [lines] for the wings, measured by six barleycorns.
From corner to corner, there should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgula);
it is said that for an octagon, there are sixteen [sides], provided with four barley-corns (yava).
One should fashion a polygon from one corner to another using twelve finger-breadths.
In the nine-sided [figure], from the center of the navel, mark four *yava*s;
at the corners, mark ten *aṅgula*s plus six *yava*s, according to the number of fingers for the wings. From corner to corner, one should mark the ten-sided [figure]; listen, O beloved! (18.81)
From the center, the placement [of the lines] in the corners is made with four [fingers] joined by barley-corns;
then from one corner to another corner, the Guru should fashion [the layout] using five barley-corns together with nine fingers.
From the center of the eleven sides, one should place the wing-fingers endowed with four barley-corns; at the corner regions, they should be joined with six barley-corns.
Eight finger-breadths are said to be from one corner to the other corner.
At the center of the twelve-sided [figure], the wise man should mark the middle point of the central pin at fifteen finger-breadths,
increased by four barley-corns; he should then mark each of the eight corners with a single finger-breadth in the case of a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit.
A cord eighteen finger-breadths long should be wound ten finger-breadths from the navel region around its two sides; thus, forty-eight [finger-breadths] are placed.
One should place fourteen finger-breadths in the center of the wheel within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

And one should wrap a single thread; that itself shall be the lotus [line]. In the bow-shaped pit (*cāpakuṇḍa*), from the point of the *śaṅku* on both sides as well, there is a placement at eighteen finger-breadths; that very same [measurement] is the bowstring for the bow.
O Goddess, when the cord is wound from that point toward the north from the south,
it forms a bow-shaped pit (*dhanuṣkuṇḍa*), as declared by the wise who are learned in the scriptures.
One should perform the specific ritual action for whatever purpose corresponds to whichever particular pit is used.

Therefore, having first consulted the scriptures, one should fashion each respective *kuṇḍa*. Thus, I have described the general construction of the four types of *kuṇḍas*— quadrangular and so forth— for the abodes of the gods.
In the case of emanations, consecrations, festivals, daily worship, rites for peace,
fire-offerings, and in all rituals such as expiations,
one should construct sacrificial pits according to the scriptures and perform the oblation within them.
Where an oblation is offered without having first performed [the preliminary rites], there the Fire-god is not satisfied.
As long as I am unsatisfied while residing within the Fire, how can the accomplishment of one’s own purpose occur?
Therefore, having prepared sacrificial pits in this manner, one should offer oblations into them during these rituals.
One should construct the perimeter of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with a length of ninety-six finger-breadths;
leaving two finger-breadths on all sides, twenty finger-breadths remain within the pit.
Alternatively, that [measurement] may be half, a quarter, or even four finger-breadths.
One should have three girdles dug all around; these are thus described.

The first should be one *tāla* in height, the second should be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the third should be four finger-breadths; and the width of each one [should be equal to its height].
The girdle (mekhalā) should also be fashioned, measuring four finger-breadths [in width] according to each respective pit, situated in the middle space within the pit.
A lotus with twelve petals and a pericarp should be fashioned there.
In a lotus-shaped pit there should be no lotus, and in a yoni-shaped pit there should be no yoni.
Wherever the officiating priests stand to perform the oblation in a lotus-abode,
one should fashion a yoni there above the girdle, winding it like a serpent.
The stalk is two finger-breadths at the bottom, four finger-breadths in the middle, and said to be six finger-breadths at the top; it should be shaped like the hood of a serpent.
Outside the altar of the pitcher, at a distance of four tālas, one should delight [in the surrounding space].
In the eastern direction, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square; in the south, it should be bow-shaped.
In the west, the wise man should fashion either a circular pit, a lotus-shaped one, or a triangle. In the north, however, he should fashion the string of a bow.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made by the preceptor from the finest metal or from a sacrificial tree;
the *sruk* should be measured by a staff equal to one's own forearm plus one finger-breadth.
Its thickness is said to be six finger-breadths, corresponding to its width.
Taking that wood, one part of it shall be nine finger-breadths [in width];
the mouth of the trough should be equal to that, one and a half finger-breadths in length;
the neck shall be one [part] and its half, and the binding-ring shall be circular and long.
Then one should also fashion another neck and mouth;
the sacrificial vessel (yajñapātra) should be six finger-breadths in both width and height, being equal in those dimensions.
Its thickness at the middle, however, should be three finger-breadths, and there should be a hollow in it.
One should fashion a lotus provided with a pericarp and joined with twelve petals.
Then, upon the raised portions, one should slightly fashion a sixteen-spoked wheel complete with a rim;
its rim shall be one finger-breadth wide, while its height shall be one finger-breadth.
If it should be quadrangular, one should mark it with conches at the corners;
there should be three girdles all around, each measuring one barley-corn in width.
The back portion may be shaped like a tortoise or like a lotus.
One should fashion the channel for the clarified butter (ājyapraṇāla) at the opening with a measurement of one full and one deficient finger-breadth (samanyūnāṅgula).
Then, the long handle shall be two parts, arising from the mouth of the lotus;
one should plane away the remainder from that which is one and a half fingers thick and two fingers wide.
That staff, O Rame, should be either square or circular;
it should be provided with three folds, and at its end one should fashion a lotus.
A long wooden staff measuring one cubit in length should have a thickness and width of two finger-breadths.
In front of that, one should make a circle two finger-breadths in diameter;
in its center, there should be a pair of depressions, each half a finger-breadth deep, with a barley-corn-shaped ridge between them.
O auspicious lady, the wall surrounding it should be provided with a thickness of half a finger-breadth.
O slender-waisted one, that place for the clarified butter (ājyasthāna) should be like the hoof of a deer;
the formation of the neck is desired to be one-third of its width. At both ends at the base, one should fashion a svastika two finger-breadths long.
The remainder shall be circular, and the handle adorned with various colors.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā;
[now begins] the nineteenth chapter.
At the four doors of the pavilion for the installation, there should be archways (toraṇas) made of *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* trees, starting from the east. However,
if all four types of wood are unavailable, one may fashion them from a single tree.
Or rather, one may make everything out of sandalwood according to the prescribed rule.
It should be seven cubits long, or perhaps five cubits long;
it may be circular or square, with a thickness of twenty-two finger-breadths.
It should be joined together, two finger-breadths thick and six finger-breadths wide;
it may be bound with the previously mentioned cord or fashioned in the shape of a plank.
One should fashion the udumbara beam above the archway to a length of two cubits.
By a difference in designation, that very same thing is called a "tablet" (paṭṭikā).
|| 19.5 In its center there should be a single wheel, and on both sides two Garuḍas; these should be fashioned upon the tablet itself at each archway (toraṇa). || 19.6
At each gate there were two banners, adorned with various colors;
they were twenty-two finger-breadths in length and half that in width.
The planks, made from sacrificial wood, were two finger-breadths thick.
Alternatively, having fashioned [the image] from gold or other metals, the wise man should subsequently inscribe upon these the names of the eight auspicious symbols:
the Śrīvatsa, the forest garland, the kettledrum, and the mirror; || 19.8–19.9 ||

One should also depict a pair of fish, a conch, a discus, and the son of Kaśyapa; for these lotus-seated deities, one should likewise draw lamp-stands and chowries on both sides, and a parasol over their heads.

One should prepare a bathing place and a consecrated water-vessel corresponding to the image. For the preceptor and the officiating priests, one should provide seats made of udumbara wood, as well as thrones and sandals fashioned from sacrificial wood.
O Rame, all the sacrificial vessels, such as the *śarāva* and others,
are six finger-breadths in height, and likewise in width and length;
their centers are hollowed out, being four finger-breadths deep at the bottom.
The preceptor should fashion the upper portion five finger-breadths wide.
O Rame, he should provide banners, water-pots with their lids, various grains, loads of *śāli* rice,
unhusked rice, sesame seeds, and indeed garments.
The preceptor should first procure jewels, grains, cows, maidens, earth, clarified butter, and other such items.
The jars should be smooth, without holes, and twenty-four finger-breadths in height.
They should be fashioned from gold, silver, or copper, free from any flaws.
Likewise, from the middle of its width, its neck should be three finger-breadths high;
its mouth is known to be six finger-breadths wide and three finger-breadths deep.
The girdle (*mekhalā*) surrounding the lotus-base should be known to be three finger-breadths wide;
or else it may be half that measure, all of which is determined first by its height.
Or, O auspicious lady, in the case of the most excellent of the excellent, they fill a *droṇa* measure.
Half of that, or even less by a portion, up to the limit of two *prastha*s of water;

in the secondary rite (*anukalpa*), they may be made of clay, provided they are free from holes, cracks, or fissures, not double-heated, well-burnt, and devoid of black coloration and the like. || 19.20–19.21 ||
One should fashion a *karaka* (small water-pot) with a measurement half that of a *mahākumbha*.
In its belly, there should be an outlet for the water provided with corners.
O Rame, [these] jars, such as the door-jars (*dvārakumbha*) and others, are for the purpose of bathing and for installation.
Or the preceptor may fashion [the vessels] from metals with the dimensions previously mentioned.
O beloved, hear now the characteristics and the number of the *pālikā* and other vessels:
the height is one hand (twenty-four finger-breadths) and the mouth is sixteen finger-breadths.
Its length up to the neck should indeed be that many finger-breadths;
the circumference of the neck is declared to be seven finger-breadths.
From the neck down to the feet, the length is nine finger-breadths.
Its width at the bottom is said to be ten finger-breadths.
When it is made thus, with the upper part like a lotus from the central cavity and the lower part like an unmatta flower, they know it as a *pālikā*.
I shall describe the characteristics of the water-clock (ghaṭikā); listen, O lotus-born one!
It should be twelve finger-breadths in length and sixty finger-breadths in width;
its belly is the principal part, with a width of six finger-breadths.
On the belly, one should fashion four faces, each four finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide, extending in the four directions.
Thus is the characteristic of the *ghaṭikā*; they are five-faced and shaped like jars.
The width of the rim of the bowl should be twenty-two finger-breadths;

its height should be twenty finger-breadths, and its depth below should be eight finger-breadths. O Rame, these are the measurements for the best type; the middling type is thirty-six [finger-breadths].
The minimum number should be sixteen; however, eight is not considered a minimum.
For all purposes, there may be eight *pālikās*, according to one’s wealth.
In rites such as the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of deities, the *pālikās* must be in pairs.
The installation of clay images and other rites for humans are auspicious when performed with an odd number of vessels and so forth;
one should never make an even number for them,
for if one were to do so, it would lead to great misfortune.

Around the pavilion, there should be decorative water-pots (pālikā) for the sake of ornamentation. These should be prepared by the most excellent gurus in such a way that they contain sprouts on the seventh or even the ninth day prior to the day of the consecration. || 19.35–19.36 ||
For the sake of providing a place for the proponents of the Vedas to stay around the consecrated pavilion,
one should construct water-stalls (prapās) originating from the Ocean of Milk for those who have come from other regions and belong to the branches of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
