For the sake of dwelling, sleeping, and eating for all the other Brahmins who excel in every branch of knowledge, one should construct water-stations (prapās) everywhere within the third enclosure and along the walkways, starting from the third [enclosure]. || 19.38-39 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter on the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhākarma*) in the illustrious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
Chapter Twenty: Having determined the day for the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the preceptor—
Then, on the preceding day, [one should prepare] the consecration pavilion (pratiṣṭhāmaṇṭapa),
as well as the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and all other structures, the kitchen,
the assembly hall (āsthānamaṇṭapa), and likewise the gate-towers (gopura).
First, one should cleanse the doors and door-panels with water; then,
O Lotus-born One, an artist should everywhere paint the walls of the temple with colors such as white, red, and others.
And with garlands of darbha grass and coconut fruits— [and of jackfruit,
betel-nut, and plantain fruit]—
one should tie bunches all around on every side.

In all places, such as the pavilions, one should fix two plantain pillars on each side of every door, provided with fruits. One should adorn the entire sanctuary on all sides with banners and garlands of homage.

Likewise, having consecrated a water-shed and performed the rite of planting seedlings for the foundation, one should decorate those two with canopies and other ornaments; then, in due order from the east and other directions,
it is taught that an *aśvattha* tree is to be placed in the eastern direction (Indra’s quarter) and an *audumbara* tree in the south.

One should dig two *tāla*s deep into the ground at the western side for a *nyagrodha* tree and at the northern side for a *plakṣa* archway; having dug thus, one should firmly install the archways. One should then place two banners above each gate in successive order.

One should conceal the pavilion everywhere with a curtain. One should fill the hall with camphor, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, *devadāru*, and especially with the exudations of trees and incenses. || 20.10–20.11 ||
Then, the twice-born should smear the ground with cow-dung as prescribed;
they should clean it with wooden sticks and decorate it with lime and other materials.
Outside the water-shed, at the four gates, which possess a golden luster—
One should then fasten the banners inscribed with the Truths and other mantras above [the image].

(20.13) Now, the preceptor, who knows the true principles of the treatises on the arts, should inspect all the primary images in the workshop according to the path prescribed by the scriptures. (20.14)
The opening of the eyes should be performed by an artisan in his workshop for an image made of stone, wood, or cast metal;
likewise for an image made of plaster or fashioned from cloth.

The wise artisan should have the installation of the eyes performed for a [deity] to be painted on walls and the like, as well as for one made of clay, within the inner sanctum (garbhageha). For images made of stone and other materials, he should perform the consecration with mantras.

Having placed [the image] upon a chariot and other vehicles amidst the sounds of all musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas, one should indeed circumambulate Hari through the streets and then bring him to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) onto a pedestal made of the Brahma-stone.
In the nine pits, one should first place gold, jewels, and so forth;
for each pit, there are five items—of which I shall tell you the specific varieties:
a diamond together with gold, uśīra root, and likewise rice.
Likewise, in a pit to the south of the Aindrī [direction], there is one made of sapphire;
in the west, sesame, lead, and sandalwood, as well as pearl;
and in the north, silver, mercury, mung beans, and uśīra root.
Having placed the ruby, the finest bell-metal stone, and the king of gems (diamond) in clockwise order, and likewise starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise,
he should place iron together with lapis lazuli, the discus-marked stone, and mica.
One should place the *ṣāṣṭika* grains in the direction of the Lord (the northeast), and cast the *puṣyarāga*, *harīta*, *gairika*, *śārika*, and tin in the place of Vāyu (the northwest).
One should place the *masūra* lentils in the place of Nirṛti (the southwest), as well as the *mahānīla* and *vaṅgaka*.
Stone, realgar, barley, and likewise *sāgarikā*;
in the southeast [quarter], crystal, copper, and likewise *manogupta*;
wheat and *śaṅkhapuṣpā*—uttering the mantra along with its ancillaries.
In the center, one should first smear all [the areas] with lime;
then the Guru should divide the ground from the door to the edge of the wall into seven parts.
The central part shall be the station of Brahmā, and immediately following that, the station of the Deity.
After that, the human [form] and then the piśāca [form] are proclaimed.
In the case of a single-liṅga [temple], one should deposit the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) in the Brahma-place;
however, in the arrangement of multiple liṅgas, it is in the positions of the Deity and the Human.
In the pavilion of Śrī, Bhūmi, and Vainateya, situated at the sides [of the temple] in ancient times,
the middle of the door must not be abandoned, nor its side, nor its back;
for it is free from defects and exists for the benefit of all through its sixfold nature.
Therefore, one should remain slightly toward the north-eastern direction from the seat of Brahmā (20.31).
Indeed, for the sake of attaining the fruits such as liberation,
one should first install the Blessed One in the form of an image upon the throne without hesitation (20.32).
The artisan should first establish the state of unity among the image, the pedestal, and the stone; then, while standing upon the temple structure,
he should fix the stūpī onto the peg and likewise establish them in a state of unity.
Likewise, the opening of the eyes for the gods residing in the celestial chariots (vimāna) is performed;
in this manner, the preceptor, having caused the artisans to perform the opening of the eyes and other rites for the primary images and so forth, as well as for the celestial chariots and the rest.
One should perform the joining of the pedestals for the images of the deities, such as Karmamūrti and others.
Then, having spread out a cloth, one should place lotuses upon it.
Over that, again, a cloth [should be placed], and above that, a load of *śāli* rice.
Having placed half that amount of rice upon it, one should indeed place sesame seeds on top of that.
Then, having drawn a lotus upon it and spread a layer of *kuśa* grass,
one should spread out a new cloth and place a seat adorned with a lotus upon it.
Then, having cast down the lotus or [the image], the Guru, with that very mantra, performs the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) and other rites for Viṣṇu using the Gāyatrī;
he offers one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter and sixteen with the Nṛsūkta.
Then, O Goddess, one should sprinkle [the deity] with water from the *puṇya* vessel;
with the thought "well-established" (*supratiṣṭha*), one should place the God upon the pedestal.
And on all sides, they should chant the *Sāman* hymn: "Thou art established" (*pratiṣṭhāsi*).

The preeminent artisan should make it with firm bonds; the lord should satisfy him with wealth, ornaments, garments, and the like, and then the Guru should dismiss him. Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Twenty-first Chapter:
On the third day from the day the consecration begins,
or even on the preceding day, one should commence the ritual for the consecration-seed-sprouts (aṅkura).
On that day, the preeminent teacher should select four officiating priests who are approved by himself for the purpose of consecrating the temple. He,
O Rame, should also request four officiating priests [to serve as] the Ācārya and others.
"You are knowers of the truth of the Śrī Pañcarātra and exponents of Brahman.
Therefore, for the sake of the consecration of Hari's temple, perform the ritual work together with me according to the rules, so that no transgression occurs."
Having thus prayed, he should bathe together with them, preceded by the shaving of his head;
all [the participants] wearing white garments, adorned with the five-fold ornaments,
marked with the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, pure, and wearing clean sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*).
Formerly, Bhaṭṭācārya worshipped the God of gods in his own home;
formerly he gave gold, betel, and garments to the Brāhmaṇas,
and having obtained their permission, he was honored as equal to the patron of the sacrifice.
Accompanied by officiating priests and brahmins, with the sounding of all kinds of musical instruments,
and by excellent attendants holding parasols and chowries in their hands,
[he was offered] betel, areca nuts, flowers, and fruits in golden vessels.
Having had [the ground] marked out by the best of fortune-tellers with the chanting of the Vedas,
and thus observing the most auspicious omens through all the necessary implements, the preeminent guide, carrying a full water-pot in his hand at a favorable moment, [proceeded].
From his home, he should go either northward or eastward while mentally recollecting Hari; indeed,
he should do so while other excellent teachers recite the Śākuna Sūkta and the Bhadra-karṇa [Sūkta],
O Goddess, as he performs the circumambulation of Hari’s abode.
Having constructed the pavilion, the preceptor should enter it together with those who have been initiated.
Then the officiating priest, using long bundles of *darbha* grass along with fire,
should draw [the deity] into the entire pavilion, the abode of the gods.

And everywhere along the walls, one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) while reciting the mantra "śucī va" (O pure ones); by this, purification shall become certain. Then, having washed one's feet and sipped water (*ācamana*) according to the rule, [one should proceed].
In daily rites, one should wear a purifier made with two blades of darbha grass;
in rites for the ancestors, with three; in rites of sorcery, with four;
in rites for prosperity, with five; and in rites for peace and at meals, with six.
The purificatory ring (pavitra-valaya) is made with two [strands] for all rites, or with seven;
the ring is said to be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide, and the knot should be one finger-breadth.
The length is four finger-breadths, and the kuśa grass blades should measure five fist-lengths.
"The *pavitra* is said to be a ring fashioned from gold and precious gems.
(21.18) Then, having performed the purification of the hands, one should wear the *pavitra* on the hand;
having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should sit upon a seat of grass (*viṣṭarāsana*). (21.19)
Having first recited the "caraṇaṃ pavitram" verse, one should wash the feet;
then, with the "viṣṇorarāṭam" mantra, one should sweep them with *darbha* grass.
With the mantra "gandhadvārā," one should smear them with cow dung.

One should moisten [the ground] with water while reciting the mantra, and adorn it with powdered lime. With the mantra "devasya tvā," one should scatter unbroken rice grains upon the earth; with the mantra for the winter season, one should prepare a seat of grain.
With the mantra "śaṃ no devī," the wise one should draw a hundred-petaled lotus;
with the mantra "dhanvanāga," he should spread darbha grass upwards around it.
Upon that [lotus], he should place [the image] endowed with the proper characteristics, fashioned from gold or other materials.
Having placed a jewel, gold, a tuft of coconut fibers, and an ashvattha sprout [into it],
one should fill the jar with water and fragrant substances;
one should also adorn it with sandalwood, unbroken rice, garlands, and ornaments.
Around that pitcher,
one who knows the single path should place [the syllables] from the right hand of Hari, who stands in the center of the solar disc;
having invoked the thousand-spoked [wheel], one should remember Nārāyaṇa within the pitcher.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present fruits and the like.
Together with jars touched by *darbha* grass, the preceptor should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
This consists of the first four mantras, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word *pavitra*.
Then, for the sake of purification, let there be the discourse on the Self and the manifestation of the Self beyond this; may the supreme deity Vāsudeva be for purification.
May Saṃkarṣaṇa be for purification, and may Pradyumna be for purification.
May Aniruddha and the glorious Keśava, as well as Nārāyaṇa, be for my purification;
may Mādhava be for my purification, and likewise Govinda;
may the primordial Viṣṇu be for my purification, and Madhusūdana be for my purification.
May Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara be for my purification;
may Hṛṣīkeśa and Padmanābha, the Lord of the World, be for my purification.
May Dāmodara be for my purification, and may Padmanābha be for my purification.
May Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātmā, and Madhusūdana be for my purification.
May Kapila, the presiding deity of knowledge, and Viśvarūpa be for my purification.
May Vihaga, Kroḍātman, and Vaḍavānana be for my purification.
May the Lord Dharma, the Master of Speech, and likewise the one reclining upon the single ocean, be for my purification;
may the god Kūrma, the supporter of the netherworld, always be for my purification.
May Varāha be for my purification, and may Narasiṃha be for my purification.
May he who brought the nectar and the Lord of Śrī also be for my purification.
May he whose soul is beloved and the conqueror of Rāhu be for my purification;
may he who seized the Pārijāta tree and the Lord of the World also be for my purification.
May the Blessed One Dattātreya likewise be lying upon the banyan tree;
may he be Ekaśṛṅga-tanu and Vāmana for the sake of purification.
May Trivikrama, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and Hari likewise [be so].

May Rāma, bearing the flaming axe, and Kṛṣṇa be for the sake of purification. May Rāma be the wielder of the bow and a knower of the Vedas for the sake of purification; may Kalki, the destroyer of all defects, always be for the sake of purity.
May the Lord who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātālaśayana) always be for the purification of the world;
may all beings everywhere and at all times be for the purification of everyone.
May they always be for prosperity, nourishment, peace, and spiritual accomplishment.
For the sake of Śiva, for the increase of liberation, and for the unimpeded success of all actions;
for the sake of mantras, the foremost of teachers, female and male servants, and even cattle;
and for the sake of the Vedas, Śāstras, Āgamas and the like, of vows, and of desired accomplishments.

May there be well-being and auspiciousness for the ascetic Vaiṣṇavas who are purified by the five times and possess long life, health, intelligence, and the abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches;
may there be auspiciousness again and again!
May there be no obstacle, may there be constant and long life for us.
May there be a concentrated mind; may this be an auspicious day that brings about all purity—the Lord of all lords, endowed with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
"May this Vāsudeva, the Lord of Śrī and bestower of all perfections, be pleased!
May all the deities mentioned previously be pleased today, be pleased!
Thus, the most excellent initiates proclaimed the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) according to the *Ekāyana* tradition.
Having had that recited, he should first sprinkle himself with water.
Then [he should sprinkle] the disciples, the practitioners, the officiating priests, the attendants,
all the ritual materials, and the sacrificial pavilion itself.
The Guru should first sprinkle the abode of the God of gods;
the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) derived from a tawny cow and a goat are highly recommended.
One should take the pañcagavya in a new and auspicious earthen vessel.

One should not accept [cows] that are distressed, pregnant, or within ten days of calving, nor those that have lost their calves; furthermore, one should not accept what has already been accepted [if it was obtained under such conditions], as it does not effect purification.
The five products [of the cow] are cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
While [the urine] is being discharged, one should collect it; likewise, cow dung that is still on the ground, warm, and free from worms and such, should then be squeezed.
[One should also use] its juice, freshly drawn ghee, or curd that has been left to stand for a day and night.
Milk that has not been heated should be taken; these [substances] are always pure.
Cow’s urine with the *viṣṇugāyatrī*, cow dung with the *gandhadvārā* mantra, milk with the *āpyāyasva* mantra, and curd with the *dadhi krāvṇa* mantra.
One should combine the substances together with the mantra "Ghṛtaṃ śukram asi" (The ghee is the seed),
or else with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī or even the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
The ghee should be one measure, the curd two measures, and the milk three measures.

Six parts of urine, four parts of water, and one part of feces are prescribed for bathing; for sprinkling, equal parts of each are recommended. Urine should be mixed with an equal amount of cow dung, and twice that amount of curd should be added.
Clarified butter is said to be four times [the quantity], and milk eight times that;
this is declared to be the measure for consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
By means of this pañcagavya, even all the grounds of the temple—
The Guru should sprinkle the sacrificial hall, the pavilion, and so forth on all sides.
He should incense them everywhere with incenses, along with unbroken rice grains and flowers;
he should also scatter white mustard seeds and drench them with fragrant waters.
One should adorn the abode in every direction with colored powders, garlands, and so forth; O Rame, one should light many lamps that do not go out using cow's ghee.
[If one performs the ritual act without first declaring it an auspicious day, it shall be fruitless.]
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter on the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhākarma*) in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
If a temple has been constructed without first establishing the location for the child-god (*bālasthāna*), [the following must be done].

Prior to the commencement of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the most excellent Guru should prepare a pedestal (*pīṭha*) upon the altar (*vedikā*) consisting of five *bhāras* of grain, half that amount of rice,
and half that amount of sesame seeds. || 22.1–22.2 ||
Then, having drawn a lotus upon that [surface], or else an image endowed with the [auspicious] marks,
together with a beard, and joined with a coconut and so forth, as well as mango sprouts—
having placed a water-pot in the center of the solar disc:
Oṃ, salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, Blessed Lord, who are affectionate toward your devotees!
O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive me for this dwelling which I have constructed without having built a house for my child, out of a desire to show favor to your devotee.
"O Blessed One, come here; O Hari, accomplish our rite!

Having thus prayed and invoked him, one should worship with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. Then, having offered milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
From the completion of the rites such as the consecration of the site up to the construction of the temple,
if the fashioning of the images is performed without mantras,
then [the rite should be performed] in front of a small image, or in a sacrificial pit, or even upon a sacrificial mound.

Having generated the fire according to the prescribed rule, the best of teachers should perform the oblations and other rites at their respective times; indeed, having drawn [the disciple] in, he should take delight [in the practice]. He should offer the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta), ending with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
The characteristics of the primary image, the secondary images, and the sanctuary are such that even the gods do not know them, let alone the humans on earth;
therefore, at the time of afternoon, for the sake of purifying the measurements, [one should perform the rite]. || 22.10–22.11 ||
When the fire has been established in front of the image of the child,
the preceptor, remaining composed, should first offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) together with *śamī* leaves one hundred times for each, using the seven *vyāhṛti*s.
Thereafter, with the *Nṛsūkta*, one should offer sixteen oblations for each [verse];
likewise, with the five *Upaniṣads*, one should offer a hundred oblations for each.
Then, having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the preceptor should dismiss the fire.
Then, at the time of evening, for the sake of accomplishing the seed-syllable of the installation (pratiṣṭhāṅkura),
one should place betel, plantain fruit,
coconut fruit, rice, flowers, and sandalwood in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
A bundle of *darbha* grass, a water-pot, an umbrella, and a fly-whisk; a fan, a hand-lamp, and likewise items such as golden handles—
all these were carried by attendants, both local guides and others.
Accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and the resonance of musical instruments, one should go joyfully to the child’s chamber;
having arranged the curtains and other decorations before the image of the Child,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground four times before the Lord of the World.

Having personally worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings up to the *naivedya*, the Guru, taking flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in both hands, should pray to the Lord:
"Salutations to You, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator. (22.19–22.20)
To the one who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus; who reclines upon Śeṣa;
who is served in the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha by the eternal, liberated, and wise sages;
the creator of the world; the all-pervading one within all things.
For the welfare of all the world and for the prosperity of the king and his kingdom,

I shall commence the ritual sowing of seedlings (aṅkurārpaṇa) for the sake of accomplishing the great consecration (mahāpratiṣṭhā). May he appoint the commander-in-chief to the task of bringing the clay.

Having made this request, one should worship the lotus-feet with flowers and other offerings, upon a seat made of sixteen *darbha* grasses and covered with a cloth of gold or other materials. Having invoked the commander of the army (*senāpati*) onto the *kūrca* mat at the pedestal of the child-image, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped him with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should pray to Gaṇanāyaka:
"O Lord saluted by the immortals, you have been commanded by the Master for the sake of protecting this great consecration; come with me to fetch the clay. (22.25–22.26)
Having thus made this supplication with the chanting of the Vedas preceded by the sounding of musical instruments,
and taking up the ritual vessels and other implements while holding parasols and fly-whisks in their hands,
they should go toward the east or the north for the purpose of collecting earth in a large quantity.
Having established the commander-in-chief upon a golden seat within a pavilion purified by the waters of the *puṇyāha* rite,
and having placed the ceremonial canopy and other items on the ground before him,
she should then place her head upon the ground in front of him, toward the northeast.

Having thus drawn the earth with its surface marked by the tips of her feet placed toward the southwest, her face turned upward and her hands joined in *añjali*, the Guru should then prepare a pedestal of grain for her head,
either to the south or to the north.
Having placed a golden spade there, adorned with *darbha* grass and other items,
and having strewn around it a seat of grain upon the ground,
one should likewise decorate it in due order with garments and ornaments.
Having placed a *kūrca* made of seven blades of *darbha* grass, one *tāla* in length,
upon the heart of the earth, and likewise a *kūrca* upon the spade,
he should sprinkle them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite while reciting the mantra "Bhūmir bhūmnā."
There, one should indeed pray to the goddess Earth, the beloved of Viṣṇu:
"O Earth, please be present here for the sake of bestowing the auspicious sprouts as I begin the installation of the divine Lord Vāsudeva."
Having thus invoked [the deity] and worshipped him immediately thereafter with offerings of water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth—
O you who attained the earth as the Kṛṣṇa incarnation and destroyed Hiraṇyākṣa—
for the purpose of the consecration, during the rite of collecting the clay for the Blessed One:
"Be present in this spade for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Having thus invoked [the deity] in the form of a boar, one should worship him with water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other offerings;
then, having offered molasses and cakes, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the two of them.
Taking up a spade, O Rame, and reciting the Gāyatrī mantra of Viṣṇu in the form of a boar,
I took earth from the netherworld with the spade for the sake of the face, arms, breasts,
and feet of the Earth.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Hari as a boar emerging from the water;
then, with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by Viṣṇu, one should place earth into vessels made of gold or other materials,
as well as sand and powdered cow-dung therein.
Having prepared those [offerings] and placed them in vessels,
the knower of mantras should then joyfully cover them with new cloths while reciting the root mantra.
[He should place them] upon a chariot, on the shoulder of an elephant, or upon the head of an attendant.
Having set down [the vessel] accompanied by all musical instruments and the resonance of the Vedas,
the best of preceptors, having circumambulated the temple and sprinkled the water-shed with the waters of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), should lead it to the pavilion of sprouts (aṅkuramaṇḍapa).
The wise practitioner should consecrate all the vessels, such as the *pālikā* and others, immediately;
he should arrange their positions according to the scriptures.
He should spread threads moistened with sandalwood paste upon the altar.
First, one should clearly draw twelve straight lines extending eastward;
then, one should draw sixteen horizontal lines from south to north with their tips pointing north.
Among these, starting from the fifth line up to the sixtieth line— || 22.46–22.47 ||
Then, from the tenth sūtra up to the eleventh,
and from the eighth sūtra up to the ninth,
extending horizontally from four sūtras up to the fifth sūtra. (22.48)
From the eighth thread-drop up to the ninth thread,
and from there up to the twelfth thread, as far as the thirteenth line—
[the area] provided with three horizontal paths is proclaimed to have two lengths.
When this is done, O Lotus-born One, there are thirty-six positions for the *ghaṭikās*, and likewise for the *śarāvas*. In this manner, O Lotus-born One, there are one hundred and eight positions.
It should be provided with three horizontal rows and two vertical rows in length;
furthermore, each individual square shall contain exactly nine vessels.
For each of the sixteen types [of deities], the laying of the lines begins from the west.
The lines extending from south to north should be nine new ones;
one should strike twelve lines for the determination of the positions.
From the third and also from the sixth line-drop, one should establish the pathway (vīthikā).
One may calculate from the ninth up to the tenth line;
then, from the third straight northern line,
as far as the fourth line, the central path (vīthikā) extends.
From the sixth line down to the seventh line,
by establishing eight units for each, the arrangement of the paths is conceived;
one should likewise arrange nine [units] from the western line.
I indeed delight in the six diagonal lines of the thread;
from the third [square] of the north, one should fashion the path as far as the fourth line,
and from the sixth to the seventh, one should likewise arrange the straight path.
A path-line should be drawn across the middle of the horizontal space according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus first laid out the paths, and having constructed an altar one cubit high within each of those respective paths and previously adorned it, the preceptor—
One should construct separate pedestals using *pramāṇa* measures of grain;
upon them, one should draw eight-petaled lotuses while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Then, one should cover the cavities of the small pots with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass.
One should first fill it with earth, immediately thereafter with sand;
then with powdered dried cow-dung, and subsequently with the products arising from the Ocean of Milk,
together with the shoots of the *aśvattha* tree, *dūrvā* grass, and the tips of *darbha* grass.
The preceptor, with *sahadevī*, *niśā*, and *āmrā*, and by means of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*),
should bind them around the necks; immediately thereafter,
he should place the *pālikā* vessels on the right and likewise the *ghaṭikā* vessels in the center.
In the northern [direction], there are shallow bowls (*śarāva*) and seed-vessels (*pālikā*) and so forth, in due order. In the western position among these, upon a pedestal (*vedikā*),
is the Soma-pitcher together with eight subsidiary pitchers (*upakumbha*) around it, along with grain.
One should place the Sudarśana [image] in a water-pot on the northern spot,
wrapping each one with cloths while reciting the root mantra. Then, while reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one should place the small earthen vessels (pālikās).

With the *pārameṣṭhya* mantra, the teacher should place the water-jars (*ghaṭikā*) using the *viśvamantra*; O Goddess, he should establish the bowls (*śarāva*) with the *viṣṇugāyatrī*. He should also fill the *somakumbha* and the others with scented water.
One should place brushes made of mango sprouts at the openings of coconut shells.
[These should contain] wild rice, śāli rice, wheat, mung beans, niṣpāva beans, bamboo shoots, 70. priyaṅgu, sesame, māṣa beans, kuluttha, mustard seeds, and barley.
O Lotus-born One, the preceptor should first place each of these vessels upon golden plates;
having covered these vessels containing grain with cloths,
he should place them upon the heads of the attendants.
Accompanied by all kinds of ritual implements, musical instruments, and the chanting of the Vedas,
one should circumambulate the temple and lead [the image] back to the pavilion.
First, one should purify it with milk while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by [the name of] Viṣṇu.

Having placed [the image] upon a seat of grain, one should sprinkle it with meritorious water. Having formally requested the deities at the gate, the archway, and the jars, the self-possessed preceptor should worship them according to the ritual rules from the seat of the child-image.
O Rame, having fashioned a pedestal ending with the lotus out of unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*) upon all the vessels— the *pālikās*, the two jars (*kumbha*), the two chariot-wheels (*somarathāṅga*),
and the secondary jars (*upakumbha*)— one should worship Viṣṇu, who is born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, within the *pālikās*.
And he installed Brahmā, born from a portion of Aniruddha, in the water-jars;
Śarva, born from a portion of Pradyumna, in the shallow bowls produced from the lake;
and the Lord of Herbs (Soma), arisen from a portion of Pradyumna, in that very pitcher.
One should worship Indra and the other deities in the small jars (*upakumbha*), and Sudarśana in the water-pot (*karaka*).
One should worship Keśava and the others in the grains such as *nīvāra*,
and in the sixteen vessels that protect all purposes, O Rame, one should worship them in due order.
One should worship the four beginning with Vāsudeva, the ten, and the two beginning with Keśava.
One should worship the twelve beginning with Keśava, the eight beginning with Viṣṇu,
and the four beginning with Janārdana, having invoked them in sequence.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), one should then wrap [the image] with a new cloth.

Having prepared a pedestal ending in a lotus in the eastern part of the vessels, or in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or even on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship Lakṣmī’s Lord there.
"O Blessed One, Lord of all the worlds, I am now prepared to perform the consecration.
Having previously kindled the fire to provide the sacrificial fuel for its limbs, I desire to offer oblations for its successful completion; you ought to grant me your permission."
Having thus prayed, the wise man, dwelling in the house of the child,
should meditate upon the fire arisen from my presence and dismiss it into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
After offering oblations (āhutis) into the mouth [of the fire] until its conclusion, he should then proceed with the rites for the fire in due order.
O Rame, one should indeed perform for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies;
however, the consecration of the fire is performed in this manner when there is an oblation to a deity other than me.
But when an oblation to both of us is performed by the preceptor, [the procedure is as follows].
Then, one should mentally visualize fire arising from my mouth.
For this [fire], there are never any rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and so forth.
[However, it is used] in consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), festivals (*utsava*), and other rituals dedicated to me.
Having thus generated [the fire], the best of instructors should offer oblations into the fire.
For, having first invoked us two into the sprout-fire according to the rule and offered the oblation,
he should then dismiss [us] and perform the arrangement of the pedestal for Soma.
Having invoked Soma into that [liṅga], one should perform its six-limbed ritual;
then, having offered the arghya and other oblations with clarified butter using the Soma-mantra,
the best of preceptors should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter.
The preceptor should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, and *bilva* with the root mantra; furthermore,
he should offer one hundred oblations with the mantra of Soma.
Having uttered the names of the presiding deities of the *pālikā* and the other vessels,
the preceptor should offer oblations of clarified butter either one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times,
or eight times; he should then take the *saṃpāta* clarified butter.
Then, O auspicious lady, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*),
the most excellent of gurus, meditating upon the Lord of the Wind (*Pavanādhipati*),
[should pour] clarified butter into all the vessels, such as the *pālikās*, and indeed into the *somakumbhas*, using the tip of the *kūrca* grass.
One should cast out what remains and place it in the seed-vessel;
then, having dismissed Soma who resides in the fire, one should dismiss the fire itself.
One should deposit the seeds into the small earthen vessels and other containers with the twelve-syllable mantra.
With the mantra "mūrdhānam," one should cover the seeds with earth; then,
with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa," one should sprinkle the collections of seeds with water infused with turmeric.
One should also sprinkle them with water from the Soma-pitcher using a *kūrca* [bundle of grass].

Having worshipped the Soma residing in the Soma-pitcher and the deities in the *pālikā*s and other vessels with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (*pāyasānna*) as an offering.
One should offer the *kumuda* and other oblations until the day of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
One should perform worship at the two [morning and evening] times and sprinkle water with turmeric.
[One should observe] sprouts that are dark-green, black, or red, even those growing horizontally.
The practitioner of mantra should abandon those [obstacles] that have not yet fully grown and create them anew as before;
he should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of that defect.
In the case of daily and occasional rites, creation [of the mandala] proceeds as usual, but in the case of optional rites, it should be abandoned—of this there is no doubt.
In the case of dark-colored [spots], there shall be loss of wealth; in red ones, there will be quarrel.
In black ones, there is mental anguish, and if they are in the form of animals, disease.
If they are not fully developed, death occurs there; of this there is no doubt.
When [the lines] are auspicious, yellow, white, straight, and upward-pointing,
there shall be the full prosperity of all attainments for both the performer and the one who causes the performance to be done.
Thus it is in all festivals, whether regular or occasional.
Having thus offered the sprouts, one should perform the auspicious rite.
Or, O Rame, if due to the lack of materials and so forth, or because of the exigency of the occasion, one does not install the eight-and-a-half *pālikā* vessels and the rest; || 22.107–108 ||
For all purposes, sixteen, twelve, eight, or even four *pālikā* vessels may be prepared; in that case, they should be arranged individually in a pleasant place.
One should not prepare a water-station (*prapā*) for them; rather, they should be placed within the sacrificial pavilion itself.
Having bathed [the deity] on the altar in the northeast, one should worship him.
Among the sixteen and other rites to be performed, the worship of Soma is in the center.
This offering of sprouts is indeed recommended to be done at night alone.

For Soma is indeed the lord of herbs, and Night is his beloved; when Soma is honored during that night, all [the herbs] are indeed honored. It is said that for the teacher, the master, and the abode, there shall surely be prosperity in every respect.
One should light lamps on all sides with cow’s ghee and keep them burning without extinguishing them.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter [concerning the rite of installation] in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-three.
Then, one should consecrate in the pavilion jars containing gravel,
as well as door-pitchers and jars suitable for the ritual bathing;
these should be purified with clean water and freed from any cracks or defects.
One should carefully wrap [the vessels] with thread, leaving a space of one finger-breadth between each.
(23.2) If one uses jars made of gold and other such materials, or those fashioned from metal, no wrapping with thread should be performed for those produced from water [i.e., clay]. (23.3)
To the west of the sacrificial ground, one should cover the earth with rice grains;
there, one should spread out *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward.
One should indeed place all the jars upside down in a row.
Having spread kuśa grass over [the vessel], facing eastward, with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra;
then, having displayed the darbha-mudrā and having sprinkled it all around with scented water, one should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣatān*) with the *viśva-puruṣa* mantra, O Rame. (23.5–23.6)

O Goddess, in former times, on the altar of the pitcher (*kumbhavedī*), the Guru should first prepare a pedestal (*pīṭha*) of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) using individual grains of rice, half of that with rice-grains (*taṇḍula*),
and half of that with sesame seeds (*tila*); upon this, he should fashion either a lotus or a wheel.
Having written [the mantras] upon them, one should indeed place the jars and the water-pot there.
Likewise, for the consecration of the jars beginning with those at the doors,
there should be a pedestal of rice six finger-breadths high, and half of that amount of rice-grains.
Having fashioned a seat out of sesame seeds and half of that [quantity], one should indeed place the jars and other vessels upon them; otherwise, the ritual act is fruitless.
And for the wheel and lotus, when fashioning the seat on the altar with rice and other grains...
If, however, there is no sesame seed, the Guru should draw a lotus upon it;
he should fashion its petals with rice grains of five colors,
the pericarp with yellow-colored [grains], and the filaments with red and white ones.
Then, having performed the daily rites such as bathing at dawn,
the wise man should go to the temple with the officiating priests and perform the worship of the *pālikās* and the child-image, as well as the worship of the doors and other parts.

One should perform the worship at the two times in this very manner until the conclusion of the consecration. O Rame, one should indeed place five jars— previously consecrated and wrapped with threads— in the intermediate directions and also in the center.
One should mix the five products of the cow with mantras for the consecration;
then the Guru should fill five jars with the five products of the cow. In each jar, he should likewise place a bundle of kuśa grass and a coconut fruit.
One should cover the jars with clusters of mango sprouts.
On the ground area of the great pavilion, one should place the bathing seat;
upon that pedestal, one should install the metal images for the ritual actions and so forth.
One should purify the water-pots placed upon a seat of grain in front of that pedestal,
and one should also dry the articles for worship.
Having sprinkled them with water from the "auspicious day" (puṇyāha), one should display the cow.
Having rendered all objects immortal with their milks,
the preceptor should worship the deities presiding over the five elements within the jars;
he should then offer the bathing-cloth to all the deities, beginning with the Mūla-mantra.
Having worshipped [the deities] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present the *madhuparka*.

One should consecrate the primary images (*mūlabimba*) with the central jar alone. Then, O Rame, all the images belonging to the ritual actions and so forth should be consecrated by means of the fire-abiding [deity].
With the *nairṛta* [mantra] one should [cleanse] the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and with the *māruta* [mantra], the clay images (*bhaktabimba*).
Then, with the *kumbha* [mantra] from the *aiśa* [direction], one should sprinkle the entire temple;
thereafter, the plastered (*sudhāmaya*) and other types of images should be sprinkled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then the supreme guru should consecrate the images with pure waters;
this is proclaimed as the bath for the purpose of removing defects caused by the artisan.
Furthermore, having prepared a pedestal of grain in front of the deity, [he should proceed].

The preceptor should place there a jar filled with cow's ghee. O Rame, having invoked the god Nārāyaṇa therein, he should worship him with the mantra "ghṛtasnātā" and smear the flowing images [with the ghee].
Having cleansed [the image] with fragrant powders, one should sprinkle it with warm water;
for all images, beginning with those made from clay, [this should be done] using a quantity equal to a *darbha* blade.
One should offer a pair of garments with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ."
Then, with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, the preceptor should offer the arghya, pādya, ācamana, fragrance, garland, incense, lamp, and food offering; thereafter,
he should offer them to the goddesses beginning with Śrī using their respective mantras.
Then one should perform the rite for the pacification of the site (vāstu-śānti); first, one should worship its presiding deity.
In ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, Bhṛgu protected the Daityas;
his wife also constantly carried all the asuras within her womb.
Then, overcome with anger, he cut off his wife's head. When Bhṛgu was possessed by great wrath, sweat fell from his body onto the surface of the earth; from that sweat, the best of Daityas was born.
Then he was born from the earth and set out to slay the gods;
all the gods, having assembled, struck down his body,
and those led by Ravi stood firmly, having stepped upon his head and the rest of his form.
Then he began to cry out to the lotus-seated one born from the lotus.
Thereupon, the four-faced one granted him a boon regarding his true nature:
"O son of the Earth, since your origin has arisen from the ground, [you shall be known as Vāsudeva]."
Therefore, when men on earth construct for you a house, or a village, or a town,
or even a temple for the god,
they shall worship you thus installed by the gods, by virtue of my boon.
If one should become satisfied by that [offering], they will not worship with reverence;
there will be the destruction of sons and others, and one will be deprived of prosperity.
Therefore, a wise person should pray for the sake of the welfare of all.
On the southern side of the water-shed, having spread out loads of sesame seeds,
one should, applying effort, draw a figure with its hands and feet extended, lying face down with the head toward the east, in the four corners in succession.
Having invoked the gods, one should worship them therein; I shall describe that to you:
having invoked Sūrya on the head, Manmatha at the base of the arm, Subrahmaṇya on the elbow, and Vināyaka in the left hand. (23.41–23.42)
On the two feet are the two Aśvins; in the middle [of the body] is the full moon;
on the hand is Durgā, and on the elbow is the root of the Mothers;
on the region of the navel is Umāpati; in the heart is Brahmā; and [on the head is] Hari.

Having placed a seat made of seven blades of darbha grass upon the heart of the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), while mentally meditating on the eight Lords of the World in the surrounding directions and Kṣetrarakṣaka in the north, the preceptor or the officiating priests [should proceed].
The practitioner of mantra should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) in the western worldly fire and offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣadic mantras;
immediately thereafter, [he should offer oblations] with fuel-sticks of *śamī*, *apāmārga*, and *khadira*.
Uttering each syllable of that mantra with the root-mantra, O Goddess,
one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times,
or even eight times, using the Puruṣasūkta which has the Puruṣa as its essence.
And on an auspicious day, the preceptor should offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with sixteen oblations;

having offered it once for each [deity] with the *caru*, he should utter the names of those residing within the body of the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*), and after making the offering, he should cast the ritual food-offering (*bali*) to them alone.
The best of teachers should dismiss the deities, such as the Sun and others, who have entered into that [liṅga].
Immediately thereafter, he should smear that spot with cow-dung and water;
and having had the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited, he should sprinkle the ground with those waters.
Then, however, one should generate a body for the site using a bundle of *darbha* grass;
having invoked [the deity] into that with sesame seeds and sprinkled it with water from the *puṇyāha* rite,
one should set fire to that site along the pathways by means of attendants.

O beloved of Hari, one should summon [the guardians] from the eight directions for the purpose of the consecration; O lotus-born goddess, one should then offer an oblation (bali) to the invited lords of the directions.
Then, having returned to the temple, one should cleanse one's hands and feet.
Having sipped water according to the scriptures, the preceptor should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon those images in due order, beginning with the base,
using betel leaves, fruits, flowers, and the like, as well as golden threads and other such materials.
Having taken up the eye-patches and other items, the preceptor, together with Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas,
initiated officiating priests, and the patron himself,
circumambulated the sacred abode preceded by the sound of musical instruments.
Having reached the inner sanctum, one should place [the image] upon a seat of grain;
then, having bowed down again and again and praised [it] with various hymns,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited and thereafter sprinkle the threads.

One should purify great silver threads and the like by means of drying and other such methods. One should consecrate protective cords with the Aparājita mantra; having invoked Śrī into them from the midst of the Ocean of Milk, [one should wear them].
Having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, one should then worship the images;
the most excellent of teachers, having tied the *kautuka* (protective thread) to the primary images,
should proceed to the great pavilion and perform the thorough worship of the ritual image (*karmārcā*) and the others.
Having performed the ritual binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) according to the rules upon his own hand,
as well as those of the officiating priests, he should afterwards perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord.
Then, having ascended the celestial chariot (vimāna) and worshipped it according to the rules, [he should proceed].
Having first tied a protective cord (pratisara) on the frieze of the temple with twenty-five threads, and afterwards [tying one] for the preceptor,
the most excellent of preceptors should then perform the consecration by shadow (chāyādhivāsa).
For the purpose of accomplishing the preliminary consecration (chāyādhivāsa) before the primary image,
one should place upon a bed of grain either a water-vessel made of gold or other materials, or one made of wood, or even one made of clay, or a large cauldron. || 23.65–66 ||

On all sides, the most excellent preceptor first places eight jars— equipped with coconut fibers, threads, and brushes, arranged according to their respective rites, and adorned with leaves of the *aśvattha* and *āmra* trees— along with a water-pot (*karaka*) at the head portion.
One should fill the troughs and other vessels with water and flowers upon a lotus-seat.
Then, having sprinkled the pedestal with meritorious waters, one should arrange them;
Indra and the others in the subsidiary jars, and Sudarśana in the *karaka* vessel.

One should meditate on Hari upon a seat made of twenty-eight blades of *darbha* grass; indeed, one should worship the goddesses, beginning with Śrī, having invoked them upon seats made of twenty-one blades of *darbha*, according to the proper sequence.
When that water has been purified with the *pāvamānī* verses and the five *upaniṣads* and so forth,
one should then cause Hari, who is seated upon a *kūrca*, to lie down therein while reciting the Lord’s eight-syllable mantra.
One should perform worship up to the offering of food (naivedya); this is the sequence for Śrī and the others.
Then, having displayed the wheel-mudrā (cakramudrā), one should cause the water-vessels to be covered.
The best of preceptors, knowing the mantra, [should address] the living soul (jīva) that presides over the image.

Having drawn it into his own heart, he should lead it along the path of withdrawal; O lotus-eyed one, he should then unite that [consciousness] with the Supreme Brahman. Thereafter, however, the primary forms [of the deity] [should be dissolved] by means of drying, flooding, and so forth.
Having cleansed the images, the Guru should then cover them with cloths;
in this same manner, he should perform the rite for the forms of the celestial palaces (vimāna) and for the palace itself.
Alternatively, for the sake of each individual palace, the most excellent Guru should do so in a wooden vat filled with water.
One should perform the preliminary consecration by water (jalādhivāsa) on the ground in front of the temple structure.
Having prepared bundles of seven darbha grasses,
the preceptor should indeed invoke the Goddess Rame along with the temple structure for the preliminary consecration by shadow (chāyādhivāsa).
Having thus prepared the pavilion and proceeded to the rite of installing the water-pots,
[the officiants] should be well-bathed, wearing clean garments, with clear clay applied as vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) on their foreheads,
their limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents, and adorned with flower garlands and the like.

All the excellent attendants, commanded by their master, took up the jars that had been previously consecrated; accompanied by the requisites for the procession and the sounds of musical instruments, they circumambulated the palace.
Having reached the bank of a river or similar body of water, and having filled jars with filtered water,
O Brahmins, and having adorned those jars with coconuts and other ornaments,
they should be placed with devotion upon the shoulders or the heads of elephants.
Having performed a circumambulation, he should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
In the center of the altar, he should place the great pitcher, and to its right, the small water-vessel;
then, from the direction of Indra (East) up to Īśāna (Northeast), he should arrange the other pitchers in equal positions.
In the intervals between the jars, [place] the eight auspicious objects beginning with the conch,
as well as ruby, coral, diamond, lapis lazuli,
topaz, sapphire, emerald, and pearl.
And gomedaka—these are the nine gems, O lotus-eyed one.
Likewise, Vāsudeva, the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the banner;
as well as the Śrīvatsa, Vainateya, and the king of tortoises.
Immediately thereafter, the most excellent of gurus should place these objects made of gold and other materials, together with gems, into the central jar and the other jars;
and he should place the Kālacakra and the fire-gem into the *karaka* vessel.
In this very manner, one should install the pitchers of the celestial chariot (vimāna) in the Rame [chamber].
One should cause the image of Aniruddha to be placed in the great pitcher (mahākumbha),
and one should indeed set gems such as rubies in the door-pitchers.
One should cast musk, sandalwood, camphor, saffron, ushira root, and aloe-wood into the ritual jars at the sacred sites (ghaṭatīrtha).
[One should avoid] those who are nihilists, those who have transgressed the bounds of conduct, and those who revile the gods and Brahmins.
Having expelled those who act contrary to the law, those of evil conduct, those afflicted by diseases such as leprosy,
those with missing limbs, the deaf, the blind, and those who have abandoned their daily duties,
the Guru should sprinkle them outside with meritorious waters.

The best of teachers should cause the students of the Ṛgveda to recite at the eastern gate, those of the Yajurveda at the southern, those who know the Sāmaveda at the western, and those belonging to the Atharva branch at the northern gate; he should have them recite by beginning with their respective Vedas. (23.94)
The Vedānta, the Purāṇas, and hymns of praise should be recited in the fires.
Without contradicting these, one should have other musical instruments played.
Then, the officiating priests, instructed by the Guru, should worship the eastern door and the others.
Thus, on the southern and northern branches of the archway at the eastern gate, one should worship the very beautiful Indra;
above and on both sides, the two Vainateyas; and in the center, one should worship the Sudarśana.
O Goddess, one should worship the two red banners, Kumuda and Kumudākṣaka;
the wise man should worship the two jars with full openings using offerings such as *arghya* and others.
One should worship the *Ṛgveda* in the middle of the door, and on the two right door-panels— 23.98–99.
Subhadra and Dharmarāja on two yellow-colored banners;
Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana on the two jars, O lady of auspicious countenance;
and the two gods Ānanda and Nandana, as well as the Yajurveda, in the center.
Sugandha and Varuṇa are to be worshipped on the two door-posts of the western gate.
One should meditate upon Śaṅkukarṇa and another [deity] on the two blue banners;
and upon the two jars, Sarvanetra, Vīrasena, and Suṣeṇa.
In the middle [of the altar], one should place the Sāmaveda; on the two door-panels of the northern gate, the Sugotra and Dhanada; on the two white banners, the two Ramas;
and on the two jars, Sumukha, Supratiṣṭha, and likewise Sambhava.

One should worship Prabhava in the middle position and Atharvan as well. For the other doors, the Guru should perform the worship of Vainateya and the others in sequence, starting from the eastern door, just as was done for Yama and the rest.

O Beloved, having invoked the previously mentioned deities from the pedestal of the child-form (bālabimba) into these [liṅgas], one should worship them in sequence with unbroken rice grains (akṣata), water for honor (arghya), and other offerings—
[the gods] who hold the conch, discus, and mace in their hands, and are adorned with crowns and earrings.
One should meditate upon the beloved attendants who stand with palms joined and bowed in devotion.
Then, one who knows the Sāman chants should cause this female gatekeeper to recite the Sāman;
standing facing east at the western side of the Cakra-kuṇḍa.
Seated in the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), meditating on Hari, the most excellent guru,

holding a pavitra grass ring and reciting the mantra "Svāhā to the discus that is the destroyer of the asuras," should then perform the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with three blades of darbha grass, O Rame.
Having smeared [the area] with sandalwood paste and other substances, one should then scatter unbroken grains (akṣata).
First, one should meditate upon the deity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍadeva); learn from me its true form:
the head is in the east, the arms are extended toward the northeast and the southeast.
The feet [are located] in the southwest and northwest, and the belly likewise in the center of the pit;
such indeed is the visualization for all pits, O Lotus-born One.
Then, one should worship the person in the form of the pit with perfumes and other offerings.
Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should take up a pair of *darbha* blades. With those two, O Rāme, one should draw three upward-pointing lines extending toward the east;
while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should likewise draw three channels (*nāḍī*).
With the *guṇamantra*, the preceptor should cast those two *darbha* blades into the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
along with a bundle of soft *darbha* grass, like dried cow-dung powder.
He should fill it with husks while reciting the mantra "Gandhadvārā."
One should strew sixteen *kuśa* grasses around the perimeter of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having spread [grass] even within the center of the pit, one should arrange the *yogapīṭha*.
Upon that seat, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva, the Lord of Ramā.
Having worshipped him with the *arghya* and other offerings, he should pray with the appropriate mudrā:
"O Virāḍ-rūpa, O Source of the Universe, served by Brahmā, Rudra, and the others!
For the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), I pray for fire from your mouth, O Lord! (23.118)
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods,

one should take fire from a sun-crystal or from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and place it in a copper vessel in the northeast of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), following the procedures beginning with drying.
One should purify it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), strike it, and sprinkle it;
[visualizing it] as resembling a thousand suns, with two heads, seven hands, seven tongues,
three eyes, three feet, and a pale-red luster.
With his two principal hands joined in *añjali* and holding other weapons with his remaining arms—
the conch, the discus, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the spear—
the Guru should meditate upon Agni, the Lord of *svāhā*, seated upon a lotus in the sacrificial pit. (23.122–123)
One should display the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), in their proper order.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the six-syllable fire-seed mantra (agnibīja).
O Rame, one should worship [the deity] with clarified butter (ājya), beginning with the water for honor (arghya) and ending with the food offering (nivedya).
With both hands filled with parched grain, the Guru should pray to the Fire:
"O Anala, I begin the installation of the Lord Vāsudeva;
remaining here in the form of the Gārhapatya and other fires, fulfill this rite."
Thus the self-possessed preceptor should satisfy that fire with parched grains;
for the other sacrificial pits, however, having performed the circumambulation with a handful of *darbha* grass and having previously prepared the pedestal in them according to the rule.
Thereafter, one should pour the fire from the central pit into those [other pits].
Then, for all the fires, one should worship with offerings such as *arghya* and clarified butter (*ājya*).
Four cows should be stationed in the south, facing north.

Then, having worshipped the cows known as Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godā, and Yamunā, the most excellent of teachers should milk them. With their milk, one should cook sacrificial porridge (caru), and with that, the oblation (āhuti) should be performed.
Having washed the cooking vessel with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra and having placed rice grains into it,
one should fill it with water using the mantra called Cakra or Sucakra,
and then purify the rice grains.
Then, one should place a three-legged tripod made of iron in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O Rame, having placed the cooking vessel upon it with the mantra called Sūryacakra,
one should ignite the fire with the mantra called Jvālācakra.
One should perform the cooking of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with the vessel named Mahāsudarśana.
One should cook milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the eastern pit, kṛsara-rice in the southern,
rice mixed with jaggery in the western, and pure rice in the northern.
At the time of cooking the *caru*, one should offer one hundred and eight fuel sticks (*samidh*) with the mantra called *Jvālācakra* for the increase of the fire.
For the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the east and other directions, [the wood should be] from the *pālāśa*, *plakṣa*, and *khadira* trees.
O Goddess, fuel-sticks made of *bailva* wood are to be known as appropriate for all rites.
Alternatively, fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood are prescribed for the sacrificial pits in the east and other directions;
or else, one *āḍhaka* measure of rice grains may be cooked in the kitchen.
On the northern side of the sacrificial pit, upon a bed of darbha grass,
the officiating priests should place [the materials] for the purpose of pacifying the fire within the seven tongues of flame.
I shall now describe the procedure for that oblation, as well as the substances and the colors of those tongues.
At dawn, one should offer fuel-sticks and clarified butter with the *mūla-mantra*;
at *manojavā*, food with the *vidyā* called Vāsudeva; and at *lohitā* and *dhūmrā*, parched grain with the *vidyā* called Saṃkarṣaṇa.
One should perform oblations with sesame seeds using the Pradyumna-mantra in the Sphuliṅginī fire; with milk using the mantra called Aniruddha in the Viśvarūpī fire;
and with honey in the Karālikā fire, one should offer the sacrificial pap (caru) with the Puṃsūkta.

The middle position belongs to Kālī, while Karālī is in the eastern direction. Manojava is in the southeast, and Lohitā is in the western direction. Sudhūmrā has the moon as her abode, and Sphuliṅginī has the wind as her support.
This is declared to be the location of Viśvarūpiṇī in the northeast. Now, regarding the tongues on the right face, there are four;
listen, O beloved, as the distinction of colors for three of them is described.
Black, blue, red like a lotus, and shining like lightning—others likewise, as well as blood-red and white, and blue: thus the supreme guru should meditate.
By the command of Bhaṭṭācārya, the officiating priests prepared to offer the oblations.

Having performed all the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as well as the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of the east and so forth, and likewise in those of the temple (vimāna),
and having first prepared the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha), [one should install] Vāsudeva and the others in their proper sequence.
Having visualized [the deity] from the worlds known as Ānanda and the others, one should invoke [Her], O Rame.
From the beginning of the mantra-installation (nyāsa) until the end of the offering of food, one should perform the oblation preceded by the mantra.
[One should then invoke] Vāsudeva, who is composed of consciousness, from the Vaikuṇṭha of Supreme Bliss.
Having invoked [the deity] into the great jar, the most excellent guru should perform worship;
I shall now describe that ritual sequence to you, O daughter of the Ocean of Milk.
The earthly realm, protected by Viṣṇu, is joined with [the worlds of] humans and others.
One should meditate upon [the deity] in the sky above the earth, accompanied by Gandharvas and others;
one should meditate upon him protected by the Daśārhas, and above that, the circle of the twelve-fold self protected by Keśava and the other [Vāsudevas]. 23.152–153.
One should meditate upon the lunar orb, which is protected by Śrīśa;
above that is the realm protected by Mukunda and frequented by the Siddhas;
and the heavenly world (svargaloka) protected by Upendra and frequented by the gods.
There, in various places, are the cities of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), accompanied by their eightfold subtle bodies (puryaṣṭaka);
there also are the rows of palaces belonging to the hosts of gods beginning with the Vasus.
Above that is the world of that Great Splendor (Mahas), which is remembered [by the wise] and inhabited by Sanaka and the others.
Janaloka is constantly and well-inhabited by other great seers;
in that place, the god Janārdana is perpetually and most highly honored by them.
Above that, however, is Tapoloka, which is occupied by the Vairāja and others.

One should remember that it is protected by me in the form of Puruṣottama. Having meditated in the heart upon Satyaloka, which is served by the gods beginning with Brahmā and protected by Padmanābha, one should then mentally contemplate the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
Outside the egg as well, O Rameśvara, water is pervaded by fire;
fire is enveloped by air, and that [air] is pervaded by space from the outside. Beyond that is ego (ahaṃkāra), and beyond that is intellect (buddhi).

Then one should meditate upon the Unmanifest, which is declared to be the source of supreme joy (pramodana). That indeed is the Vaikuṇṭha of the same world (sālokya), [reached] by means of celestial chariots fashioned of gold,
and by variegated palaces and gate-towers made of various jewels.
It was surrounded by extraordinary, heart-stealing *kalpavṛkṣa* trees;
it possessed jeweled floors, stairways, and costly gem-encrusted altars;
it was a hundred *yojanas* in width and many hundreds in length.
In that first divine, supramundane realm, honored by the gods,
the Blessed One Aniruddha dwells together with Queen Māyā.
One should then remember Sāmīpya-Vaikuntha, which is full of fragrance, situated above.
As before, it was beautifully adorned with celestial palaces and gate-towers;
it was graced by five divine and most wonderful ramparts, ten thousand yojanas high and possessing a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns.
Its length was likewise a thousand yojanas, and its breadth was equal to that.
It was adorned by hundreds and thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu, who were intent on the deeds of the Blessed One and running here and there.

In that divine, supreme world, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, Pradyumna, who is affectionate toward his devotees, dwells happily together with Jayā. One should meditate upon Sārūpya-Vaikuṇṭha, which is described as full of joy.
It was endowed with a dust-free perimeter, adorned with seven enclosures,
measuring ten thousand yojanas in both width and length,
and radiant with palaces and other structures possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred thousand suns.
[He was surrounded] by divine beings bearing conchs and discs, endowed with four arms,
wearing yellow garments, broad-chested, with eyes like lotus petals,
praising, dancing, and singing with devotion.
Surrounded by them, the Lord of the World, the Teacher of the World,
the divine Saṃkarṣaṇa, dwells upon that easy throne together with Kīrti.
Above is the vast Vaikuṇṭha of union, known as Ānanda.
Extending for a hundred thousand yojanas in width and of equal length, it was auspicious,
endowed with nine enclosures, and possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it shone with celestial palaces and was adorned with archways and other ornaments.
[He was surrounded] by those who were self-luminous, embodiments of Viṣṇu, as pure as the rays of the autumn moon;
by various and innumerable hosts like clusters of stars,
glorious, with dark-complexioned limbs, and possessing prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Surrounded by them, Vāsudeva sat upon the seat of enjoyment with Lakṣmī;
he held the Sudarśana for the sake of stability, the Pāñcajanya for the granting of liberation,
and the Kaumodakī for the destruction of enemies and the establishment of dharma.

Holding the Nandaka sword and the Śārṅga bow, he sits upon a throne to be enjoyed by Lakṣmī. And then, O lotus-eyed one, ten million yojanas above that is the supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, named Paramānanda.
Extending for ten million *yojanas* in width and rising to the same height in length,
it was adorned with variegated walls and gate-towers made of divine jewels,
and it shone with rows of houses fashioned from various kinds of gems.
It was adorned with lofty palaces resembling a multitude of Indra’s rainbows,
and graced by men possessing the luster of a thousand moons;
all were pure, four-armed, and possessed forms equal to their own Lord.
All of them bear the conch and the discus, wear garlands, and are clothed in yellow garments;
they are composed of the non-material, eternal, and free from rebirth.
They are [honored] by the Veda known as Ekāyana and also by hymns beginning with "Jita."
The radiance of their bodies was equal to ten million autumn moons;
all those women had eyes like lotuses, were graced with eternal youth,
were endowed with every auspicious mark, and were like Lakṣmī herself.
They rejoice in the supreme, imperishable sky, which consists of eternal bliss;
they too worship and praise the Lord of Ramā,
who is composed of splendor, resides within that [palace], and is endowed with four gates.
It was adorned with walls, divine staircases, and gate-towers;
it was well-guarded by gatekeepers such as Caṇḍa and others, as well as by Kumuda and his companions;
and it was perfumed by the fragrance of divine sandalwood, musk, and camphor.
It was adorned with archways fashioned from various kinds of jewels;
it possessed a thousand pillars of gems, was provided with canopies and altars,
and was surrounded on all sides by celestial wish-fulfilling trees such as the Pārijāta and others.
A pavilion of supreme bliss with stairs constructed on all sides;
[in its center, at a spot of stainless stability, joined with twelve pillars, provided with doors on both sides, and adorned by a pavilion of liberation].
The celestial chariot of Soma, adorned with three peaks,
possessed a divine lion-throne in its center, supported by the wise ones beginning with Dharma;
it was divine, consisting of the four Vedas, and equipped with all their limbs and sub-limbs.
In the center of that is an auspicious eight-petaled lotus consisting of the eight syllables.
Upon it, on a couch of Ananta variegated with the jewels of his hoods,
[is the deity] who has two hands, one face, and resembles pure crystal.

[His lotus-feet were adorned with heroic ornaments and anklets; his lovely golden garment shone with the splendor of the morning sun. The regions of the sky were illuminated by the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem shining upon his chest. 23.196-23.197ab.
His chest was resplendent with a forest garland composed of gems, gold, and fine pearls,
together with a sacred thread;
his hands were adorned with magnificent and precious finger-ornaments consisting of ruby bracelets.
With his left arm draped down to his knee and the other likewise,
resting his face— which resembled the rising moon— upon the lap of the Ocean of Compassion,
and with brilliant earrings clinging to his radiant cheeks.
His facial orb shone with the moonlight of a gentle smile;
his eyes were like slightly reddish cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses;
and it was radiant with a tilaka mark rising upon his forehead, resembling the young crescent moon.
He possesses the form of a priceless jewel, shimmering with the luster of his crown;
his body is illuminated by the light from the rubies upon the hoods of his serpent-couch.
He is easily accessible through true devotion, yet difficult for all [ordinary] scriptures to reach.
Invisible to all beings, yet through compassion he has become visible;
his form is inexhaustible nectar, consecrated for the protection of the distressed—
the divine Vāsudeva, higher than the highest, lying upon his back.
The Teacher of the worlds is to be worshipped by means of the twelve-syllable vidyā and others;
he alone is the Blessed Lord, the god who is immutable, immovable, and eternal.
He is inconceivable to all beings, ungraspable, and indeed the Imperishable (akṣara).
He is eternal, truth, the immortal, the unmanifest, beyond darkness;
stainless and devoid of qualities, he is forever established in his own self.
He who is called both being and non-being is the primordial Brahman, higher than the highest.
That very Lord, the God, is served by the conch, the discus, and other [emblems];
his consort is likewise equal to him in virtue, beauty, and qualities.
She is steady, resembling a mass of radiance from a thousand rising *campaka* flowers.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she was graced by a divine garment as white as the foam of the milk-ocean;
she was distinguished by a mass of hair that was exceedingly glossy, dark blue, and beautifully lustrous.
Shining with four arms, adorned with armlets and bracelets,
she always joins her palms in the añjali gesture with her two principal hands;
with her other two hands, she holds the lotus-feet of the Blessed One.
Śrī, assuming a divine form, always remains there, touching him with devotion.
O Rame, having meditated upon that Vāsudeva in the mind,
the best of gurus should offer prayers during the consecrations of the images of the manifestations such as the Fish and others.
In the Vaikuṇṭha known as Dharmānanda, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent and surrounded by a pure ocean of milk as bright as ten thousand full moons,
it is beautified by seven walls fashioned from refined gold.
In that [city], which is adorned with divine gate-towers (gopura) and other structures shimmering with the nine gems,
and which is frequented by the wise, including the gatekeepers such as Jaya;
in its central pavilion, upon the auspicious couch of Śeṣa—
Born from the array of emanations, Padmanābha is endowed with Śrī and Bhūmi;
he has four arms and is adorned with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the bow.
Thus [one should meditate upon] the Lord of Gods, the primordial cause of manifestation, as he lies thus asleep.
Having thus meditated upon the lotus-eyed one, one should then worship him within the water-pot (kumbha).
In whichever world Vāsudeva and the others reside,
one should first mentally worship the Lord of the World in that respective realm.
Then, holding a handful of flowers, he should praise the Lord of the World:
"Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one! Salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One!"
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, whose self is peaceful, infinite, and victorious;
salutations to the sovereign, the independent, the eternal, the one who is without need, the infallible, the changeless, the treasury of splendors.
Salutations to You, the embodiment of the six perfections, untouched by afflictions, karma, and the like;
salutations to You, whose inner self consists of the three types of knowledge, power, sovereignty, valor, and potency;
salutations to You, the Lord of the Three Ages; salutations to You, the fourfold Self.

Homage to you, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, O Supreme Person! Homage to you who possess four, five, nine, manifold, ten, and twelve forms; to you who are of many forms, yet formless, and of a single form.
O Nārāyaṇa, homage be to you, whose eyes are as long as lotuses;
O you with beautiful brows, forehead, and nose, and with lovely-smiling lips like young shoots;
O you with full, rounded, and long arms, marked with the Śrīvatsa.
O you of slender waist, wide eyes, and lotus-navel, homage be to you!
O you whose lotus-feet have traversed the three worlds with graceful prowess,
homage to you, wearer of yellow garments, adorned with shimmering makara-earrings!
O Lord adorned with a shimmering crown, armlets, the Kaustubha gem, and bracelets;
O wielder of the five weapons, homage be to you, homage to you, O Pāñcakālika!
O Lord who brings about the security and well-being of those solely devoted to the five-fold time-observance!
O Acyuta, whose eternal knowledge, power, sovereignty, and enjoyments are self-sustained!
Homage to you, the initiator of the worldly course for Brahmā, Rudra, and the rest!
From birth onwards, I am your servant, your disciple, and your son.
"And you, Mādhava, are my master, my guru, my mother,
and my father. Even now, O Blessed One, even Brahmā, Śarva, Śakra, and the great seers are not able to see, worship, or praise you."

O Lord, for those sinking in the ocean of existence, made terrifying by the great crocodiles of the three-fold suffering, this prostration offered at Your feet is a boat. O Lord of the World, protector of the helpless, to me who seeks refuge, [grant protection].
Be gracious to me who am sinking; salutations to You, O lover of Your devotees!
Whatever worship has been performed by me—whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion—[may it be accepted].
Therefore, you must forgive those who have sought refuge, for you are indeed one who endures the offenses of others.
O Hari, I am a vessel for a thousand offenses, fallen into the belly of the terrifying ocean of existence;
I am without recourse and have come to you for shelter—out of pure compassion, make me your own.
O Supreme Person, O Lord of the World, forgive all these transgressions committed by me day after day under the pretext of ritual service,
according to the procedure taught by you in the *Pāñcarātra*.
Having fashioned gate-towers and other celestial palaces according to the prescribed rites,
O Janārdana, I desire to worship you with devotion there— you, the Lord who assumes the form of an image together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
