O you whose form is mantra, O you who pervade the universe, having arrived together with Viṣvaksena and the other attendants, as well as Garuḍa and the celestial chariot,
please enter into this image out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world.
"O All-pervading Lord, accept this worship being constantly performed by me.
O Lord of the World, come here out of a desire to show me favor.
Having meditated thus, the solar orb then arrived from that world.
Then, O Lotus-born one, one should first place the jewel-encrusted sandals upon the feet of Vāsudeva residing in the world of the Sun;
likewise, having offered them to Śrī, one should then place them upon those of Viṣṇu and the others.
Having meditated thus upon Vāsudeva, who consists of the universe, the consecrated lord,
having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) together with the eight forms beginning with Viṣṇu,
should meditate upon him within the great jar and the other jars, and then offer prayers.
Form characterized by bliss, the primordial form, unchanging, extremely subtle, self-dependent, independent, the supreme light, free from affliction,
eternal, one, consciousness-bliss, the nature of consciousness, all-pervading, and supreme.
It is eternally pure by its very nature, waveless, and undisturbed; it is boundless, beyond all qualities, yet endowed with qualities and the granter of all desires;
it is the object of meditation upon meditation, a marvel that transcends the reach of speech and mind.
[He beheld] the Lord, the omnipresent one named Vāsudeva, whose form embodies the six political expedients (ṣāḍguṇya),
seated comfortably upon the throne of Śeṣa, which was variegated by the luster of jewels covering his thousand hoods; his right foot was extended.
His right foot is bent, with that arm resting upon the knee;
his left arm is placed on the couch of Śeṣa, and Lakṣmī rests upon his chest.
He is adorned with a crown and earrings, and shines with a forest garland.
The Guru should meditate upon [the deity] in the central pitcher as wearing yellow garments, gentle, adorned with bracelets and other ornaments, and being served by his attendants:
"O Vāsudeva, source of the universe, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss!"
"As long as I pray to the image, so long remain firm within the jar.
O Supreme Person, accept this worship offered by me.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Lakṣmī with the mudrā of prayer, the Guru—
Having offered prayers, one should first worship the deity in the central jar according to the prescribed rite.
Then, in the jars of the east and other directions, one should worship those [deities] seated upon lotus-thrones,
facing Vāsudeva, and clad in pure yellow garments.

[He should visualize] Viṣṇu and the others, endowed with these characteristics in their proper order: four-armed, with gentle faces, adorned with crowns and other ornaments, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wearing forest garlands. || 23.256–23.257 ||
The preceptor, the most excellent knower of mantras, should invoke and worship them all;
having fashioned the supreme wheel of a thousand spokes, whose form is blazing radiance,
he should perform the invocation for the removal of all obstacles.
For the sake of pacifying the fatigue of all [beings], one should thus worship with water for the hands and other offerings.
And that guru who has been appointed for the consecration of the temple [should visualize Vāsudeva] as having arrived,
situated within the solar disc.
Having meditated upon that vimāna together with its retinue and the deity presiding over it,
and having visualized Aniruddha within the central pitcher, one should then offer this prayer:
"O You of wondrous form, with a thousand heads, feet, hands, and eyes!"
"O you who possess the form of a celestial chariot, remain steady here until I have invoked [the deity] into this jar, within the inner sanctum, and into the aerial vehicle. Then,
in the jars of that [sanctum], starting from the east, [one should invoke] Narottama and Madhokṣaja."
The wise one should then meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, Acyuta, Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa in the water-pot, and the King of Discuses (Cakrarāja) within the vessel.
O Rāma, one should thus invoke the deities within the mandala of the discus and lotus.
One should worship the gods, Puruhūta and the others, in the outer enclosure (23.265).
In the doors of the middle enclosure, starting from the east and in due order,
one should worship the gods Caṇḍa and the others in pairs on the ground situated in front of the eastern door (23.266).
One should meditate on the god, the son of Vinatā, facing the maṇḍala;
and [one should visualize] the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in the middle of the doors starting from the east. Then, one should meditate on Senāpati in the northeast within the inner enclosure.
In the corners beginning with the southeast, [one should place] Varāha,
Narasiṃha, Ananta, and Hayagrīva;
these are seated upon their thrones in the center of the pericarp of the lotus within the wheel, adorned with a thousand hoods.
Upon the seat of the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, [He] bestows creation, maintenance, dissolution, and liberation;
dark-complexioned like the neck of a peacock, with one face and four arms,
resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, the Nandaka sword, and other weapons.
His chest was radiant with the Śrīvatsa mark, and he was adorned with a forest garland;
he shone with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments;
wearing yellow garments, he was gentle and the primordial cause of the worlds.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Vāsudeva, who has arisen from the Supreme Vāsudeva, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, seated comfortably within the solar disc.
On the filaments [of the lotus] is the twelve-syllable mantra, and on the eight petals is the eight-syllable mantra.
One should meditate upon Keśava and the other [forms] on the twelve petals, starting from the east and proceeding in order,
adorned with the Śrīvatsa and other marks, just like Viṣṇu and the others; having invoked them,
the wise man should worship them with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and so forth, for the sake of quelling fatigue.
Having thus invoked the deities, Vāsudeva and the others, who reside within the fire situated in the pitcher-maṇḍala,
one should then worship them up to the offering of food (prāpaṇa), O Goddess, preceded by the seat of the mantra, but excluding the bathing seat.
At the time of the ritual placement of the mantras for the twenty-five deities beginning with Vāsudeva,
the instructors should, while moving clockwise across the four cubit [mandala], likewise visualize their divine weapons.
O Rame, those who know the mantras should show him the respective mudrā;
there is a second Vāsudeva, and both of them are born from that.
Likewise, there is another Vāsudeva who is known as Nārāyaṇa.
One should likewise visualize the deities beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa in their hands, in due order:
the lotus, the discus, the conch, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow.
Now, the ritual placement of the mudrās for the twenty-four forms is described.
The all-pervading Vāsudeva, bearing the mace, conch, discus, and lotus;
Saṃkarṣaṇa, endowed with the mace, conch, lotus, and discus;
and Pradyumna, adorned with the discus, lotus, mace, and lotus.
One should meditate upon Aniruddha, who holds a discus, a mace, a lotus, and a conch;
upon Keśava, whose hands are adorned with a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a mace;
and upon Nārāyaṇa, resplendent with a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus.
Mādhava, the all-pervading Lord, who holds the divine mace, discus, conch, and lotus;
Govinda, adorned with the discus, mace, lotus, and the Pāñcajanya conch; Viṣṇu, the wearer of the forest garland, who bears the mace, lotus, conch, and discus.
Madhudviṣa, endowed with the discus, conch, lotus, and mace;
Trivikrama, the all-pervading Lord, bearing the lotus, mace, discus, and conch;
and Vāmana, holding the Pāñcajanya conch, the enemy-slaying mace, and the lotus.
The Lord Śrīdhara, who holds the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the conch;
Hṛṣīkeśa, endowed with the mace, the discus, the lotus, and the conch in his arms;
and Padmanābha, joined with the lotus, the discus, the conch, and the Kaumodakī mace.
One should meditate upon Dāmodara, who bears the lotus, conch, mace, and discus;
upon Narottama, joined with the discus, lotus, conch, and Kaumodakī mace;
and upon Adhokṣaja, adorned with the weapons of the lotus, staff, conch, and spear.
[Nārada saw] Nṛsiṃha with four arms holding a discus, a lotus, a mace, and a conch;
Acyuta, resplendent with a staff, a lotus, a discus, and a conch;
and Janārdana, bearing a lotus, a discus, a conch, and the Kaumodakī mace.
The Guru should meditate upon Upendra, adorned with the lotus-stalk and the Pāñcajanya conch;
upon Hari, whose body is embellished by the conch, the enemy of the lotus (the mace), and the lotus;
and upon Kṛṣṇa, endowed with the conch, the mace, the lotus, and the discus.

Having thus recollected [the deity], one should display the mudrās, O Lotus-born One, on the seventh, the fifth, or even on the third day and so forth. One should perform the consecration of the Lord; one should not conceive of it otherwise, O All-pervading One.
Excluding the day of the consecration,
one should perform worship of Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, for twelve, eight, or even four periods of time, offering either a thousand or eight hundred oblations in each instance.

O auspicious lady, the worship previously described should be performed individually upon the pitcher (kumbha), the mandala, and the fire at those respective times, or rather, as the most excellent guru may direct.
Having indeed performed the worship upon the pitcher, one should then complete the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
At those respective times,

having performed the worship according to rule with the corresponding number of offerings in the three vessels beginning with the *kumbha*, and having offered the four kinds of food, O Rame, those who know the mantras should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā;
[now begins] the twenty-fourth chapter.
Then, in the afternoon, having especially adorned the images with garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth, consecrated with the mantras of one's own deity,
and having worshipped them with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should bind the *kautuka* thread in the proper sequence.
Having installed the Lord of the World upon an auspicious throne made of gold and other materials, along with Śrī and Bhūmi,
and having consecrated other divine images, the supreme guru—
while others were reciting the *Śākuna-sūkta* and the hymn beginning with "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ"— [performed the rite].
Likewise, with Brahmins chanting the Rathantara Sāman and even the three Vedas, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, conchs, and those bearing parasols and other regalia,
[he circumambulated] the temple clockwise with other requisites for the procession.
Having led [the deity] to the bank of a river or similar place and having sprinkled it with holy water,
the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should establish the Lord facing east upon a pedestal there and perform the *puṇyāhavācana* ceremony.
It was situated in the midst of pure water, capable of withstanding wind and rain;
it was provided with four gates and adorned with four archways,
equipped with canopies and banners, and hung with nets of pearls.
In the center of the pavilion, upon a delightful bed-platform provided with pillows and adorned with a soft covering, one should place an image in accordance with its size; then,
having sprinkled the pavilion and other areas with meritorious waters, one should consecrate them.
First, one should purify the water of rivers and other sources by means of draining and similar methods;
then, having displayed the image of the daughter of Surabhi, one should perform the worship of the gateway.
Then, having mentally conceived a pedestal upon a bed situated in the midst of the water, one should worship it.
Above that, having reached the shore, the preceptor should place the bed of Śeṣa;
O fair-faced one, he should set down nine jars and a water-pot upon a prepared seat of grain on the ground in front of the deity.
Having invoked Viśākha and Yūpa into the *kumbha*, and the radiant Cakrin into the *karaka*,
one should worship Indra and the other deities in the *upakumbhas* in due order.
With the root mantra of the deity, the preceptor should offer the *arghya* and other oblations.
One should gradually withdraw the individual soul (jīva), which identifies with the physical form, into the Heart-lotus.
Having meditated upon the Self as all-pervading, omniscient, partless, and sovereign, the practitioner,
endowed with the proper disposition, should perform that consecration (adhivāsana) of Viṣṇu.
Having established the individual soul, which identifies with the image, by means of the *praṇava*,
and having caused it to ascend and achieve oneness with the Self, one should contemplate Lord Hari, the Master of the Self, within oneself.
Having purified the defiled earth and having burnt the seeds with the fire, [one should proceed].
Having drenched it with water and dried it with air, one should dissolve it in fire; then,
having withdrawn the fire by means of the air, one should lead the air to the state of space,
together with the internal and divine instruments and their objects.

Having withdrawn those [elements] established in their respective subtle states (tanmātra) in due order, the teacher should dissolve space into the mind, and that mind again into the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti). He should then lead that [ego] into the Great Self (mahat), and bring even that into oneness with the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta).
One should meditate upon him in Vāsudeva, the self of all, who is peace, the infinite, the supreme ether, partless, and whose form is knowledge;
in whom the unmanifest is dissolved, and whose very nature is that state.
Having withdrawn the earth and the other elements into that very [liṅga], the preceptor should cover the images with cloths from the feet up to the head,
by the command of Bhaṭṭācārya, while the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) are most proficient in the mantras.

Reciting the Śākuna hymn at evening, they should lead the imperishable Viṣṇu to his bed situated upon the water, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi; with the mantra beginning "ambhasya," they should place Hari there with his head toward the east and facing north.
First, one should have [the deities] lie down with the two goddesses; then, in the surrounding quarters, one should place the other [vessels].
One should place the central jar and the water-pot (karaka) at the head-end.
Having placed jars around the images, one should deposit them in their respective directions.

With the mantra "rakṣohaṇa," one should display the wheel mudrā. O lotus-eyed one, the officiating priests, instructed by the preceptor, having entered the sacrificial hall, should perform worship at the three locations according to the rules.
The preceptor, together with the devotees of the Lord, shall narrate Vaiṣṇava stories;
the Brahmins shall cause the Purāṇas and the four Vedas to be recited. On the banks [of the river], those skilled in lutes shall play all kinds of musical instruments.
Then the dancing girls, along with singers, should delight Hari with their dances.
Having thus spent the night there, all of us, filled with devotion,
shall enjoy ourselves for a day, or three watches, or even two watches.
One should practice dwelling in the water for a watch (yāma) or even half a watch;
as long as Hari lies within the water, so long should mortals remain in that water.
Having entered, they may perform bathing, drinking, and so forth, as well as treading with their feet [as they wish].
The best of teachers should not perform [the rite] in such places; rather, protection should be established [elsewhere].
This applies even to waters that are foul-smelling, astringent, muddy, alkaline, bitter, or frothy.
O Hari, O Rame, one should not perform water-dwelling and other such rites in places defiled by cremation grounds and the like, or those inhabited by Caṇḍālas; however,
in the absence of pure water, one may do so in a water cistern or a natural water source.
The consecration of the water for Hari must be performed right at the water-shed (*prapā*).
At dawn, the preeminent teacher, having bathed and performed his daily rites,
and having sipped water (*ācamana*) when the time for rising has arrived, the Guru—
One should offer the *kumuda* and other oblations together with the officiating priests and the image-protectors.
Having raised the images from the water, as well as the large jar and the smaller vessels,
and having placed the images upon their pedestals, the preceptor should remove the cloths.
One should perform the creation of the principles (*tattva*) for the images preceded by their ritual installation (*nyāsa*).
First, one should purify the metal images with the water of *tintriṇī* (soapberry), and then,
having smeared them from head to foot with the aforementioned clays.
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with the central jar, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Immediately thereafter, having dismissed the deities residing in the subsidiary jars,
one should place the images upon vehicles and adorn them with garments and ornaments.
Together with the requisites for the procession, one should lead [the deity] to the temple;
and the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ) should place the representative images upon the seats.
The preceptor (ācārya), the most excellent knower of mantras, [should proceed] together with the teacher of the temple (prāsādaguru).
One should contemplate the deities within the images, starting from the shadow, the consecrated seat, and the pedestal.
With the central jar, one should bathe the primary image, as well as the pinnacle;
this applies to large images made of metal and the like, as well as those made of clay.

In the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), the most excellent of gurus should likewise perform the ritual dwelling of the shadow (chāyādhivāsa), the ceremonial bath (snapana), and the offering of the gaze (dṛgdāna) for those images made of lime (sudhā), as well as for those situated on walls and those half-painted with frescoes.
The preceptor of the temple should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the reflected images of the deities made of sudhā and other materials in a mirror provided with a tuft of wool;
he should perform the preliminary consecration of the reflection (chāyādhivāsa) in the forenoon and the immersion in water (jalavāsana) in the afternoon.
Likewise, there should be the gift of the eyes and the laying down [of the image] during the great night;

at dawn, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) prescribed by the scriptures. Furthermore, this applies to the ritual immersion in water and likewise to the opening of the eyes.
O Rame, there should be no other time for the installation on the bed;
one should first bathe [the image] with nine or five jars before the opening of the eyes, and only then perform the opening of the eyes.
Having performed the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), the fire-oblation (homa), and other rites, the best of preceptors should again bathe Puruṣottama with the previously mentioned jars;
then he should lay the Lord of the gods upon the bed together with his two consorts.
Having awakened [the deity] in the morning, one should present the enjoyments (bhogas) in succession, like a queen. Then,
having consecrated the deity with seventeen, sixteen, or twelve jars, one should offer food made of mung beans.
On the day of the consecration, at dawn, one should sprinkle the Victorious One with thirty, twenty-five, or twenty-one jars.
On the following morning, [one should do so] with one hundred and eight jars.
Or else, O Rame, one should bathe the Lord with eighty-one jars, or with a number diminished by one,
or with fifty jars accompanied by two goddesses.
Having bathed the Lord according to the rite, the Guru, prior to the gift of the eyes, [should proceed].
Having adorned the image with garments and the like, and covered it with a cloth,
the supreme guru, having placed an excellent golden vessel upon a pedestal of grain in front, and having set down another silver vessel... [24.56]
One should fill [the vessel] with honey measured by one āḍhaka, and likewise with clarified butter.
Having sprinkled a golden or silver probe eight finger-breadths long with water from the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) rite, one should purify it by means of drying and other such methods.
One should meditate upon the flawless Nārāyaṇa, who has the luster of a *pāṭala* flower in his honey-cupped hand, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, who is endowed with the *tejomudrā*,
and who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace, emerging from the orb of the sun.
Resembling ten million moons and accompanied by the *dhenu-mudrā*,
Hayagrīva is situated within a lunar disc in the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*).
With the mantra "madhuvātā" one offers honey, and with "savirāja" one offers ghee.
Having performed the mantra-ritual, the Guru should then cover [the vessel] with a new cloth;
he should then invoke the Eight Lakṣmīs, well-adorned young maidens, into the eight vessels filled with eight kinds of grain.
And one should also station cows at the side while the sound of the Veda is being intoned.
When the doors have been closed without gaps by means of a curtain,
[one should take] a golden probe consecrated with the Netra-mantra.
Having taken up a blade smeared with honey, one should scrape the right eye;
then, with a blade smeared with clarified butter, one should thoroughly scrape the left eye.
One should visualize Nārāyaṇa and Hayagrīva within the two vessels at the eyes.
One should show the eight grains, cows, and maidens to Hari and Rame. Then the preceptor, with a vessel containing honey and clarified butter and two probes,
[should perform the rite] for Śrī, Bhūmi, Vīra-lakṣmī, and also for Tārkṣya, Senā, and Payas.
And for those situated on the ramparts, he should perform the opening of the eyes;
then, O Lotus-born One, the Guru should bathe the God of gods according to the prescribed ritual for the images installed at the gate-towers.

O Goddess, in former times, the preceptor of that [temple] should provide the installation of eyes for the temple, for the deities of the directions, and for other divine images. Having thus performed the installation of eyes, he should perform the consecration with shadows (chāyābhiṣecana).

Then, at the time of afternoon, the preeminent teacher should have the officiating priests bathe the metal images of the ritual objects and so forth according to the prescribed method. He should wipe the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) and the two goddesses with dry cloths.

Having adorned [the image] with garments and other ornaments, one should place it upon the previously prepared pedestal for the purpose of opening its eyes; having laid it down supine, [one should cover it] with threads made of gold.
Having completely covered all the limbs of the Lord of the World with blankets and other coverings,
when the evening hour has arrived, the preceptor, having placed vessels of honey, clarified butter, and grain upon a seat of grain as before, should perform the worship.
One should perform the opening of the eyes for the ritual image, the face, and so forth.
The most excellent of teachers should show eight kinds of grain, cows, and girls with auspicious marks at the eastern fire-pit for the sake of the rite of opening the eyes.
O Rame, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times each with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, using honey and likewise clarified butter;
having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings by means of the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Then, having offered the madhuparka, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the deity,
O Rame. The preceptor, having first covered with pure *darbha* grass the auspicious altar— which is one *tāla* high and situated to the left of the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)— [should proceed].
Having prepared a seat of grain, one should then place parched rice upon it;
above the parched rice, a new cloth, and above that, a jewel-embroidered blanket.
The Guru should then place a fresh linen garment together with a pillow.
Having sprinkled the bed with *puṇyāha* water, the preceptor,

together with the guardians of the images, should worship the Lord of Serpents upon it along with the goddesses; then, while recollecting the heart-mantra, he should lay him down on the bed with his head toward the east.
Having worshipped [the deity] seated upon the bed with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), perfumes, and other offerings, O fair-faced one,
the Guru should perform the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*) for the one seated on the bed by means of the root mantra (*mūla*).
This applies to the painted image and so forth, the primary icon (*mūlabimba*), and the portable image (*kautuka*) situated within the temple.

From the great root-icons (mūlabimba), the Guru should contemplate the principles beginning with the individual soul (jīvatattva) within the action-icon (karmabimba); then he should perform the oblation of the principles (tattvahoma). Having resolved upon the purpose of the principle-oblation, he should sprinkle that fire with water.
First uttering the *praṇava* (oṃ) of the presiding deity of each respective principle (*tattva*),
the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations at dawn with the names of those deities in the dative case, ending with *svāhā*, using the ghee of a tawny cow— twice or four times, O Rame.
The Guru should perform the placement (nyāsa) in those respective locations with the *sampāta* [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*,
while likewise recollecting their powers (śaktis), such as Śrī and the others.
He should then cause the place of the *sampāta*-placement to be sealed with the *praṇava*.

The wise practitioner should install Brahmā and the others, as well as the images of the devotees, in their respective places using the names of the principles (tattvas), and should then cover them with the Sāvitrī mantra.
Having first withdrawn the principles, one should then perform the installation according to the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa).
One should meditate on the seed-syllable *aṃ*, resembling the sun, which is called Vāsudeva;
one should place that principle of Īśvara in that location.
One should place the seed-syllable *maṃ*, the principle of Jīva, which has the luster of crystal, within the lotus of the heart.
Nārāyaṇa is the presiding deity (adhideva) of that which is known as primordial nature (prakṛti);
its seed-syllable is *bhaṃ*, and its deity is Aniruddha, who is white in color.
Upendra is the deity of the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), and he has the luster of crystal.

The seed-syllable *baṃ* is to be placed as before upon the lotus-eyed heart; egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) is pale-red in hue, with *phaṃ* as its seed-syllable and Hari as its deity—one should know its placement as before. Janārdana, however, is the deity of the mind.
One should know that which resembles white and black; one should place the seed-syllable *paṃ* in the heart.
Madhuhā (the Slayer of Madhu) is sound in the two ears; it is white, and its seed-syllable is said to be *naṃ*.
Trivikrama is touch on the skin; it has a reddish luster, and its seed-syllable would be *dhaṃ*.

The wise one should place the seed-syllable *daṃ*, which is the god Vāmana and the essence of form (*rūpatattva*) with the luster of his eyes; the learned one should place the seed-syllable *thaṃ*, which has a pale-white radiance, on the tongue as the essence of taste (*rasatattva*), known as Śrīdhara.

That seed-syllable *taṃ* is black in color; its presiding deity is Hṛṣīkeśa, the essence of sound. Its placement upon the nose is sanctioned by the scriptures. The sense-organ of hearing is pale-red in appearance; its seed-syllable is *ṇaṃ*, and its deity is Ramā.
The wise declare that Aniruddha is the placement in the region of the ears.
The seed-syllable *Ṭhaṃ* is gold-colored; the principle of the skin (*tvaktattva*) is Puruṣottama.
The placement upon the roots of the arms as the deity is enjoined by the scripture.
The principle of the eye is black in color; its seed-syllable is *ḍaṃ*, and its presiding deity is Adhokṣaja.
O Kamalasambhavā, one should place this in the middle of the eyes.
The principle of the tongue is fair in color; its seed-syllable is *ṭhaṃ*, and its deity is Nṛhari, O Ramā.

One adorned with the five-limbed ornaments should also place [the deity] upon the tongue of the goddess Rasana. Acyuta is the deity of the principle of the sense of smell; one should place the seed-syllable *ṭa* above the nose, which is said to be black in color.
Padmanābha, white in luster, is the presiding deity of the principle of speech (vāk-tattva).
By placing the seed-syllable *jñaṃ* upon speech, one shall attain all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The deity of the principle of the hand is red in color, and its seed-syllable is *jhaṃ*.

Dāmodara is the placement on the two arms; the lotus-born [Brahmā] is the principle of the feet, red in color, with *jaṃ* as the seed-syllable, and Saṃkarṣaṇa as the presiding deity. This placement on the feet is enjoined in the Pāñcarātra scriptures.
The seed-syllable *caṃ* shall have a red luster; its principle is the anus, and its deity is Vāsudeva.
O lotus-eyed one, one should place [this] upon the seat of the anus.
Pradyumna, however, is the presiding deity, and the seed-syllable *caṃ* possesses a golden color.
"The wise one should place [the syllable] *me* in the genitals, for they call *tattva* the organ of excretion.
Keśava, who resembles collyrium, is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of space (*ākāśa*). The seed-syllable *ṅaṃ* is the principle (*tattva*) of space; space is said to be formless. (24.108–109)
One should place [the mantra] originating from the crown of the head down to the end of the nose in that which arises from milk;
the deity is Māruta, the principle (tattva) is the stalk, and the seed-syllable is declared to be *gham*.
One should then place Nārāyaṇa sequentially from the region of the nose down to the navel.
The seed-syllable *gaṃ* is pale red and triangular, like the fire element (*tejas-tattva*).
The deity is Mādhava; from the navel to the end of the genitals, there is the sprinkling of clarified butter (*ājya*).
The seed-syllable *khaṃ* is white in color, and it is the water element (*ap-tattva*) joined with a half-moon.

Then Govinda, as the presiding deity (adhideva), should perform the placement up to the knees; the seed-syllable "Kaṃ," which is yellow in color and square in shape, O high-minded one, is the earth-element (pṛthvītattva) with Viṣṇu as its deity. One should perform the placement in sequence down to the feet.
The placement of the ten vital winds, beginning with Prāṇa, will now be described.
The seed-syllable *Yaṃ* is silver-colored; its presiding deity is the Fish (*Matsya*).
It should be placed in the Suṣumnā channel, from the navel to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), in due order.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, O Goddess, the preceptor should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*). The Lord of Apāna, whose seed-syllable is *raṃ*, who is dark-hued and assumes the form of a tortoise,
is intended to be placed upon the earth from the navel to the tip of the left nostril.

One should place the seed-syllable *laṃ*, which is dark blue in color, belonging to Vyānadeva, the bull-faced deity of the Lord of the World, upon the right nostril at the level of the navel within the Piṅgalā channel. Then, one should place the Nārasiṃha mantra, whose lord is Udāna, with the white-colored seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the navel and ending at the left eye within the goddess Gandhinī.
The lord of the *samāna* breath is golden; the seed-syllable *śaṃ* is the lord Vāmana.
One should place [the syllables] within Hastirasajñā, beginning at the navel and extending to the eyes.
Then one should place the seed-syllable *Saṃ*, which has the serpent as its presiding deity and is yellow in appearance, belonging to Bhārgava Rāma,
from the navel up to the left ear in the region called Pūṣan; there,
the turtle (*kūrma*) shall be the presiding deity of the channel, and the seed-syllable *Saṃ* shall have a dark-blue luster.
The preceptor should place Rāma at the end of the right ear in Yaśasvinī;
Balarāma is smoke-colored, his seed-syllable is "Haṃ," and he is the lord of Kṛkara.
The placement [of the deity] in Alambuṣā is desired from the navel down to the anus.
The blue Devadattādhipa, whose seed-syllable is *ḷaṃ*, is the slayer of Kaṃsa and Māra;
one should place him in the *kuhū* channel from the navel-center to the genitals, O Rame.
The white-colored Kalkī, the god Dhanañjaya, has the seed-syllable *kṣaṃ*. || 24.123–24.124 ||

O lotus-eyed one, the wise one should place the principles (tattvas), beginning with the individual soul (jīva) and the conceit of being the image (bimba-abhimāna), in the *kaiśinī* channel from the navel down to the tips of the toes,
in their proper order within the fire, for the sake of attaining the state of non-materiality (*aprākṛtatva*).
Having offered oblations in the manner previously described and having purified [the body] of the Teacher of the World,
O high-minded one, by repeatedly placing the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) upon his limbs,
one also abandons the state of being material through the installation of the deities.
Therefore, one should meditate upon me, the Lord, who am non-material, devoid of flesh and bone,
all-pervading, pure being, a mass of consciousness, and the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
by contemplating the reality of the forms of Brahmā and the others, one becomes non-material.
The placement of deities (*devatānyāsa*) and so forth should be performed for the image of the Blessed One alone;
for others, it should not be done, as there would be no rule for such a procedure.
Padmanābha, the sovereign lord of Brahmā, is situated to the right of the navel.
O Goddess, the place of Saṃkarṣaṇa is above the navel;
one should assign Indra to the right, and likewise perform the assignment on the left arm.
Then [one assigns] Narottama, Prajādhīśa, and the Lord of Sages.
Viṣṇu should be placed on the right shank, and the Lord of Yakṣas on the left.
Śrīdhara is the placement on the feet, while Gandharveśa is Vāmana. One should place Saṃvatsareśa, who is yellowish in complexion, and Acyuta upon the head.
One should place Keśava and the other lords of the months from the top down to the feet;
Vāsudeva, who is crystal-like in appearance and the lord of the syllable *praṇava*, [is placed] in the heart.
Nārāyaṇa, the lord of the skin and dark-complexioned, one should place upon the head.
O Goddess, [the placement] of the two deities Yajus and Sāman is on the south and north [shoulders].
Then, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna are at the region of the navel of the Atharvan;
and there is the placement of Aniruddha, Vṛkṣeśa, and Acyuta.
The Guru should place Abdhinātha, who is white as a conch, at the secret place; Trivikrama, the yellow Lord of Mountains, on the two shanks;
and Aniruddha, who has a dark-blue luster, the sovereign of the worlds.
One should place [the syllables] on the head, at the navel of Hari, and on the two feet, O Rame.
Having offered oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should then perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*.
One should place the six mantras beginning with the heart-mantra upon the locations starting from the heart.
One should place the crown on the head, the Śrīvatsa on the right shoulder,
the Kaustubha gem on the left side, and the forest garland around the neck. The placement of the discus and the conch is prescribed for the right and left hands respectively.
The supreme preceptor should place a mace in the left hand and a lotus in the right;
a Śārṅga bow in the left hand and an arrow in the right, along with the Kaṭinanda sword.
To the right of the God is Lakṣmī, and on his chest to the north is Bhūmi.
I shall describe the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two-armed form upon the lotus-seat: Vainateya at the base of the thighs and Ananta upon the lotus-feet.
On the right hand of the Lord is the discus, and on the left is the conch.

One should install the Kaumodakī and the Nandaka maces preceded by the Dhava rite. This installation applies to new images and temples; however, no such installation is prescribed for them during the restoration of old structures or rites such as sprinkling consecration (prokṣaṇa).
Having meditated upon the Śakti, who possesses a thousand heads, feet, hands, eyes, and so forth,
and who resides within the inner sanctum, one should perform the invocation preceded by visualization using twenty-five *kuśa* blades, each a span (*hasta*) in length and without a tuft.
Then the teacher, standing facing east in his sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
should thereafter deposit the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) upon the ritual grass (*kūrca*) by offering clarified butter, O fair-faced one;
the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is considered additional, as is the deposition of the celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
One should place Satyaloka on the head and Tapoloka on the face;
Janaloka in the middle of the throat and Mahaloka between the arms;
Svargaloka in the lower part [of the body] and Bhuvarloka on the belly.
One should place the intermediate space (antarikṣa) at the region of the navel, and the world known as Bhūrloka in the middle.

Then, one should assign the path of the feet, extending downward as far as the forepart of the feet; furthermore, one should place the Atala world in the private parts and the Vitala world, so named, in the thighs.
The region called Nitala is on the two thighs; Rasātala is at the region of the knees;
Sutala is on the two shanks; and Talātala is on the two feet.
Then, O Goddess, the Guru should assign Pātāla to the two foreparts of the feet.
Then, O Rame, one should perform the placement of time and space according to the sequence of the emanation-arrangement (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*):
one should place the first *parārdha* on the head and the second on the hair;
one should place the *Svāyaṃbhuva* on the nose and the *Svārociṣa* on the speech.
One should place the mantra called Tāmasa on the chin and the throat;
one should place the one called Raivata in the middle of the throat and Cākṣuṣa on the chest;
the Vaivasvata mantra and the one named Sūryasāvarṇi in the heart.
O one born from the water, [he placed] the one named Dattasāvarṇi in the region of the navel in the belly;
likewise, he placed Brahmasāvarṇika on the two roots of the thighs,
and the one named Rudrasāvarṇi between the thighs.
O lotus-eyed one, one should place Dharmasāvarṇika on the knees, the one named Raucya on the shanks, and Bhaucya on the pair of feet;
O blameless one, one should place the Kṛta Yuga on the face and the Tretā Yuga [on the chest].
One should place Dvāpara on the thighs and Kali on the feet. The best of gurus should place Saṃvatsara on the forehead and Parivatsara on the heart, and Idāvatsara in the region of the navel.
One should know that the *idāvatsara* year is placed on the two knees, and the *vatsara* year on the two lotus-feet.
O Lotus-born One, one should place the *dakṣiṇāyana* in the right hand,
and the *uttarāyaṇa* in the other, left hand.

One should place Spring, Summer, and the Rainy season on the shoulder; Autumn, Winter, and the Dewy season on the middle, the right side, and the left side respectively. One should place Mārgaśīrṣa on the head and Taiṣa between the eyebrows.
One should place the month of Māgha in the nose and Phālguna in the mouth;
O Lotus-born One, one should place Caitra in the throat, Vaiśākha on the chest, and Jyeṣṭha in the heart;
likewise, the Guru [should place] Āṣāḍha in the belly and the navel.
O Goddess, one should place Śrāvaṇa at the root of the thighs and Bhādrapada;
likewise, Aśvayuja at the knees and Kārtika at the shanks and feet. One should place the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) in the left eye and the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) in the other.
One should place [the letters] from *kalā* up to the end of the day from the head down to the soles of the feet;
one should assign the night to the hair on the head and the day to the forehead;
the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) to the joints, and the watches (*yāmān*) to the two eyes.
Having placed [the breath] for a moment in the mouth, for a nāḍī in the throat, for a kṣaṇa in the region of the chest,
for a kalā in the navel, for a kāṣṭhā in the secret place,
for a lava at the two knees, and then for a truṭi in the two feet, one should thereafter proceed along the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan).

The preceptor should thus place [the mantras] on the respective limbs of the one born from a lotus: a Brāhmaṇa on the face, a Kṣatriya on the two arms, one born from the thighs (an Ūruja) on the two thighs, a Śūdra on the two feet, and those born in the natural order (Anuloma) on the joints. (24.170)
Having placed the *udgītha* at the crown of the head, one should place the six-syllable mantra in the mouth;
the twelve-syllable mantra in the heart, and the six-syllable mantra in the region of the navel.
Then, having raised the image with the mantra "Arise" (*uttiṣṭha*), [one should proceed].
Having brought [the image] to the bathing pavilion, the preceptor should bathe it according to the prescribed rite, having offered sattvic foods, betel leaf, and mouth-perfume. Then,
having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for that image, the wise one should lead it to the place of the bed.
And in a beautiful pavilion, having prepared a seat of grain upon the altar,
[one should place] a very firm, smooth, auspicious pedestal made of wood,
ivory, silver, gold, or other materials, which is four-cornered and elongated, and provided with four legs.
O Rame, one should place a couch known as a *khaṭvā* upon that;
on it, a swing made of jewels, adorned with hundreds of small bells, filled with soft pillows and cotton, and draped with hanging strings of pearls.
Having prepared such a bed, perfumed with agallochum and scented with camphor and other fragrances, the Guru,
having spread a mass of sesame seeds upon a couch known as a *khaṭvā* near the swing, [should proceed].
Above that, O beloved, one should place either a tiger skin or a deer skin;
then one should arrange eight water-pots (kalaśas) in order, starting from the east.
One should place the *vyūhakumbha* at the head-side and the *karaka* on the right.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water consecrated for a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha), one should perform the worship of the door and other rites.
One should meditate upon Viśākha on the sacrificial post (yūpa) and Sudarśana in the large pitcher (kumbha) and the small jar (karaka);
having invoked Indra and the other deities in the secondary pitchers (upakumbha), one should worship them.

The best of teachers, having worshipped the Lord of the Gods upon a swing with the goddesses using the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," should place Him, whose head is toward the east, upon a couch in a palanquin. || 24.182 ||
O Rame, one should have [the image] lie upon a bed with the mūrtipās, with its head toward the east;
having worshipped it thoroughly with arghya and other offerings, [one should present] foods cooked in ghee,
the four kinds of food, and various fruits.
Having offered cow’s milk, fresh butter, and likewise sugar combined together,
one should present betel leaf accompanied by mouth-fresheners.
Then, reciting the *varma* mantra, the best of the initiated should perform the *nīrājana* rite.
Then, one should cover all the limbs with fragrant clothing.

Next, for the sake of protection, one should display the wheel-mudrā accompanied by the mantra. Then, during the remainder of the night, one should [entertain] the Lord with lute music and other such performances.

The preeminent teacher (deśikendra), having thus spent the time until dawn with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), should satisfy the patron (yajamāna) and have him lie down for the sake of the success of the dream, once he has fasted, bathed well, and is endowed with self-restraint. || 24.188 ||
Having performed the daily rites such as bathing and having entered the pavilion with the officiating priests,
and having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods preceded by the worship of the door, O Rāma,
I raised him from his bed along with the goddesses.

Having offered food, milk, and other substances along with the *arghya* and other honors, the preceptor, after meditating on Hari, should ask the awakened patron— who has bathed and arrived at the pavilion— about his dream, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.

If there is an inauspicious omen, the lord of the place should, for the sake of its pacification, perform an oblation in the fire with the mantra of the Lord of Dreams, encased by the *astra* mantra, reciting "Destroy the fault, destroy it! Svāhā! twenty-eight times.
Having offered clarified butter (*ājya*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the foot up to the knee upon the image (*kautuka*).
Then, having offered curd (*dadhi*), one should touch [the image] starting from the knee up to the navel with it.
Having offered milk (*kṣīra*), one should perform the placement starting from the navel up to the nose.
Having likewise offered oblations with honey, he should touch [the deity] from the nose up to the head.
Having brought the Lord, together with the goddesses, to the bathing pavilion,
he should bathe him according to the scriptures and worship him according to the prescribed rule.

Having offered the food and other items, one should meditate upon the Śakti who has come forth from the primary image as being present in the vessel used for invocation, and then join her back to the root [image].
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should pray with this verse:

O Lord, you are omniscient and perfected through the six divine attributes. O God, you cannot be reached even by many years of practice by yogis or even by the gods; how much less can mortals behold your body?
O Bearer of the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Person!
Just as fire is hidden within pieces of wood, so you, the all-pervading Lord, abide [within all].
Nevertheless, for the sake of the world, I pray to you with devotion through this image.
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, O Acyuta, reveal yourself to your devotees!
Accept this worship offered by me out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods, one should worship him with offerings of water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Having offered food and other oblations, one should then praise Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World;
and one should cause the Brāhmaṇas to recite the mantra beginning with "O Creator," as well as the verse "He who has eyes on all sides," and the verse "The Lord of the Universe."
Following that, he recited "dvā suparṇā," then "ato devā," the Puruṣa-sūkta consisting of Ṛg-verses, then "paratamān," "ajasya nābhau," and "arcata" for the Sāman-chanters. (24.204–205)
Then, having performed the *anīrājana* rite for Lakṣmīśa, as well as for the Lord of the Celestial Vehicle (*vyomayāna*),
one should invoke the Śakti from the *kūrca* and worship her in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Then, the most excellent among those who know the mantras, having performed the daily fire-offerings (*nityahoma*) and so forth up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [should proceed].
Holding the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in their hands, accompanied by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas reciting the *Śaṃ no mitra* prayer and the *Upaniṣads* with the sound of musical instruments,
the supreme preceptor, together with the officiating priests, circumambulated the sacred abode.
Carrying the *saṃpāta* clarified butter, he enters the inner sanctum and should place it, consecrated with the *Puruṣasūkta*, upon the head of the deity. Then,
having ascended the temple structure (*vimāna*), his preceptor should indeed place it there.

Thus, from the day of the commencement until the conclusion of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the remainder of the clarified butter (ājya) should be deposited at the two times; otherwise, the rite is fruitless. Then, one should deposit the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya) into the central pitcher as if it were a daily (nitya) offering.
One should perform five expiatory oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the Upaniṣadic mantras;
then, having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) for those situated in the four locations, one should cast the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
A wise person should act in this manner until the day of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
O Goddess, if the time for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should fall at midday,

one should perform the ritual bathing during the previously mentioned period, preceded by protective rites. O Lotus-born One, if that auspicious moment (lagna-kāla) should occur at dawn, [one should proceed accordingly].

On the evening of the day preceding that [day], one should perform the consecration for the images of Vīra, Lakṣmī, and the others, as well as for Tārkṣya and the commander of the army. Having adorned the four-armed images made of clay or metal, [one should proceed].
The Guru should install each respective [deity] in its appropriate place in due order by means of the image-worshippers (mūrtipas).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter on the rite of installation in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
When the night has turned to dawn, having performed the rites such as bathing and so forth, [he should proceed].
Having entered the sacrificial hall together with the officiating priests, the sacrificer, and the preceptor of the celestial chariot,
he should perform the daily oblations and other rites.
Then, O Rame, he should offer oblations for the sake of pacifying any omissions of mantras or other defects.

For the sake of pacifying the omission of mantras, the most excellent of teachers [should perform oblations] in his own fire-pit with clarified butter, sesame seeds, milk-rice, prepared foods, and edible substances,
along with honey— each substance twenty-eight times.
Then, O Rame, having offered oblations with the root mantra,
one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the sacrificial pit known as Kodaṇḍa to pacify any omission in the ritual,
using ghee, milk, curd, seeds, grains, and rice.

Having offered oblations with fruits, roots, and the like, as well as bilva leaves, according to the previously mentioned number, using the mantra known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the circular sacrificial pit (vṛttakuṇḍa),
O fair-faced one, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency of materials.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with white lotuses, other flowers, clarified butter, and even sprouts of *dūrvā* grass,
using the *pradyumna-vidyā* mantra and the previously mentioned number of times;
this should be done with milk in a triangular fire-pit for the sake of pacifying defects such as the elision of vowels.
Having offered oblations into their respective fire-pits with dhātrī fruits, bilva fruits, ghee and cooked rice,
plantain fruits, sugar, and lotus seeds, using the vidyā known as Aniruddha,
the officiating priests should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
An oblation of a heap of sesame seeds is performed with the Hariṇānana mudrā.
An oblation of ghee measuring one karṣa is prescribed, as is that of milk specifically;
an oblation of curd is the measure of a śukti, while that of milk-rice (pāyasa) is one prasṛti.
For other types of food, the measure is half a mouthful according to their own size;
for all seeds, however, one should offer a mere handful.
For rice grains and parched grain, the offering is likewise the tip of a finger.

The fruits should be of their own natural size, and the same applies to the sprouts. Gula should be the size of a jujube fruit, guggulu should be the size of a fist, and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be a span long; they must not be crooked and should be possessed of their bark.
The preceptor, along with the Bhaṭṭācārya and the two Mūrtipas, should offer blades of *dūrvā* grass— measuring either eight finger-breadths or four finger-breadths— at the appropriate time,
reciting the mantra "uttiṣṭha" (Arise).
Having requested [permission] from Bhūmi and Nīla, and having established the ritual image on an auspicious seat,
one should then adorn the icons with garments, garlands, ornaments, and fragrant substances,
and subsequently worship them with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites.
Then, having offered foodstuffs and the like, as well as betel-leaf and a mirror,
one should subsequently meditate upon Vāsudeva and the others who were previously invoked in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
as well as Hari, even though he resides in the image of the child, within the central pitcher.

In the center of the pericarp of the lotus within the wheel, one should place Vāsudeva, who consists of the universe; on its petals, one should assign the deities beginning with Keśava. One should likewise meditate upon the Lord situated in the pericarp as being present in the jar.
One should place the King of Wheels (cakrarāja), which resides in the *karakastha* vessel, at the entrance of the womb-chamber (*garbhadvāra*).
One should then dismiss the preeminent attendants (*pārṣadapuṃgava*) who reside in the door-flags (*ketana*) and the water-pots (*kumbha*),
[placing them] upon the great seat (*pīṭha*) of Bali, which is situated in the east and produced from a lake.

Having meditated upon the Moon from the water-pitcher and the presiding deities of the *pālikā* and other vessels in their respective places, the most excellent Guru should then perform the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice; however,
in the case of a single-liṅga shrine, he should do so to the south of the entrance of the sanctum.
Having summoned those who have bathed well, who wear washed garments, who bear clear vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*) made of clay,
whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, and who are adorned with flower garlands—
even the servants— he should purify them with holy waters.
Having honored the Lord of Birds among them when that auspicious moment had arrived,

he— being the best among those who know mantras— should give gifts for the journey to the Vaiṣṇavas and to the knower of the science of astrology, and then pray to the God stationed within the pitcher.
O you whose self is the mantra, withdraw your own form and your sovereign power for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, and for the stability of the worlds, O Lord!
Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; arise, O Lord of the worlds!
"And for the sake of favoring me, O Lord, take recourse in the primary image.

Having thus entreated [the deity] within the great jar (*mahākumbha*) preceded by the secondary jars (*upakumbha*), one should raise it with the words "Arise! and place it upon the heads of the messengers.
The lords of birds shall carry Hari, who is seated upon his auspicious throne, even above the multitudes of celestial chariots hovering over the heads of the attendants;
and Bhaṭṭācārya shall lead them from the front, together with Dhārayācchidrayā.
Taking up the *karaka* vessel, he should proceed while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).

Between those who hold the *bimba* and the *kumbha*, and between the preceptor himself—no others should pass through that space; if one who is uninitiated should pass through it, [the ritual is spoiled].
Or, O Goddess, if he is initiated, that rite shall become fruitless by that [act].
Therefore, while the patron stands before everyone,
I, Hari, and the Guru must look on with an attentive mind.
Then one should proceed in front [of the image], preceded by the chanting of the Vedas (24.34).
O Rame, they should cause all musical instruments, such as trumpets and the like, to resound;
and behind the image, those who know the Vedas should likewise recite the Śākuna [texts] (24.35).
"May auspiciousness attend your ears in the south, and may you find security in the north;
as great crowds scatter various jewels and flowers, let us go slowly with the King out of respect, O Rāma. (24.36)
In this manner, the most excellent of teachers should pour out the water from the image-vessel and other vessels.
O Goddess, that spot where the vision of the celestial vehicle occurs is the place;
then, he should install the Lord of Gods in that location after performing a circumambulation.
Having reached the summit of the temple, his preceptor first performed a subtle consecration with a large pitcher at the top of the spire for the Lotus-born One;
then, at the base of the celestial chariot, he should contemplate the yoga-pedestal.
Having covered the great pitcher and the pinnacle with a silken cloth,
and having worshipped Aniruddha situated within the pitcher—
He who is adorned with a thousand heads, feet, hands, and eyes— || 24.40–24.41 ||
"Grant your eternal presence in this image that resembles your own form.
Having thus prayed, one should contemplate [the deity] within the vessel situated in the celestial vehicle (*vyomayāna*).
Then, upon the altar-base supporting the jar (*kalaśa*), one should visualize the Sudarśana.

Having meditated upon Vāsudeva within the jar, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other rites. One should tie a tuft of *kūrca* grass, as well as an *aśvattha* sprout and a cloth, around the neck of that jar, and then perform the consecration (*abhiṣecana*).
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the deities stationed in the various directions, one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of minced meat,
powdered turmeric, parched grain, and curd-mixed barley flour. Having combined these with the food of the bali, one should recite this verse:
And you beings who abide in the eastern direction— both those who are primordial and those born of karma—
be gracious and accept with respect this offering given by me.
Likewise, those who abide in the southern direction, on the tops of trees and upon mountains.
Those who dwell on the earth and in the sky, let them accept my offering;
the Vināyakas and Kṣetrapālas stationed in the western direction,
and those attendants beginning with Pūṣan, let them accept my offering today.
"May Caṇḍa and the others, as well as Kumuda and the others, who are stationed in the direction of the Moon—
may all these attendants of Viṣṇu accept this supreme offering.
Having thus presented the offering in the four directions, [he should do so] with other waters from the ritual jars.
Stationed in the forms of the directions within celestial vehicles, they should sprinkle the pavilions, the gate-towers, the sacrificial hall,
the kitchen, and other areas.
After the offering of the *bali* sacrifice, [they should sprinkle] the ground in front of the great pedestal of the deity.
Or else, having blocked the door of the inner sanctum with the articles for the *arghya* offering and having performed worship up to the *nīrājana* rite using the image, the ritual jar, and so forth,
the supreme preceptor should enter within while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should place the Mahākumbha and Upakumbha vessels upon a bed of grain,
situated on a Jāmbūnada-golden altar in front of the permanent image (dhruvārcā).
Then, one should install the ritual image (karmārcā) on the Brahma-pada, with Śrī and Bhūmi on its two sides.
On the left, however, one should install the images of the sacrificial deities and others in the worldly realm.
One should install an image made of gold or other metals upon the desired ground.
Having led the auspicious throne outside, the supreme guru [prepares] the inner door.
Having concealed [the deities] with a curtain and having bound them in the posture called the lotus-seat (padmāsana),
one should then designate the yoga-seat upon the pedestals of the primary image and so forth;
and having worshipped those [deities] residing in the great jars and other vessels with the arghya offering and other rites.
In the handful of flowers, one should meditate upon the lotus; in that lotus, upon the yoga-throne,
[one should meditate upon] Viṣṇu Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest, lying down or reclining,
having arrived from the supreme bliss of Vaikuṇṭha together with Śrī.
Seated comfortably upon the seat of the infinite serpent, four-armed,
and adorned by his attendants such as Tārkṣya, Seneśa, Caṇḍa, and others—
one should then pray to the God residing within the jar with this verse:
O Vāsudeva, source of the universe, perfected through the six divine attributes; O boundless one, beyond all qualities, self-luminous, undisturbed,
free from conceptual construction, formless, stainless, and free from affliction.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million times ten million suns, fires, and moons,
and endowed everywhere with heads, eyes, faces, arms, and feet—
for the sake of securing the welfare of the worlds and for the destruction of evil-doers.
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, you ought to manifest your presence within this divine image from this pitcher.
Having thus prayed to the flawless Vāsudeva,
who had arrived in the great pitcher from the supreme bliss of Vaikuṇṭha— || 24.64–65 ||
Having meditated upon the handful of flowers within the pitcher and having joined it with the primary image (mūlabera),
one should sprinkle that water from the pitcher upon the head of the deity using the *kūrca* grass-bundle.
Then, one should contemplate it as having entered the image through the path of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
One should close the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) with the *Tāra* [syllable] of the Supreme Self.
Having turned [the mind] toward one's own self by means of the *Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā*,
and having risen, one should prostrate four times to the Lord of Kamalā.
One should display the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), preceded by the mantra.
Then, one should perform the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
The placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) occurs during the act of emanation, as well as during lying down and sitting.
One should perform the *sthitinyāsa* during the state of stability and the one called *bhoga* during the state of reclining;
likewise during *yoga*, during the *viśvarūpa* [state], and everywhere in postures such as sitting.
During the *saṃhāra* [state], the *saṃhṛtinyāsa* is performed; when mounted on a vehicle, all three should be present.
Then, having worshipped the deity, one should offer the *madhuparka*;
one should then mentally visualize the auspicious rite (*karma-kautuka*) situated within the mandala of the discus and lotus.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *Puṇḍarīkākṣa* mantra.
One should remember those who have come from the worlds of bliss during festivals and other such occasions.
One should perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) upon the images using the eight-syllable mantra.
Having invoked the Lord residing within the image of the child (*bālabimba*) into the image used for sleep (*svāpārcā*), [one should proceed].
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the six-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu, one should worship according to the rules;

O Goddess, one should worship Śrī and Bhūmi on both sides of the Śrīvatsa mark. Having meditated [upon the deity], one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsana*), and thereafter the worship.
Having gone to the abode of Vīralakṣmī with the great pitcher, the preceptor should invoke Lakṣmī—
who has come from Śrīvatsa and is resplendent with four arms—
into the Dhruvārcā and other [images], and sprinkle them with the waters from the pitcher.
Having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsana*), one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
One should [worship] the Lord of Birds (*khageśa*) and the Commander of the Army (*senanāyaka*) located at the threshold and the *udumbara* tree of the inner chamber;
Lakṣmī residing in the kitchen; and also Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.

O Lotus-born one, the devotees should sprinkle with the water from the great pitcher, using their respective vidyās, the vehicles such as chariots, those stationed at the gates such as Caṇḍa, the flagstaff, the images of the deities, the ponds, and so forth. (24.79–24.80)
The Guru himself should pour the remaining water upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
The creation and arrangement belong to Brahmā; the dissolution belongs to the Lord of Pārvatī.
Having taken the Gārhapatya fire from the eastern pit (kuṇḍa), [he should perform the rites].
O Lotus-born One, having established [the fire] in the hearth of the kitchen for the purpose of the daily *homa* with the *tejas-mantra*, one should enter the inner sanctum; thereafter,
one should pray to the deities at their seats for the meal with the root-vidyā.
Having offered the four kinds of food along with eatables, fruits,

and betel leaves in abundance, and having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the most excellent preceptor enters the kitchen where the fire has been established in the south-eastern corner.
One should perform the daily fire-oblation according to the rules during the worship at the conclusion of the homa;
otherwise, having offered an apology, one should present a lamp made of flour,
bowing four times with the eight limbs of the body and with palms joined in reverence.
Having approached the side of the Deity, one should utter this verse:
"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, eternal embodiment of mantra,
O Lord of the World, from the commencement of the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) up to the end of the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa)..."
Whatever rite has been performed by me for your pleasure, O Lord,
and whatever has been done by the officiating priests authorized by me,
may all that be fully perfected and any deficiency or excess be pacified.
O you who are affectionate toward devotees, O bestower of the desired objects of your devotees,
I pray to you, O Lord, with the desire for your grace:
remain for a long time in this place prepared with this faith.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods; accept this worship from me as well.
O Hari, Lord of Śrī, grant nourishment, contentment, and likewise the supreme goal to the village, the king, the kingdom, and the subjects.
Having thus informed the Lord, the preceptor (deśika) should offer pearls and other such things, the nine gems, stars, and golden flowers at the Lord’s feet;
thereafter, he should complete the Vedas and the Vedic rites.

When the deity is seated upon the seat of food, the officiating priest, instructed by the preceptor, shall go to the abode of Vīra-lakṣmī; having offered balls of food made of molasses and other ingredients, and having displayed a lamp of flour, he should then offer this prayer: ||| 24.94–95 |||
O Goddess seated upon the lotus, born from the interior of the lotus;
O you who wear a garland of lotuses, whose eyes are like lotuses, O Indirā, sovereign of all beings!
O omniscient one, dwelling within all beings, witness of all!
O Sovereign of the entire world, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu,
you who bestow land, prosperity, sons, grandsons, and all else upon your devotees:
it behoves you to maintain your presence within this image for a long time.
Thus, one should offer gems and other items at the lotus feet of Lakṣmī;
then, O Lotus-born One, beginning with Caṇḍa and the others situated by the side of the door of the Blessed One’s dwelling, [one should proceed] up to the Great Seat (mahāpīṭha).

One should offer the *bali* oblation in the house of Śrī and to Caṇḍī and the others in their proper order. Another practitioner [should offer it] to the deities stationed on the courtyards, the ramparts, the walls, and the gate-towers, preceded by the *arghya* offering.
Having offered food to the attendants (pārṣadas), one should cast the bali-offering while recollecting the verse:
"May the devotees of the Blessed One and the beings dwelling outside the temple accept this;
as well as their followers who are purified by the power of mantras. (24.102)
"Having accepted this Vaiṣṇava offering (*bali*) with water given by me at the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*),
and having attained satisfaction, protect the abode of Hari.
Having spoken thus, one should offer the *bali* into the air, preceded by the sounding of musical instruments.
Then, O Rame, having worshipped the God of gods according to the prescribed rites with arghya and other offerings,
[I offered] divine vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like cooked with cow's ghee,
as well as pure rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), and various foods prepared with clarified butter.
Having offered [the food] together with curd and soup, the most excellent teacher,
desiring the satisfaction of Hari, should then feed the Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas.
Then, when the time of evening has arrived, having completed the daily worship, [he should proceed].
Having adorned and worshipped the deity whose vehicle is Tārkṣya and others,

the preceptor should cause him to be paraded through the streets, together with the requisites for the procession and numerous lamps of ghee, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments.
Having restrained the Teacher of the World in front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
and having worshipped him with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites for the pacification of defects of sight,
one should then display a lamp in a jar and offer puffed rice (pṛthuka) and other foods.
Having performed the *nīrājana* rite, he should lead the Lord of Gods from the vehicle into the inner sanctum (*garbhamandira*).
He should then present abundant, pure food of the four kinds.
Thereafter, he should cause the food and other offerings to be distributed among the Brahmins and the devotees.
Then, having worshipped the end of the bed, the Guru should fasten the door-panel.
Thereafter, at dawn, having completed the daily worship of the Deity and having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, he should offer food such as mung-bean porridge.
Then, having removed the curtain and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), he should pray to the Lord:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the worlds, my beloved! O source of all, O you who are the beginning, middle, and end of all, O All, O Acyuta, supreme over all!"
O Govinda, lotus-eyed one, ancient Supreme Person!
You are capable of ferrying [beings] across the ocean of saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross and shoreless;
you are the knower of the manifest and the unmanifest, who has fashioned the fourfold states known as Time.
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World; O Saṃkarṣaṇa, Master of the Universe;
O Pradyumna, Blessed One, Śrīman; O Aniruddha, Unconquered One! You who abide in manifold manifestations of power, you who bring about manifold manifestations of power!
O divine one, embodiment of the arising of the six qualities and the bliss of both tranquility and emergence;
O you whose crown, armlets, necklace, anklets, and Kaustubha gem are shimmering;
O wearer of yellow garments, most noble one with eyes like lotuses!
O four-formed one, O fourfold manifestation, you who possess the luster of an autumnal blue lotus;
O Nārāyaṇa, treasure-house of compassion, whose beauty equals ten million gods of love,
without you there is nothing for me, and without me there is nothing for you.
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, be gracious so that you may take me as your own.
For those whose feet have stumbled upon the earth, the earth alone is their support;
for those who have gone astray from you, you alone, O All-pervading One, are their refuge.

Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the preceptor should prostrate with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga). At the conclusion of the offerings including the madhuparka, the patron, bowing low with devotion and having received the preceptor’s permission, [should offer] water first into the hand of Hari.
On the right, for the purpose of perpetual worship, [he should give] land filled with grain,
as well as a grove, golden ornaments and the like, the nine gems, a woolen blanket, coverings, female and male slaves, musical instruments, and vehicles.
Having given away vessels such as basins, as well as articles for worship,
along with water, and subsequently his wife and children,
his male and female slaves, his entire property, himself, and his riches; ||| 24.126 ||
The most excellent lord should place [the disciple] at the feet of Vāsudeva;
then, honoring him as mother and father, as a kinsman, and as a supreme teacher— as a friend and as one's own self— he should prostrate before him again and again.
With armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and golden sacred threads;
with fields, groves, houses, and wealth; likewise with living and non-living assets;
with male and female slaves, elephants, horses, gold, palanquins, and so forth.
O blameless lady, the patron should indeed gratify the Bhaṭṭācārya. At that time, a thousand cows should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru;
half of that should be given to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and to the practitioners (sādhakas) as is appropriate.
The Bhaṭṭācārya himself shall take all the sacrificial materials without exception,
as well as those for the learned Brāhmaṇas who have studied the Vedas,
for the reciters of Purāṇic verses, for the chanters, and for the mantra-reciters.
To the members who possess knowledge of the proper timing, according to their respective duties,
he should give cows, land, gold, silver, garments, and ornaments,
as well as for their proficiency in the arts, conduct, and various musical instruments.

Having placed upon a vehicle the garments, ornaments, musical instruments, and wealth belonging to each hermitage, and having led the Teacher around the village clockwise with the sounds of all musical instruments, along with banners, parasols, and yak-tail whisks; || 24.135 ||
O Goddess, one should lead [the deity] to that house and ask for forgiveness through prostrations and other such acts.
(24.136) But in the ritual procedure for a single image (*ekabera*), O Rame, after the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), one should then cover the image with fresh silk garments. (24.137)
Having covered the door-panel for three days, one should place a discus at the entrance.
For those three days, Brahmā, Rudra, and the other gods, as well as the celestial sages,
the Siddhas, and the Brahman-sages, worship the Lord of Ramā.
When the fourth day has arrived, the knower of mantras, having opened the gate and performed the ritual ablution according to rule preceded by the hoisting of the banner,
should conduct a festival as far as the sacred bathing-place (tīrtha) for the sake of pacifying that fatigue.
One should perform a single festival for the pacification of that exhaustion;
the patron [should give] a hundred gold coins, as well as cows, woolen blankets,
highly valuable sheep’s wool, garments, and ornaments.
He should give to the preceptor, the practitioners, and the officiating priests in due order; he should employ his dependents for the protection of the deity.
Likewise, he should not cause distress to the devotees or the attendants.
Having thus performed everything, the patron (yajamāna) should then enter his home.
He who performs [the rites] from the initial plowing up to the final consecration (pratiṣṭhā) for the Lord of Ramā is indeed the Bhaṭṭācārya; he alone should perform the daily worship (nityapūjā).
If his son, or even one devoid of qualities, or likewise a descendant of his lineage,
should worship [the Lord], the Omniscient One would always manifest His presence there;
however, the worship of others is not pleasing to Me.
Therefore, let those born of his lineage always worship me.
O Goddess, I shall declare the auspicious fruit of worldly enjoyment and liberation for whoever thus performs the installation of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
If the sacrificer is a Brāhmaṇa, he shall become a master of all sciences;
if a Kṣatriya, he shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth; and if a Vaiśya, O Lotus-born One, he shall possess abundance of cattle, gardens, houses, fields, wealth, and grain.
If the sacrificer is a Śūdra, he rejoices through wealth and other such means.
(24.149) One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth.
Whatever the performer desires, he obtains all that with speed. (24.150)
From the ground of the temple up to the tip of the banner, including the pavilion equipped with all its implements and throughout all the enclosures—
within the entire expanse of all atoms surrounding it.
O fair-faced one, a count is produced among them for each individual;
having dwelt in the world of Viṣṇu for hundreds of millions upon millions of years as both instigator and sacrificer, they finally go to the supreme state.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The twenty-fifth chapter:
O fair-faced one, if the consecration of Lakṣmī and the others takes place at a different time [than prescribed],...
I shall now declare its ritual procedure; pay close attention to the specific details.
A shrine for Śrī should be established in the direction that is the abode of Nirṛti, while Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and likewise Parā [should be placed] in the four directions of the vimāna.
One should likewise arrange Sāvitrī and Vāgdevī in the corners,
and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) or a lion at the two sides of the inner door;
and similarly, Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī at the two sides of the second door.
The best of artisans should fashion a forest garland of *balākini* flowers.
O beloved, this is the rule for the dependent [temple]; now hear it for the independent one:
on the southern and northern sides of the third gateway (*gopura*).
Then, on the two sides of the fourth door, [one should place] Jayā and Vijayā;
and in the fifth enclosure, Vibhīṣikā and Śāṅkarī. Then, facing the lotus, one should place Tārkṣya in the northeastern direction and Hrīmatī.
Having envisioned all the sacrificial halls and other structures as before,
one should contemplate Vanamālikā, Śacī, Balākinī, Kālanāyikā, and Vibhīṣikā upon the door-panels of the eastern and other directions.
Immediately thereafter, [one should worship] Śītalā, Śāṅkarī, and the goddess Saṃpat;
then Jyeṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śraddhā, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kriyā, Kṣamā, and Jayā—
in this sequence, upon the pitchers at the doors and on the eight banners.
One should worship Dhṛti, Lañjā, Sāvitrī, Māyā, Śuddhi, Tuṣṭikā, Śānti, and Kīrti; these are four-armed and very beautiful,
holding a discus, a conch, and water, and seated upon lotus-thrones.
At the time of worship,
one should meditate upon Vijayā situated in the center of the wheel within the middle of the door-leaf, and the devourer of serpents (Garuḍa) on both sides.
