In the middle of the door, the Guru should worship the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas as before.
Then, in the four pits (*kuṇḍa*) in order, [one should worship] from Padmā down to Yoni;
and in the eight auspicious jars (*kumbha*), Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā;
and then Śakti, Vibhūti, Icchā, as well as Prīti and Rati.
One should worship Māyā, Dhī, and Mahimā in the central jar,
and Śrī in the water-vessel (karaka) upon the pericarp-seat of the lotus of the wheel.
One should worship the goddess Śrī in the twelve petals in due order.
The best of preceptors should worship Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śakti, Vibhūtikā,
Icchā, Prīti, Rati, Māyā, Dhī,
and Mahimā upon the door-panels starting from the east.
One should worship Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī, and Tārkṣya facing toward the mandala. In the northeast, one should meditate upon Hrīmatī, who is endowed with the tarjanī mudrā.
In the corners beginning with the southeast, one should worship Vasudhā and Narakesarī.
One should then recollect the Vāruṇī-vidyā and worship her with the *arghya* and other offerings.
One should contemplate all these Śrīs as looking toward the face of Rame;
one should place Māyā in the jar at the center of the temple and likewise recollect her in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having invoked the goddesses previously mentioned into the secondary jars (*upakumbha*), one should worship them. The best of teachers should perform the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) with either nine or five jars for Śrī and the others, as well as for the rest.
Whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform entirely according to the previously stated rules.
Having thus established the Fortune of Heroism (Vīra-lakṣmī), one should perform her worship;
every year, one should hold a festival preceded by the celebration of a marriage ceremony.
O Goddess, having been deprived of his kingdom by the curse of Durvāsas, Indra,
the preeminent among the gods, performed austerities for a thousand years on the shore of the Ocean of Milk in order to regain it.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, in order to grant him the fruit of his ascetic penance,
the King of Bestowers of Boons appeared, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
he appeared before the one who was bowing with palms joined in reverence and praying for the heavenly world.
I said: "O gods and Daityas, first establish a state of friendship.
O, I shall provide assistance to you through Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
Then, having cast all medicinal herbs into the Ocean of Milk together with the Daityas, [I acted].
If the auspicious nectar is churned by Mandara,
Lakṣmī will arise there; seek her, O best of gods,
after making yourself strong by consuming the ambrosia.
"Having conquered the gods, you shall then obtain the blameless Lakṣmī, preceded by the heroes;
having regained your entire kingdom, you will undoubtedly protect it.
Having heard all that was thus spoken by me, together with the hosts of gods, [he replied:]
At that time, for the welfare of the worlds, you caused the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
On the auspicious day of the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kanyā, on a Friday,
you entered into the milk ocean and the essence of the medicinal herbs.
Having distinguished between both nectar and poison for the welfare of the world,
you emerged from the ocean on the full moon day under the Uttaraphalgunī constellation in the month of Phālguna, [revealing] the Lord clad in yellow garments.
Seeing the garland upon my neck, O Goddess, you lowered your face in shame;
then, having ascended, you came to my *śrīvatsa* mark.
When the Lord was gazed upon by you, he attained the splendor of a hero.
Having conquered the hosts of Dānavas and blazing with glory, the king of the gods,
having regained his entire kingdom, indeed celebrated a festival for you.
In the same way, the preceptor should perform a festival for you even during the worship of the image.

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, or on the full moon of Phālguna joined with the Phālgunī nakṣatra, or indeed on the anniversary of my manifestation, having determined the date for the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), O Rame,
one should perform the collection of clay while placing Hrīmatī at the forefront.

If [the rite] is independent, this should be a ritual injunction; but if it is dependent on another, one should have the commander of the army worshiped, as well as the door, the pitcher, and so forth, just as before.
Having worshiped the Eight Lakṣmīs in the *pālikās* and the Intellect (*dhī*) in the pitcher, [one should proceed].

In the central pitcher, [the preceptor should worship] the goddess Śrī; in the directions starting from the east, in due order, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā; and in the regions starting from the southeast (Āgneya), the teacher [should worship] Harī, Prīti, Vāgdevī, and likewise Amṛtā in the west (Vāruṇī).
Having meditated, invoked, and worshipped [the deity] in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and the water-pots (*karaka*),
one should worship [it] as before upon the mandala of the lotus within the wheel (*cakrābja*).
Now hear the sequence of deities for the ornaments and ritual implements.
Having invoked the respective deities into the crown, the Kaustubha gem, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the forest garland; into the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the sword Nandaka;
having invoked Radiance into the light, and Prosperity into the other ornaments; || 25.43–25.44 ||

The preceptor should worship [Viṣṇu] upon an auspicious seat, in sandals, in a palanquin, on a banner, as well as on an elephant, a horse, a chariot, a lion, a swan, and Tārkṣya; and likewise in the images of Śeṣa, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the Moon, the Sun, and others.
One should worship those respective deities in the central jar and in the eight lotuses surrounding it;

one should worship Indra and the others in the secondary jars, excluding the door-worship, and likewise perform all rites such as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) according to the prescribed rules.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should sprinkle [the image] with water from the pitcher;
the most excellent lord should give the teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
O Goddess, their ritual bathing may be performed with nine pitchers.
One should establish the devotees in the fourth enclosure and beyond.
Having fashioned the temple devoid of the lion-faced directional deities (siṃhamukha),
[one should install those] whose conduct accords with their respective caste and stage of life, and whose forms and gestures are appropriate.
Having fashioned the devotee’s image and other forms in the temple within the human station,
and having established them upon the lotus-footed pedestal of Padmanābha,
one should pray to that divine soul and contemplate it within the center of the water-pot.
One should not perform the eight rites beginning with *upakumbha*, nor the consecration (*adhivāsana*) upon the bed.
One should perform everything else as before, up to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
One should then contemplate those disciples within the sandals (*pādukā*) as being born from the ocean.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Completion of the Installation," in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-six.
Śrī said:
O Lord worshipped by the gods, whose two lotus feet are a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, at the conclusion of my festival, let there be the marriage festival for us both. (26.1)
"It has been said that this must certainly be done; O Lord, tell me the procedure for it.
The Blessed One replied:
"O Rame, who delights in the moonlight-like smiles arising from the fatigue of churning the Ocean of Milk! 26.2
I shall describe that procedure for you, O daughter of the Ocean of Milk. O Goddess, on the day following the final day of the festival, the Guru,
having first performed the daily worship of the God and the Goddess, O Rame, [should proceed].
Salutations to you, O daughter of the ocean; salutations, O sister of the moon!
Salutations to the dweller of Śrīvatsa; salutations again and again to her who is the source of the three Vedas and more. O beloved of Hari, I entreat you for the sake of the wedding festival.
"Therefore, O daughter of Bhṛgu, manifest your presence within this ritual image.
Having thus informed Lakṣmī and immediately invoked her,
the Guru should go to the temple of the Lord and petition Him as well.
Salutations to you, the one worthy of worship by the gods of gods, the Great Lord of all worlds! O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, ocean of the six divine attributes, free from fault and untainted,
grant your presence within this image for the successful accomplishment of the marriage festival.
Having thus offered prayers, he then bathed Lakṣmī and Lakṣmīśa individually upon golden seats with fragrant oils and other substances,
and honored them with garments, ornaments, garlands, and golden sacred threads.
Having adorned [the deity] and placed it upon [the vehicle], together with the requisites for the procession,
and having performed the circumambulation of the enclosure wall, the preceptors should lead [it] to the marriage pavilion,
having seated the God and the Goddess upon a golden lion-throne.
Then, one should pray to the divine fire in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila).
Next, one should fasten a golden marriage-thread (kautuka) upon the hands of the God and the Goddess.
Then, having offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka), one should place the Lord of the Universe within the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having worshipped together with the Goddess and having prostrated with palms joined in reverence:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, Nārāyaṇa, who pervades the universe;
O Lord of the beautiful body, resplendent in yellow garments. (26.13–14)

"I shall give this maiden Mahālakṣmī to you, Viṣṇu— she who was born from the ocean of milk, who is a sister to the Pārijāta tree and others, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament. (26.15)
"Accept this, O Supreme Person, for the welfare and security of the worlds.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should place [the gift] together with gold, cows, and land into the hand of the Blessed One, O auspicious lady, preceded by the pouring of water.
Then the preceptor, having worshipped the God and Goddess and offered them the *madhuparka*, should join the hand of Lakṣmī with the hand of Viṣṇu,
taking the auspicious gem with the permission of the Vaiṣṇavas.
And having consecrated it with the Aparājita-mantra and others, like a thread:
"O you who are the fruit of the exertion in churning the Ocean of Milk, O form of the Enemy of Madhu!
Homage to you, the sister of the Moon; homage to you, the source of nectar! (26.20)
O Mother, Daughter of the Ocean, I entreat you, Lakṣmī:
I have been appointed by the Lord to fasten this auspicious thread upon your neck (or in your bowl); please accept it, O Supreme Goddess.
Having made this request, while recollecting Hari, he should fasten [the garland] around the neck of the Goddess.
Taking the sandals of the God and the Goddess together with the practitioner,
the Guru should first perform the circumambulation of the fire while reciting the Puṃsūkta mantra.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer parched grains (lājā) while reciting the Śrīsūkta;
then, with the Bhūsūkta, one should perform a circumambulation for each [deity] along with sacrificial fuel-sticks,
cooked rice, and clarified butter, accompanied by the Lakṣmīgāyatrī.
One should offer twelve oblations for each [verse] with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
Then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should subsequently perform the expiatory oblations (prāyaścittāhuti) with the five Upaniṣads.
One should pray to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) residing in the fire and to Lakṣmī within their two forms.
Having dismissed the fire from those two images, one should present the oblations and other offerings.
After performing the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the God and the Goddess, one should satisfy the Brahmins with wealth.

One should cause the offered food, edibles, and other items to be given to the Vaiṣṇavas. When the time of evening has arrived, having sprinkled the palanquin, adorned with flowers and other ornaments, with holy water, one should [place] the lotus-like Lord within it.
Having placed [the image] there, one should adorn it with garments, ornaments, and the like, as well as with garlands of flowers,
with the various requisites for the procession, and with many lamps of ghee. Then,
having circumambulated the temple according to the rules, the most excellent preceptor—
One should lead the divine Śrī from the palanquin to the inner sanctum of the womb-chamber.
The learned and devoted Bhaṭṭācārya should worship her at the end of the bed.
In this manner, one may perform the rites for four days according to the worldly path.
The marriage of the goddesses, beginning with Jāmadagnyā, is performed according to the path of the Smṛtis.
Thus, for whoever causes the marriage to be performed after having installed Lakṣmī, Śrī makes her eternal residence in that person's home; of this there is no doubt.
The increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as the acquisition of land, shall come to pass;
having become long-lived and free from disease, one shall thereafter go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-Seven:
Śrī—
Many consecrations have been proclaimed for the purpose of installation.
"I wish to hear the number of those jars, the deities, and the substances, as well as the mantra. You, who are learned in the scriptures, ought to tell me all of that.
The Blessed One said:
O sinless one, whatever you have asked regarding that which arose from the Ocean of Milk,
listen now to all of it in detail as it is proclaimed in this single path.
Those who desire to perform the ritual bathing before the sanctum of the single-liṅga [deity]...
But when there is an extensive arrangement [of shrines], I am pleased even in front of the temple,
or indeed in all directions throughout all the surrounding grounds.
Having constructed a water-shed (*prapā*) provided with a foundation, measuring one span in height—
There, one should prepare the altar according to the number of jars.
First, the Guru should divide it according to the distinctions of the Brahma-sthāna and other locations,
leaving out the pathways for the sake of worship with rice, husked grain, and sesame seeds.
One should fashion a pedestal for each [vessel], marked with the wheel of the jars.
Upon those pedestals, one should place the water-pots with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
When the great consecration is to be performed, there should be one hundred and eight pots.
In the central position of the Brahma-sthāna, O Goddess, one should establish four [vessels] at each of the eight directions surrounding it; in the intermediate quarters (kāṣṭhā),
nine vessels each should be placed by the Guru, and indeed eight [vessels] in the [cardinal] directions.
O Goddess, for the jars representing the deities located in the east and other directions in due order,
[one should offer] the central jar, as well as water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācāma), milk, curd,
the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), honey, and fragrant water.
One should fill the jars all around with pure water using the weapon-mantra (astra-vidyā).
In the station of Brahmā and in the eight directions, beginning with that of Indra,
one should place fruit-water and cleansing water in each of the four jars.
The wise man should fill [the vessels] with honey-mixture (madhuparka), leaf-water, jewel-water, and thereafter iron-water, sugarcane juice,
and molasses; in the central position of Brahmā and in all four pitchers.
Having filled [the vessels] with ghee, warm water, and water containing flowers and all medicinal herbs, one should place blades of grass (*kūrca*) within them while circumambulating; likewise,
one should place sprouts of the *aśvattha* and *āmra* trees, as well as coconuts.
The preceptor should cover the mouths of the jars with the *cakra-mantra*,
and the Guru should wrap the neck of each jar individually with a cloth;
or else, O Rame, he may wrap all of them with a single cloth, according to his means.
Having covered the jars with new cloth, facing the northeast,
he should prepare a bathing seat in the western region of the jars;
on the northern part of the bathing altar, there should be one filled with scented water.

The preceptor should place a large vessel for the purpose of the preliminary bath (upasnāna), which has been strained through the Pavamāna and other [mantras], consecrated with mantras, and provided with a lid; likewise,
he should set out the conch-vessel, the discus-vessel, and the hundred-streamed vessel.
One should prepare a thousand-streamed vessel made of gold for the purpose of bathing, as well as a bowl filled with powdered sandalwood and a container for the thick paste of *tintriṇī* fruit.
One should arrange the articles of worship, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the lamp-vessel.
Having entered within, one should [worship] the ritual images (*karmabimba*) in sequence, starting from the root-mantra.
Then, having completed the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), the best of gurus should offer this prayer:
O you who are all-eating, O soul of all living beings, O omniscient one, O Lord of all! (27.23) O Blessed One, I now earnestly entreat you to perform your consecration;
for the sake of gladdening the world, adorn yourself with the reflection of [your] activity. (27.24)
Having thus offered prayers and performed the invocation, one should lead [the deity] to the bathing pavilion.
One should bring the God of gods, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, to the seat for bathing.
First, those devoted to the five-fold daily ritual (pañcakāla) should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited.
Having sprinkled water upon the ritual jars and other items, one should commence the worship of the door.
The best of Vaiṣṇavas should recite the Niṣadvara hymns;
outside, instrumentalists should play music, and groups of dancers should dance.
Formerly, having prepared the flower-sprout according to the rules, the best of preceptors,
having established the divine fire in a vessel to the east, or in a sacrificial pit, or even on a sacrificial mound, should perform the arrangement of the seats for the jars.
Having fashioned the respective deities of those materials and having invoked them into the jars, one should worship them.
Then, having prepared a pedestal in the fire, the preceptor should worship Vāsudeva,
offering oblations of clarified butter while specifically intending for the presiding deities of those respective materials.
Having offered oblations with the eight numerical formulas, sixteen oblations with the *caru* rice,
and one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
he should sprinkle the remaining ghee from the oblation into the central jars.
During the ritual performance, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self abiding within the fire. Thereafter, having extinguished the fire for the sake of bathing the Teacher of the World,
and having offered a bathing cloth, one should worship Hari with the *arghya* offering and other rites.
The preceptor should bind the protection cord upon the hand of the deity and himself;
it should be made from the seeds of the *gandhamārjāra* plant and cooked in fragrant oils. The preceptor should indeed purify it with *astra-mantra* and sesame oil.
One should perform the anointing of the Lord from the head down to the feet.
Then, O Rame, one should lift up the vessels of substances with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra;
one should bathe the Lord with the water-pots for the feet and other rites, preceded by the recitation of mantras.

Having worshipped each individual substance with mantras, along with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), touchings, garlands, incense, and so forth, one should then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with it.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the substances in their proper sequence is proclaimed as "their extraction" (*taduddhāra*).
O Goddess, having cut the cord measuring a span that encircles the jar with which the Guru bathes the Lord of Gods,
O Goddess, one should tie it to the hand of Hari and bathe Him with the water from that jar.
At the conclusion of the bathing ceremony with the vessels containing water for the feet and other substances, the supreme preceptor,
having then anointed the limbs of the deity with fragrant pastes,
should worship it with the arghya and other offerings and present food such as mung-bean rice.
Standing behind the Lord, the Guru should, above the head of the Master,
hold a canopy of a thousand streams with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
[He should also hold] a conch, a lotus, and two jars of treasure filled with water from sacred bathing places (puṇyatīrtha).
Having taken up their positions on the right and left of the Lord, the two most excellent teachers should direct that sacred water onto the body of the Lord of Ramā with the root-mantra,
using a thousandfold stream; thus one should perform the bath.
Then the twice-born should satisfy Hari with the Puruṣasūkta.
Having thus consecrated [the deity] three times, one should likewise consecrate the two goddesses;
and having removed the bathing-cloth, one should offer a covering cloth.
Then, with a paste made from tintriṇī wood and many kinds of fragrant substances, the preceptor should cleanse the limbs of the Lord; afterwards,
he should bathe him with waters intended for the preliminary bath and bring his limbs to a state of relief using a cloth.
Having formally requested the deity onto the ornamented seat, one should worship according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having led [the deity] to the seat for the meal, one should offer the sacrificial food and other offerings;
however, if one possesses the means, one should arrange the ritual of the "great oblation" (mahāhavis).

Those who drink or carry the consecration water of Viṣṇu indeed obtain the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas). The offering of water for the feet (pādya) and the placement of ritual substances in the jars and other vessels is prescribed.
One should place these four substances— śyāmāka, viṣṇuparṇī, dūrvā, and lotus— into the water-pot for the feet (pādyakumbha). [Likewise, one should place] barley,
white mustard, fragrant flowers, unbroken grains, fruit, and sesame seeds.
These eight, including the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, are proclaimed as the components of the *arghya*.
One should add cardamom, cloves, and camphor to the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Likewise, one should include plantain, coconut, sugar, honey, and ghee.
Having combined these substances, one should place them in the jar of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should likewise offer sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, the king of perfumes (gandharāja), murā, uśīra, saffron, and spikenard into the jar of fragrance.
Plantain, bilva, mango, jackfruit, citron, coconut, emblic myrobalan, and pomegranate— from the juices of these fruits;
along with turmeric, sahadevī, śirīṣa, and sūryavartinī.
One should always cast auspicious tips of kuśa grass into the water for sprinkling.
Indeed, honey, milk, curd, clarified butter, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be placed in the jar.
[Likewise, one should use twigs] from the nyagrodha, aśvattha, vakula, kadamba, mango, and śirīṣa trees.
Also, sprouts from the *palāśa* and *bilva* trees,
leaf-water, moonstone, sunstone,
magnetite, coral, lapis lazuli, ruby, *brahmarāga*, and *gāruḍa* [gems].
The best of preceptors should place these— sapphire, topaz, crystal, diamond, and pearl— into the jewel-pitcher;
as well as gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin into the water-born [pitcher].
One should place these five metals into iron jars. O lotus-eyed one, one should place wheat, barley, wild rice, śāli rice, mung beans, priyaṅgu, black gram, and brīhi rice into the seed-jar.
One should throw the inner bark of these trees— of the *śamī*, *udumbara*, and *bilva*, as well as the *palāśa* and *aśvattha* trees,
and likewise of the *vaṭa*, *khadira*, *cāmpeya*, and *vikaṅkata* trees—
into water that has been boiled with astringent decoctions.
One should place costus, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, vacā, kacora, and mustā into the jar containing all medicinal herbs;
likewise, one should add nīvāra, sesame, siddhārtha, barley, and bamboo-seeds.
One should cast tulasī leaves into the water of pacification (śāntyambhas),
as well as the lotus, the blue water-lily, the buds of land-lotuses,
and the flowers of ketaki, mallikā, jātī, and nandyāvarta.

Into that vessel made of lotus leaves, one should place flowers of Campaka, Megha, and Bakula; likewise, the essence of cow dung, cow urine, curd, milk, and ghee— these five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— along with water.
One should take auspicious earth from fields of merit, oceans, rivers, and from the beginning, end, and middle of sacred sites;
and also from the roots of *tulasī*, *bilva*, and lotuses.
Having taken these, one should fill a jar of earth with water.
These collections of substances, according to one's wealth and capacity,
should be placed— either individually or all together— into their respective jars. Or else,
the jars may be filled with scented water, strained pure water, or clear water.

One should fill jars with five-pronged cow-products (pañcagavya), ghee, milk, and honey, each measuring one droṇa; likewise, one should fill others with other liquids and an equal amount of molasses-water, O Rāma, using wise ones to fill the vessels with water from the material jars.
One part out of eight is prescribed as the measure of the materials,
such as gold, various metals, and gems, according to the available wealth.
Having invoked the presiding deities of each respective material, one should worship them.
The eternal Vāsudeva is the presiding deity of the jar of ghee; Saṃkarṣaṇa is the deity of the jar of heated water and of excellent fragrant water;
and Pradyumna, O Goddess, is the deity of the water containing all medicinal herbs.
Aniruddha is indeed the deity of the jar for the sacred bathing water (puṇyatīrtha);
Vāsudeva is remembered as the deity of the jar of pure water, and Nārāyaṇa likewise.
Keśava is the deity of the jar for water for the feet (pādya), and Nārāyaṇa is likewise [the deity of the arghya jar].
Mādhava is the lord of the water for the *ācamana* rite of the *arghya* jar;
Govinda is the lord of the milk jar; Viṣṇu is the lord of the curd produced from the lake;
and the deity named Madhusūdana is the lord of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

Trivikrama is the presiding deity of the jar of honey, Vāmana of the jar of perfume, Śrīdhara of the jar of fruit, and Hṛṣīkeśa of the water for cleansing, O lotus-born one; Padmanābha is the presiding deity of the madhuparka offering.
Dāmodara is indeed the lord of the juice of leaves, and Ratnanīra;
Narottama and Adhokṣaja are the lords of the vessel of molten gold,
while Nṛsiṃha is the lord of the water of *gulā* (jujube), and Acyuta is the lord of the juice of sugarcane.
The deity of the seed-vessel is remembered as Hari;

Kṛṣṇa, however, is the deity of the vessel for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the jar for the rite of peace (śānti). Indeed, he is the presiding deity of the five principles (pañcatattva) and the water-pitcher.
And Ādisūkara-deva— thus are the deities proclaimed.
Having worshipped each of these deities with incense, lamps, perfumes, and so forth,
the chief practitioners, reciting the Gāyatrī and the name of Viṣṇu, [should proceed].
Having taken up the pitchers according to the sequence of the ritual placement of substances (*dravyanyāsa*),
O Rame, the preceptor (*deśika*) should place them in the hand of the *ācārya* along with the others;
reciting the mantra, he should consecrate the deity while facing north.
Then, with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra, one should bathe the deity with water from the foot-bath pitcher;
then, with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should bathe him with the water for the arghya offering; and reciting the mantra "na te viṣṇo," one should offer the water for ācamana.
One should sprinkle [the image] with cow's milk while reciting the mantra "āpyāyasva";
one should bathe Hari with curd while reciting the Yajus formula "dadhi krāvṇo akāriṣam.
One should bathe the Lord of Gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) while reciting the root-vidyā.

One should bathe the Lord with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) while reciting the mantra "madhu vātā," and with fragrant waters while uttering the mantra "gandhadvārām. One should bathe him with water infused with fruits while reciting the anuvāka beginning with "phalinī."
One should bathe [the deity] with purificatory waters while reciting the mantra "śaṃ no devī";
one should bathe [him] with water infused with leaves while reciting the mantra "yā oṣadhīḥ";
and there is the consecration with precious gem-water and metallic water while reciting the mantra "iṣetvā."
One should perform the bathing with jaggery-water using the mantra "madhu vātā";
with water and unbroken rice-grains (akṣata) using the Sāvitrī;
and one should bathe [the deity] with seed-syllable water using the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ".
The bathing of the Lord with decoctions and waters of pacification is performed with the mantra "vedāham";
the bathing with ghee is performed with the mantra "ghṛtasnātā";
and the bathing with a stream of warm water is performed with the Yajurvedic mantra "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ".
The preceptor should perform a bath with "puṣpāmbu" (flower-water) using the mantra "yo 'pāṃ puṣpam";
then an ablution with water containing all medicinal herbs accompanied by the *puruṣasūkta*;
and an ablution with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the mantra "viṣṇoḥ karma."

With the mantra "Thou art lifted up" (uddhṛtāsī) using water from a funeral rite, or with the *gaṅgā* mantra "This [water] for me," or by means of the pure *tīrtha*, one should worship the Lord of Gods; or else with the *mūla-vidyā*,
or with the mantra "Victory to Thee" (*jitaṃ te*), or with "Of waters" (*ambhasya*)— O Rame!
One should consecrate each object with its own respective mantra;
or else with the Puruṣasūkta, or with the twelve-syllable vidyā,
or with the Viṣṇugāyatrī, or with the six-syllable mantra of Rāma.
Or else, the Guru should bathe the Lord of Śrī with the vidyā of his own form;
likewise, by means of the placement of eighty-one jars,
or forty-nine, thirty, twenty-five, or twenty-one.

Likewise, O Lotus-born One, I shall describe the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the jars established by the number one for the seventeenth, as well as for the sixteenth, which arises from the union [of the others], and for those numbered twelve, nine, and five. (27.101–27.102)
O Goddess, when one is consecrated with eighty-one jars,
the wise man should place nine [jars] in the central Vairiñca [mandala];
likewise, in each of the eight directions of the divine site, he should place nine [jars] each.
The meritorious holy site (puṇyatīrtha) of the pitchers placed at the positions of the Creator (Vidhātṛ) is in the center.
Around it, in the eight pitchers located in the directions starting from the east and so forth,
in due order, there should be fruit-water, cleansing water, honey-mixture (madhuparka), and [water] with leaves.
Water with gems, water with iron, water produced from sugarcane,
and the water for pacification (śāntivāri) [are placed] in the feet of the deity, beginning from the front.
As for the substances in the middle jars, there are one hundred and eight, as follows:
In the same manner, listen now regarding those numbering forty-nine surrounding it: having placed nine jars filled with the ritual substances as before in the station of Brahmā,
one should place them in the eight directions at the stations of the deities in due order.

Having placed five [vessels] each into those central jars, one should fill them with the very same substances as those used for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. One should fill the corner jars with pure water, [reciting the mantra] "O you born from the churning of the ocean of milk! (27.109).
O Goddess, when the god is consecrated with thirty jars—
two jars filled with meritorious water and unbroken grains being placed in the center at the station of Parameṣṭhin— and likewise in the eight directions around them...
One should place each [substance] individually, beginning from the front, together with the ritual materials:
curd, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), likewise honey, scented water, fruit-water,
water for rinsing, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with leaves.
One should place five jars each in the four directions at the site of the deity.
In those central jars, one should fill them with water for washing the feet (pādya), respectful offerings (arghya), and sipping water (ācamana);
the others should be filled with milk or with pure water according to the twenty-five-fold [mantra] ritual.
In the Vairiñca rite, there should be an ablution with jars; having placed five pitchers [filled] with meritorious water, one should offer them into the central jar.
In the four directions around it, one should place four [pitchers] containing curd, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and honey.
Scented water [is placed] at the location of the deity and in all four directions. There is an arrangement of thirty jars, as well as their filling with ritual substances.
Of the twenty-one jars, there is one jar at the location of the Creator (Sraṣṭṛ).

Having filled [the vessels] with water from sacred bathing-places (puṇyatīrtha) in the four intermediate directions in due order, and having placed five jars each in them, one should indeed place in those central jars unbroken rice-water, as well as water from the bīja-mantra, decoction-water, and peace-water (śāntivāri).
One should fill other jars with pure, strained water,
O auspicious lady, using seventeen jars so that the deity may be consecrated.
[The seat] should be fashioned from grain, featuring a pericarp and sixteen petals.
Upon that pedestal, in the pericarp, one should place a single jar, and likewise other jars; having placed them, one should fill the central one with water from a sacred bathing place (puṇyatīrtha).
With the five [substances]—water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācāma), milk, and curd—one should [fill the others].
O Goddess, one should pour in the nectars (amṛtas), honey, and fragrant water;
one should also pour in fruit-water, cleansing water, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
as well as leaf-water, jewel-water, metal-water, and molasses-water.
When there are sixteen jars, the [consecration] derived from sugarcane would be of middling quality;
the Guru should then consecrate the God of gods and arrange the jars.
With twelve [jars], he should place them with rice grains in sequence from the west to the east.

Having first arranged three rows, one should place four jars in each; thus, when placed in the three [rows], there will indeed be twelve. One should fill them with water containing the substances for the foot-washing and so forth, ending with leaves.
When I am present in the nine jars to be established—
with the sacred water from holy pilgrimage sites in the central jar and indeed in the eight jars surrounding it—
one should perform the placement of the ritual substances, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the fragrant paste (gandha).

Among the five jars, the sacred water from a holy bathing place (*puṇyatīrtha*) should be placed in the middle one. In the corners starting from the southeast, one should fill the single jar with water containing unbroken rice (*akṣata*), seed-water (*bījavāri*), pacifying water (*śāntitoya*), and saffron-colored water (*kāṣāya*).
Having filled a jar with meritorious water, one should bathe Hari;
yet in this scripture, an initiation even greater than this has been proclaimed.
Nevertheless, O beloved, I have described it to you only in brief.
During the consecration and festivals, in rites such as penances,
and on occasions such as the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*),
one should perform worship in four locations according to one’s means and then bathe Hari.
This principal consecration has been described to you, O lotus-eyed one;
without the fire-oblation (homa), it would be middling, as would be the case with the mandala of the wheel-lotus.
Devoid of worship, O auspicious lady, it is inferior; the wise man, having understood this, should perform [the rite].
The preceptor himself should collect the substances required for the bath— curd, milk, honey, and all other materials—
before the bathing of the Lord Hari is completed by the patron.
One should satisfy the teachers and the practitioners with various kinds of wealth,
and one should also satisfy all other Vaiṣṇavas according to one's capacity.
At the conclusion of the ritual bathing, if one has the means, one should arrange a festival.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter of the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter: The Sequence of Worship [The Ritual for Daily Sacrifice].
[Śrī: O lotus-eyed one, O Hari, sovereign of the entire world!
Having established Hari, one should worship the imperishable one constantly with devotion. 28.1
"You should explain that worship which was mentioned by you in its entirety.
The Blessed One said: "O Goddess, from the day of completion until the day of the installation, the preceptor... [28.2]

A devotee of the Lord should worship with devotion daily according to his means— either six times, or three times, or twice, or once. O Rame, I shall explain that method according to the injunctions prescribed in the scriptures.

Rising from bed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, with his senses restrained, the teacher—the preceptor—having washed his hands and feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), and remained silent while praising Hari with hymns beginning with "Victory! (*jitaṃ te*), should go to the temple and so forth. (28.4–28.5)

Having performed the purification of the body and other preliminary rites, one should then bathe according to the prescribed rule; or else, O Goddess, having carefully considered the qualities of the place, the time, and so forth, as well as the state of one's own body, one may bathe with warm water, O Rame.

Or, having performed the ritual bath with mantras and other rites, one should carry out the daily obligatory duties (nityakarman). One should adorn oneself with a pair of garments, earrings and other ornaments, white clay, vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and fragrant substances such as sandalwood.
The best of preceptors should adorn [the disciple] with golden sacred threads and garlands;
he should cleanse his mouth with betel leaves accompanied by mouth-perfumes.
Having washed his hands and feet in the area outside the gateway, [he should enter].
Having sipped water for purification, he then proceeded clockwise within the great sacred precinct (mahāpīṭha).
Upon reaching the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa), he recited the twelve-syllable mantra;
at that time, the bards and panegyrists also cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory! (jaya jaya).
With various other hymns and pleasing sounds of lutes and other instruments,
the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) should likewise awaken the Lord of Gods;
having reached the gate, they should praise him with devotion through divine songs.

Having first mentally worshipped the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the gods stationed at the door-panels and those standing on the door-posts, as well as Śrī situated on the Udumbara post, and Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Standing facing the door-panel, he should meditate upon the Lord of the Wind;
having performed three claps with his hands while standing with palms joined,
the best of teachers should effect the opening of that door.
Having mentally divided [the space] into three parts, and having further divided the middle portion into two,
he should stand with his palms joined in *añjali* and enter within by means of the right foot, accompanied by the gentle *devavrata* chant.
Having lit lamps with the six-syllable vidyā-mantra,
and having bowed my head to the Lord, the Master of the World, as he lies upon his bed,
O Rame, I shall awaken him from his sleep with hymns characterized by the signs of awakening.
Having seated the God upon the pedestal, one should apply the Śakti at the base.
Then, removing the curtain, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) of Hari;
at that time, [one should offer] to the God the back of a cow, the face of a horse, and the face of an elephant.
One should show the blue-locked deity, the great mirror, and also the maiden;
one should praise the God, who is endowed with universal power, with hymns headed by the *Jitantā* and other verses,
as well as with other songs, [offering] cow’s milk mixed with sugar.
Having offered curd-rice and other such items, one should then commence the daily worship (nityapūjā).
At the time of worship, the most excellent guru should first perform the fivefold purification:
the purification of the place, the purification of the vessel, and likewise the purification of the image.
Then, O Rame, I performed the purification of the elements for myself according to the syllables of the mantra;
likewise, I prepared a canopy for the inner sanctum of Hari with clusters of peacock feathers or handfuls of *darbha* grass,
as well as a lion-throne.
The preceptor should first sweep the ground, the wall, and the area around the altar-platform with the mantra "śucī va," using water mixed with powdered saffron, agallochum,
camphor, and sandalwood.
Having thoroughly smeared the inner sanctum, he himself should scatter unbroken grains;
if the vessels are made of gold and so forth, they should be cleansed with sugar, and those of silver with lime and other substances.
Copper and brass vessels [should be cleaned] with water infused with the fruit of the *tintriṇī*.
O Rame, the vessels for worship should indeed be made of bell-metal or wood;
one should cleanse them with ash and clay respectively,
having consecrated the vessels with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by [the name of] Viṣṇu.
Having removed the ornaments, garments, garlands, and sandalwood paste from the primary image (mūlabera) and other icons on the previous day, I then take delight [in them].
One should purify them with a clean cloth while reciting the mantra "tac chaṃyoḥ."
Starting from the half-pavilion up to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) for the lotus-born [Brahmā],
the attendant or the practitioner, by his command, should purify the kitchen, the sacrificial ground, the vessels, and all other items. (28.31–28.32)
On the day before, the archways and other decorations made at the gates with flowers and sprouts of mango and other trees should be removed;
then one should join new ones and arrange colorful festoons.
One should meditate upon Senaśa with the mind for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the sacrifice.
Then, for the purpose of purifying one's own body, as well as the sacrificial materials,
the sacrificial hall, and the kitchen, the Guru should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
With that, one should thoroughly purify everything— the self as well as the temple.
Then, while the resonance of the Vedas and the sound of musical instruments proceed,
one should go inside the inner sanctum and fasten the door.

Having covered that door with a curtain, the most excellent of gurus went to the right side of the deity and sat upon a seat. The seer is said to be Mount Meru, and the meter is the ground of the seat.
The deity is Śrī Kūrma; one should employ him upon a lotus seat.
The wise practitioner should place a *kūrca* made of seven *darbha* grasses upon the seat.
Upon that, he should meditate on the god Kūrma as either a *svastika* or a lotus.
Having tied [the cord] and sat down, one should then bind the directions with the Astra-mantra (28.40).
One should perform the burning with the Vahni-mantra and the Agniprākāra-mudrā;
one should meditate on the sky situated within the enclosure by means of the Cakra-mudrā (28.41).
Having covered [the area] with the Cakra-mantra, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the Praṇava, and its metre (chandas) is called Gāyatrī.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the deities who preside over exhalation (recaka) and the other phases [of breath control].
The seed-syllable is the letter *ha*, the power (*śakti*) is *hāṃ*, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is remembered as the letter *ka*.
One should contemplate the mantra, endowed with a smoke-colored hue, during breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
having assumed the yoga-mudrā, one should purify the evils of the body.
Having meditated upon the smoke-colored seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is square and located in the bulb of the navel,
one should purify the impurities of one's own body by means of that wind.
The fire-seed-syllable, triangular and pale-red in luster, is situated in the lotus of the heart.
Having meditated [on this], the Guru should burn away impurity with the splendors arising therefrom.
Having meditated on the seed-syllable of Mahendra, yellow in luster and square, located at the throat,
he should then arrest the wind with the wind arising therefrom.
Having meditated on the seed-syllable of Varuṇa situated at the crown of the head— circular and resembling crystal—
one should wash the body with the nectar-water arising from it. Then,
one should purify sin through the *recaka* breaths and subsequently burn it away with the *pūraka* breaths.
One should arrest the fire by means of *kumbhaka* breath-retentions; in this way, one shall purify evil.
One should emanate the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth, preceded by their reabsorption.
For the mantra of earth, the seer is said to be Brahmarṣi and the meter is Gāyatrī.
The deity is declared to be Varāha, resplendent with the syllable *huṃ*.
One should withdraw the earth, which is square, yellow in color, endowed with five qualities,
and characterized by the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of smell, along with the sense organs of the nose and the genitals.
The region of the earth is said to extend from the feet to the knees.
Sindhu-dvīpa is the seer (ṛṣi) of water; its meter is stated to be *tal*, and its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *vaṃ*;
its presiding deity is Varuṇa, and its form should be like that of the moon.
The tongue, white in color, together with the ether and the anus, is in the *Rama* [channel];
water has four qualities, and in the lotus of taste, it should withdraw the smell.
The region from the knees to the end of the secret place is declared to be the abode of water.

The seer is Kāśyapa of Agni; the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Tanūnapāt. They say the seed-syllable is the letter *ra*; at the time of dissolution, the Guru should contemplate it as fire—possessing three qualities, triangular, and pale-red—consisting of sight, feet, and the sense organ.
The teacher should contemplate the subtle element of taste within form;
the wise know the region from the secret place to the navel as the locus of fire.
For the seed-syllable of wind, Kiṣkindha is the seer and the Jāgata is the meter.
The deity Pavana should contemplate that seed-syllable during the process of withdrawal;
it is smoke-colored, endowed with two qualities, and possessed of the hand, skin, and sense of touch.
Then, one should withdraw the wind and the form from the sense of touch.
The Guru should touch the locus of air, extending from the navel up to the nose.
Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of space, and the Gāyatrī is its metre.
The seed-syllable is "Ṣaṃ," and the venerable Lord Aniruddha is proclaimed as its deity.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, joined with the organ of speech and hearing;
endowed with the quality of sound, formless, and very extensive—this is called the location of space (ākāśa), extending from the nose to the top of the head. (28.61–62)
One should withdraw touch into sound, and delight in that which is characterized by the subtle element (tanmātra).
Having withdrawn sound into the internal organ (svānta), one should then withdraw the internal organ into the ego-principle (ahaṃkṛti).
One should withdraw the ego into the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), and the intellect into primordial nature (prakṛti), and therein I find delight.

Having restrained the breath through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the teacher should withdraw the primordial nature (prakṛti) into the individual soul (jīva). Having meditated upon the wind situated in the navel-center (nābhikanda) by means of the kumbhaka breath,
[he should contemplate] that which is extremely subtle, located in the navel-wheel (nābhicakra), and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The Guru should cause the life-force, rendered helpless by the vital wind, to ascend through the *suṣumnā* channel— which is as subtle as a lotus fiber— to the head;
having caused it to exit through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), he should lead it to the orb of the sun.
One should join that [soul] from its maṇḍala into the Blessed One, the supreme Brahman.
One should purify the gross body born of a womb through methods such as drying.
Then, one should lead the individual soul (jīva) of oneself out from the abode of the supreme Brahman.
Having caused [the soul] to enter the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the path of the lunar orb,
one should then remember it as having entered again through the suṣumṇā channel into the heart-lotus;
from that living soul (jīva), one should emanate [the elements] up to Prakṛti, and then from the Blessed Lord Hari.

For the sake of propitiation, one should contemplate one's own body as pure being (*śuddhasattva*). Having visualized the celestial river arising from the lotus-foot of Trivikrama, one should properly contemplate oneself as having bathed therein. (28.70–71)
Having thus purified his own self, the most excellent guru, possessing perfected mantras, should commence the daily sacrifice (nityayāga) for Hari of wondrous deeds;
just as I take delight in the installation of images, including their postures and seats.
With whichever mantra and whichever image [the deity] was assigned by the practitioner,

with that very mantra the Guru should perform the worship and also assign [the deities] upon himself. First, one should commence the assignment of the hands (karanyāsa) through the stages of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution.
One should purify the palms and backs of both hands with the Astra-vidyā; likewise,
one should perform the placement of the Praṇava upon all the joints of the fingers, both at the beginning and the end, and specifically upon the middle joints.

Those who know the mantras understand this as the "arrangement of the syllables of the mantra. O Rame, beginning from the joint of the right index finger and proceeding through the joints of the fingers up to the end of the joint of the left index finger, this placement constitutes the "creation" (sṛṣṭi).
But by reversing [the order], there is withdrawal; while for maintenance, one begins at the joint of the index finger of both hands and rests on the little finger.
This is declared to be the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight-syllable mantra.
Listen, O fair-faced one, to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the twelve-syllable mantra:
the placement is on the palm with the middle finger, and with the index finger on the joint of the thumb.
Then, having performed the eight-syllable placement, the wise practitioner should perform everything [else]. (28.79–28.80)
Resting on the left palm is for creation; with the other [right palm], it is for dissolution;
and for preservation, O Goddess, the Guru should proceed as before with both palms.
He should place his own rest upon the two little fingers.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-syllable mantra has also been taught by the ancients:
beginning with the middle finger of the right hand,
and likewise for the left hand, one should perform the placement up to the middle finger, O Rame.

O auspicious lady, this *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (creation-assignment) is said to be the reverse of *layanyāsa* (dissolution-assignment). Beginning from the middle fingers of both hands and proceeding to the little fingers, this assignment is called *sthitinyāsa* (maintenance-assignment).
Now, first of all, the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) for the Jewel of Mantras is described.
A wise person should perform this placement of the six-syllable mantra upon the head, the face, the heart, the navel, the knees, and the feet during the rite of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
In the rite of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), the placement (*nyāsa*) is prescribed from the feet up to the crown of the head.
In the placement of the eight-syllable mantra, however, the eyes and the secret place [are included], and it is further augmented [by the others].
For the twelve-syllable mantra, [the placement is performed] on the head and the four [limbs] in sequence.
The arrangement in the directions starting from the east has been proclaimed as additional.
Now I shall describe to you, according to the proper application, the ritual of placement for the three mantras consisting of twelve syllables and so forth, upon the fingers.
Then, one should place [the thumb] on the eastern part of the head with the thumb;
on the southern position with the index finger; on the western with the ring finger;
on the northern with the little finger; and in the middle, one should place it with the middle finger.
One should visualize the Yogapīṭha lotus on the Mantrāsana, and elsewhere one should contemplate it [differently].
One should meditate upon Tārkṣya on the Mantrāsana and Ananta on the Śayanāsana;
furthermore, one should perform the placement of the eyes with the middle and index fingers.
The knower of mantras should place [the mudrā] on the mouth with the ring finger and the thumb;
one should perform the placement on the heart with the thumb and forefinger;
likewise, the placement on the navel is proclaimed to be performed with the thumb and little finger.

Without the thumb, one should place [the mudrās] with the remaining fingers on the secret parts and on both knees; with all fingers together, they are placed on the two feet—these are the stages for the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should assign these to the respective locations of the eight-syllable and six-syllable mantras.
I abide in the limbs during the placement [of mantras] from the navel to the end of the heart;
I shall now declare the eight-syllable mantra, complete with its deity, ṛṣi, and other elements.
First, one should utter the Praṇava (Oṃ), and after that, the word "namaḥ."
The sage is remembered as Nārāyaṇa in the dative case (nārāyaṇāya), the inner controller (antaryāmī).
The deity is the manifest Nārāyaṇa; Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter.
"Aṃ" is the seed-syllable, Āya is the power (śakti), and "hrīṃ" is proclaimed as the pin (kīlaka).
They say that Vaikuṇṭha is the sacred field (kṣetra), and Śrī is proclaimed as its armor;
[it is] four-armed, with noble limbs, attended by weapons such as the discus,
resembling a dark rain-cloud, and having eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Wearing yellow garments, gentle, with earrings blazing with jewels,
adorned with shimmering bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and the Kaustubha gem,
the Lord sits upon a jeweled lion-throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
One should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation to those who have taken refuge in him—
white, golden, black, red, resembling saffron,
like the filaments of a lotus, and eighthly, possessing all colors.
In this manner, one should contemplate the colors of the syllables at the time of their placement.
O Goddess, I shall now declare the seers and deities of the twelve-syllable mantra:
having first uttered "Udgītha," one should then say "namo bhagavate. (28.103–104)

Vāsudeva ending in the dative case is declared as the seer (ṛṣi); Brahmā is said to be its meter (chandas), while the goddess Gāyatrī is the meter and Vāsudeva is the deity (devatā). Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Āya is the power (śakti), and Hrīṃ is declared to be the pin (kīlaka).
"Śrīṃ" is the armor, "Om" is the weapon; the color is proclaimed to be white.
White, black, smoke-colored, dark-blue, and like the stars (white), as well as crystal-like, conch-like, red, pale-white, and crimson. || 28.106–28.107 ||
One should meditate upon the forms of the syllables in their proper sequence: [the form of] Tamas as yellow-colored,
two-armed, lotus-eyed, with a body like pure crystal,
wearing a crown and earrings, and adorned with a forest garland.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Vāsudeva, who has the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest, whose neck is bent by the shining Kaustubha gem,
whose middle of the arms is embraced by the Goddess of Yoga, who is higher than the highest,
and who dwells in the supreme ether.

Now I shall declare the six-syllabled mantra for the sake of attaining the presence of Viṣṇu. Having uttered the first of the meters, one should then remember the wife of Fire (Svāhā). Thereafter, the one skilled in mantras should meditate upon the word "Viṣṇave."
O Rame, for this Śrī Viṣṇu mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi);
the meter (chandas) is Devīgāyatrī, and Viṣṇu is declared to be the deity.
The seed-syllable and other elements should be as before; one should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu.
[He saw] the Lord, dark as a rain cloud, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
the inner controller, the Sovereign, resplendent with a crown and other ornaments,
accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and surrounded by Sanaka and the other great sages.

One should meditate upon the six-syllable [mantra] served by hosts of wise sages, seated upon a lotus throne; [one should meditate on it as] a white water-lily, a bandhūka flower, a blue lotus, a lotus filament,
and a lotus resembling the flower of the atasī plant.

O Rame, at the time of performing the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the Guru should indeed perform the placement of the twelve-syllable mantra twice, from the heart to the weapon (astra). First, the placement of the eight-syllable mantra should take place upon the six limbs.
The placement [of mantras] on the heart and the head is prescribed using the two remaining syllables.
One should perform the placement of the six-syllable mantra upon the six limbs in sequence;
furthermore, one should place the previously mentioned syllables of the mantra using the mantras beginning with "jñānāya."
Having mixed [the substances], the preceptor should place them on the limbs in their respective locations:
the crown-mudrā on the head, the śrīvatsa on the right arm,
the kaustubha-mudrā on the left, and then the forest-garland on the neck.
O Goddess, one should place a lotus and a discus on the two right arms;
a mace and a conch on the two left [arms]; likewise, Garuḍa at the tips of the feet;
and for Śeṣa and Aśeṣa, one should display them in their respective locations.

Having meditated on the limbs, beginning with Kruddholka, upon the five [fingers] starting from the thumb, one should place the remaining [limbs] on the human face; and on the palm, the discus together with the lotus.
One should likewise visualize the conch and the Kaumodakī mace on the left and right palms respectively.
One should perform the pervasive placement [of the mantras] from the aperture of Brahmā down to the tips of the feet by means of those two [breaths].
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should worship Hari with the mind.
Then, by means of the air of breath-retention (kumbhaka), the navel-lotus, which is facing downward, [is raised].
Having raised and opened [the door], one should fashion a pedestal therein;
from the primary image (mūlabera), [one should bring forth] Vāsudeva, adorned with a forest garland,
wearing yellow garments, four-armed, and bearing various divine, uplifted weapons.

One should meditate upon the Lord seated on the previously mentioned pedestal, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, resplendent with the Goddess of Yoga (Yogalakṣmī), and accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi; then,
with the most purifying enjoyments born of that contemplation, [one should worship].
The Guru should first worship the Deity and then address him:
"Welcome, O Lord of the gods; please grant your presence within the lotus of my heart.
Accept this mental worship, offered according to your merit."
Having known that the Lord is well-pleased and inclined toward grace,
O Rame, one should pray for his presence, his withdrawal, and his manifestation;
then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon Hari, omitting the placement on the hands (hastanyāsa).
One should display all the mudrās, beginning with those of the crown and the forest garland;
then, having offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the best of preceptors should meditate upon the Lord seated for the bath,
and likewise meditate upon the bath consisting of anointing with oil and so forth.

Having meditated upon the mental ornaments, one should adorn [the deity] with the crown and other regalia. One should mentally present to the Lord everything from the parasol down to the incense and lamps; then, having made a request, one should place the God upon the seat for food with various kinds of foods to be licked, sucked, and eaten as side dishes.
Having offered the four kinds of food to the God immediately thereafter,
and having mentally envisioned the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should satisfy Puruṣottama.
Having performed the sacrifice of dissolution (layayāga), one should then perform the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga).
I shall explain its ritual procedure; listen, O Paṅkajamālinī.
One should place the pedestal for the vessel (pātravedikā) upon a seat in front of the Blessed One.
One should set the receiving vessel (pratigrahapātra) upon the ground and place it facing that [pedestal].
Or else, O Rame, one should place the vessels on the altar in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) or in the directions starting from the east;
and one should deposit a single vessel in the center,
filling those vessels with pure, filtered water.
One should purify the materials for worship brought by those who are uninitiated and others.
One should meditate on the Sun, situated in the center of a wheel, upon the palm of the left hand;
with that [hand], one should touch the materials and burn them with the fire produced therefrom.
One should meditate on the moon situated in the center of a lotus within the palm of the left hand.
One should contemplate that the masses of burnt materials, having been touched by the nectar-water produced from it,
are sprinkled and thus become fit for sacrifice once again.

O Rame, one should place a *cāmpeya* bud, *dūrvā*, and *śyāmāka* grain in the water for the feet (*pādya*); and cardamom, cloves, and camphor should be placed in the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*).
[One should also offer] turmeric, saffron, flowers, camphor, and yellow sandalwood.
The one most skilled in mantras should place these [substances] into the bathing water.
One should cast sesame seeds and *tulasī* into pure water, and touch them while reciting the *Nigama* and other [mantras], saying: "I prepare the *arghya* and the rest."
One should place the substances in the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings while reciting the *hṛdayamantra*.
One should display the *surabhimudrā*, [visualizing] them as filled with nectar. Having meditated thus and taken the *arghya* water with the *uddharinī* [ladle], one should place it upon the altar.
Having placed [the vessel] there, one should pray to the Virajā river from Vaikuṇṭha—
[visualizing her] with four arms, clad in yellow garments, her body like pure crystal,
standing before [him] with two hands joined in *añjali* and holding lotuses.
Having meditated upon her with two other hands as the bestower of liberation to those who have bathed,
and having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, the Guru should fill the vessels with that water from all sides and sprinkle himself with it.
Then, one should draw water from the *arghya* vessel using the *uddhariṇī* (ladle).
Having placed it in the left hand, one should cover it with the right hand;
having drawn it up as far as the forehead, one should recite the root mantra seven times.
Having sprinkled the ritual substances, oneself, and the deity with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra* using the *kūrca*, one should commence the sacrificial offering (*bhogayāga*) for the Lord:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, Janārdana, whose form is the mantra!"
"O Lord of Gods, I perform this worship according to the very path taught by you.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, accept it with affection, desiring to show me grace.
Having thus informed the lotus-born one at the feet of the Root [Mantra], [he offered it].
One should worship with the *prārcasāman* chant; the preceptor should quickly cast a handful of flowers.

Having offered the guest-water (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), as well as perfume, garlands, and incense, and having presented a lamp to the deity, one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
Or else, having offered the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should perform the worship of Śrī and Bhūmi.
Whether on a karma-pīṭha, an arcā-pīṭha, a sahaja-pīṭha, or a separate lotus-throne (kamalālaya),
one should prepare the yoga-pīṭha for the deity’s placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).

Having first meditated upon the support-power (ādhāra-śakti), who is red in color, four-armed, and possesses seven faces, at the base of the pedestal; and immediately after that, the tortoise (kamaṭha);
and above that, the fire of time (kāla-dahana), who has seven faces and three eyes.
He is resplendent with three legs and a pair of seven arms;
above that [is another form] wearing blue garments, adorned with a thousand hoods,
four-armed, white in color, and equipped with a conch and a discus.
Above that, one should visualize the goddess upon the square ground;
upon it, in the corners starting from the southeast, [one should place] Dharma and the others, human in form, four-armed, lion-faced, and seated upon the positions of the yoga-pīṭha.
Having first meditated on those of white complexion in the east and other directions, holding their seats with both hands joined in the *añjali* gesture,
and then [meditating on] Adharma and the others in the four directions, who are red in color and arranged in due order; || 28.161–28.162 ||
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the center, adorned with fifty arms,
possessing twenty-five faces and seventy-five eyes;
he is white-complexioned with a blue throat, together with his heads and hands.
The wise one should meditate upon the Yoga-pīṭha supported [therein], and above that,
he should meditate upon the fourfold [elements]: the Upānaha, the Jagatī, the Paṭṭikā, and the Pota,
in the order of the Ṛgveda and the others, having the form of a wooden plank.
One should then visualize the elements as a mattress, and likewise the individual soul (jīvātman) as the bedspread;
above that, one should meditate on the disks of Fire, Moon, and Sun in their proper order,
and upon them, a white lotus with twelve petals.

In the center, one should visualize the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of a lotus that is joined with a pericarp and well-filled with filaments (*kesara*) and other parts; at the beginning of the Vedas, O Lotus-born One. On its twelve petals, starting from the east and proceeding in due order— || 28.167–28.168 ||
Śrīvatsa, the forest garland, and Vaiṣṇavī Yogamāyā; likewise Vimalā, Sṛṣṭi, and the power Utkarṣiṇī; Prabhavā, Satyā, and Īśānā, as well as Anumantī, the Grandmother (Pitāmahī).
Holding joined palms with their front arms and likewise with their rear arms,
these lotus-eyed goddesses bear blossoming golden lotuses;
they [should be placed] in the directions beginning with the southeast circle of fire, starting with Indra and the others in due order.
O Goddess, within the orb of the sun, in the positions beginning with Kumuda, one should place these weapons—
conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, thunderbolt, sword,
and likewise the lotus and pestle— in human form.

Furthermore, within the orb of the Moon, one should remember these eight Śaktis— Vyāpti, Kānti, Tṛpti, Śraddhā, Vidyā, Jayā, Kṣamā, and Śānti— each holding a chowrie, positioned in order in the eight directions starting from the east.
In the outer enclosure, one should visualize Tārkṣya in the northeast corner and the General,
all standing with palms joined in reverence, facing toward the Lord. Having thus meditated upon the Yoga-pīṭha and the deities of power residing therein, [one should proceed].
Thereafter, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
At the commencement of the worship, one should remember in the heart the preceptor who belongs to the lineage of the Blessed One.
O Rame, [this applies] indeed to the ritual image whether it is seated or reclining.
At the time of conceptualizing the pedestal, one should first remember the lotus;

then, O Goddess, one should remember Ananta, adorned with a thousand hoods. One should contemplate Tārkṣya as being beneath the image that is mounted upon the vehicle [of Garuḍa], starting from the lotus.
One should contemplate the *yogapīṭha* as a lotus upon the *mantrāsana*;
elsewhere, one should meditate on Tārkṣya for the *yātrāsana* and Ananta for the *śayanāsana*.
For the goddesses such as Śrī and others, however, there is a tortoise at the base of the pedestal (*pīṭhamūla*).

In the center of that, [the worshipper] should meditate upon the Lord of Serpents; in its corners, O Lotus-born One, one should meditate upon Dharma and the others in sequence; and above that, the unmanifest lotus. At the commencement of the worship, the preceptor should remember the lineage of the Blessed One and his own Guru.

I shall describe the procedure for invocation; listen, O lotus-born one! During the invocation, the deity is drawn from the heart-lotus of the primary image into the vessel, and then, by means of the *puṅgalā* [mantra], into the lotus of the heart of each respective image.
Having invoked [the deity] through the Suṣumṇā channel, one should then perform the worship and other rites;
at the conclusion of each respective rite, one should likewise re-join [the deity] with the root mantra.
Before three muhūrtas have passed since the commencement of the worship, one should worship Puruṣottama.
Having performed the worship without performing the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), one should then perform the dismissal.
Just as fire shines from the sun-gem due to the sun,
so too [the deity] manifests from the root-mantra through the prayer of the worshipper during the preliminary rites and the consecration of the image.
O Rame, Hari is present in the three locations and in the bathing pitcher.
One should fill the vessel—the seat of invocation—with fragrant waters.
Then, having cast *tulasī* into it with the root mantra, [one should proceed].
With both hands, one should raise that vessel up to the forehead.
It stands at the base, possessing a splendor equal to millions upon millions of suns, fires, and moons;
it has two arms, a single lotus face, and is attended by weapons such as the discus.
One should pray with this verse to Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, who is adorned with a crown, a forest garland, and the Kaustubha gem:
"O You of dense radiance, born from the milk-ocean of the essence of compassion!"
"Come, come, O Acyuta, for the sake of the daily worship into this vessel.
Having thus prayed, [he should contemplate] the primary image as having arrived in that vessel,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and Śārṅga bow, and clad in yellow garments.
[Vasudeva] whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, adorned with a forest garland and other ornaments,
resembling a dark blue rain cloud, four-armed,
seated upon a lotus throne, and possessing a golden luster.
He was resplendent with a crown inlaid with priceless jewels,
and [his hair] resembled crushed collyrium as dark as a fresh rain-cloud,
its interior intermingled with *mādhavī*, jasmine, and *jāti* flowers.
He was beautifully adorned with divine masses of hair grey as camphor;
his lotus-face possessed locks of curly hair as soft as swarms of bees,
and it was radiant with a tilaka mark rising upon his forehead that put the moon of the eighth day to shame.
His side-glances ripple with a flood of unrestrained compassion;
his eyes mock the white lotus frequented by bees.
With his cooling glances, he brings joy to the entire world.
His beautiful nose was radiant with golden campaka flowers;
his teeth gleamed with a gentle smile, and his lips were like the bandhūka flower.
He was adorned with jeweled earrings resting upon mirror-like cheeks.
Adorned with a chin that has the form of a casket of beauty,
it is radiant with a necklace shimmering like a crescent moon resting upon his conch-like neck;
its chest is exquisitely perfumed with saffron, agallochum, and musk.
He has four arms and noble limbs, long arms, and is in the full bloom of youth;
he is adorned with shimmering bracelets, armlets, and precious finger-ornaments,
and his sprout-like hands are joined in readiness to bestow the four aims of human existence.
With his primary right hand he grants fearlessness to those who have taken refuge;
with his left hand, resting playfully upon the lotus-seat,
he holds the Kaumodakī mace and the Śārṅga bow with his right paw.
He bore the Sudarśana discus with its thousand spokes, possessing the brilliance of ten million fires of cosmic destruction;
it resounded with the resonance of the syllable Om and was adorned as if by a hundred Himalayan mountains.
In his left hand, he held the perfectly pure conch, Pāñcajanya.

His chest shone with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, its borders illuminated by the horizon; his broad breast was resplendent with ornaments of jewels, gold, and fine pearls, as well as a forest garland and a sacred thread.
Adorned by swarms of bees wandering about in the fragrance of the *tulasī* garland;
its interior cavity beautified by many shining cosmic eggs;
and made exceedingly beautiful by the navel-lotus, the birthplace of the Creator.
His waist shone with yellow garments resembling a mass of thousands of *campaka* flowers;
his girdle was joined with the *Nandaka* sword that humbles the pride of the lord of serpents;
and he was radiant with a pair of beautiful thighs as majestic as the trunk of the lord of elephant herds.
Adorned with the beautiful circles of his divine knees, which shine like bursting pearl-oyster shells;
enchanting with the smooth shanks that captivate the pride of fish-women;
and possessing a pair of feet shaped like tortoises, resplendent with jeweled anklets.
His webbed fingers shone with coral-like luster, adorned with rings of gleaming jewels;
his rows of nails were resplendent, shining like the ten moons of autumn;
he was complete with all the auspicious marks and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
With a beautiful, divine, and manifested form,
emitting from his body a constant light characterized by wisdom—
the Lord of meditators who destroys ignorance without effort— (he sat).
With a heart full of compassion and striving for the upliftment of the world,
augmented by the power of his indivisible and perfect sixfold attributes,
he is the God of all gods, a treasury of all splendors.
Situated in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of his own body— worthy of meditation by yogis, unborn, eternal, and the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe—
having thus remembered the Lord of Lakṣmī, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, with devotion; [28.216–28.217]
Having meditated, one should sprinkle the head of the ritual object with that water using the *kūrca* brush;
one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra four times and say "Come" in unison.
One should contemplate the Supreme Self residing in the vessel as being present within the ritual image.
Having displayed the *āvāhana* (invocation) mudrā, thereafter comes the *sthāpana* (establishment):
"O All-pervading Lord, Sovereign of all worlds, served by the son of Vinatā;
for the protection of the entire universe, welcome to You, O Lord of the World! (28.219–28.220).
Thus one should display the gesture of welcome (*svāgatamudrā*) and the image, saying:
"O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship,
remain present within this image through your devotion to me."
O fair-faced one, he should display the *sānnidhya-mudrā*, the prayer, and the boon-granting gesture (*vara-mudrā*).
Having addressed him thus: "Be well-disposed, O Lord of Gods, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Janārdana," he should also display the *sānnidhya-mudrā*.
"O consort of Govinda, you who possess the splendor of thick streaks of lightning arising from the nectar-ocean of beauty, come to this vessel for invocation!
Having thus prayed, one should then meditate upon Śrī, residing within the vessel, as being present in the [divine] image.

"O auspicious Earth, come to this vessel for worship— you who support all living beings, who are beloved, and who are the essence dear to the Supreme Self. Having thus invoked the Earth residing within the vessel, one should unite her with the image.
The best of teachers should display the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana);
in the absence of a primary [image] for Śrī and the others, he should do so from the primary image of the Lord.
Having invoked the Śaktis into the ritual images of Śrī and the others, he should worship them.
At the time of the deposition of mantras, however, having meditated upon the Lord of Gods seated on the yoga-throne within the body of the deity, one should perform the deposition of mantras;
one should display all the mudrās, beginning with the crown and ending with the Lord of Serpents.
One should likewise place *śrām* and so forth upon the body of Śrī, as well as that of Bhū;
O lotus-eyed one, one should then place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *hrām*.
Then, having displayed the lotus mudrā, the Guru should pray to the Lord of Gods.
"I am your slave, O Lord of the World, together with my sons, wife, and home.
Employ me in whatever must be done; I am your servant, ever devoted to your welfare.
Today, O Hari, I worship you with devotion through offerings such as the *arghya* and other enjoyments. (28.231–232)
"O Supreme Lord, accept this worship as mine.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Ramā, one should then worship Him with the *arghya* offering and other rites.
After performing the worship of Śrī and Bhūmi, one should present the *madhuparka*.
[The Lord] was seen engaged in yoga, or in adornment, or likewise on a journey, or at a meal; bathing, or sitting comfortably, or reclining on a bed;
or in other services, whether standing or indeed seated. (28.234–235)
