The wise preceptor, like a mother toward her infant or a virtuous wife toward her beloved husband during dalliance, should contemplate [the disciple] facing eastward, either according to the sequence of the directions of the gods or on the seat for bathing and mantras upon the ritual grass-mat, just as he would treat his own disciple.
In matters of adornment, the worshipper should serve the guest like a householder;
on the journey-seat and the excellent couch, he should serve the King like a minister or a servant; and in prayer, he should meditate upon the God like a friend. (28.237–28.238)
But when performing the rite for a single *bera*, O Rāme, the Guru should first worship the deities seated upon the *yogapīṭha* in their proper order;
then he should perform the worship according to the rules, beginning with the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and ending with the fire-oblation (*homa*). (28.239)
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others within the images during sacrifices, worship, and other rites.
Now I shall describe for you the procedure for the invocation in the case of multiple forms: Vāsudeva is four-armed and endowed with the six qualities beginning with knowledge.

At the festival and the *kautuka* [consecration] of the Root [deity], one should visualize Saṃkarṣaṇa, who resembles pure crystal; at the *balikautuka*, Pradyumna, who has a reddish luster and is the embodiment of knowledge (*jñānamūrti*);
and at the bathing ceremony (*snānakautuka*), Pradyumna, who is the embodiment of power (*balamūrti*) and golden in color.
Having invoked Aniruddha— who possesses the form of prosperity, has dense radiance,
is the embodiment of Dharma, has a lotus-navel, and is dark like a peacock’s neck—
into the dream-image at the appropriate time, one should worship him.

One should meditate upon all those who have arisen from Vāsudeva—Keśava and the other leaders—as having four arms, bearing the conch, discus, lotus, and mace; their chests marked with the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha jewels, and adorned with forest garlands and other ornaments. (28.245)

Having duly worshipped the bathing seat, one should perform the worship of the sandals (pādukā). One should meditate upon the Lord Garuḍa, who consists of the Vedic meters, as the ornament of the King of Mountains (Meru) with its golden depth, within the sandals.
One should bathe the sandals with mantra-infused water while reciting the Tārkṣya-gāyatrī.
Having worshipped them with flowers, incense, and other offerings on the ground in front of the bathing pedestal,
one should arrange from twelve to one jar according to one's means.

Having prepared the jars and worshipped them, one should bring forth the auspicious bath. "O Lord of Gods, this time for the bath has arrived; if it is your will, I shall anoint you and cause you to perform a beautiful ablution."
Having made this request, one should offer a sandal made of gold to the God;
one should meditate upon the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" during the mounting of the sandals of the Lord.
The Guru should then cause the God to rise with the mantra "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate."
One should lead [the deity] to the bathing seat with the mantra *bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*.
One should place [the deity] upon the bathing seat with the mantra *viṣṇor nu kaṃ*.
And one should offer the *arghya* and *pādya* with the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī* and the mantra *trīṇi padā*.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to Hari with the purifying mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ"; then, one should clean the teeth with a wooden stick;
and one should perform gargling with the tongue for the sake of Viṣṇu using the *Viṣṇugāyatrī* and the *Nigama* mantras.
The preceptor should cause [the image] to be bathed and should clothe Hari in two bathing garments; then,
with the Vāmadevya Sāman, he should perform the rubbing of the Lord's body with scented oil,
beginning from the head down to the feet.
Then, one should comb the hair with a comb while reciting the *Rāmāgāyatrī*,
using oils, fragrant powders, and scented water.
Thereafter, one should purify [the body] from the hair down to the feet with the mantra "tac chaṃyoḥ."
Immediately thereafter, [he should bathe the image] with milk and curd using the mantra "āpyāyasva";
with coconut water and yellow water using the *dadhi krāvṇa* mantra, the *gāyatrī* preceded by Viṣṇu, and the *lakṣmīgāyatrī* respectively.

Then, having offered a pair of garments, the preceptor should bathe [the image] with fragrant paste using the mantra "Gandhadvārā," and thereafter apply an ointment of saffron. He should then adorn the Supreme Lord with necklaces and garlands for the head.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present the *madhuparka*.
Likewise, having invoked the Lord of the Sun (Bhāskara) into a cloth marked with a thousand streams,
and Śrī into a vessel called *śaṅkha* or *padma*, one should worship them.
Having filled those two with water from the *kumbha*, together with the one having a thousand holes,
and accompanied by two preceptors, one should bathe the Lord of Lakṣmī with the *Puruṣasūkta*, or else, O Rame, with the great *kumbha*.

One should sprinkle the Lord of Ramā with streams of jambīra juice while reciting the mantra "śucīva," and then with pure water; one should consecrate the Lord of Gods with water from a conch shell while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra.
One should purify [the head] with a dry cloth while reciting the mantra "agnir mūrdhā";
one should dry the moist hair with fragrant incense while reciting "mūrdhānam. Then, having offered a pair of garments, one should place [the image] upon a lion-throne.
One should propitiate those who occupy the places of adornment and petition them for the performance of ritual acts.
"O Lord of the worlds, please take your seat upon this great and supreme throne of ornaments, together with its lotus pedestal, for the purpose of wearing these finery. (28.267–268)
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should meditate upon him while seated on the decorative throne;
then, having removed the ancient pair of garments with the *vyāhṛti* mantras,
one should cause him to don two new garments with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.

Afterwards, one should smear his body with fragrant sandalwood paste while reciting the Vedic mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; then, one should adorn the Supreme Self with ornaments while reciting "jitaṃ te," and with a resplendent crown.
One should fashion a tilaka on the forehead of the God of gods with garlands made of jewels and ornaments such as the discus;
one should also provide him with a cloak and a sacred thread made of silk cloth and the like.
One should worship the Lord with flower garlands and other offerings while reciting the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ. With the mantra "irāvatī," one should scatter unbroken grains (akṣatān) at His feet.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual purification for each of the images, such as those used in the sacrifice.
One should worship Goddess Kamalā in the mirror, the Lord of Wind (Vāyu) in the fan,
and the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) under the umbrella, each with their respective vidyā-mantras.
With the vyāhṛtis, one should show the mirror and the other objects to the Supreme Self.
Then one should worship the images, such as those made of clay or other materials, with offerings such as *arghya* and so forth.
One should offer betel leaf for cleansing the mouth with the *Ramā-gāyatrī*,
and one should offer *agaru* incense with the mantra beginning "jitaṃ te."
[With the mantra "Be inflamed," one should offer a lamp to Rame.
Upon the clusters of lamps, one should indeed show the stars; upon the central lamps, the moon.
Having invoked them, one should show the lamp to Hari with the verse "Be inflamed" (uddīpyasva).
Then, having removed the curtain and taken up a lamp,
the preceptor [should perform the rite] three times with the Guṇamantra, from the feet up to the head of the ritual image and the other images; having done so, the Guru then—
Betel, rice, mung beans, clarified butter, gold, fruits,
a morsel for the cow, cows, and clothing— these are declared to be the materials for the *mātrā* offering.
One should personally display these materials for the *mātrā* before the deity.
[Having shown it to the deity, one should take it immediately thereafter.
Having withdrawn Vainateya and the others, one should worship them in sequence with the *arghya* and other offerings.
Then the Vaidikas should commence the study of the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas.
The chanters of the hymns should praise with a very loud voice.
In the beautiful dance pavilion, the courtesans and the people should perform dances,
and there the singers should sing auspicious songs.
Then the preceptor should worship the deity with *tulasī* sprouts,
using names such as those of the *vyūhas* and others, as well as names beginning with *vibhava*.
Then, having covered the entrance of the womb-chamber with a *kāṇḍa* cloth, the preceptor [proceeds].

Having placed various kinds of food, such as those fried in ghee and other edibles, upon the sacrificial altar (vedi) in front of the deity, one should purify them by means of drying and other methods;
then, having displayed the Surabhi-mudrā, one should indeed render them nectar-like (amṛtīkṛtya).
One should request all the forms, beginning with the root [deity], with this verse:
"O Lord of the World, these various kinds of pure, clean, and solid foods—eatables and chewables—are prepared; please grace our dining seat."
Having thus informed the Lord, one should place the two sandals upon Hari.
O Rame, one should remember that the food and other offerings are reduced by one-tenth in successive order;
one should present seven-tenths for the seven images beginning with the Mūla-bimba.
One should place one portion of the śāligrāma stone in the vimāna,
another for the fire-oblation (homa), and deposit yet another portion in a separate vessel.
Having meditated upon the Lord seated upon the seat of food, one should worship Him with the arghya and other offerings.
The Guru should place the *arghya* flowers in the Blessed One’s right hand:
"O Lord, please accept with compassion this well-prepared food offered by me, your servant, which grants freedom from fear. (28.292–293)
Having thus informed the deity, one should present the *madhuparka* with the left hand placed upon the right,
while bowing the head with devotion and displaying the gesture of taking a mouthful.
With the mantra "Of the god Viṣṇu," the preceptor should offer thirty-two morsels of food,
such as various kinds of eatables, into the right hand;
and at intervals, he should give water mixed with cardamom and other ingredients.
[Combined with cool water and mixed with cardamom and camphor, or lukewarm and infused with fragrance— this is known as *arhaṇāmbha* (water of honor).
|| 28.297 One should offer this water of honor at the beginning of the meal and seating, and also at the end of the meal.
One should perform the washing of the hands for the God, the Supreme Self.
Then, having offered water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa), one should worship again with arghya and other offerings.
One should purify the lotus-like hands, face, and feet with pure water.
In this manner, one should offer all six— the images of Karma and the others—
as well as Śrī and Bhūmi, and likewise food and other offerings;
then, O Rame, having offered them to Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the Sālagrāma stone.
One should offer food and other items to the Lord of the Temple, who is unobstructed by hunger (Aniruddha).
Then, one should present betel-leaf along with fragrant substances to the primary images beginning with Dhruva. After that, one should lead the power of the bathing image into Dhruva.
At the conclusion of the offering, one should set aside half a portion of the various foods and edibles for the purpose of worshipping Viṣvaksena and others; then,
having drunk the water of acceptance (*pratigrahodaka*), one should place the sandals upon one's own head.
Endowed with humility, the best of worshippers should consume the leaves and flowers that have been used for the sake of completing the worship;
having sat facing the deity, he should eat a small portion of food while observing silence.
The first limb is the worship at the yoga-pīṭha according to the heart-āgamas;
the second limb is the ceremonial bathing; the third is the worship of the attire;
the fourth is the worship of Viṣṇu at the seat for food; and the fifth follows thereafter.
The sixth is the Guru’s partaking of the *siddhi*, and the seventh is the daily worship of the fire. The eighth is said to be the perpetual festival;
thus is the eight-limbed worship prescribed within the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*).

One should begin the external worship starting from the fourth [limb] up to the end of the sixth limb. When both the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*) rites have arrived at the same time, one should first perform the occasional rite and afterwards the regular worship (*nityasamarcana*).

For when both the occasional (*naimittika*) and the permanent (*nitya*), whether they be impermanent or permanent, occur simultaneously, one should first perform the impermanent rite and afterwards the occasional-permanent one. When both the occasional and the optional (*kāmya*) arise, however, the optional should be performed first. (28.310–311)
When these times have arrived for the expiation, the preceptor,
having first performed the expiation, should then perform those [rites] in due order;
in that case, the fault of exceeding the prescribed time shall never occur.
And in all courtyards, palaces, and dwellings,
where magnificent forms were established for the sake of beauty;
likewise in the gate-towers, doorways, directional images, and pavilions.
When they have arrived in his presence, he should always worship them according to his ability—
either three times a day, twice a day, or once a day in times of distress—
and likewise perform worship with the eight offerings (aṣṭopacāra) during occasional rites as well.
In that case, ritual service to the image and so forth, as well as bathing, festivals, and the like— namely,
the offering of oblations (bali), fire-offerings (homa), the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), and so on—
should especially not be performed for the images situated in the courtyards and other such locations. (28.316–28.317)
In those [deities], one should perform only the subtle consecration (sūkṣmābhiṣeka),
as well as for the hosts of attendants such as Khageśa and Viṣvaksena; likewise,
in houses where [the deities] have been installed, they are to be worshipped like the foundational forms (āśrayamūrti).

One should offer the bali-oblation on the ground before Vāsudeva for Ananta, Tārkṣya, Sena, Īśa, and the Devas in the pavilions and other structures; for Kumuda and the other Gaṇeśas who dwell in the door-surroundings; and for those who are formless. || 28.319–28.320 ||
Where the general of the army, though a devotee, is worshipped independently,
the best of Vaiṣṇavas should certainly not eat the substances offered there.
[The worship of the devotee should be performed by excellent attendants or by disciples.]
Having praised [the deity] with various hymns, one should then perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
Chapter Twenty-nine.
Having thus performed the daily worship, the preceptor [should visualize] Nārāyaṇa for the sake of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma)—
four-armed, resembling a lotus in its origin,
adorned with a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and graced by a forest garland.
Resplendent with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; the Lord, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, and who wears yellow garments—
having invoked him into the vessel for invocation, one should cover the bowl with a cloth.
Having taken that with both hands and placed it upon the head of the messenger at the conclusion of the fire-offering,
the Guru, reciting the *śaṃ no mitra* mantra while ringing a bell,
should proceed slowly toward the kitchen accompanied by lamps.
Having reached the gateway of the sacrifice, one should worship Caṇḍa and the others mentally.
Having gone to the south of the inner fire-pit (kuṇḍa) upon a bed of darbha grass,
one should place the vessel on a tortoise-seat to the west of the pit.
Having sat down facing the east and performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the oblation,

one should then cast six *kuśa* blades facing eastward in the region to the north of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), O Rame. Upon them, one should place the vessel of clarified butter, the sacrificial offering, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the fuel sticks, and *kuśa* grass.
The most excellent of gurus placed the *praṇītā* vessel, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the ladle, the fan, and likewise the stirring-spoon;
then, O Rāma, he set down the unbroken rice, dry wood, and sesame seeds in pairs,
having arranged the vessels with their openings facing downward.
To the right side of yourself, place the water-pot and the flower-vessel;
around the sacrificial pit, spread five, seven, or nine kuśa grasses. O Sāmbavat, strew these around the fire and the ritual materials upon the darbha grass.
Having placed that [vessel] upon the *praṇītā* [water-vessel], one should worship the Wheel-King (*cakrarāja*).

Having laid down a *kūrca* of grass measuring a span, made from a pair of *darbha* blades with their tips pointing north, and having covered it with three *darbha* blades, one should place that [vessel] [upon it].
Having first placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel before himself, the best of teachers should join the water from that *praṇītā* vessel with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] in the *prokṣaṇī*. Then,
using both the thumb and ring finger of each of his two hands, he should take hold of that *kūrca*.
Having taken those [materials] and purified them three times, the knower of the scriptures,
having turned the vessels face upwards, sprinkles them with water and the *pavitra* using the *cakragāyatrī*, while pronouncing the respective names of each.
O Rame, one should also touch the ritual substances and the vessels in due order;
with the remaining water, one should sprinkle the *praṇītā* vessel.
Having refilled the *praṇītā* vessel once more, [one should place] the four-armed deity within it.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, who is adorned with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, Nandaka sword,
and other [emblems], one should place a bundle of twelve kuśa grasses (kūrca) upon the northeast seat of the sacrificial pit in the southern location.
Having placed [the image] on the sacrificial grass (saṃstara),

one should meditate there upon Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed, holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), accompanied by the sacred syllable (girā), golden-hued, and measuring a finger’s breadth in height.
Having kindled the fire with sacrificial fuel consecrated by mantras,
O Goddess, the preceptor should place a vessel of clarified butter before himself upon *darbha* grass, reciting the mantra "nāpyāyasva. (29.20–29.21)
O Rame, one should fill [the vessel] with clarified butter from a cow that has been strained and melted;
taking the *kūrca* from the *praṇītā*, one should place it in the vessel for the clarified butter.
Then, having taken embers from the north of the fire, [one should place them] beyond the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having placed her in the western part of the northern side and established her in the seat,
one should light the vessel of clarified butter and the *darbha* grass over that fire and show them;
then, with the *guṇamantra*, one should discard those *darbha* blades upon the northern ground.
Having cut off the tips of two *darbha* blades, he should purify them with water;
then the preceptor, having thrown two bunches of *kuśa* grass into the clarified butter (*ājya*) and set them ablaze,
[should show the clarified butter again and then perform the circumambulation by fire three times].
Then, having discarded the pair of *darbha* blades, the Guru should place embers into the pit.
Having placed that vessel of his own before himself with both the left and right hands,
he should purify it three times with the *kūrca* brush.
Having untied the *kūrca* bundle and touched water, he should cast it into the fire;
having displayed the *surabhi-mudrā* and covered [the fire] with eight blades of *darbha*,
he should likewise take hold of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles while displaying the *cakra-mudrā*.

Having washed [the two blades] with warm water, one should purify the root of the blade made of five *darbha* grasses by means of the root [of the other], the middle by the middle, and the tip by the tip; then,
one should heat them over the fire.
Having sprinkled with water and then placed the *kūrca* toward the north, O Rame,
the preceptor should untie its knot, cast that *kūrca* into the fire,
and then invoke and worship Indra and the other deities around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in due order.
Having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, one should sprinkle the oblation materials.
O Rame, one should touch the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the three mantras beginning with Śrīdhara;
one should place the two *āghāra* fuel-sticks and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with the water from the *karaka*.

Having filled the pit all around with water using the three mantras beginning with "aditi," and having strewn those waters with their tips pointing eastward and northward, the preceptor should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) with the mantra beginning with "devādi" and ending with "prasuva."
Having meditated upon the god Brahmādhipa, and having taken fifteen fuel-sticks sprinkled with clarified butter, he should grasp them with the fist-mudrā; then,
remembering Vāyvadhipa, he should kindle the fire with a palm-leaf fan.
The Lord has one face, the luster of coral, and is adorned with matted hair and a crown;
he has three eyes, seven tongues, is mounted upon a ram, and possesses four arms.
He is the all-pervading deity holding a conch and a discus, with his palms joined in reverence.
Having thus reflected in his mind,
the Guru, for the sake of the fierce pacification of the fire, offered eight oblations of sesame seeds with clarified butter and *nigama* verses to the elder Agni by means of the Pradyumna mantra.
One should offer fuel-sticks with the root mantra according to the previously stated number;

one should worship the fire with clarified butter, from the offering of perfume up to the lamp, ending each with "svāhā. Then [one recites]: "O Agni, you have assented," and finally, "I have granted permission; O Rati..."
Then, having sprinkled with water, one should prepare a seat upon the fire.
One should contemplate the Supreme Self residing in the vessel as being upon the yoga-seat:
"O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, you possess the brilliance of ten million suns."
"O Lord, remain present in this sacrificial pit until the conclusion of the oblation.
Having thus entreated the deity, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
One should offer the *arghya* and other substances into the fire, up to the point of the food offering (*naivedya*), each time only once.
With the *puṃsūkta* and with sacrificial porridge (*caru*) sprinkled with clarified butter, he should offer sixteen oblations;
immediately thereafter, for the sake of recitation, he should also offer oblations of ghee.
Then the Guru [should offer] a ball (*piṇḍa*) resembling a citron and drenched in clarified butter.
Having cast the *sruk* ladle into the pit, the preceptor, O Lotus-born One, should cover its opening with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with fuel-sticks and flowers,
using the *sruva* ladle smeared with clarified butter.
Then, holding that vessel up to his head with both arms, the preceptor—
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer oblations and perform the sprinkling.
Having offered the expiatory oblations with the five Upaniṣads, O Rame,
one should fill the *sruc* with clarified butter and cover it with the *sruva*.
Then, having lifted [the vessel] with both hands up to the tip of the nose, one should offer it as an oblation. Thereafter,
the Guru should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa within the sacrificial pit or the vessel used for invocation,
and visualize the God seated within the lotus of his own heart.
During great festivals and other celebrations, one should perform the oblation (havana) into that fire.
One should dismiss the Creator (Vidhātṛ) and place the *sruk* ladle in front of oneself;
to its right, one should place the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and on the left, one should place the *sruva* ladle.
In the daily fire-offerings (*nityahoma*),
the best of teachers, having taken all the used *kuśa* grasses,
[places] the roots, middles, and tips of the *kuśas* into the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyapātra*), the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and the offering-ladle (*sruc*).
Having touched [the materials] in this manner three times, one should employ the *darbha* grasses in the fire.
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with water, one should sprinkle it clockwise outside the sacrificial pit;
then, O Rame, one should sprinkle the remainder of the water upon one's own head.
Having made a tilaka with ashes and taking the vessel as before,
the Guru, holding a handful of flowers, approaches the inner sanctum and transfers the Supreme Lord residing in the vessel to the primary image (mūlabera).

"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, please accept out of compassion this worship performed with devotion in the fire according to one's ability and according to the rules. Having thus addressed the Lord of the World, one should perform the offering of the sacrificial oblation."
For that purpose, one should worship [the deity] beginning with the primary image (mūlabera) and ending with the offering image (balibimba).
Then, having presented food offerings (naivedya) and so forth to Tārkṣya and Seneśa in due order,
and having likewise presented them to the one residing in the offering image, one should pray to the imperishable Hari.
"O Lord, the attendants dwelling in Dvārakā, headed by Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, are all intensely longing for service such as that of your lotus feet;
they have remained there, down to the great sacred seats (mahāpīṭhas), for the sake of serving you. (29.59–60)
"Mount the palanquin for their service and gift-giving.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the Guru should lead the palanquin forward and place the offerings,
such as food for the bali sacrifice, upon the head of the servant.
Accompanied by the ringing of bells, the sounds of musical instruments, and the recitation of the Vedas,
he proceeded with the sacrificial offerings to the deities residing at the gates, such as Caṇḍa and others,
and to the lords of the Gaṇas, Kumuda and the rest, who dwell within the door-surroundings.
Saying "I give," one should offer the bali-oblation with water before the image of Balyarcā;
having meditated upon the attendants (pārṣadas), the servants of Viṣṇu, all around the pedestal,
one should cast all the remaining bali-materials upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
Having circumambulated the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*), one should cause [the deity] to enter within the temple.
One should unite the Śakti residing in the image of the offering with the primary image (*mūlārcā*).
Alternatively, having meditated upon Saṃkarṣaṇa upon the seat called the heart-lotus, [one should perform the union].
Starting from the entrance to the womb (garbhadvāra) and ending at the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha),
one should place [the offerings] upon the two pedestals situated at the sides of the doors for the door-keepers beginning with Caṇḍa,
and upon the great pedestal for the devotees who have become one with Viṣṇu.
Once the pedestal has been washed everywhere, the offering of the *bali* as previously described should be made.
In the absence of a pedestal, the preceptor should offer the *bali* upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
In the absence of musical instruments, one should cast the *bali* with a single *maḍḍuka* drum alone.
One should employ Saṃkarṣaṇa, who resides in the heart-lotus, for the worship of Balarāma.
From the image of Bala, O Rame, one should request his Śakti to enter the primary image (mūlabimba).
Then, the Guru should pray to the Lord of Gods for the daily festival.
"O Hari, accept this vehicle-seat given to you by me;
for the sake of serving you, Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the other denizens of heaven wait at the gateway with their palms joined in reverence. (29.71–72)
"Therefore, O ocean of affection for your devotees, take up a vehicle.
Having thus petitioned the enemy of the Daityas, one should indeed carry him in palanquins and the like;
having adorned him with flowers and other offerings, one should present betel leaves and other such items.
With white umbrellas, peacock-feathered parasols, and those made of gold and silver;
with banners, yak-tail whisks, and numerous lamps fed with ghee;
and with female dancers, musical ensembles, singers, lute-players, and the like.

Having performed a circumambulation of the temple of the deity, the preceptor should then worship the deity with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings in the area in front of the altar for the sacrificial oblation (balipīṭha).
Then, having displayed the lamp of the jar, he should offer parched rice (pṛthuka) and other such items.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should lead the Lord into the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*).
One should contemplate the Śakti residing in the sacrificial image as being present within the permanent image (*dhruvārcā*),
whether that image is self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*), divine (*divya*), or even devoid of a sacrificial image.
In that regard, O lotus-eyed one, I shall describe the procedure for the perpetual festival:
upon a pure surface made of gold or other materials, one should fill [the area] with a *droṇa* measure of rice.
Having drawn a lotus upon it, one should purify it by means of sprinkling and other rites.
Having prepared a pedestal in the center of that [space] and having invoked Vāsudeva, who has four arms,
from the primary image (mūlabera), one should then worship him with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites—
[him] wearing white garments, gentle in appearance, and wearing a white sacred thread.
Having visualized that auspicious and excellent attendant, the joy of Vinatā, wearing an upper garment and a turban and adorned with sandalwood paste and other ornaments;
and having placed the protective amulet upon his head along with the requisites for the journey.
Having circumambulated the abode and the Supreme Lord situated within the vessel,

one should subsequently unite [the deity] with the root-mantra, O fair-faced one, using that very mantra by which the rite of mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*) was previously performed for both the God and oneself. (29.83–29.84)
Having purified the phonemes of that mantra through the processes of drying and so forth, the self-possessed practitioner should perform their awakening by means of the Vedas and other scriptures,
repeating them one hundred and eight times or twenty-eight times.
Or the mantra-practitioner may recite eight [times] with a rosary of lotus seeds and so forth;
with whatever number of recitations was previously performed for mental worship,
with that same number the best of gurus should recite during the external sacrifice.
"One should perform the recitation (*japa*) at the conclusion of all worship, but one should not do so in the case of a minor rite.
O Lotus-eyed One, Soul of the Universe, Embodiment of Mantra, Janārdana!
O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, accept this worship performed by me, which concludes with the recitation. (29.88)
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should place a *tulasī* leaf along with water on the ground before the Blessed One, like a gift offered with pure devotion (*sāttvika-dāna*):
"Salutations to You, the waveless; salutations to You, the witness of all. (29.89–29.90)

Salutations to you, O Vāsudeva; salutations to you, the Supreme Self. [I seek refuge] in you who [protects] the one of wicked pride, the one beyond all bounds, the ungrateful, the evildoer, the impure, the merciless, the cruel, the deceitful, and the one of fickle mind.
A storehouse of the undisciplined, lacking self-knowledge, and a temple of greed;
one who insults others, deceitful, devoid of devotion, and the foremost among the wicked;
always intent on censuring others, mean-spirited, and devoted to praising oneself. (29.92–29.93)
[He is] a slanderer, one under the sway of desire, an abode filled with malice,
cruel, a deceiver, wicked, and an ocean of offenses—
sunk without a raft in the mass of waves from the milk-ocean of your [virtues]. (29.94)
O refuge for those seeking shelter, this one is slain, wretched, and without a protector;
you ought to rescue me by means of the boat that is your lotus feet.
O ocean of compassion, friend of the helpless, benefactor of the entire world! (29.95–96)
"Be gracious, O Beloved of Kamalā! You are indeed an ocean of affection;
O Supreme Lord, accept these prostrations offered by me.
Thus lamenting, he [prostrated] with both hands, his feet, his head, his intellect, and his heart.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the earth four times with the utterance of "I am," he should offer salutation to Vāsudeva.
At the conclusion of the worship of the God of gods, [he should bathe in] the sacred ford consecrated by the gods.
Or, at other times during the performance of rites for minor deities, the Guru should first drink water from his feet, which is as pure as the Gaṅgā-tīrtha;
having drunk it himself using a water-pot, a vessel, or another container.
And of the perfected ones, the great seers, the ascetics who discourse on Brahman,
of the Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who devote themselves to the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas,
and of the devoted kṣatriyas and vaiśyas born from the feet [of Viṣṇu].

Gradually, the best of preceptors should cause the devotee to receive the water from the feet of the God of gods; at the conclusion of the worship, he should offer the sacred water (tīrtha) and the grace (prasāda) of Viṣṇu.
If one does not drink it oneself, or gives it to others, the worship is indeed fruitless.
Those who drink the water from his feet and smell the leaf of the *tulasī* go, liberated from sin, to the eternal, supreme state.
One seeking the world of the gods should [worship him] at dawn; one contemplating dharma at midday.

One desiring a son should worship Vāsudeva in the afternoon; one seeking wealth at the onset of night; and one seeking liberation in the forenoon or at night, O Rame. The worship of the Enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu) until the conclusion of the daily festival is indeed the most excellent of all.
Know that which ends with the fire-oblation (*homa*) is the highest; that which ends with the attainment [of the deity] is the middling;
that which ends with incense and lamps is the lowest; and worship consisting merely of the water-offering (*arghya*) and so forth is trivial.
Among the previously mentioned divisions of time, two are primary and bestow liberation.
O Goddess, worship performed at those two times bestows all accomplishments;
the offering of oblations, the daily fire-sacrifice, and the festival preceded by the daily rites—
the Lord of Teachers himself should perform these, or at other times, O Rame.

One who contemplates liberation should perform or cause to be performed the worship of Viṣṇu until the end of the fire-oblation (homa) or until the end of the offering (prāpaṇa), either by himself or through an adept. At dawn [the worship is] with rice grains, in the forenoon with lotuses, and at midday [with lotuses].

In the forenoon, the afternoon, and the evening, O fair-faced one, and at night with sesame and blue lotuses, one should meditate upon the Lord and perform the daily festival. In the forenoon, the bathing of the image for the ritual ablution is enjoined by the scriptures.
At other times, or at the end of the fire-oblation (homa), or at the conclusion of a festival,
during worship one should sprinkle the bathing image with the waters used for bathing.
However, the ritual bathing of Śālagrāma stones may be performed at all times.
If at other times the initiated one has only food and a seat [to offer],
O Rame, he should invoke the Śakti from the root and perform the ritual worship (karmārcā).
He should worship the Deity during the six-fold daily rites with the mantras as prescribed.
Or else, with the Puruṣasūkta or with a twelve-syllable mantra and so forth,
one should worship Hari on his bed during the last half-watch of the night;
for that purpose, having invoked Śakti from the root-mantra into the couch-image.
One should worship the lords of the serpents in their fixed rites and sacred images with offerings such as the *arghya* water and so forth;
having presented milk-rice mixed with cow’s milk and ghee, along with fruits and various kinds of edible foods, one should place the lord of the *pannagas* upon the bed.
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should then pray to the image for rest:
"O Blessed One, the time for the sleep of enjoyment has now arrived; O Lord of the World, prepare your bed upon the serpent-couch. (29.119–120)
Having thus offered this prayer, one should place that image upon the bed;
and having offered cow’s milk mixed with sugar, white candied sugar and the like,
fresh butter, and betel leaf, in due order.
If [the deity] is naturally reclining upon a bed of infinite serpents,
one should not separately worship the remaining couch on the image-bed;
one should perform the locking of the door while reciting the armor-mantra.
The Guru, having alerted Sudarśana at the gateway as well as the doorkeepers, should go to his own home by way of circumambulation, O Rame.
In the worship and other rites of the images, beginning with those of mortals and ending with those of the Siddhas—
Listen, O blessed lady, to the invocation, its sequential application, and its defining characteristics.

In the ritual worship of the image, one should invoke the Śakti from the primary icon (mūlabera) and perform the worship. Following that rite, O Rame, one should invoke her from the ritual image into the bathing image.
Again, one should dissolve that power into the ritual action, and from that into the offering and the festive rite (*balikautuka*).
Then, having performed the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*), one should again dissolve the power into the ritual action and the festive rite as before.
Furthermore, having invoked [the deity] once more during the festival, one should do so again when the performance of those rites has ceased.
Having engaged her in the ritual acts of worship and the rite of sleep, one should then pray to her.
One should unite her with the root [deity] in the action-image (karmabera) of the image used for the sleep-rite;
while meditating upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, [one should do so] in the festive images and others.

During great festivals and other celebrations, one should likewise invoke and worship [the deity]. At the conclusion of the worship, the preeminent teacher (deśikendra) should first honor the guests with the articles offered to me, and thereafter [honor] his sons and other kinsmen.
One should satisfy the God who is the inner controller of all according to the path of the scriptures.
O daughter of the Lord of the Ocean of Milk, I am pleased by that;
for there is the worship of both Yogalakṣmī and Bhogalakṣmī together with the God.
I have described the supreme propitiation of Vīra-lakṣmī;
now I shall explain the procedure for that—listen, O Lotus-garlanded One!
Having performed all the observances such as bathing, the best of preceptors [should proceed].
Having approached the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the abode of Lakṣmī, who stands before him,
and having worshipped Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī in his heart on both sides of the door of the womb, he then enters within and beholds the Mother of the World upon her couch.

Having awakened [the deity] with various hymns of praise, one should unite the Śakti at the root. Beginning with the purification of the site (sthalaśuddhi) and performing everything up to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should proceed with the six-syllabled mantra of Lakṣmī: *oṃ namaḥ śrīṃ śriyai*.
One should perform the placement of the hands and other rites upon one's own limbs with the six syllables of Viṣṇu.
Bhārgava is its seer, the *paṅkti* is the metre, and Lakṣmī is the deity;
one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the syllables: *śrāṃ śrīṃ śrūṃ śraiṃ śrauṃ śraḥ*.
In the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), within the ocean of burnt nectar, in a palace of jewels,
in a forest of celestial wish-fulfilling trees and beautiful women, and on the mountain of grace,
she sat comfortably upon a lotus throne, surrounded by the eight Lakṣmīs.
Golden-hued, tawny, with eyes like lotuses,
four-armed, with full shoulders, adorned with all ornaments;
in two hands she holds lotuses, and in the other two she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I take refuge in Mahālakṣmī, whose limbs possess the fragrance of a lotus.

Having meditated thus and performed the pervasive ritual placement (*vyāpaka*), one should worship Śrī with the mind. [In the lotus of the heart, one should contemplate the Supreme Self, Vāsudeva, the eternal.]
Resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, Nandaka sword, and other [emblems],
he was like a gem filled with its own radiance, like the ocean with its depth,
like the sun with its brilliance, and like the moon with its moonlight.
Having first meditated upon the Lord of the World, whose face and eyes are gracious,
and having subsequently worshipped Him mentally, [one should contemplate] the golden-hued, tawny [Goddess] who has emerged from the primary image onto the right side of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should meditate upon the Fortune of Yoga, seated comfortably and pervading every limb of Hari:
"Welcome to you, O lotus-eyed one; take up residence in the lotus of my heart. Accept this mental worship, contemplated according to its true nature. (29.146–147)
Having thus informed Śrī, [he offered] the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana);
likewise, the bath, the lower garment, and the upper garment along with the sacred thread (upavīta);
perfume, flowers, a lamp, incense, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should offer a handful of flowers along with betel leaves and a lunar disc (*sendu*).
Thus, the Guru should worship [the deity] mentally with various enjoyments;
having prepared the *arghya* and other offerings, he should then perform the sacrifice of enjoyments (*bhogayāga*).
Seated comfortably in the lotus posture, possessing the radiance of ten thousand full moons,
with a face like a lotus marked by a gentle smile, she is yellow in complexion and has four arms;
with her two principal hands, she bestows fearlessness and boons upon her devotees.

Having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī in the primary image (mūlabera), holding divine lotuses in her two other hands for the sake of sport, one should worship her with the arghya and other offerings. One should then contemplate the Yoga-pīṭha upon the Sahaja-pīṭha, which serves as the seat for the ritual image (karmārcā).
On the lotus petals of the yogic seat, in the eight directions beginning with the east,
one should visualize Vīra-lakṣmī, pale-red in hue, bearing a sword and a shield;
and Dhana-lakṣmī, of variegated color, attended by the conch, the lotus, and the treasure-vessels.
The Fortune of Lineage, green in color and accompanied by a conch, milk, and a jar;
the auspicious Fortune of Victory, yellow in color and bearing a bow and arrow;
and the Fortune of Grain, with the luster of a Palāśa flower, marked by hands holding clusters of grain.
The Fortune of Fortitude is white in luster and resplendent with the conch and discus;
the Fortune of Sovereignty is red in color and holds a goad and a whip.
All of these have four hands and are adorned with divine ornaments.
With limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garments,
their principal hands joined in the añjali gesture, while their other hands are equipped with weapons—
the Guru should meditate upon all these Śrīs as gazing toward his face. (29.158–159)
O Rame, for the sake of invocation, those [deities] beginning with Pūjyā are indeed to be worshipped in that vessel;
therein one should meditate upon Vīra-lakṣmī, who has arrived from the primary image,
endowed with all auspicious marks and radiant with a crown of excellent jewels.
She is enchanting with two ears adorned by blooming lotus-earrings;
she is radiant with a tilaka-mark upon her face which resembles the full moon;
she has four arms, beautiful limbs, and is captivating with a gentle smile.
Her limbs are the color of the interior of a lotus, and she is adorned with various ornaments;
she bestows desired boons upon those who take refuge in her two hands,
while with her other two hands she holds two red lotuses.
Then, having invoked Vīra-lakṣmī seated comfortably in the lotus posture for the sake of the auspicious rite, one should display the six mudrās:
"O Omniscient One, who dwells within all beings, O Witness of All! (29.165)
O Goddess without beginning or end, welcome to you who benefit the world!
O you who emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, O Consort of Vāsudeva,
out of compassion, please remain present within this image until the end of the worship.
"Be well-disposed, O Omniscient One, whose nature is the bliss of knowledge.
(29.167) After each such petition, one should display the corresponding mudrās;
one should perform the deposition of the mantra upon the image without the deposition of the hands. (29.168)
Having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should display the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).
Having worshipped her thoroughly with the water for honoring (*arghya*) and other offerings, one should present the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
[One worships] Lakṣmī, the bestower of the fruit of sovereignty, who is Padminī and wears a garland of lotuses.
In the worship of the sacrificial image, one should [visualize] the smiling-faced *baliberam*;
during the rite of bathing, one should [visualize] Jayā, who bestows fame, whose splendor is like the *cāmpeya* flower, who is golden-hued, and who grants victory. (29.170–171)
Having invoked, according to the prescribed rite, Śrī— who performs all wonders, who is yellow-hued in her form as a Tīrtha deity,
who has the brilliance of lightning in her image for sleep, and whose nature is Dharma—
one should perform the ritual bathing with the Śrīsūkta.
Having prepared the seat and ornaments with the Bhūsūkta and other hymns, one should meditate upon it; then,
having worshipped with either sixty-four, thirty-two,
or even sixteen ritual offerings (upacāras), one should present the sacrificial oblation (havis) to the deity.
Having cooked it, one should offer it separately to the Goddess;
or else, at the end of the meal or the end of the fire-oblation, one should worship Śrī as before.
At the time of the oblation, [one should visualize] from the primary image into the vessel a radiance like a flash of lightning.
[Nārada saw] Nārāyaṇī, the queen of Vāsudeva and the mother of the world,
adorned with ornaments such as jeweled bracelets, armlets, girdles, and waist-bands;
she was dressed in white garments and graced by a forest garland.
Having meditated upon that, one should then invoke [the deity] into the fire and worship it;
having visualized [the deity] departing from the fire, one should unite it with the root-mantra within that vessel.
This is the procedure when there is dependence on another; however, for the welfare of the world, it is performed in a state of independence.
One should perform the daily worship, as well as the offerings of strength (bali) and the festivals.
Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, destroyer of worldly affliction, regarding those who are dependent and those who are independent..."
"Tell me in detail about the schism and the performance of that sacrifice.
The Blessed One said:
"For the sake of the prosperity of Ālaya, in the temple of Vāsudeva..."
If, having established the Fortune of Heroism (Vīra-lakṣmī) and worshiping her according to the rules,
one says of her, "She is dependent on another," she bestows the fruit of desire upon the seeker of desire;
and the seeker of desired objects performs a festival for her, preceded by the binding of a protective thread (rakṣābandha).
One who seeks liberation should perform worship at the four sites, but not with a banner nor with ritual offerings; he should not give gifts at holy fords, yet he should practice everything [else].
Whether on the bank of a sacred ford or on a delightful mountain peak, he should act accordingly.
Or, one who desires the fulfillment of specific wishes should dwell according to the rules in either a city or a village.
Having constructed a temple there, he should indeed install Śrī;
the follower of the Pāñcarātra school should address Lakṣmī as independent, perceiving her through his intellect in that way.
One should perform the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) and other rites for her during the daily worship (*nityārcā*);
however, during a festival, one should also perform the raising of the banner (*dhvajāroha*) and the rite of offering oblations.
One who desires specific results (*kāmyārthin*), or even a devotee, should perform all such acts as the giving of gifts at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and so forth.
One should have [the image] fashioned according to the rules for the sake of the abundance of all prosperity.
For one who thus worships Lakṣmī, her fortune shall be imperishable.
Now, my dear, I shall explain the worship of Sudarśana.
In that self-manifested place, a divine field supremely purifying,
for the sake of protecting that sacred site and for the attainment of desired goals by those possessed of longing,
there is to the south of the celestial vehicle a dwelling in the form of a discus.
Whether outside the abode, on a riverbank, or even on a mountain,
having constructed a sanctum with a surrounding wall according to the rules,
the wise one should worship the deity in the form of the Wheel, installed there, three times a day.
O Goddess, in the abodes of mortals and others, known as the inner maṇḍala,
or else within the inner enclosure (antarhāra),
the [deity] previously established in the center of the circle [should be worshipped] for the sake of protecting Viṣṇu’s abode, to the right of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
At the conclusion of the worship of the God and Goddess, the Guru should enter the maṇḍala-hall.
Having performed the purification of the site and other preliminary rites, he should then install the six-syllable mantra.
The Gāyatrī meter is declared for the six-syllable Sudarśana mantra.
O Maheśvarī, the Cakrarāja deity has the letter *repha* as its seed-syllable (*bīja*),
*svāhā* as its power (*śakti*), and the syllables *sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ* in sequence.
One should first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the two hands, and thereafter upon the body.
The best of teachers should place [the mantras] ending with "svāhā to Sudarśana" in the heart and other locations upon the six planes, according to the sequence beginning with the Vedas;
[he should visualize] the Lord of Śrī, seated in the center of the discus, resembling a hibiscus flower.
With hair like flames, bearing a discus, two-armed, and with crooked eyes;
his face formidable with fangs, he is the terror even of fear itself;
wearing red-colored garments and adorned with a crown and other ornaments.
One should meditate upon the remover of the distress of those who bow down, resplendent with a thousand rays.
Then, one should assign the crown, the forest garland, and so forth, as well as the mudrās, to their respective limbs.
Having meditated on the primary image within the heart-lotus, one should worship it mentally until the end of the recitation.
As before, one should worship Sudarśana with offerings such as the *arghya* and other enjoyments;
having meditated upon that Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) of a thousand spokes, possessing the brilliance of ten thousand suns,
one should [meditate] upon the God, resembling saffron, in the center of its pericarp.
The quarters of the sky were set ablaze by the flames issuing from the eye in his forehead;
the Rākṣasas and Dānavas were terrified by the roar produced as he spat with his fangs;
his limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste, and he was clothed in garments and ornaments of blood-red hue.
His chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he was adorned with a forest garland;
he possessed great splendor and a massive body, graced by eight arms holding a noose,
a goad, a mace, and a wheel of most fierce radiance.
Having thus meditated upon the incomparable hero, the pervasive Lord born of Saṃkarṣaṇa, who holds a conch, the Kaumodakī mace, a bow, and an arrow resembling a half-moon,
one should then worship him in the primary image with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites.

Then, in the vessel for the invocation, one should visualize the solar disc (sūryacakra), which has sixteen spokes and the brilliance of the sun; within it, [one should visualize the deity] with sharp fangs,
three eyes, a red tongue, a gaping mouth, and eyes crooked with a frown.
With the tips of his hair fierce and tawny, resplendent with garlands of flames;
wearing red garments and shining with garlands of red flowers;
adorned with the edge of a crown licked by masses of upward-flaming tongues of fire.
Adorned with armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments made of rubies,
his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he is beautified by glowing earrings.
[He holds] an extremely fierce eight-spoked discus, as well as a mace and a goad.
And in the right portion, he holds a lotus with four arms;
adorned with conch, bow, mace, and arrow in his left hands,
he terrifies the piśācas, asuras, and rākṣasas with his own boisterous laughter.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement of the mantra upon the ritual image (*karmabimba*).
Then, one should visualize that three-eyed, terrifying form upon the bathing image (*snapanabera*), possessing four arms and holding a conch, a discus, a noose, and a goad. (29.213)
In the ritual of offering (balyarcā), one should contemplate the Lord as abiding within the wheel of flames;
in that very form, the All-pervading One resides within the primary image (mūlabera) [or, in the ritual of sacrifice (makhārcā),
the All-pervading One holds a hook, a lotus, a conch, and a noose].
One should meditate upon the four-armed, terrifying form of the Lord of Kālacakra,
the presiding deity of the wheel of flames within the *bilibi* image, originating from the primary statue—
four-armed, with broad shoulders, and granting boons and fearlessness with his two principal hands.
One should meditate upon him holding the conch and discus with his two other hands.
The wise one should worship him as before, ending with the offering of food accompanied by mantras,
[the deity] who is established within the abodes ranging from those self-manifested ones down to those of mortals.
"Those who know the scriptures understand that for [these] there should be only daily worship, and neither fire-offerings nor the ritual of bali, nor even a daily festival;
such is the case for those images enshrined [in temples], O Rāma, as well as for an image of a devotee."
If one performs worship outside the temple of Hari,
O Goddess, then for those [deities], one should perform all rites such as offerings (bali) and worship within their own dwellings; even so, this applies to the Lord of the World.

When the festival has commenced, for the sake of protection, he should lead the one in the form of the discus through the streets by that very means for as long as the festival lasts. [In a place constructed of mortars and other materials, if there is a lapse in worship or the like, the Guru...]
Only after performing the expiation (prāyaścitta) should one perform the daily sacrifices and other rites.
When an omission of worship occurs in a self-manifested or divine [liṅga],
one should perform the expiation while the worship is still in progress.
In a self-manifested abode, in one called most divine and fashioned by the gods,
in a dwelling fashioned by the Siddhas, or fashioned by divine sages and others,
or even in one fashioned by the Sāttvika twice-born, the Kṣatriyas, and the Vaiśyas; || 29.224 ||
In a temple constructed by those born of the feet [Śūdras], women, and those of lower castes,
one should practice the scripture known as Tāmasa.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the Śrī-Śrīpraśna-saṃhitā.
The Thirtieth Chapter:
Śrī— O Blessed One, lotus-petal-eyed one, saluted by all the gods!
O Lord, immediately after the consecration, the daily propitiation is prescribed.
Within that [consecration], the daily festival and the fire-oblation (homa) are declared;
likewise, during the great festivals and other such occasions, the Guru performs the daily sacrifice and the rest.
"One should perform [the rites] only in the sacrificial fire, and not in the kitchen fire"—
this was said by you, O Lord, and indeed a doubt arose there in me.
(30.3) Is it that while the great festival is already underway, another festival is now taking place?
What is this so-called "Great Festival," and of what nature is its procedure?
At what time should it be performed, and what is the number of days?
O you who are served by the virtuous, tell me all of that in detail today.
The Blessed One said:
"O sinless one, born from the ocean of nectar and dwelling upon my chest,
regarding that which you have asked concerning what is called the Great Festival (Mahotsava):"
I shall now tell all of that in detail; listen, O beloved! Among all rites beginning with propitiation, this increases my supreme joy—the festival by which great delight shall come to me.
And because it generates joy, this is called a "great festival" (mahotsava).
That great festival is threefold: constant, occasional, and optional.
O daughter of the Ocean of Milk, I shall describe its various types here for you.
Whether on the day the image is manifested,

or on the day of its consecration, or on the lunar day corresponding to that [consecration], having decided upon the pilgrimage to the sacred site preceded by the rite of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), the banner is hoisted; that indeed is the eternal great festival.
During an eclipse or a planetary conjunction, when great portents and the like occur;

during the restoration of a dilapidated deity, during the consecration (prokṣaṇa), or during a royal calamity; and whatever festival takes place when the Guru enters the sign of Leo for a sacrifice—[on these occasions, one should perform the rites].

Indeed, that which is preceded by the hoisting of the banner is remembered as occasional (naimittika); it may also be performed on the king’s birthday or at his imperial consecration. For the sake of wealth and desire, one should certainly perform it during specific months, asterisms, and so forth.
Under Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, or Śravaṇa, as well as on the anniversary of the death (sārvamāsika),
that great festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner is performed for specific desires;
yet that great festival should be characterized by purity (sāttvika), while the pilgrimage (tīrtha) takes place on the ninth day.
The pilgrimage occurring on the seventh or fifth day is considered rājasa and tāmasa;

that which is constant (nitya) is declared sāttvika, while the occasional (naimittika) would be rājasa. That which is performed for specific desires (kāmya) is said to be tāmasa; thus it is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
During an occasional festival, at a self-manifested site, or at a divine occasion, the wise man should have the rite performed for nine days; otherwise, O Rame, it is for seven days.
Indeed, when the festival of a divine self-manifested site has arrived, [this is the rule].
O beloved, for Viṣṇu and the other deities who reside in village temples,
no festival should be performed until the conclusion of the pilgrimage site [the Tīrtha].
If a festival for them should occur, it must be one that excludes the hoisting of the banner.

One should have them perform circumambulations in the processional paths by means of a self-manifested [image], O Lotus-born One. One should not perform offerings of oblations, pilgrimages to sacred sites, and so forth;
for if one were to do otherwise, the kingdom, together with its king, would perish.
When the great festival for the deities residing in villages and other such places has commenced,
one should perform the remaining rites of that festival within those very enclosures.
O lady of beautiful countenance, while the festival is underway, [one should do so] in its streets.
At that time, men shall not obtain the performance of auspicious rites in their own homes.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall also describe the sequence of the festival:
from the day the festival begins, even after twenty-two months.
Eighteen days prior, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment,
the best of preceptors, having performed the morning worship and other rites,
shall wash his feet and sip water according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed fragrant paste along with plantains and other fruits,
betel-leaf, unbroken grains of rice, and flowers upon the head of the messenger,
[he should proceed] amidst the chanting of the Vedas beginning with the Rigveda, accompanied by musical instruments, umbrellas, and chowries.
Having circumambulated the sacred abode, he should go into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having been saluted by the image-keepers and having placed the vessel upon the pedestal,
the Guru should indeed worship [him] in due order with water for honoring, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
Having offered perfumes and garlands, and having presented fruits and other offerings,
[he said]: "O Vāsudeva, source of the universe, uniquely worshipped by all the worlds,
for the sake of securing the welfare of the worlds, [perform] this unsurpassed great festival."
O Lord of Gods, I wish to perform [this rite];
for that purpose, O Hari, I shall now purify the sacrificial hall, the temple, and the mounts, as well as have a water-shed constructed for the festival.
"Grant me your permission, O God, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods and obtained the permission of the Teacher of the World,
the preceptor came outside accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments.
In the past, O Goddess, the King of Birds was established upon the vehicles and other items;
having dismissed him from there and meditated upon him in the heart, one should lead him into the primary Garuḍa.
[One should likewise establish] artisans, chariot-makers, and the chariots and so forth, in due order.
Then, having appointed [the master] to level [the ground] at an auspicious hour and a favorable conjunction,
one should place the water-shed pillar (prapā-stambha), adorned with all ornaments, outside the temple in the northeast corner amidst the sounds of Vedic recitations and musical instruments.
Then the preceptor should cause the Blessed One’s remaining sandalwood and other materials to be given to all the Vaiṣṇavas and also to the artisans;
he should employ them to properly construct all the vehicles, such as chariots and the like. || 30.37 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter:
On the ninth day prior to the commencement of the festival...
On the sixth day, or the third, or even on the preceding day,
the most excellent of gurus should perform the sowing of seeds during the night itself;
he should carry out the collection of earth for the purpose of the rite of planting the sprouts.
On the morning of the day for collecting the clay, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests,
should bathe preceded by a hair-cutting ceremony for the sake of initiation into the great festival;
he should be adorned with pure garments, sacred threads, and vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, and earrings, and decorated with perfumes and garlands, the Guru,
having reached the temple of the Blessed One, began the daily worship;
he [honored] the gatekeepers such as Caṇḍa and the images of the devotees.
Then the practitioner should worship the forms residing in the *ālaya*.
Having taken betel, coconut, unbroken rice, and other offerings in a vessel made of gold or similar materials,
the preceptor should approach the presence of Viṣvaksena.
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should pray to him for the sake of taking the clay:
"O Lord, Master of those who possess the sacred thread, you who are saluted by all the gods!
Today I have commenced the great festival of Vāsudeva. (31.8)
For the sake of his unimpeded success, by the command of Vāsudeva,
you, O General, must today be present for the task of collecting the earth-clods.
Indeed, let him come to the abode of Hari to seek the permission of the Teacher of the World.
Having thus informed the commander of the army and helped him onto a vehicle,
the guide went at an auspicious moment to the inner sanctum in the presence of the Lord;
having placed fruits and other offerings there, he paid obeisance according to the prescribed rite.
Then the excellent preceptor [addressed] all the Vaiṣṇavas, the Pāñcarātrikas, the ascetics, the Brahmins learned in the Vedas, the wise ones, and the exponents of Brahman;
for the great festival of the God of gods had commenced.

For the sake of completing [the rite] without obstacles until the conclusion of the sacred ford (tīrtha), you must remain alert during the time of the ritual performance. Having completed the sacrificial duties and obtained permission from Hari, [you may depart]. || 31.13–31.14 ||
"You ought to go, O All-Knowing One; accept my request.
Having thus entreated them and received their permission, he then [proceeded] for the sake of purifying his own body and for the purification of the officiating priests and practitioners.
O Rame, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) for the articles of worship;
with those waters, one should effect the purification of oneself and others as well.
One should personally sprinkle all the ritual substances and worship Hari.
Having offered fruit and betel, he should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then, having prostrated on the ground with palms joined in reverence, the preceptor [should pray]:
"O Lord of the world, whose nectar is never-ending; O Lord of Ramā, whose desires are fulfilled!"
"O Hari, this festival has been commenced by me, a fool, for the sake of you;
O Lord, Master of Ramā, command the Lord of the Army to bring it to completion.
Having thus obtained the permission of Hari, he should then pray to the Lord of the Army.
"You have been instructed by Hari for the sake of protecting the sacrifice;
from the gathering of the earth-clay until the concluding purificatory bath of the festival,
O General, accomplish all tasks together with me."
"Come to fetch the clay for the rite of the festival-germ (utsavāṅkura).
Having thus entreated Vighneśa, the preceptor should place a garland upon the head of the Lord Viṣvaksena, as well as his sandals.

Accompanied by all kinds of requisites and the sounds of every musical instrument, as well as the chanting of the Vedas beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, I shall cause Viṣvaksena to reach the eastern direction of Soma; there, indeed, I shall delight in a water-shed.

Having sprinkled [the image] with water from the Puṇyāha rite, one should install the commander of the army. In front of him on the ground, one should place [the image of the goddess] with her crown resting in the northeast (Īśāna), her feet resting in the southwest (Nairṛta), facing upwards, and with palms joined in reverence.
Having thus drawn upon the earth, the preceptor should then prepare a seat of grain at either the head-side or the right side of that [drawing].
Upon it, he should place a clean spade adorned with *darbha* grass and other offerings.
Having established and strewn a seat of grain upon the ground,
one should likewise adorn it with garments and other ornaments.
One should also prepare a *kūrca* made of seven blades of *darbha* grass, measuring one *tāla* in length.
Having placed [the ritual materials] upon the heart of the earth and also upon the spade and the *kūrca* grass-bundle,
and having sprinkled them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite while reciting the mantra "bhūmir bhūmnā," the preceptor then consecrates both that [earth] and the spade.
O Goddess, one should prepare a pedestal and there indeed supplicate the Earth:
"O Goddess, beloved of Vāsudeva, for the sake of the success of that great festival, be present here in this auspicious clay, which is beneficial for that festival. (31.31–31.32)
Having thus invoked [the deity] and worshipped him immediately thereafter with water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other offerings, [he addressed him]:
"O You who are intent upon slaying Hiraṇyākṣa, having attained the earth as the site for Your incarnation as the Boar,
for the sake of the festival, [please engage] in the act of collecting the clay."
"Be present soon, O God, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Having thus invoked him, one should worship the one in the form of a boar with offerings of water for the hands (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth;
then, having offered a bean-cake (*māṣāpūpa*), one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the two of them.
The preceptor, taking up a spade while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra over the earth— which has the form of a boar—
should [dig] at its mouth, arms, breasts, and feet. Having taken the earth from the spade with the Gāyatrī preceded by Viṣṇu...
O Rame, he should deposit that clay either in an iron vessel or one made of bamboo;
from that, the Guru should prepare sand and cow-dung.
He should then cover each of the three vessels separately with a new cloth.
Having placed him upon a chariot, or on the shoulder of an elephant, or on the head of an attendant,
and accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the Vedas,
he should circumambulate the temple and lead him to the pavilion for the Lotus-born One.
Having placed that clay in the pavilion, one should prepare all the pathways;
one should employ laborers to cleanse the walkways,
and they, having leveled the uneven paths with dust, [should make them smooth].
One should cleanse [the area] with cow-dung water and perfume it with fragrant water;
one should fumigate all the streets with incense of sandalwood and agarwood.
One should decorate the *sarvatobhadra* water-shed on all sides with canopies and other ornaments.
Then, with various variegated garments, garlands, and salutations,
one should place lamp-stands with lamps on all sides;
for the sake of beauty, they should be set up along both sides of every street.
In the vessels, small pots should be placed, and indeed, O beloved, near each pillar,
plantain trunks joined with fruits and wrapped in cloths and garlands [should be set].
There are also coconuts, betel nuts, and jackfruit as well.
One should cause water-pots to be suspended above the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
and likewise provide them in all the walkways (vīthikā) and in all the dwellings on every side;
furthermore, banners (patākikā) should be placed upon the pitchers (kumbha) of the gate-towers (gopura) and in the pavilions.
O fair-faced one, one should bind birds of variegated colors, adorned with the king of birds, for my devotees who have come from various lands,
either in the third enclosure or even in the fourth enclosure.
For the purpose of sleeping, eating, drinking, and for the sake of comfort,
as well as for cooking, there should be various beautiful halls;
and sacrificial altars (vedīs) should be constructed by capable people together with physicians.
The patron, beholding them every day, should satisfy them all—
whether in the first enclosure or even in the second.
Its width should be twelve cubits and its length ten cubits.
Or one should construct a pavilion for seven *pālikās*;
it should have four doors on the four sides and be well-adorned with lattice windows.
In its center, for the installation of the *pālikās* and other vessels, there should be no pathway.
The ground of the altar-platform, being elevated, should be purified with meritorious water;
thereafter, one should adorn it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with lime powder.
And upon all the altars, one should prepare sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains.
One should draw lotuses upon them, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
The Guru should place the *pālikās*, the *ghaṭikās*, and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*).
In the west, he should place the Soma-pitcher and also the water-jar (*karaka*), O Rame.
One should place eight secondary jars (upakumbha) around the Soma jar;
one should first worship the door-arches, the jars, and so forth, with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other substances.
This applies to all [the vessels] beginning with the *pālikās*, as well as to the Soma jar itself.
Having prepared a pedestal ending with lotuses using unbroken grains (*akṣata*) near the small jars (*upakumbha*),
one should worship Viṣṇu, who is born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
in the *pālikās*; and Brahmā, who is produced from a portion of Aniruddha, in the *ghaṭikās*.
One should indeed remember Śarva, born from a portion of Pradyumna, within the shallow bowls (śarāva);
and the Moon, arisen from a portion of Pradyumna, within the water-pitcher (somakumbha).
One should worship Indra and the other deities upon lotus-seats within the subsidiary pitchers (upakumbha).
For the sake of protecting these, one should worship Sudarśana in the water-pot (karaka).
One should worship Keśava and the other [deities] among the grains such as wild rice (nīvāra).
The Guru [should perform this] in the sixteen [vessels], in due order, for those who protect all goals.

O Goddess, the worship of the four beginning with Vāsudeva, the ten and two beginning with Keśava, and the eight beginning with Viṣṇu, preceded by Janārdana, is prescribed; one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as the sacrificial food.
Having covered each [image] individually with a new cloth, the most excellent Guru,
having prepared a pedestal in the eastern part of the hour (ghaṭikā) either in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
should worship Lakṣmīśa there, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya).

"O Blessed One, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, for the sake of the festival procession and for the successful accomplishment of the sprout for the purpose of the banner, I shall produce fire, sir! Having thus made this request and produced the fire there, he should then perform the oblation.
Then, having offered oblations to the Lord Soma, the best of teachers should perform the sowing of the seed-syllables and pour the *saṃpāta* clarified butter;
this is for the sake of the festival in the sacrificial hall, beginning with the second enclosure.

Wherever there may be space, one should prepare a site; therein, one should determine the width and length of that pavilion and the arrangement of the altar. Listen, O lotus-eyed one, as I describe the sacrificial pits according to their measurements.
One should construct an altar measuring five cubits on each side and one cubit in height at its center, with its length and width commensurate with fourteen measures;
it should be provided with a girdle, and the preparation of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be made around it.
In the northeast (Pauruhūtī) a square [pit], in the south a bow-shaped one (dhanu),
in the west (Vāruṇī) a circular pit (cakrakuṇḍa), and in the north (Cāndramasī) a triangular one;
having thus had the pits constructed by those skilled in craftsmanship, thereafter—
For the purpose of the sacrificial implements, the wise man should prepare an altar two cubits in length in the south-east or the south-west corner;
[another] for the installation of the sacrificial image in the north-west, and one for the mandala.
One should arrange that [altar] for the placement of the *pālikā* and other vessels in the northeast corner;
however, when following the rite of a single *kuṇḍa*, it should be on the ground to the east of the altar.
The *kuṇḍa* should be square, while the vessel-altar (*pātravedi*) should be to the south.
To the west of the sacrificial image and to the north of the mandala,
the Guru should prepare an altar for the sake of the *pālikās* in the northeast;
O Goddess, this applies if he prepares the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) within a pavilion made of stone and other materials.
One should fashion the depressions there according to the requirements;
likewise, one should construct the altars and sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) precisely according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, first of all, one should purify the entire temple with water.
One should provide plastering with lime, hoist banners, set up archways adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass, and arrange respectful offerings joined with plantain pillars everywhere—
in the streets as well as in the palace once it has been thus prepared.
Then, having placed the army commander upon the vehicle with the equipment for the journey,
the Guru, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the Vedas, should indeed circumambulate it and show him the streets and the palace on all sides.
Then, having worshipped him with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should lead him to his house.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*, concerning the ritual for the Great Festival.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Then, on the following day,
having completed the daily rites and being accompanied by the officiating priests, the master practitioners, and the instructors,
he should enter the temple and thereafter worship the glorious deity.

The preceptor, remaining unwearied, should then have everything performed by the officiating priests: the worship of Garuḍa as the commander of the army, the door-keepers residing in their abodes, the worship of the threshold and the doors, and the propitiation of the *pālikās* and other vessels. (32.2–32.3)
Whether made of dukūla, silk, or even cotton,
the cloth for hoisting the banner should be very firm, smooth, and endowed with auspicious marks;
it should be white or free from blue hair and other such blemishes.
The length should be fifteen, ten, or seven [parts];
or it may be equal to the height of the main image (mūlabera), or the length of the inner sanctum door.
O fair-faced one, the width should be five or three cubits.
Having first taken the dimensions of the cloth suitable for the King of Birds' [Garuda's] design, one should, from the center of that [cloth], using sandalwood powder and water,
draw a central line with a thread from corner to corner.
One should strike [the image] from the middle part down to the head and the feet.
