Whatever remains on the two sides must be removed by the artisan;
[the image should depict] Garuḍa, ready to depart, with golden limbs and squinting eyes.
Joined at the tip of his blue nose, beautiful in all his limbs,
with palms joined in reverence, gentle, the all-pervading Lord bearing the conch and the discus;
with a tilaka-mark placed upon his forehead and accompanied by the flapping of his wings— 32.10.
Adorned with all ornaments, white in color, and four-armed;
wearing a crown and a small basket, and graced by a white garment;
with his right leg drawn up and the other placed behind.
Upon his head, he wears a serpent fashioned like a garland, and a conch shell with the luster of snow;
on his right ear, a lotus with a crimson glow in the form of an earring;
and on his left ear, a great lotus with a tawny hue as an earring.
He wore a dark-blue *gulika* bead on his neck in the form of a necklace;
he bore the fearsome, blood-red Vāsuki, adorned with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*),
and the smoke-colored Kārkoṭaka in the form of a pearl necklace, O Lotus-born One.
One should depict Takṣaka, with a yellowish complexion, adorned with a girdle;
and Ananta, resembling fine linen, as a bracelet on the right hand.
On the left hand, one should draw Mahāśveta acting as a bracelet.
On all sides were the conch and the discus, as well as the mace, the sword, and the bow;
on the head of Tārkṣya was a parasol, and on both sides were two chowries;
at the feet were lamp-stands, and likewise flower-pots with sprouts.
The instructor, or even an artisan, should thus paint it with five colors.
Therefore, the instructor, having satisfied the artisan, should take the cloth painting,
place it upon a palanquin, and proceed preceded by the sound of musical instruments.

Having circumambulated the *dhāma*, one should lead [the deity] to the consecration pavilion (*pratiṣṭhāmaṇḍapa*). Then, for the purification of the village and other such places, one should perform the *vāstuśānti* rite.
Upon a seat prepared with grain and other materials, one should spread out the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) there.
One should sprinkle the cloth with water from an auspicious day and [the materials for] the pavilion and so forth;

having worshipped the deities of the doors and other [locations], one should prepare an auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) in either the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), [and thereupon worship] the omnipresent Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite, O Lotus-born One, one should pray:
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Master of the World, for the prosperity of this great festival and for the performance of the flag-hoisting ceremony, [I have drawn You] upon this cloth with five colors."
"O God, this Garuḍa has been depicted for the pacification of all defects;
O Supreme Lord, look upon him with your cool eyes.
O sir, I shall now produce the fire that is an integral part of the rite for the consecration of Tārkṣya."
Having thus informed [the deity], one should contemplate the union of those two within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The best of preceptors should meditate upon that Vaiṣṇava fire born therefrom;
by the command of Vāsudeva, he should contemplate Tārkṣya on the cloth (paṭa) from the root-mantra.
One should perform the rite of curiosity (*kautuka*) for Tārkṣya and the consecration (*adhivāsana*) upon his shadow;
then, with five jars, there shall be a ceremonial bath (*snapana*) performed before a mirror.
One should then carry out the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*) for both Tārkṣya and the serpents.
Then, having displayed grains and other offerings, he should have the cloth laid upon the bed.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his own body with the Tārkṣya mantra;
he should recite it one hundred and eight times, joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end.
Having performed the recitation, O Rame, one should fill five jars with fragrant waters;
having placed them upon a pedestal of grain and adorned them according to the rite,
one should prepare the pedestal and worship the birds within those jars.
Holding a handful of flowers, he should pray to the Lord of Birds:
"O Lord of Birds, born from Vāsudeva, possessing a golden luster,
please manifest your presence in this jar for the sake of the festival of the Blessed One."
Having thus prayed from the heart, one should contemplate Tārkṣya within the pitcher;
having displayed the six mudrās beginning with the invocation, one should worship him with the arghya and other offerings:
"O you who are born from a portion of Vāsudeva, embodiment of truth, with the luster of lightning!"
For the conquest of untimely death, O Lord born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, establish Your presence in this jar for the increase of the knowledge of the twice-born.
O Suparṇa, possessing the luster of crystal, come and establish Your presence in this jar.

O Garuḍa, you who possess the brilliance of lightning, born from a portion of Pradyumna, establish your presence in this jar for the increase of the strength of kings. Born from Aniruddha, [establish your presence] for the accomplishment of the wealth of Vaiśyas.
"O Lord Tārkṣya, who resembles a star, grant your presence within this pitcher.

(32.38) Having diligently invoked [the deities] into the pitchers located in the corners beginning with the southeast, one should then perform the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation, as well as the ritual worship. (32.39)
Then, having provided a seat for the meal, one should offer sweetmeats (modaka) and other foods.
Having gratified the fire according to the rule, one should perform the *tattva-homa*.
Taking the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*), one should place it upon the cloth using the *kūrca* brush.
Having duly conceived the Yoga-pīṭha within the fire-altar,
the Guru should cause [the deity] to descend from the heart with the mantra of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
He should display the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), upon the Lotus Seat.
Then, one should offer oblations with clarified butter (ājya) for everything from the seat of the mantra up to the food; thereafter,
one should offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Puruṣasūkta,
and one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī of the Lord of Birds (Vihagādhipa).
With that same number of fuel sticks made of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and *khadira* wood,
as well as *bilva* wood, one should offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred and eight times.
Then, having taken the residual clarified butter, one should proceed with the *Tārkṣya-gāyatrī*.
The best of gurus should place [the deities] in all the jars and upon the cloth;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) from the sacrificial pit, O Rame, he should dismiss Viṣṇu and his chariot from the jar,
and thereafter release Satya and the others.

One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the sake of pacifying deficiencies or excesses. Having extinguished the fire from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer rice mixed with sugar and present an oblation (bali) of white water-lilies and other flowers, reciting the mantra of Vainateya.
"Established in his observance, he should spend the night in recitation and remain awake.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter [on the rites of festival] in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-three.

Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor, having performed his daily rites such as bathing along with the practitioners, should enter the delightful abode. Sandalwood, agallochum, jasmine, *kakubha*, *campaka*, and *śamī*—
The khādira, sārabilva, kesara, saptaparṇaka, varuṇa, tilaka, nimba, arjuna, and śamīruha—
these trees have hard wood both internally and externally when growing in water.
The *kramuka*, the coconut, the palmyra, the *hintāla*, and the bamboo—these have their strength in the outer layer; the preceptor should employ them for immediate use.
Among those mentioned that have their strength in the inner layer, one should select that which is free from cracks and other defects.
One should take a single tree according to the mantra for the conception of the eternal pillar; it should be one hundred *tālas* in height for the primary conception,
eighty *tālas* for the inferior, and sixty *tālas* is proclaimed for the middling.

One should determine the height of the vimāna, or its neck-height, or the measurement of the gate-tower (gopura), by means of the *mānāṅgula* or according to another system of measurement, as far as one's ability permits.

The wise man should fashion the flagstaff as sixteen-sided, eight-sided, or square, or even circular, according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. He should divide the staff into four parts and set aside the first portion.
Having divided the three parts into five, one should take the last from them;
having further divided that also into five, the first among those shall be the lotus.
One should make the last [part] the *stūpikā* (the pinnacle) upon the three middle [sections].
With a length equal to the final portion, a width of one and a half *tālas*, and well-expanded,
it should be provided with a flagstaff and a peg, and adorned with small bells; one should join three wooden panels to these sections, O Rame.
O fair-faced one, having encased the central portion and the end portion of the planks with lead using armor-plates, the first part of the pillar [should be so treated];
as for the remaining three parts, they should be covered with gold or silver.
One should cover it with armor made of copper or even brass. Having thus prepared the flagstaff for the sacrificial pedestal, O Rame,
one should then dig the earth for the pillar, either to the west or to the east.
Seven, five, or even three cubits in detail,
[the foundation] should be bound with bricks or stones until it is level with the ground;
having left space for the flagpole-hole, one should bind it all around, O Rame.
Then, one should construct a pedestal (upapīṭha) all around the ground;
it should be one tāla in measure all around and one cubit (hasta) in height.
After that, one should then fashion a square altar (vedi).
It should be four cubits or two cubits in size, adorned with painted images and the like; its altar should be equal in length and height, and its edge should be furnished with lotuses.
It should be decorated with coverings and other such items, and made beautiful with stairs.
Having thus had the pedestal for the flagstaff constructed by artisans,

one should first sprinkle the holes for the pedestal with water from an auspicious day, and then place all the materials, such as gems and other items, into those holes while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by [the name of] Viṣṇu.
Having cast [the image] together with the practitioners and the Vaiṣṇava officiants,
while the preceptor raises the pillar amidst the practitioners chanting the Tārkṣya-mantra, along with the sounds of the Vedas and the sounds of musical instruments; 33.22.
Having placed a pillar facing the primary image and having filled it with sand,
one should have the best of artisans properly finish it with lime and other materials;
then, one should wrap it with cloths such as garlands of *darbha* grass, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Having reached the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) and performed the daily worship according to the rules, and having completed the fire sacrifice (homa), the Guru, at an auspicious moment,
[should offer] betel, fruits, flowers, and so forth, together with a golden thread.
Taking a plate of gold and other materials, together with the initiated officiating priests,
and having circumambulated the temple while accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the like,
they enter the inner sanctum and place it upon a pedestal of grain.
One should sprinkle all the materials for worship with meritorious water;
one should purify the threads of fine silver by means of drying and other such methods,
using pastes of saffron mixed with the powder of turmeric.
He should likewise anoint me with the essence of sandalwood. Having thus fashioned threads made of silk, the supreme guru,
having placed them in a vessel of gold or another precious metal, [should hold them] indeed with his right hand.
Touching the protective threads with the Aparājita mantra,
the wise preceptor should recite the Gāyatrī of the Sudarśana seven times. Once those threads have been purified, the preceptor should pray for prosperity.
O you who possess eternal, faultless, and boundless auspicious qualities,
for the sake of the festival of the Blessed Vāsudeva and of yourself,
I entreat you through these verses: be present for the welfare of the world!
Having thus prayed to Lakṣmī residing upon the chest of the permanent image (dhruvabera),
and having invoked Śrī from the Śrīvatsa mark, one should worship her within the protection cords (rakṣāsūtra).
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should pray to the primary auspicious knot (mūlakautuka).
O Vāsudeva, source of the universe, by your command I shall today perform this unsurpassed great festival; I bind the auspicious *kautuka* on my wrist— accept it with affection, O Lord of Kamalā!
"You ought to grant the presence of the images [used] for festivals of ritual action and the like.
Having thus informed [the deity], one should worship the primary image (mūlārcā) with the god [offered] water for honor (arghya) and other offerings.
(33.37) I shall describe the sequence of invocation; listen, O Goddess garlanded with lotuses.
"O you who cause the creation, maintenance, and end of the world, presiding over the deities beginning with Brahmā;
remain present in this image until the concluding bath of the festival.
Having thus invoked [the deity], one should perform the ritual service upon the action-image (karmabimba).
Then, for the sake of the festival, one should pray to Hari within the image:

"O Lord of Lakṣmī, please grant Your presence in this image for the purpose of worship at the four stations. Having thus prayed, one should offer the water of honor (arghya) and other ritual offerings.
O you whose eyes resemble a full, steady, and six-fold auspicious lotus,
be present for the sake of performing the *bali* rite during the worship of the *bali*.
Having thus invoked [the deity] into the images in due order, one should perform the worship.
Having offered milk-rice and various kinds of edible foods,
[he said]: "O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge,
please accept this protection-thread for the fulfillment of the worship of the sacrifice."
Having thus offered prayers, the preceptor takes the thread from the vessel;
grasping it with both hands using the thumb and ring finger,
he [places it] to the right of the primary image (mūlabera) with the mantra "viśve tvā tāta."
Having tied it to the hand, one should recite the Astra mantra ten times;
in this manner, one should bind the protection cord upon the images of the [deities] such as Karmaprasādhinī and others.
Furthermore, for the goddesses such as Śrī and the rest, one should bind it on the left hand.

He should then tie a protective amulet (*kautuka*) consisting of a golden thread and the like upon his own right hand with the root mantra, and likewise for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Then the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipa*), [should perform the rite] for the one established as the Lord of Birds (*vihagendra*).
Having approached the pavilion, O Goddess, one should perform the worship of the door-jars and other items,
as well as Garuḍa, the great jar, the four subsidiary jars,
and the water-pot; thereafter, one should proceed until the offering of food (naivedya).
Then the Guru, having dismissed all the deities of the doors and other locations,
places the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) upon his vehicle; and having had the ritual jars brought by the practitioners,
he proceeds with the sound of musical instruments and other offerings, circumambulating the temple in a clockwise direction.
One should place them upon a pedestal situated near the flagstaff.
Having worshipped the gods located in the door-arches and pots all around the flagstaff, O Lord of Gods, O Rāma, may the three Bhāgavatas [worship you].
Having placed the Lord, together with Śrī and Puṣṭi, upon the auspicious throne,
[they honored him] with the sounds of the four Vedas, various musical instruments,
the blaring of conchs and kettledrums, and also with diverse hymns of praise.
With yak-tail whisks, fans, white umbrellas, and rows of banners,
one should slowly lead the God of gods to the vicinity of the flagstaff and seat the Blessed One upon the auspicious throne in the pavilion.
Having worshipped according to the scriptures, one should offer mung-bean rice, sweetmeats (modaka), jaggery-rice with various edibles, and drinks such as syrups; then,
having brought down Aniruddha from the Heart-mantra onto the flagstaff.
Having invoked [the deity] with the Puruṣa-sūktas, one should worship him in the form of the banner;
having invoked Māyā into the Guṇa, one should worship her up to the offering of food (naivedya).
And indeed, with the Vairāja Sāman, one should join the banner to the Guṇa.

Then, having worshipped Garuḍa on the cloth and the birds residing in the pitcher with offerings up to incense and lamps, one should meditate on that best of birds emerging from the pitcher and entering the bird on the cloth through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*).

Then, having sealed [the vessel] with the *praṇava* and having sprinkled [the area] with water from the great pitcher using the *gāyatrī* preceded by [the mantra of] Tārkṣya, the Guru, having invoked Satya and the others upon the great cloth-painting (*mahāpaṭa*),
should pray to the Lord of Birds (*vihagādhipa*).
O mighty one, O long-armed Vainateya, lord of birds!
Be present on this cloth, O bird, until the final concluding bath of the festival.
Being summoned, destroy all obstacles and set the ritual work in motion.
Having thus offered this prayer to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), one should present sweetmeats and other offerings;
one should also present betel, water for libation, and drinking water. Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should pray to the King of Birds.
Salutations to you, Garuḍa, the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, possessed of immeasurable splendor; salutations to the one who is the death of all the lords of serpents,
who brought back the jar of nectar, and who liberated his mother from servitude.
Salutations indeed to you, the conqueror of the lords of gods and asuras, who are adorned by the lord of serpents;
salutations to the support of that upon which all this world rests.
O Garuḍa, the Trivṛt-sāman is your head, and the Gāyatra is your two eyes.
The *stoma* is his soul, and the *vāmadevya-sāman* is considered his body;
the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are his two wings, and the *yajñāyajñiya-sāman* is said to be his tail. The meters are his limbs, and the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇiyas*) are his organs.
"Your hooves are the Yajus formulas; salutations to you who have the form of the Chandas.
Having thus praised the Lord of Birds for the pleasure of Garuḍa, the Tāla for Tārkṣya is said to be Tripuṭa and the Svara is Madhyama.

The musical mode (rāga) called Gauḍa and the dance called Viṣṇukrānta are prescribed. Thus, having gratified [the deity] with rhythmic measures (tāla) and other elements at an auspicious moment, the supreme preceptor [performs the rite] while the area resounds on all sides with the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas.
With conch shells, bells, and other instruments, and facing the cloth and the rosary,
the Guru should hoist the banner with the mantra "Suparṇo 'si" (You are the Eagle) in the delightful [temple]. He should then tie the rope around the pillar in a clockwise direction.
The hoisting of the banner is auspicious in the forenoon or at midday;
however, in the afternoon or at night, it brings about the destruction of the king and his kingdom.
One should also pray for the presence of Garuḍa within the interior of the banner.
O Lord of Birds, O Joy of the World, O Delight of Vinatā, O Beautiful One!
From this day forth until the conclusion of the pilgrimage,
remain present upon the banner, O God, for the sake of the king and his kingdom.

For the satisfaction and nourishment of villages, and especially for the sacrificer who belongs to Viṣṇu, and for the conquest of all enemies, and for the sake of overcoming untimely death— O Vainateya, be gracious! Om.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the Guru should scatter a handful of flowers,
display the corresponding mudrā, and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then, having gone into the presence of the deity, the most excellent of teachers—
One should pray to the immutable Lord Hari to display the banner.
Whether through knowledge or ignorance, whatever transgression has occurred during the rite of hoisting the banner, may Hari graciously forgive it all.
O God of noble vows, it shall indeed be complete; you ought to forgive me.
O Acyuta, Lord of the World, Janārdana, whose form is mantra!
This hoisting of the banner has been performed by me for your desired festival.
"Behold him, O mighty-armed one; remove [all] defects, O Lord.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, the preceptor placed him upon the vehicle, led him to the vicinity of the flagstaff, and showed him the flag.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you who are consecrated for the protection of devotees, appoint the Lord of Birds to summon all the devotees without exception.
Having thus prayed, he then circumambulated the temple.
Having brought [the disciple] outside the pavilion, he should show him the water-pot and the lamp.
He should establish him upon the lion-throne in the pavilion for the invocation of the deities.
The Guru should cause the devotees to be given the offered food, snacks, and other edibles.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā, concerning the Great Festival.
Chapter Thirty-four:
Then the Bhāgavata teacher prepared to perform the sacrifice.

Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, one should duly place the jars adorned with all ornaments; then, one should worship the doors and other parts. Having entered the inner sanctum and worshipped the festive image, one should proceed.

Having placed that deity upon a vehicle, one should bring him to the sacrificial pavilion. Then, having seated him upon the altar, O Rame, the most excellent Guru should generate the fire according to the procedure for the four fire-pits, beginning with the circular pit.
Having kindled the fire, one should transfer the flame into other fire-pits (kuṇḍas).
However, according to the rite for a single pit, one should worship the fire in a square-shaped pit;
meanwhile, the best of the twice-born should cause the four Vedas to be recited in the four directions.
Then, having duly conceived a *yogapīṭha* (seat of yoga) in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
one should worship Vāsudeva— who is resplendent with a discus, conch, mace, lotus, and forest garland— and pray with this verse:
"O Lord of the World, this great festival has been commenced for your pleasure. For in that festival, O Hari, I am performing worship at four locations;
there, I shall perform a sacrifice through the medium of the sacrificial fire, which has its origin in you."
I pray, O Lord of Gods, that you deign to grant me permission:
one should meditate upon [the deity] as emerging from his mouth, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
possessing three eyes, endowed with five faces, and accompanied by seven tongues of flame.

[Having three girdles, three feet, and endowed with seven tongues; the pervasive Fire-god, with palms joined in reverence, bearing the conch and the discus— O Agni, you who abide in the sacrificial pits such as the Gārhapatya, you are dear to Hari.
"O Lord, accept this worship until the final purificatory bath of the festival";
having thus entreated the divine Fire, one should then perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana).
Having duly gratified the Fire with oblations, one should arrange the pedestal upon the water-jars.
One should invoke Vāsudeva from the root-mantra into the great pitcher (mahākumbha) and worship him.
O Rame, one should worship Puruṣa and the others in the corners starting from the southeast;
likewise, one should worship Vāsudeva in the eastern pitcher and Saṃkarṣaṇa in the southern one.

One should place Pradyumna in the western jar, and likewise Aniruddha in the northern; Puruṣa in the southeast jar, and the one named Satya in the southwest; Acyuta in the northwest jar, and indeed Anantaka in the northeast.
Having invoked them, one should worship the deities in the eastern and other directions in due order.
First, one should draw a wheel-lotus on a pedestal fashioned from rice;
Vāsudeva is to be placed in the pericarp, and [the other deities] upon all twelve petals.
Having invoked Keśava and the others, the best of preceptors should worship them;
having worshipped the image according to the rules, he should duly arrange the pedestal upon the fires.
In a square [fire-pit] he should place Vāsudeva, and likewise Saṃkarṣaṇa in a bow-shaped one.

When [the fire] has been established, one should worship the one named Pradyumna in the *āvasathya* fire and Aniruddha in the *kamala* fire; or else, one should worship the primary form (*mūlamūrti*) in the *gārhapatya* fire.
Then, one should perform the invocation for their presence (*sāṃnidhyayācana*) in the *gārhapatya* and other fires in due order.

One should worship Vāsudeva and the others, who reside within the fire, beginning with their seats and continuing until the seats for the meal, throughout the festival and the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) at both times; then, one should offer oblations with clarified butter, ending each with "svāhā," up to the end of the meal.

Having offered the fourfold food as an oblation at the four locations where [the deities] reside, one should then offer a full oblation of clarified butter as the sacrificial substance with the Puruṣa-sūkta mantra, O Rame, using the remnants of the clarified butter.
For the welfare of the kingdom, one should indeed install the pitcher, the image, and the mandala;
having offered the bali-oblation to Kumuda and the others, the Guru should enter his own home.
Then, at the time of evening, having performed the daily worship, [he should proceed].
One should prepare a pedestal of grain on the ground in front of the deity. Having drawn the Kālacakra there, one should place lamps all around it.
A drum (maḍḍuka) should be placed in the position of Brahmā, and indeed two [drums] at its sides for Rāma.
Having placed the conch and the rattle (koṇa), one should arrange the stringed instruments (tata) and others around them:
the lute (vīṇā) and so forth in the east, the wind instruments (suṣira) and so forth in the south,
the percussion instruments (carma-vādya) in the west, and the gong (kāṃsya) in the north.
Having covered [the instruments] with new cloth and sprinkled them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite,
one should scatter perfumes and flowers upon them and worship the gods therein:
Saṃkarṣaṇa on the *maḍḍuka* drum, and Viṣṇu on the conch and the *koṇa* cymbal.
Having invoked the Lord of Wind (Vāyu), one should offer fruits and other such items; likewise,
one should invoke Aniruddha in hollow objects, the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) in lutes and similar instruments,
Narottama in those made of leather, and indeed Adhokṣaja in those made of bell-metal.
Having thus invoked and worshipped [the deity], one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Taking up the drum (maḍḍuka), the preceptor should chant the verse three times:
"O Rame, may all the Vedas increase, and may all the gods together with Vidhi [prosper]."
"May all Vaiṣṇavas indeed prosper; may the best of Brāhmaṇas prosper.
Having uttered this three times, the Guru should strike the drum (maḍḍuka).
His two feet are being worshipped by enemies conquered by the strength of his arms.
"May the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, prosper eternally.
Having recited this verse three times, one should then strike the drum.
[May there be] the increase of great wealth acquired through trade.
"May all those born of the thighs [the Vaiśyas] increase, augmented by grain and jewels"—
reciting this three times, the wise preceptor should strike the drum.
"The mouth-born and arm-born [Brahmins and Kṣatriyas] have arrived for the service of the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī."
Those born from the thighs and feet were followers of the natural order (anuloma) and righteous;
they were all devoted to their own duties, generous, and speakers of truth.
All other men [were likewise distinguished] by their sons, grandsons, wealth, and so forth.
"May they live for a hundred years, free from disease and free from calamity.
With this intent, for the sake of the welfare of the social classes (*varṇa*), he should strike the drum again.
Having thus struck it, the teacher [should address] the pure *pāraśava* who has completed his ritual bath.
Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, having summoned him and placed the *maḍḍuka* drum in his hand,
and having honored him in due order with divine garments, flowers, and so forth,
one should strike that [drum] and play the other musical instruments as well.
With the permission of their guru, those female attendants and musicians should play instruments and sing and dance upon the ground before the Lord.
Then [they should invite] those residing in Vaikuṇṭha, led by Viṣvaksena.
I worship the weapons, the forms of the deities, and likewise the lords of the gates, O Rame.
The Guru should first invoke Caṇḍa and the other gatekeepers,
as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and the great ṛṣis.
I invoke the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the nine treasures (nidhis),
the nine planets, and the Brāhmaṇas and others;
having uttered their names at the conclusion of the recitation of that group.
The wise preceptor should indeed strike the drum with a mace.
O you who possess the discus, the mace, the sword, the conch, and who bear the Kaumodakī;
O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, O lotus-bearer, and likewise O wielder of the thunderbolt—you are the dwellers of Vaikuṇṭha.
"O lords of weapons,
arise from the feet of Aniruddha— Tārkṣya, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍaka,
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Vijaya, Jaya, Bhadra, and Subhadraka— come for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord! (34.48)
O destroyer of the gods of Death, O Kubera-akṣa, O Kuberaka!
(34.49) O invincible one, O powerful one, O creator of the universe, O Puṣkara! O source of existence, O origin, O Lord, O most beautiful one, O Subhadra! (34.50)
Devoted to their respective services, with parasols and chowries in hand,
let all the hosts of gatekeepers, together with the groups of attendants,
come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī— the beloved of Hari.
O Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala! O Vasus, you eight divine hosts born at dawn,
you immortals, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
O Mṛgavyādha, Mahāśarva, Nirṛti, Tvaja, Ekapāt, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, O Sthāṇu, Bhava,
and Kapālin!— three-eyed, resembling Rudra, and wearing circles of matted hair.
"O eleven Rudras, you must come to this great festival!
O Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Vidhātṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa by name, Savitṛ, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra, Ravi, and Vibhu!"
O Pūṣan, O twelve Ādityas, come to this great festival!
O Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods; O Lohitāṅga (Mars); O Śanaiścara (Saturn)! O Rāhu, lord of the house; O Sūrya (Sun), O Soma (Moon), O Budha (Mercury), and O Ketus!
All you nine planets, come to this great festival!
O Great Treasure Padma, named Padma, Śaṅkha, and Kacchapa; O Treasure Makara, Kundākhya, Nīla, Vāra, and Mukundaka! 34.58–34.59
"You have been summoned for the great festival for the pleasure of the Lord of Lakṣmī;
come, O nine treasures, and bring delight to Hari!
O Marīci, Bharadvāja, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Kaholaka!"
O Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Bhṛgu, Viśvāmitra, O great sage! O sage Vedavyāsa, dear child, Gautama, Agastya, Mudgala!
O Jāmadagnya, Gārgya, Yājñavalkya, whose wealth is asceticism! (34.61–62)
O Kauṇḍinya, O tiger among sages, may Durvāsas, Romaśa, Aṅgiras,
and other preeminent sages come for the purpose of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī;
they who have issued from the mouth of the Supreme Brahman and are devoted to the fivefold ritual time (pañcakāla).

Let the most excellent Brahmins— skilled in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, proficient in the Pañcarātra, knowers of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and experts in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras— come for the purpose of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Born from the arms of Virāṭ, having acquired prosperity through the prowess of your own arms,
and filled with enthusiasm for battle, you Kṣatriyas are world-renowned. Come now, together with your ministers and others, to this great festival.
Born from the thighs of Viṣṇu, devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness,
constantly engaged in the profession of trade, and endowed with virtues such as tranquility—
may those who are dear to merchants come for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord.

"Let those born from the feet of Virāṭ, who follow the occupation of servants among the castes and are devoted to the service of Viṣṇu, come to the great festival. Having thus summoned my devotees and attendants, O Rame, [I spoke].
When the festival of self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*) and other such images has arrived,
one should perform the invocation before the deity and offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) in the streets.
O Rāma, this applies to the festivals of images consecrated as human beings and others.
One should perform the invocation and the offering of oblations (bali) specifically upon the street [altar].
[He should visualize] the Lord of the Immortals as having four arms, white in color, mounted upon an elephant, wearing red garments,
possessing three eyes, and likewise holding a thunderbolt and a discus.

Having meditated thus upon Kumuda, the leader of the Gaṇas, who stands with palms joined in reverence even with his two principal hands, accompanied by the gods in the space between the regions of Īśa and Vāsava,
the most excellent preceptor should present an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa).
"O Lord of the hosts of all the gods, mounted upon an elephant, four-armed one!
O Lord of Kumuda, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī!
Having thus invoked him and offered an oblation, one should satisfy him with perfumes and other offerings according to his preferences.
The musical note is Ṣaḍja, the rhythm is Sama, and the melody is said to be Gāndhāra.
With these, may I delight that Kumuda through dance and grace.
[I worship him] seated upon a buffalo, golden-hued, four-armed, and three-eyed.
The lord of the Dānavas, Khaḍga, bearing a raised mace,
with his principal hands joined in *añjali*, adorned with red garments—
the lotus-eyed leader of the Gaṇas— [is situated] between Indra and Agni.
Having meditated thus, the most excellent of gurus should offer a bali-oblation to him with black gram (*māṣa*) food:
"O Lord of the Asuras, whose eyes are like white water-lilies, served by Daityas and Dānavas!
O you of great strength, come here for the sake of attending the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī. (34.79–34.80)
The musical mode (rāga) is Kumudākṣapriya, the lunar day (tithi) is Kaulava, the note (svara) is Ṛṣabha, the rhythm (tāla) is Madhyama, and the dance (nṛtta) described here is Viṣṇukrānta.
[He is] mounted on a horse, red in color, wearing blue garments, and four-armed.
I delight in Puṇḍarīka, the leader of the hosts of ancestors, who has three eyes and carries a discus and a mace in his two hands,
while his two front hands are joined in the añjali gesture;
he dwells between the directions of Agni and Antaka (Yama).
Having meditated upon that, the supreme guru should offer a bali-oblation with sesame and rice.
The tāla is known as Bhṛṅgiṇi, the musical note (svara) is named Gāndhāra,
the rāga is Madhyamāvatī, and the dance is called Ketaka.

O mighty-armed Puṇḍarīka of great strength, mounted upon your horse, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī, O beloved of your father! [And likewise,] the four-armed, three-eyed one of white radiance, mounted upon his chariot.

One should offer a bali of tamarind food between the directions of Yama and Yātu to the god Vāmana, the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, who holds a vajra-spear, is adorned with blue garments, and has his hands joined in añjali.

O four-armed one, lord of the hosts of *yātudhānas*, mounted upon your chariot, O Vāmana, come here for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī. Your note is said to be the fifth (*pañcama*), your rhythm the *malla*, and your melody *śrīrāga*.
The dance, as well as Bhadramālī, shall be dear to Vāmana;
[he is] the Lord mounted upon a tiger, with spike-like ears, holding a noose and a goad,
four-armed, yellow in color, and resplendent with white garments.
One should offer an oblation of milk-rice between the Yātu and Vāruṇa [regions] to Bhīma, the lord of the hosts of serpents, who has his palms joined in reverence;
O mighty-armed one, mounted upon a tiger, with spike-like ears and four arms.
"O you who are served by serpents, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī!
The musical note shall be named Ṣaḍaja-ṣaḍava (Ṣaḍja with the omission of Ṣadhaivata), and Maṅgala is declared as the rhythm (tāla).
Bhūpāla is said to be the melody (rāga), and the dance is the Kāntārakuṭṭima."
O auspicious lady, one should satisfy Śaṅkukarṇa with these [offerings] such as passion (rāga) and the rest—
[the deity who is] mounted upon a deer, smoke-colored, three-eyed, clad in white garments,
holding a noose and an axe, and the all-pervading Lord with his palms joined in reverence.
Having thus meditated upon the leader of the Gandharva hosts, who has four arms and eyes everywhere, and who is endowed with these characteristics between the directions of the noose and the wind,
one should offer an oblation of chickpea food while reciting the mantra dear to him.
O Sarvanetra, mounted upon a deer, leader of the hosts of Gandharvas!
O high-minded one, come for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord.
Jayatāla shall be the Dhaivata note; the tone known as Kedāra shall be the Svara.

He performs a dance upon a circular paved floor, pleasing to all eyes; he is mounted upon a lion, smoke-colored, wearing yellow garments, and possesses four arms, three eyes, and is gracious with palms joined in reverence, wielding a discus and a spear— the omnipresent Lord.
Having meditated upon Sumukha, the leader of ten million yakṣas and the beloved of the Blessed One, situated between Vāyu and Soma, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.
O mighty-armed one, mounted upon a lion, bearer of the discus, spear, and bow! (34.100–34.101)
"O one of great strength, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī!
His tone is *niṣāda*, his rhythm is *bhadra*, and his voice has the resonance of a swan. His musical mode is *pāribhadra*, and dance shall be dear to Sumukha."
Mounted upon a serpent, golden-hued, three-eyed, and clad in yellow garments;
the god holding a sword and a discus, with palms joined in reverence;
the lord of the Piśācas, well-established and possessed of great strength.
Having meditated between the directions of Īśāna and Agni, the best of teachers should offer a bali-oblation of molasses and rice, saying: "O well-established one, O Ramā!
O great-armed lord of the hosts of Piśācas, mounted upon a serpent!"
"O General, come with well-established [forces] for the purpose of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
The *tāla* is said to be the *kakarī*, the note is named *gāndhāra*,
the *rāga* shall be *pūrṇacandra*, and the dance is the *kaṭibandhana*.
With these [mantras], the preceptor should inspire joy in Supratiṣṭha [by meditating upon him as]:

the all-pervading Lord mounted on a swan, possessing the brilliance of the sun; holding a bow and arrows; having two eyes, clad in white garments, with palms joined in reverence, and the leader of the Siddhas.
Having thus meditated upon the perfected state (*siddhapada*), one should offer the *bali* oblation of mirage-food (*marīcyanna*).
"O Pṛśnigarbha, Lord of the Suras, served by the hosts of Siddhas and others;
O Beloved of the Sky, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī! (34.110)
The *tāla* is said to be *jhiṅgiṇī*, and the note (*svara*) is called *niṣāda*.
O Blessed One, the *rāga* is named *megha*, and the dance (*nṛtta*) is declared to be the *maṇḍala*.
[He is] infinite, mounted upon a tortoise, white in luster, and four-armed.

Having thus propitiated Ananta— who has joined palms, wears blue garments, carries a plow and a lance, possesses two eyes, is the lord of serpents, and is adorned with a crown and the jewels of his hoods— one should offer an oblation of sugar-rice.
O King of Nagas, seated upon the tortoise and adorned with a thousand hoods,
come with your followers for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakshmi.
Ananta is the rhythm (tala), Gandhara is the note (svara), and Varalika is the melody (raga).
The dance known as the *ketaka* shall grant infinite delight.
[One should meditate on] the Lord Brahmā, seated upon a royal swan, possessing eight eyes and four faces,
holding a rosary and a water-pot, with palms joined in reverence.
Having meditated upon Brahmā, the lotus-born, at the eastern direction of the flagstaff,
one should offer an oblation of wheat-food for the pleasure of Brahmā,
O Lotus-born one: "O Grandfather, creator of the world, born from the navel of Viṣṇu!"
"Come, O Lotus-seated One, for the purpose of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī!
The musical mode is Ghaṇṭā, the note is Niṣāda, and the rhythm is Dhruva;
they say the dance is the 'Lotus,' which brings delight to the Brāhmaṇas. (34.118–119)
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, clad in yellow silk garments, four-armed and thousand-eyed, accompanied by the goddess Śacī,
holding a thunderbolt and a goad, gentle, with palms joined in reverence, and radiant as a water-cloud.
Having meditated thus, one should offer a bali-oblation of molasses and rice to Vāsava in the east:
"O Lord of Śacī, conqueror of enemies, wielder of the thunderbolt, destroyer of cities, beloved of the immortals!
Come for the sake of attending upon the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī! (34.121–122)
The rhythm is *samatāla*, the musical mode is *nāṭarāga*, and the note is called *pañcama*;
the dance is said to be *vilāsa*, which is dear to the mind of Indra.
[One should meditate on] the Fire-god mounted upon a ram, three-eyed and clothed in golden garments.

Having thus meditated upon [the deity] standing in the southeast corner— four-armed and of great splendor, accompanied by Svāhā and Svadhā, with his two hands joined in añjali and holding a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle with the other two hands— one should offer an oblation (*bali*) of rice mixed with ghee.

O Lord of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, O Fire, known by names such as Gārhapatya; come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī, you who are worshipped in the sacrifice! (34.126) The musical scale is Aṭatāla, the melody is Gaulirāga, and the note is named Vṛṣabha.

The dance known as Sarvatobhadra shall be dear to Jātavedas. [One should meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, the all-pervading Lord, who is mounted upon a buffalo, bearing a staff and a noose, with palms joined in reverence, possessing four arms and three eyes.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord, the leader of the hosts of ancestors, who wears white garments, one should offer a bali-oblation with sesame and rice toward the direction of Yama:
"O Lord of the black doe, mounted upon the buffalo-vehicle!"
"Come with your ancestors for the purpose of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Tāla is said to be auspicious, the note (svara) is declared to be Gāndhāra,
the melody (rāga) is Daiśikī, and the dance is named Sarvatobhadra.

Having thus meditated upon Nirṛti in the direction of Nirṛti— residing in a Piśāca, possessing a cruel form, clad in white garments, two-eyed, tawny-hued, and resplendent with a sword and shield, four-armed and with palms joined in reverence— || 34.132 ||
One should offer an oblation of black gram (māṣa) food, which is most pleasing to Nirṛti.
O Lord of the city of Kṛṣṇāṅganā, Sovereign of the hosts of Rākṣasas, O Nirṛti, come here now for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord! 34.133–134.
The musical note is Jayatāla, the scale is Ṣaḍja, and the melody is named Deśākṣi.
His dance is performed like a lotus and bestows what is dear to Nirṛti.
He is mounted upon a crocodile vehicle, is white in color, and possesses four arms.

Having thus meditated upon the god Varuṇa in the western direction— holding a noose and a goad, with palms joined in reverence, two-eyed, the lord of coolness, and surrounded by aquatic creatures— one should offer a bali-oblation of curd-rice.
O Lord of the city of Śraddhāvatī, O Sovereign of the western quarter,
O All-pervading One, O Lord of the lotus, come for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord!
Bhadratāla and Nāṭarāga are used, and the musical note (svara) is said to be Dhaivata.
The dance called *kamala* is said to be dear to Varuṇa.
It features the Lord who has mounted a doe, possesses two eyes, and is clad in white garments;
it is accompanied by the heroine Sadāgatī and is smoke-colored.
Having thus meditated upon the wise deity who has Vaiśvānara as his companion, who is endowed with four arms, who has joined palms in reverence, and who holds a banner and a *tomara* weapon,
one should offer a *bali* oblation of horse-gram (*kuluttha*) food in the direction of the wind.
O Lord of Śrīgandhapattana, accompanied by Sadāgatī, come here for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī, O Sadāgati! The rāga known as Jhampatāla is designated as Śrīrāga.
His voice is the Ṣaḍja note; he is said to be the dance, and is known as the Pṛṣṭhakuṭṭima.
He is mounted upon a man, white in appearance, the giver of wealth, and the lord of the Ālaka city.
He is the master of the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures, four-armed, and clothed in the directions of space.
Having meditated thus upon the gentle one in the direction of the Moon, with palms joined in reverence and accompanied by the goddess Saṃpad, one should offer an oblation of milk-rice.
"O Lord of Yakṣas, borne by men, together with the goddess Saṃpad... (34.146)
O Lord of the treasures such as Śaṅkha, Master, Leader of the city of Alakā! O Lord of the Giver of Wealth, come for the sake of serving the festival of Lakṣmī’s Lord!
Anantatāla is the rāga, and the vṛṣabha is the musical note (svara) that captivates.
There should be dancing, specifically the circular dance (maṇḍalanṛtta), and with these one should satisfy Kubera.

[One should visualize] Hara as Mṛtyuñjaya, mounted upon a bull, white in luster, three-eyed, wearing an elephant hide, four-armed, and with palms joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali). || 34.148–149 ||

Having thus meditated upon the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain King, who holds a skull and a trident in his hands, one should offer a bali-oblation of rice cooked with milk in the northeast corner.
"O Lord of Kailāsa, Lord of Gods, adorned with matted hair and the moon!"

"O Śrīkaṇṭha, O God Mṛtyujit, O Pinākin, O Lord of Beings, O Destroyer of Smara, come for the sake of serving the festival of the Lord of Lakṣmī! Having thus summoned the gods, the Guru should gratify them with dances and other such offerings.

Those people who hear the drum at the time of the invocation of the deities should not leave the village or the city until the conclusion of Hari’s festival; those desiring prosperity should indeed remain right there.
If, out of delusion, a person should disregard the festival and go far away,
he goes to hell as his destination after death and experiences suffering even in this world.
Therefore, one should remain right there until the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and not depart.
Then, having gone into the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should worship the primary image (mūlabera).
After offering the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis), one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Offering of Balis during the Great Festival," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The Thirty-fifth Chapter:
Having worshipped the image of Bali, one should present the offerings of food (balyanna).
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should carry the Lord upon a palanquin. 35.1
Then, taking the sacrificial offerings placed in the vessel, the bell, the flower-bowl,
the water-filled *karaka* pitcher, the incense burner with its lamp, and the lamps,
he proceeded preceded by the sound of musical instruments.
Taking a drum (*maḍḍuka*) accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,
the attendants should proceed in front of the image of the Lord (*balibimba*).
Then, either the supreme Guru, or the practitioner (*sādhaka*), or one who has received initiation (*dīkṣita*) [should follow].

"O best of gods, having received this Vaiṣṇava bali-offering accompanied by water, which I have bestowed during this great festival at these respective locations according to the sequence to be described,
and having attained satisfaction, protect this place."
Having thus recited the mantra together with the seed-syllable (bījākṣara),
and having thereafter uttered the name ending in the dative case,
the best of teachers should offer a bali-oblation accompanied by water to Caṇḍa and the others.
I shall describe that procedure for the lotus as agreed upon in the scriptures:
at the gate of the first enclosure, there is an offering (bali) for Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa;
and at the gate of the second gopura, for Jaya and Vijaya.
At the third gate, one should offer oblations to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ;
at the fourth, likewise to Durjaya and Prabala;
and at the fifth gate, the oblation to the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma.
Then one should offer an oblation to the Four-faced One (Brahmā) according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, having gone out into the streets, one should cast an oblation for Kumuda and the other [guardians].
Then, one should [offer] to Indra and the other gods who guard the directions, according to the prescribed rite.
Alternatively, one should offer an oblation to Kumuda and the others, then to Indra, and immediately after that to Kumudākṣa; or else, one may offer it to Agni,
while the streets are not empty and the people stand facing in the opposite direction.
One should not offer the *bali* elsewhere; rather, the preceptor should cause it to be performed only in the sanctuaries, likewise everywhere along the streets and in their respective locations.
Having cast the *bali*, he should approach the temple and the *balipīṭha*.
Having invoked the door-keepers, beginning with the southern one, along with their attendants and their weapons,
the Guru should offer an oblation (bali) to them around the pedestal.
He should then lead the image of the offering and the great pedestal in a clockwise direction.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should establish him in his own place.
Listen to me regarding the vehicles of the God of gods during the festival:
the sun-chariot, Śeṣa, the lion, and Garuḍa.
An elephant, a chariot, and a horse, as well as a tree known as the Kalpaka;
a swan, the moon, and Mount Sumeru, along with a palanquin and a splendid throne—such are the divine vehicles, O wise lady. (35.18–35.19)
Having had [the vehicle] fashioned by artisans from wood or from jewels such as gold,
and having installed Tārkṣya within them, the most excellent guru,
on the first day of the festival or on whichever day [is chosen], [should perform the rite].
Having placed [the image], one should cause the most excellent deity to perform the circumambulation of the street.
O beautiful one, I shall describe the procedure for the deity’s circumambulation of the street:
the preceptor, most skilled in mantras, [should lead] the deity accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
O Rame, one should raise the deity with the Brahma-mantra, "uttiṣṭha" (Arise).
Even by two initiated persons, [one should raise him] with the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ".
One should place the deity upon the vehicle, adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having adorned the Lord of Ramā, one should show him a mirror;
having worshipped him with the arghya and other offerings, one should present betel-leaf.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) preceded by the sounding of musical instruments— || 35.24–35.25 ||
"O Goddess, one should awaken the God with hundreds of lamps;
all the Vaiṣṇavas, intent on service, wearing white garments, carrying robes and turbans, and adorned with flower ornaments. (35.26)
The Vaiṣṇavas, meditating upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), shall indeed carry the vehicle;
or else, Śūdra Vaiṣṇavas, filled with devotion,
shall carry it while acting as protectors of the Lord’s image all around Viṣṇu’s vehicle.
Some bore bows and arrows, others were armed with spears or clubs; some carried swords, others were archers, and likewise some held shields in their hands.
Some were equipped with javelins or mallets, while others wore tunics and turbans.
The fourfold army should march in front of the God of gods.
Some, seated upon chariots and equipped with bows and arrows,
are mounted on state elephants and bear the banner of Garuḍa.
Some were mounted on dancing horses, others held banner-staffs;
some carried palm-leaf fans, and likewise others bore incense burners. There were also great golden parasols adorned with jewels.
A white parasol worthy of a god, adorned with a golden handle;
peacock-feather parasols with jeweled handles, O Rame;
and auspicious silver ones fashioned from pearls.
Others [brought] variegated archways with golden shafts and jeweled shafts, as well as thousands of diverse figurines;
and red, white, and copper-colored banners, upon which wheels and other symbols were inscribed.

There should be conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and the like, as well as jhallarīs and kāhalīs; there should be large kettledrums, the music of the nāgas, the music of wrestlers, and loud-sounding instruments,
along with various musical instruments such as the lute, flute, and cymbals.
O Goddess, these Pāraśava women— endowed with fresh youth and adorned with jewel ornaments— should perform before Hari;
they shall be dancers enacting many sentiments, such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others.
All of them sang with beautiful voices and also played various musical instruments.
(35.39) The Brahmins, skilled in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, were dressed in white garments; their bodies were adorned with twelve vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*). (35.40)
Adorned with necklaces, sacred threads, bracelets, armlets, and bangles,
their limbs were smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, and they wore jeweled earrings;
they were knowers of the true principles of the Pāñcarātra, with sacrificial grass rings (pavitra) held in their hands.
The Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to bhakti and adorned with garlands of tulasī,
compose works in various languages that indicate the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu;
and either the teacher or the practitioner should remain very close to the deity.
Initiated and carrying a jeweled vessel together with his sandals, he should proceed;
meanwhile, the bards should sing excellent songs before Hari.
On the right side of the Lord, those devoted to the Pañcarātra [should remain].
Others likewise recounted the majesty of Vāsudeva; meanwhile,
on the rear of the Lord, Vaiṣṇava reciters of the Vedas gratified Janārdana with the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda.
On his left side were those who know the Vedas and reveal the meaning of the Vedānta;
likewise, those learned in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, grammarians, logicians, followers of Sāṃkhya, performers of sacrifice, and those who purify themselves through Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya.
Desirous of conquering one another according to the paths prescribed by their respective scriptures,
they were all intent on demonstrating their complete proficiency in those treatises;
these were the Bhaṭṭācāryas and the Sādhakas, stationed to the right of Hari’s vehicle.
Golden sacrificial threads and waistbands adorned with jewels,
various and wonderful earrings, and many bracelets;
as well as pure finger-rings beautified with gems.
Wearing turbans and garments, and carrying red sandalwood paste, those who seek a vision of the deity should proceed on the vehicle;
the Bhaṭṭācārya should be at the front of the pedestal, and the Sādhaka on the left side.
And when devotees have arrived, he should place the sandals upon their heads,
while the lordly teacher, contemplating "I am the God" through his identity with Him,
should bestow all grace after gazing upon the face of the Deity. (35.53)
Having understood the king’s intention, he displayed it;
those standing near him spoke of that very favor shown by the kings.
Thus, the supreme teacher favored his devoted followers who were worthy of favor.
The most excellent of gurus should slowly lead the Lord of Gods through the four processional paths in succession,
placing Hari before the great pedestal facing the original image,
in order to avoid the defects of the gaze.
One should employ maidservants to bring the water-pot and lamp directly.
They should be well-bathed, wearing clean garments, with clear clay marks (urdhvapuṇḍra) upon their foreheads;
they should be young, modest-faced, and adorned with all ornaments.

Having herself undergone the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) and being consecrated as Vaiṣṇavī, she should, preceded by singing, purify the jar made of gold or other materials— which possesses the proper characteristics and is equal in height to the *tāla*— for the purpose of the lustration (*nīrājana*) of the Lord.
Having filled it with water consecrated by the Siddhārtha mantra and sealed it with a golden lotus,
one should thoroughly adorn the jar— which is perfectly pure— with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, garlands, sandalwood paste, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and place it within the lotus-pit.
One should place a wick soaked in clarified butter, four finger-breadths long,
having ignited it with the fire from the kitchen; preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
one should place the jar-lamp upon a pedestal in front of the deity.
Having consecrated the lamp with the Astra-mantra,
the most excellent of gurus should invoke the god Varuṇa into the water and Jātavedas into the flame,
and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other excellent offerings such as the Arghya.
Having worshipped the God of gods with the *arghya* and other offerings immediately thereafter,
the preceptor, having displayed the lamp-mudrā and then taking up a lamp,
[should proceed] starting from the right foot of the deity and ending with the other, the left.

One should cause all the limbs to rotate two or three times while reciting the Netra-mantra; then, one should place [the deity] upon the pedestal in vessels made of gold or other materials, spread out as desired.
Taking five, six, seven, or eight wicks soaked in clarified butter,
the female attendants indeed hold them before the jar-lamp,
O Rāma; thus, with all kinds of musical instruments, they carry the God three times while he stands upon his vehicle.
Having performed circumambulation of all [the deities] on the ground in front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
they should cast all the lamps, or alternatively, perform the lustration rite (nīrājana).
Then, having offered parched grain (pṛthuka) along with split mung beans and sugar.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*),
the most excellent preceptor should have Hari placed upon a throne (*bhadrapīṭha*) after descending him from his vehicle within the pavilion;
having brought him into the sacrificial hall, he should gratify him with the Vedas.
Having displayed the four locations, one should then perform the *nīrājana* rite again.
Having brought [the image] facing the primary icon (*mūlārcā*), one should perform the *nīrājana* for those two.
[This is done] in the house where the bed has been prepared outside, adorned with flowers.
Having seated the Lord Acyuta in the pavilion— which is covered with canopies and fine linen, and adorned with lamps— for the sake of pacifying fatigue,
O Goddess, one should bathe him with nine jars of scented water.
Having adorned [the image] with flowers and other offerings, and having gratified it with lutes, flutes, and small drums, one should present various foods such as gulānna and other edibles.
Then, upon a couch prepared with swan-down and flowers, [one should place the image].
One should lay the deity upon the bed and propitiate him with various hymns until the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the festival; indeed, O Rame, [this applies] to the ritual image (*karmabimba*).
One should prepare the bed every day for the Lord together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
And one should display the four locations and the primary image at the two times of day;
O Ramā, at the conclusion of each respective rite, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-Six:
The Teacher, having risen in the morning and completed his daily rites, O Goddess, went to the temple where the Lord was lying upon His bed. (36.1)
Having praised Hari with hymns and Upaniṣads, one should awaken Him;
one should present every service in the manner of royal hospitality.
Having worshipped the God with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites, one should offer milk and other substances.
Having reached the outer pavilion and raised the Lord of the World who is seated upon the couch, one should report everything to the God as before. Then,
having completed the daily worship, one should perform the worship of the four locations.

One should offer oblations to that Vāsudeva, who possesses attendants bearing weapons such as the conch and the discus, and who abides as the inner controller (antaryāmī) of all beings, from Brahmā downwards; he is the very nature of the universe.
Brahmārūpī is dark-complexioned and has a lotus in his navel, accompanied by his followers;
Saṃkarṣaṇa is red-complexioned, assumes the form of Rudra, and is accompanied by his followers;
Trivikrama, however, has the form of Indra, together with the gods and his retinue.
And Vāsudeva, the eternal, is that which is expressed by the syllable Om;
he is the Lord who resembles pure crystal and is endowed with the six divine qualities.
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme, is the lord of the Ṛgveda and is dark-complexioned.
Saṃkarṣaṇa is red in color, the lord and master of the Yajurveda;
Pradyumna is golden, possessed of a retinue, the master of the Sāmaveda;
and the god who is the lord of the Atharvaveda has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sages, is eternal and unceasing, accompanied by his retinue, resembling the filaments of a lotus.
The Blessed One, in the form of a Gandharva, is Vāmana, shining like gold.
The god Pradyumna is the inner controller of all, possessing a golden luster.
The lord of the Yakṣas, Śrīdhara, increases prosperity and has a pale-white complexion.
[The god Keśava is the sovereign of the months and possesses a golden luster. || 36.12–36.13 ||
Acyuta is of a yellowish complexion and is the great lord of the Vatsas;
Janārdana is red in color and the lord of the oceans. Hari, together with his attendants, is yellow and the lord of the mountains.
The Lord of Creatures, the best among men, resembles pure crystal;
the Lord of Beings, Padmanābha, has a luster like the bandhūka flower;
the Lord of Animals is blue-colored, as is Kṛṣṇa, together with his retinue.
Vṛkṣādhipa, however, is Acyuta, dark-complexioned and accompanied by his attendants;
Oṣadhīśa is Padmanābha, whose form resembles a dark cloud.
Vanaspatyadhipa is the god Mādhava, with the appearance of crystal.
Vāsudeva, white in radiance, is the lord of those born from a womb;
Saṃkarṣaṇa, red in color, is the lord of those born from an egg;
and Pradyumna, resembling gold, is the sovereign of those born from sweat.
The Lord Aniruddha, the teacher of the world, is the sovereign of the *udbhijja* (plants) beings;
Aniruddha is dark-complexioned, the supreme ruler of the worlds. One should offer oblations with these [mantras] ending in the dative case, together with their attendants.
Having thus offered oblations into the eastern pit, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should present the bali-offering to Kumuda and the others according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Having approached the presence of Hari, one should announce that the homa has been completed.
Having reached the base of the banner (dhvajapīṭha), preceded by the worship of the door,

one should worship the Lord of Birds (Vihagendra) and offer the bali-oblation for each respective door. Having reached the inner sanctum (garbhageha) and worshipped the image of the bali, [one should proceed].
Having placed that image upon a vehicle, either his disciple or his son should offer oblations to all the gods,
preceded by the sound of musical instruments, along all the streets.
In this manner, one should offer the *bali* at two times: on the final day of the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*) and on the night of the concluding day;
on the night of the day of commencement, in the morning on the ninth day, and on the night of the day of dismissal—at these very times, indeed, one should offer the *bali*.
One should offer [the oblation] at times not otherwise specified, but one should not offer it upon the lotus-seat (of the deity).
Thus, both by day and by night, preceded by the daily worship,
the best of preceptors should perform the special sacrifice ending with the bali offering.
After the offering of the oblation, one should lead the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā,
upon a jeweled palanquin while reciting the mantra,
adorning Him with various ornaments and likewise with diverse garments.
One should adorn the Lord Hari with fragrant flowers, garlands, and other ornaments;
having worshipped Him thoroughly with the arghya and other offerings, one should present betel nut and then display a mirror, preceded by the waving of lights (nīrājana).
Accompanied by various songs and dances performed with stringed instruments,
and together with attendants suited for royalty and other musical ensembles,
one should cause the deity to circumambulate the four processional paths in a clockwise direction.

While the Lord of Gods is proceeding through the streets, one should not offer edible foods. However, the most excellent Guru, having consecrated the garments and various garlands given with devotion seven times with the Astra-mantra, [should present them].
One should join those fruits and other offerings to the limbs of the deity and present them;
having led Lord Janārdana to the front of the great pedestal,
one should then worship with water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings for the sake of pacifying the god’s fatigue.
Then, having displayed the lamp within the jar, one should offer parched rice and other foods;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual worship, the libation, and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*).
In this manner, day after day, one should cause the Lord of Ramā to be carried in procession through the streets.
At the devotee’s request, one should lead the Lord to the pavilion prepared by him;
there, upon the bathing seat, one should bathe the Lord with fragrant waters.
Then, one should place the Lord of the worlds upon a golden throne.
Having adorned [the image] according to the rules with garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth,
one should offer boiled rice with ghee and side dishes,
as well as food made of mung beans, food made of jaggery, and food made of green gram mixed with ghee.
Milk-rice, molasses-cakes, bean-cakes, and sweetmeats (laḍḍuka),
as well as other various kinds of foods to be chewed, eaten, and licked—
delicious and pure foods, preceded by the offering of the arghya water and other rites.
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should cause those [offerings] to be given to the devotees.
At the time of afternoon, for the sake of pacifying the fatigue of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu),
one should offer sandalwood infused with fragrances and well-perfumed with camphor and other substances.
Having anointed the deity, one should adorn him with garlands;
[one should offer] cool water for libation mixed with coconut water,
as well as mouth-perfume consisting of betel leaf blended with cardamom and camphor.
And one should report other omens as well that signify the pacification of fatigue.
Then, with the playing of lutes and other instruments, one should gratify the Lord with singers;
and in the evening, O daughter of Padma, one should perform the daily worship of the God.
Then, having placed [the deity] upon a palanquin, one should lead it to the pavilion for the vehicle;
there, one should perform worship at four locations preceded by the offering of oblations (bali). Having mounted the deity upon the vehicle, one should conduct a circumambulation of the streets.

In this manner, one should perform the festival every evening and morning for five days. On the sixth day, prior to the mounting of the elephant, the most excellent of preceptors [should perform the rites] on the ground before the deity, either in a garden or in a pavilion.
On a grain-platform, one should place a water-vessel made of gold,
silver, copper, or wood, three cubits in length, not fashioned [too thin],
half a cubit in width, and elevated at its center like the navel of a discus.
Having placed [the vessel] and spread [the base], one should fill it with scented water.

Having sprinkled it with water from the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) rite, one should worship Varuṇa as its presiding deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then prepare the yoga-pīṭha upon it.

Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, who is accompanied by Śrī, with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, the Guru, holding a handful of flowers, should pray to the imperishable Viṣṇu: "O All-pervading One,
for the sake of quelling exhaustion during this festival, [be present] with Śrī."
"O Lord of Ramā, you are entitled to perform the consecration in this wooden vat;
descend as you wish and sport here together with Śrī.
Let the twice-born recite the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, all around you."
The four kinds of musical instruments should be played by those who live by them;
having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should bathe the deity with scented waters.
Or else, the preceptor, having uttered the mantras, should sprinkle [the deity] with a *kūrca* brush.
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should offer rice mixed with marīca. O fair-faced one, having thus served him for a watch or even half a watch,
one should then place the deity within the pavilion.
But those Brahmins, women, or even those born of low caste who behold [the deity] at the time of bathing, having their sins destroyed, attain happiness as well;
they enjoy the pleasures of this world and the next—of this there is no doubt. (36.59)
The Bhaṭṭācārya should collect all the wet garments;
having clothed the imperishable Hari in yellow silken cloths or other fabrics mixed with camphor, saffron, and the like.
The most excellent preceptor should adorn [the deity] with various types of sandalwood and garlands;
then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), he should worship the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having offered food such as molasses-rice and having seated [the deity] upon an auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
Having circumambulated the temple, one should place Hari in the pavilion;
when evening has arrived, having mounted the elephant— the vehicle— along with Śrī, one should cause the Lord of the World to be paraded through the streets in due order.
O Goddess, on the seventh day, there is no festival for Hari in the morning;
one should not perform the offering of oblations (bali), but should worship the Lord of Gods in four places,
bringing Him to the bathing pavilion along with Śrī and Bhūmi.

The Guru should worship the Lord seated upon the bathing throne with offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth. Having cooked oil with the substances for the consecration (*vāsana*) over the fire, the Preceptor,
O Rame, should anoint Hari for the sake of pacifying the Lord's fatigue.
One should brush the hair with a *kaṅkata* comb and massage the limbs;
having bathed [the Lord] according to the rules with eighty-one jars of water, O Lotus-born One, one should bring the All-pervading Lord, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, to the seat of adornment.

Having worshipped him, one should offer all food and other articles to the deity. When the afternoon has arrived, one should smear the ground in front of the pedestal of the banner with cow-dung water and decorate it with lime powder.
Having fashioned a grain-seat made of gold and washed it,
one should adorn the mortar and pestle with sandalwood and other substances,
as well as with blades of dūrvā grass, mango leaves, *darbha* grass, and shoots of the *aśvattha* tree.
One should place them upon a seat of grain after sprinkling them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite.
One should meditate on Śrī in the mortar and Aniruddha in the pestles;
[one should place] a golden-colored piece of turmeric, a *droṇa* measure of saffron, and that which is known as musk.
Having placed [the body] in a mortar, four excellent courtesans,
having covered the mouth and the nostrils with a cloth,
should perform the pounding in such a way that it becomes a powder.
While other celestial nymphs there were indeed singing and dancing,
the Vedic reciters should chant the Śrīsūkta and the Bhūmisūkta; then,
whether there be seven, five, or even one jar, it shall thereby become pure.
In the abode of Rameśvara, I shall place a jar filled with powders before the Lord;
having set it upon a pedestal of grain, I shall dry it by means of desiccation and other methods.
Having sprinkled it with water from the Puṇyāha rite, I shall worship the Lord with the Arghya offering and other honors.
One should offer food made with jaggery or food made with mung beans to the God.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should worship Śrī with colored powders.
Taking up a jar of powder, preceded by the sound of musical instruments, [one should proceed].
Having entered the interior of the temple by circumambulating it clockwise, the most excellent of gurus,
having recited the *Śrīsūkta* with ritual powders (*cūrṇa*), should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the primary image (*mūlārcā*).
Then, O Rame, he should bathe the ritual image (*karmārcā*) together with Śrī and Puṣṭi.
In that same manner, having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle preceded by the offering of oblations (bali),

and having caused the God of Gods to perform a circumambulation of the processional paths accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and other festivities, one should bring him back again to the pavilion.
Having thus performed the powder-consecration (*cūrṇābhiṣeka*),
the best of teachers should then purify the deity, who has been colored by the powder, with clean cloths.
Having performed the worship of the God of gods at evening according to the ritual rule, [he should proceed].
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle, one should again perform a procession through the streets.
On the eighth day, one should perform a festival in the morning and in the evening.
On the ninth day, O Goddess, one should perform worship in the morning, ending with the offering of bali.
O lotus-eyed one, having performed the festival of the excellent chariot according to the scriptures, the preeminent teacher should carry it out; I shall describe that procedure to you.
It may be made either of metal or of wood, and must be endowed with all the prescribed characteristics.
One should likewise adorn the great chariot with golden bells and other ornaments, with canopies of pearl necklaces, with clusters of golden blossoms,
and with variegated cloths made from threads of refined gold.
With fruits such as plantains and coconuts, as well as betel nuts, pillars of banana trees, stalks of sugarcane, and archways made of *aśvattha*, mango, and other trees;
topped with golden water-pots and adorned with the Garuda banner— || 36.89 ||
One should sprinkle the chariot with water from an auspicious day for the purification of the chariot.
Having worshipped the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) in the form of the chariot, O Lotus-born One,
and having performed the worship of the doors of the chariot, one should offer an oblation to those deities.
O Goddess, if the chariot is new, the preceptor, having performed the installation according to the rules,
should place the Lord upon that excellent chariot together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās).
O wearer of the lotus garland, listen as I describe that procedure.

Having adorned the great chariot, the most excellent of teachers should cleanse it with sweeping and other such means. Alternatively, having prepared a sacrificial hall to the east or in the northeast of the chariot,
provided with a single fire-pit (kuṇḍa), [he should perform the rites].
Having adorned it with plantain pillars, one should beautify the sacrificial hall as well as the chariot with lime powder; then, having sprinkled them with water from an auspicious day,
one should place nine decorated jars upon a heap of grain on the altar.
Having established the fire and performed the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies,
one should perform the *homa* for the sake of purifying the measurements of honor and weight;
furthermore, the preceptor should perform the various *homa* offerings, such as those for the attainment of that [status], with the appropriate mantras.
One should perform the binding of the protective thread for Vāsudeva, who is stationed upon the chariot;
the preliminary consecration in water should take place on a grass mat (kūrca), and thereafter one should perform the ritual bathing.
Furthermore, one should arrange the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) within all the ritual jars as well.
One should worship the deities invoked upon the chariot within the central jars (36.99).
Having propitiated Indra and the other gods in the subsidiary jars, the Guru,
having first prepared a pedestal in the fire, should indeed place the chariot-deities there (36.100).
Having invoked those [deities] arisen from Aniruddha through the sequential yoga,
reciting their respective mantras from the offering of *arghya* up to the end of the food,
one should first worship with the word *svāhā* at the end, and then [offer] the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *Nṛsūkta*.
Having designated each respective deity by number twenty-eight,
one should first offer oblations with cow's ghee; thereafter,
