having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the pitcher, the preceptor should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *Nṛsūkta*.
One should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) with five and also with nine [verses];
one should present the offering (bali) to Kumuda and the others, and then feed the Brahmins.
O Rame, one should thus sacrifice at the three times of day, or even at two times.
At an auspicious moment, the preceptor, the most excellent of teachers, having reached the pinnacle of the chariot, should indeed sprinkle it with the water from the great jar;
he should meditate upon Vāsudeva at the pinnacle and upon the gods in the various parts of the chariot.
Then, having sealed the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) with the *praṇava*, the most excellent Guru should sprinkle Indra and the other deities with water from the eight secondary jars, O Rame;
he should worship the gods stationed there in their respective chariots in due order.
O Rame, one should worship Śaṅkha and the others around the Brahmā-āsanam;
O Goddess, one should sacrifice to Kumuda and the others around the Deva-āsanam,
and one should sacrifice to Puruhūta and the others around the Mānuṣa-āsanam.
One should meditate upon Dharma and the others at the chariot pillars, and Adharma and the others at the intermediate corners;
one should remember the eight forms beginning with Adhokṣaja in the third rows.
In the second rows, one should worship the incarnations beginning with Matsya in due order.
Likewise, one should worship Keśava and the others in the supporting rows;
the Guru should worship Satya and the others in the corners of the supporting pedestal.
One should worship the Lord of Serpents (Pannagādhīśa) upon the support, and likewise the Tortoise (Kūrma) upon the support.
One should worship Māyā in the axles of the chariot, the Moon and Sun in the wheels, the Vedas in the horses, and Brahmā in the charioteer;
one should meditate upon Garuḍa on the banner and the Lord of Serpents on the parasol.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, he should then duly worship the swing. Then, having reached the bedchamber together with the initiates and the guardians of the forms,
he should lead the Lord, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, onto the auspicious throne.
Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments and other finery, one should show him a mirror;
then one should offer betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.
For the sake of pacifying obstacles to the journey, one should perform the offering of seeds and other rites.

Amidst the sounds of Vedic chants, the resonance of musical instruments, and even the blaring of conchs and bells, I delight in being fanned with chowries along with the various requisites of the procession.
Let those devotees carry the vehicle upon which Hari resides very slowly and steadily.
Then, by way of the staircase, he should cause the Lord to ascend the chariot;
having seated the God upon a swing, he should then worship Him with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites.
[He should offer] rice cooked in molasses mixed with ghee and blended with cardamom and camphor.
Having offered the oblation and given the libation, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then, one should carefully cause that chariot to circumambulate the temple by way of the four streets in a clockwise direction.
Once the chariot has arrived at its proper place, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then, the preceptor, together with the practitioners, shall enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and,
prostrating like a staff before the base [of the deity], shall pray with this verse:
"O embodiment of sacrifice, Lord of the World, O holy ford, O ocean of compassion!
For the sake of the concluding purificatory bath of the festival, grant your presence in this image.
Having thus invoked the power from the root [image] into the tirtha-image, the knower of mantras—
Having performed the binding of the protective thread according to the rules, he should then worship it;
the Guru should place the image of the Tīrtha upon the palanquin after it has been adorned.
O Rame, he should likewise cause the Lord of Gods, even when situated on his chariot, to be placed upon a vehicle.
One should lead Hari, together with the image from the sacred ford, for the ritual bath at the ford.
First, one should sprinkle the pavilion situated there with auspicious benedictions (*puṇyāha*).
Then, the supreme preceptor, having lowered the Lord onto the lion-throne there, [should proceed].
One should place the bathing pedestal in front of the ritual image (*karmabimba*).
Having placed the representation of the sacred ford (*tīrthārcā*) upon it, one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Prior to this, one should sprinkle the substances suitable for the bath and the sacred ford itself.
Having meditated upon Virajā at the sacred site (tīrtha), one should worship her in due order with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites.
Then, having performed the worship from the mantra-seat up to the ritual bath, the most excellent guru should consecrate the image of the sacred site with nine jars.
Having offered the *pṛthuka* grains and other items, the Guru should then reverently show the lamp.
Taking the image of the Tīrtha deity and holding it upon his head,
he enters the midst of the water and stands in water reaching up to his navel.

One should immerse oneself three times with the image of the Tīrtha together with the presiding priests (mūrtipās). At that time, those people who immerse themselves along with the Lord shall all be liberated from sin and attain the supreme goal.
Having reached the bank, one should place that image upon a seat in the water, O Rame;
then, having discarded the bathing garment, one should clothe it in other garments.
Then the preceptor, together with the ritual image, [should likewise treat] the image of the sacred ford.
Having led [the deity] into the interior of the temple by way of circumambulation,
and having subsequently displayed the lamp within the vessel (ghaṭadīpa), one should lead the ritual image (karmārcā) into the pavilion;
then, one should lead the sacred image (tīrthabera) into the vicinity of the primary image (mūlabera).

O Lord of Ramā, for Your pleasure, I, a fool, have performed this unsurpassed festival of the sacred waters (tīrthotsava) by enjoining the Śakti residing in the Tīrtha-liṅga with the primary image (mūlabera). O Teacher of the World, forgive that.
Having thus informed [the deity], O Rame, one should release the *kautuka* from the image at the sacred site (*tīrtha*).

In the absence of an image at the sacred site, the Guru should perform that rite with the bathing image; if even that is lacking, he should do so with offerings and worship, or else with the two sandals.
In the pavilion, one should present the sacrificial offerings and other items to the God of gods.
At the time of evening, one should worship the Lord in due order until the end of the ritual for the bed.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.
On the following morning, having performed his rites, the supreme preceptor entered the temple of the Lord together with the practitioners and the guardians of the images.
Then, having entered the fire-chamber, preceded by the worship of the door and the archway,
one should perform the worship of the sprouts as well as the veneration of the four locations,
and carry out the daily worship of the primary image and the other icons.
At the time of midday, one should bathe the Lord, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
with twenty-five jars for the completion of the sacrifice;
then, having offered the great oblation, one should cause it to be distributed among the Vaiṣṇavas.

In the evening, one should perform the flower sacrifice; hear now its procedure. For the sake of the deity’s flower sacrifice, it should be performed either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure, like the door-arches and the water-pots.
One should first construct a pavilion adorned with arches of *darbha* grass, garlands, and plantain pillars, and provided with many lamps of ghee;
having brought the God of gods there, one should install him upon a lion-throne.
One should worship the imperishable Hari with ornaments, seats, and enjoyments.
O Rame, one should prepare a grain-seat upon the altar in front of the deity,
having sprinkled the sacrificial materials with water from the *puṇyāha* rite.
Having spread a cloth upon that [altar], one should [draw] the mandala of the discus and lotus with five-colored flowers—
either seasonal blossoms that are pure and very beautiful—
or with dark green tulasī sprouts.
Having visualized [the deities] according to the prescribed method, one should place an excellent jar made of gold or other materials in the northeast corner outside the mandala;
one should also set out the *pālikā* vessels and others, and wash them with the recitation of mantras.
One should fill their bases with fragrant sandalwood;
then, one should fill their cavities with powdered *niśā* and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should place them upon a seat of grain on the northern side of the mandala.
The Guru should cause all the rites, beginning with the worship of the doors, to be performed according to the rules;
however, in this ritual, he should omit the moon-pitcher (*somakumbha*) and its associated fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having sprinkled the pitcher, the mandala, and the boundary-markers with water consecrated for the "merit-acclamation" (*puṇyāha*), [he should proceed].
O Rame, for the purpose of worshipping Vāsudeva, one should generate the fire on the eastern part of the sacrificial ground, either in a pit or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should worship the deities in their respective vessels (pālikās) in sequence, according to the path previously described.
Having invoked Śrī into the flowers, one should sow those flowers upon the twelve lotus petals as well as upon the pericarp; likewise,
having conceived the pedestal in the pitcher as being of the nature of the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
Then, having meditated upon Vāsudeva in the center of the pitcher, one should worship him.
Having propitiated the four-armed Sudarśana in the water-vessel,
the wise man should worship the gods situated in the enclosures of the mandala.

Having meditated upon Vāsudeva— the imperishable Lord of the Praṇava, adorned with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, Nandaka sword, and other weapons— seated in the center of the pericarp of the lotus within the wheel,
one should worship Him until the lamps [are extinguished].
One should worship the twelve syllables at the bases of the petals starting from the east.
One should contemplate Keśava and the others within the filaments in the middle of the petals.
At the tips of the petals, the practitioner of mantra should worship the *praṇava*, which has the luster of crystal.
Having worshipped the deity, one should thereafter meditate upon the mandala in the fire;
one should worship all the deities residing within the mandala with clarified butter as before.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Nṛsūkta, one should offer sixteen oblations with fuel-sticks.
The preceptor should sacrifice with clarified butter, dedicating it to Keśava and the others.
After offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should then sacrifice into the jars and other vessels in due order.
Then, having performed the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), he should worship those [deities] stationed within the fire-maṇḍala.
Having meditated upon the circle of flowers, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should pray to the imperishable Hari:
"O Lord of Śrī, Vāsudeva, sole protector of all the worlds! (37.26)
"For the pacification of omissions regarding the great festival rites, mantras, and ritual substances,
O Supreme Lord, accept this flower-sacrifice performed by me.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should begin the twelvefold worship.
First, from the base of the leaf, [the preceptor] should place the syllable, Keśava, and likewise the Praṇava;
having invoked [these] into the flower-vessel at the navel of the image, the best of gurus should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the *kūrca* grass and then worship the deity.
One should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), as well as the water for sipping (ācamana), the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), and sandalwood paste;
then the garland, incense, the lamp, fruit, and the waving of lights (nīrājana); and finally, one should present betel leaf mixed with cardamom and camphor.
The best of preceptors should perform the placement of the deities (*sthitinyāsa*) upon the limbs of the divine image;
in this manner, he should perform the placement of each syllable (*pratyakṣaranyāsa*) and indeed carry out the worship.
One should contemplate the deities residing in the *pālikās* as being within the lotus of the wheel.
One should pray to Vāsudeva from the lotus on the discus, and to Hari within the water-pot (kumbha).
O lotus-eyed one, one should pray to the deity residing in the pot as being present in the divine image.
Then, the preceptor himself, taking the flowers from the mandala, [should proceed].
One should indeed consecrate Janārdana with the Puruṣasūkta;
having sprinkled him with the water from the pitcher, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having offered sattvic foods and various kinds of edibles, [one should proceed].
Then, having given those [offerings] to the devotees, one should perform the festival of the God.

Or else, the most excellent preceptor, having established the Lord of Gods together with Śrī and Bhūmi upon an auspicious seat and having adorned Him with flowers and other offerings, [should proceed].
With many lamps fed with ghee and having many wicks, as well as with the various requisites for the procession, preceded by dance and song,
one should lead the God through the streets accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
Having brought the deity from within the sanctum, he should place Lord Hari upon a seat on the ground in front of the *balipīṭha*, facing the primary image (*mūlārcā*). Then,
with palms joined in reverence, the Bhaṭṭācārya [should worship] the deity with the Upaniṣads.
Having gratified Viṣṇu with hymns of praise, one should pray with this verse:
"O Lord of Gods, thousand-headed, resplendent with a thousand eyes, endowed with a thousand arms, and possessing thousand-petaled lotus-feet. (37.41)
O Lord of the Universe, whose nature is unceasing, please grant permission for the gods beginning with Brahmā,
as well as for the men who have come for the sake of attending this great festival, to return to their own abodes. (37.42–37.43)
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, O Earth, one should request permission from them [to create] Brahmā—
the sovereign of the world of truth (satyaloka), seated upon a royal swan, born from the lotus of your navel, and endowed with the Gāyatrī of Speech. (37.44)
"O Lord of the World, command this best of Vaiṣṇavas, who has come for the purpose of serving Your great festival, to go to his own abode.
[Command] Purandara, the lord of Śacī, who was born from the lotus-like mouth of You."
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvaṇa, the sovereign of Amarāvatī,
that foremost of Vaiṣṇavas has arrived for the purpose of attending your great festival—
he who possesses the splendor born from the lotus of your face and is the lord of the city.
[I salute] the Lord of Svadhā and Svāhā, the Fire-god (Vahni), seated upon a ram, holding a spear in his hand;
the best of Vaiṣṇavas who has come for the sake of serving Your great festival;
and the powerful Kāla, born from Your left arm, the leader of the Śyāmalās.
[He saw] the lord of the city of Saṃyaminī, the three-eyed one seated upon a buffalo,
the best of Vaiṣṇavas who had come for the sake of serving your great festival,
the Nirṛti whose vehicle is a ghost and who was born from your lotus feet.
The fierce lord of Kṛṣṇāṅganā, accompanied by the mistress of the long pond,
has arrived for the sake of serving your great festival; he is the best of Vaiṣṇavas,
born from your secret part, bearing a noose, and the sovereign over Śraddhāvatī.
Varuṇa, the lord of coolness, who rides upon a great makara, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, has indeed arrived for the purpose of serving your great festival;
he is born from your vital breath, mounted upon a deer, and is the sovereign of Gandhavatī.
[Vaishampāyana said: Vāyu, the Lord of the Ever-Moving, who holds a banner in his hand and possesses great strength;
the best of Vaiṣṇavas who has come for the sake of serving your great festival;
the one born from your thigh, the holder of treasures, the friend of Śiva, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera). || 37.54–37.55 ||
Mounted upon a human vehicle, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, the lord of the goddess Lakṣmī, has arrived for the sake of attending your great festival;
he is Hara, the lord of Yaśovatī, who was born from your right arm.
The Lord of Umā, the wielder of the trident, the three-eyed one who has the bull as his vehicle—
the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu who has come for the sake of serving your great festival—
has arrived. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas have gathered together from various regions.
"And all these Śūdra Vaiṣṇavas have come for the purpose of serving the God;
O Mādhava, grant them permission to return to their own country.
Having beheld the face of Hari and received the permission of the Teacher of the World, [they departed].
The best of teachers should grant them permission to return to their own country.
Then, having brought the deity to the sacrificial hall, he should show it [to them];
the Guru should cause the worship of the four stations and the completion of the Veda to be performed.
One should place the deities residing in the small vessels into the wheel-lotus;
then, having brought forward the vessel containing the sprouts, one should pray to the imperishable Hari:
"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge!"

O Lord, whatever rite has been performed by me for your pleasure, beginning from the offering of the seed-syllable (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and ending with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the festival,
as well as that which has been performed by other officiating priests authorized by me; [37.63–64]

O Lord of Kamalā, accept this worship of the auspicious sprouts for the sake of fulfilling those various needs and for the pacification of deficiencies and excesses, performed by practitioners and other diverse attendants.
Having made this request, he should thereafter worship the Lord with the Śrīsūkta.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), he should display the lamp of the water-pot.
Thereafter, by way of the staircase, the most excellent guru [should lead] the Blessed One.
One should lead the Lord of Ramā very slowly into the inner sanctum;

having placed him facing the primary image (mūlārcā), one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the two of them. Then, by the command of the preceptor (ācārya), the practitioner (sādhaka) should go outside.
O Lotus-born One, one should dismiss all the gods, beginning with Brahmā. Then the practitioner, having placed the sacrificial image upon a palanquin or vehicle,
should offer the bali-oblation according to the rules, starting from Caṇḍa and ending with Supratiṣṭha.
Having removed the *kumuda* and other [offerings], one should place them upon the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*).
One should cast the water-offering (*bali*) toward the deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
Those most excellent gods, Brahmā and the others, by whom [the offerings] were previously summoned—
Having awakened [the deity] with those very verses, the wise one should lead him to his own respective region.
Having offered the *bali* at the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*) while performing circumambulation,
and having reached the flag-seat (*dhvajapīṭha*), he should worship the Lord of Birds (*vihagendra*).
Having offered sattvic food and then dismissed the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) who was stationed upon the banner, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the primary Lord of Birds;
thereafter, having lowered the banner, the preceptor should carry it on his head.

Having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha) and offered the ceremonial banner and cloth to the lotus feet of the primary image (mūlārcā), one should perform the worship of the four locations and then unite the deity residing in the mandala fire with the physical form (bimba).
One should place the [deities] located at the door-arches and the water-pots upon the great pedestal.
Then, having mounted the sacrificial image upon a vehicle, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should carry it,
along with the great water-pot, the secondary pots, and the requisites for the procession.

Accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and the sounds of musical instruments, they should proceed to the temple of the god. Taking up the water-pot (*karaka*), the Bhaṭṭācārya should walk at their head, reciting the Astra-mantra along with the *Chinnā-dhārā*.
One should place the jars upon a pedestal of grain in front of the deity.
O Rame, one should establish the images of the ritual acts and so forth in their respective places upon the seats.
One should worship, beginning with the offering of the *arghya* and ending with the image of the bali-offering for the root-mantra and the rest.
Then, having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), the preceptor, holding a handful of flowers,
should conceal [the image] behind a curtain or a screen for the sake of the great festival, according to his capacity, during the ritual of the primary image.
Visualized within the sacred thread, the sacrificial offering, the image, and the water-pot,
one should pray to Śakti with joined palms of flowers and rejoice before her.
Then, established in meditation, one should offer those flowers upon the head of Hari.
Having removed the curtain, one should display the jar and the lamp.
Sprinkling the deity with water from the jar while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*,
one should then pray to the deity with palms joined in reverence after having offered salutations.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, saluted by all the worlds;
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, abiding in the hearts of all beings!
O Blessed One, you are Vāsudeva, and she who dwells upon the expanse of your chest—
And Kamalā—you two are the primordial causes of all the worlds.
You are Viṣṇu and Kamalā is Lakṣmī; you are Rudra and Kamalā is Śivā.
You are Brahmā and Kamalā is Vāṇī; you are Śakra and Kamalā is Śacī.
You are Agni, Śrī, Svadhā, and Svāhā; you are Yama, while I am Hariṇī.
You are Nairṛti, Dīrghikā, and Śrī; you are Pāśī, Śītalā, and Ramā. You are Sadāgati, Śrī, Vāyu, Śrīda, Saṃpat, and Indirā.
"You are the moonlight, Lakṣmī, and likewise the moon; you are the sun, and I am the radiance.
Thus, O Hari, you two are the parents consecrated for the protection of the world;
in this way, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you shall manifest at various times."

O Lord, whose form is composed of consciousness and bliss, and who is never separated from true generosity— by me, a fool who did not recognize what was pleasant or unpleasant for you, an omniscient being such as you, this [wrong] has been done.
Whether it be according to the scriptures or contrary to them, you alone are worthy to know.
O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, O Lord endowed with glory, accept whatever transgression I have committed during this festival, for I am a devotee who has come to you for refuge.

Having thus informed the Lord, one should contemplate the Śrīvatasa, wherein resides the auspiciousness of the protective thread; O Goddess, one should then release the protective threads. O Rame, one should also cause the removal of the *kautuka* (sacred thread) for the preceptor and all others.

The most excellent preceptor should worship the deity at the end of the bed according to the prescribed rite. Then, on the following day at dawn, the patron should respectfully honor the supreme guru with garments, ornaments, cows, wealth, and lands.
Having honored him with two chowries, two umbrellas, banners and the like,
and with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, as well as with divine ritual implements,
the wise man, accompanied by his followers, should lead the preceptor to his home.
The patron (yajamāna) shall also depart accompanied by the assembly of attendants stationed at the temple.

Having returned to his own home, the preceptor (ācārya), the most excellent of gurus, should worship all [the implements] in due order; then the supreme guru [should take up] the flagstaff and its cloths.
After the festival, O Goddess, one should personally take for oneself the materials remaining from the sacrifice for the sake of pacifying the exhaustion of the Deity. Then,
having completed the daily worship in the first enclosure and the others, [one should proceed].

Having brought the deity into the pavilion, one should worship him with the materials required for the shrine (chaityavastu). In pavilions constructed in gardens and other such places, the preceptor, having been entreated there by the devotees, should likewise bring [the deity] and worship him with devotion.
Having first bathed the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rite with scented water and other substances, having anointed him with perfumes,
and having adorned him with jasmine flowers and other blossoms as well as ornaments, [he should fan him] with palm-leaf fans made of uśīra grass.
Sprinkled with water from the Himalayas, their bracelets jingling "jhaṇajjhaṇ," adorned with all ornaments and beautified by flower decorations,
these fragrant maidservants in white garments attend to me on all sides.
Some maidservants should fan the Lord of Gods, others should dance,
and still others should sing while playing the lute, flute, and drum;
thus they should gratify Hṛṣīkeśa with these cooling services.
Then, at the time of evening, one should worship the God with the *arghya* offering and other rites.
Immediately after presenting foods such as rice mixed with sugar and other edibles,
the preceptor should lead the God of gods very slowly back to His abode.
The most excellent of instructors should perform the night worship in due order;
for this festival of Śaitya, there is no fixed number of days,
O fair-faced one, nor is there a requirement for worship at the four locations.
"In this very manner, even during the spring, one should perform the festival for the Lord.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā. [The thirty-seventh chapter.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Śrī said:
O Puruṣottama, tell me all of this: what is the time for the worship of the Vasantotsava, what is its sequence, and how is it performed? I wish to hear all that. 38.1
The Blessed One said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the worship of Hari in the spring;
or even during the season of spring, or in summer, when the bright fortnight prevails. (38.2)
On the full moon day, O fair-faced one, or on a non-pierced [lunar day],
or if it is pierced, on the first [tithi], the Guru, having determined the time for the avabhṛtha bath,
should worship Puruṣottama for seven nights after that determination. (38.3)
Except for the hoisting of the banner,
one should perform the worship of the four locations preceded by the rite of sowing seeds and followed by the binding of the protective thread,
starting from the day the festival begins and continuing every day thereafter. || 38.4–38.5 ||
At the two times [of day], there should be the offering of oblations (bali) and the worship of the door and the archway.
One should dig the ground into a square measuring thirty-two cubits in width and the same in length, extending twenty-eight bow-lengths.

In its center, according to the prescribed measurement, artisans should construct a level pavilion (maṇḍapa) twenty cubits in size, using either stone or brick; in the middle of that, there should be a pedestal (pīṭha) one cubit high, facing south.
Having established it within the enclosure, one should fill it with fragrant waters;
it should be adorned with plantain trunks, betel-nut trees, fruits, and flowers,
scented on all sides with sandalwood and various perfumes, and likewise fumigated with incense.
Having made the pavilion cool, the best of preceptors,
who knows the mantras, having entered the inner sanctum at the arrival of evening,
performs the worship during the rite of the Spring Festival.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he should pray to the Lord of the gods of gods:
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, wearer of yellow garments, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace!
For the sake of the worship during the spring festival, grant your presence for this ritual performance. (38.12)
"O Joy of the World, act out of a desire to bestow grace upon your devotees.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, the preceptor should invoke Śakti,
whether she is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi or not, as well as the *kautuka*.
Having specially adorned [the deity] with ornaments, sandalwood paste, and garlands, one should place him upon a pedestal made of jewels or even in a palanquin,
and carry him in procession through the streets of Puṣpaka.
Then, having brought [the deity] to the pavilion, one should establish him upon a seat of jewels.
One should fan the deity with fans perfumed with fragrant substances,
and having worshipped according to the scriptures, [one should offer] various kinds of edible foods.
One should offer pieces of cucumber, water infused with fragrances,
pieces of sugar mixed with the leaves of black mung beans,
and curd-rice together with various kinds of fruits.
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should cause dance and song to be performed.
One should cause the offered food, snacks, and other items to be distributed to the devotees in due order.
Thus, having propitiated that Lord of the World with all the ritual services (*upacāra*), [one should proceed].
Then, O Rame, one should lead the Deity into the inner sanctum;
having withdrawn the Śakti from the festival [procession], one should enjoin her into the root [image].
"O Ocean of Compassion, Lord of the World, you who are consecrated to the protection of devotees!"

"O Lord of Gods, I have no power for the rites such as worship according to the scripture spoken by you; please forgive whatever I have done out of delusion. Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
Having thus performed the six festivals during the latter part of the day, he should,
in the evening, place the Lord upon a chariot or even upon Vainateya,
and together with Śrī and Puṣṭi, cause him to circumambulate the streets in due order.
Having descended from the chariot, [the officiant] should lead the deity— who is equal in measure to the image at the sacred ford—
to the riverbank or a pond and perform the avabhṛtha bath.
Then, having brought [the deity] to the pavilion, one should worship him in due order as before.
Having offered everything as before and having assigned [the deities] in their proper order,
the best of teachers should dismiss the deities of the door-pitchers and so forth.
He should then project the Śakti from the pitcher, the maṇḍala, and the fire into the image.
Having led [the deity] from the image at the conclusion of the festival, the Guru should unite the Śakti with the root [deity].
With water from the pitcher, the Guru should sprinkle the root image using the *kūrca* [grass-bundle];
then, having released the protective binding, he should perform the daily worship.
Whoever worships the Blessed One in this way during the spring season with cool and fragrant substances goes to my abode.
This festival should be observed during the bright fortnight according to the path of the scriptures.

If it were performed during the dark fortnight, O Rame, it would surely bring about the destruction of the king’s kingdom, as well as that of the patron and the preceptor; therefore, it should somehow be done during the bright fortnight, but never during the dark one.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Vaiśākha festival for the lotus-born one,
the Lord of the World, for the purpose of pleasing the deity of the spring season.
A wise man should worship him with branches and fruits produced in that season.
Listen, O Lotus-born One, to the fortnight, the asterism, the month, and the lunar day:
on the full moon of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha conjoined with the Viśākhā asterism, on that day,
the Bhāgavata preceptor should perform the worship under that asterism.
Even when there is a conjunction of lunar days (tithi) and constellations (nakṣatra), the primary festival is said to be [on the day of] the constellation.
O Lotus-born One, they know that worship on a lunar day devoid of a constellation is demonic.
Therefore, one should perform worship on a day possessing the constellation; that indeed becomes Vaiṣṇava.
On that day, in the evening, the Guru, having performed the worship of the deity as usual,
said: "O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, worshipped by the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Makaradhvaja),
grant your presence within this image for the sake of the Viśākhā festival worship."
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods regarding the ritual worship of the Moon (Kalānidhi),
and having invoked [the deity] and placed him upon the vehicle, he brought Hari down from that onto a seat within the outer pavilion using twenty-five jars.
Having bathed the deity, the most excellent of gurus then adorned him with ornaments;
having likewise decorated him with jasmine, mālatī, kunda, kurava, and damana flowers, as well as mango blossoms, lotuses, blue lilies, and other such flowers, the best of teachers [proceeded].
One should perform the worship of the four locations, beginning with the doors and the archways;
[offering] jackfruit, plantains, mangoes,
pieces of coconut, lac-dye, and dates.
One should take milk and sugar in quantities equal to these [ingredients],
along with a little marīca, elā, and one *pala* each of karpūra;
having purified these according to the rules, one should cook them in the cooking vessel.
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rites, one should offer all four kinds of food and various types of edibles to him.
One should also offer a refreshing drink, coconut water, and cool, satiating water.
Then, having offered betel leaf, he should cause it to be distributed to the devotees in due order.
Beautiful young female attendants should dance before them,
and thereafter the singers should perform songs accompanied by the lute and other instruments.
The twice-born should cause the sounds of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas to resound;
having thus performed the festival, the preceptor, having placed the deity upon a vehicle,
should lead him to the inner sanctum and install him facing the original [image].
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, one should apply the *śakti* mantra at the base.
"Without knowing the path of the scriptures and without reflecting upon what is pleasing to You, whatever action has been performed by me—You ought to forgive all of that. (38.49–38.50)
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
If the Vaiśākha festival should fall during the middle of the Vasantotsava,
one should perform both festivals on a single day.
Thus, for one who worships the God with leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth,
there shall be an increase of crops and the fruit thereof shall be very great.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-nine:
Now, O Daughter of the Ocean, I shall describe the great festival of the Milk Ocean;
it should be held during the cool season or the summer, on an auspicious day in the bright fortnight.

The festival of the raft (plavotsava) should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; or, having held the festival for eight, six, four, or even two days prior to the day of the raft-festival,
one rejoices on the following day.
The boat festival (plavotsava) must be performed according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
One should offer the germinating seeds (aṅkura) on the night preceding the day of raising the banner;
or one may perform the boat festival either before the raising of the banner or without it.
The preceptor should perform the binding of the protective thread for the deity and for himself as well,
starting from the day of commencement, twice every day.
He should perform worship at the four locations and cause the offering of oblations to be made.
At the beginning and at the end, one should bathe the Lord of Gods with twenty-five jars every day, and perform the ritual of mounting the vehicle; furthermore,
one should construct a pavilion near the lake.
Adorned with plantain trunks, betel-nut fruits, and the like, with arches for worship, canopies of variegated cloth and other materials, and flower garlands—
having thus prepared the pavilion according to the prescribed characteristics, the most excellent of preceptors [proceeds].
On the day of the festival's commencement, having completed the morning worship, one should then pray to the Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees for the sake of the boat festival:
"O Lord of Ramā, you who lie upon the serpent Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk... (39.9–10).
"Be present in this image together with Śrī for the festival of the boat procession"—
having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should subsequently invoke the Power (Śakti) from the root-mantra into the primary image and the festive icon, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi.
Having consecrated the god with the offering of *arghya* and other rites in due order,
I placed him upon a jeweled palanquin at dawn;
having adorned him with ornaments such as a crown and even with flowers, I indeed took delight.
Accompanied by parasols, chowries, peacock-feather fans, banners, and staffs,
as well as various kinds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas,
he circumambulated the village together with the two goddesses and the Lord.
Having brought [the deity] to the bank of the lake and placed it upon a golden throne in a pavilion,
one should then perform worship according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, at the time of evening, one should lead [the deity] back from there to the temple.
When evening has arrived, having performed the daily worship,
he should then mount the vehicle, accompanied by lamps fed with scented oil and by the sounds of all kinds of musical instruments, amidst crowds of actors and dancers.
With the dancing of courtesans and by circumambulating the processional paths,
O Lotus-born One, one should slowly lead the God to the temple;
and having performed the worship, one should then conduct the festival of the couch.
In this manner, one should cause the festival of Hari to be celebrated prior to the day of the *plava* [year].
Then, on the morning of the *plava* day, having performed the worship up to the conclusion of the festival,
the preceptor should place Vāsudeva, together with Śrī and Puṣṭi, upon a vehicle.
Having adorned [the image], I indeed delight in the four processional paths in due order.
One should lead it around clockwise accompanied by the sounds of Vedic recitations and musical instruments;
having brought it to the pavilion on the bank, one should place it upon a golden seat.
Having performed a special worship there, the best of instructors should then offer food, edibles, soft foods, and drinks;
coconut water and cool water for libation.
One should offer to the God the honey-mixture (madhuparka), along with betel-leaf containing camphor and powder, together with cardamom,
cloves, nutmeg, and jasmine fruit,
as well as two areca nuts and a betel vine.
Then, first of all, he saw an excellent boat constructed by the best of craftsmen,
equipped with sixteen masts, adorned with banners and other ornaments,
beautified with variegated garlands, canopies, and two stories.
O Rame, the preceptor should first sprinkle the area, which is adorned with rows of plantain trunks and canopies, with the waters of an auspicious day; he should then sprinkle the jar,
the Lord of the Ocean of Milk, and the ground, along with Śeṣa, in due order.
Having invoked them with their respective mantras, one should then perform the worship of the fire.
Then the Guru himself, having invoked all [the deities] of the fire into the water of the pitcher,
takes up the central pitcher accompanied by the sounding of bells and musical instruments.
Having gone to the bank of the pond, the preceptor should invoke the Lord of Waters from the water in the pitcher, Śeṣa upon the float, and Bhūmi in the celestial chariot (vimāna), [reciting]:
"O Overlord of the Milk Ocean, adorned with hands holding a noose and a lotus! (39.30–39.31)

"O Goddess, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands, please establish your presence in the lake for the sake of the Lord’s boat festival. Having thus entreated Varuṇa, one should worship him in the lake, O Rame. (39.32)
O Goddess, sovereign of Śvetadvīpa, be present upon this raft!
O Lord of Serpents, praised by the immortals, adorned with a thousand crest-jewels, bed of Viṣṇu, assume the form of a raft, O Master! (39.33–39.34)
Having thus offered prayers to the Earth, one should worship Śeṣa with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites.
Then, having consecrated the raft (plava) by sprinkling it all around, one should worship the lotuses and other flowers.
Thereafter, one should cause the Lord, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, to ascend the raft.
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments mingled with conchs and the chanting of the Vedas,
one should circumambulate the lake three or five times in a clockwise direction and then place the raft in the central pavilion, O Rama.
When the sun has set, one should worship the Blessed One.
Around the lotus pond, in the prepared and elongated [spaces],
one should continuously arrange ghee-lamps provided with flames.
Having placed the Blessed One back upon the raft with the chief attendants,
one should cause the vessel to be circumambulated three times with lamps, musical instruments, and other offerings.
Having brought the Lord of Gods to the shore, one should perform the procession through the streets.
Then one should perform the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) for the festival of the Lord Hari.
Having brought the sacrificial image to the temple and entered the fire-chamber,
one should unite the Power (*śakti*) residing in the circle of fire with the image of the sacrifice.
The wise practitioner should lead the primary pitcher and the other pitchers to their fundamental place.
He should place the image-pitchers in front of the root-icon;
he should then unite the power residing in the pitcher and the image with that [power] in the root.
Having sprinkled [the image] with water from the pitcher, one should utter this verse:
"O God, whatever boat-festival has been performed by me as a service dear to you,
it may certainly have become deficient therein due to ignorance, pride, and so forth."
"O Lord of Kamalā, forgive this which has been done by me.
Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods and having paid obeisance to the All-pervading One,
one should perform the worship, the ritual sleep, and the festival according to the scriptures.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter of the illustrious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Forty:
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the festival of the ceremonial bath for the eldest [brother].
Either under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā during the month of Mithuna, or on the full moon day;
or indeed on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Kaṭaka—
whether the lunar mansion is joined with or separated from the sun, O Rame.
On the eleventh lunar day of Hari, the consecration must certainly take place;
having first performed the daily worship, one should then pray to Hari:
"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, beloved of Lakṣmī, ocean of compassion! (40.3)

"I pray that you perform the great consecration for me. Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods, and having prayed from the root-mantra for the ritual action, [he says: "May you graciously accept my worship, having entered into the ritual image. 40.4–40.5.
Having brought the ritual image (karmabimba) outside the pavilion, the preceptor first uncovers the armor (kavaca) of Hari and places it before Him in the sacred abode (Rame). Then,
having established eighty-one jars, the preceptor [proceeds] with those vessels.
One should fill all the vessels with ghee and other substances using their respective mantras.
First, one should offer the sprouts and also tie the protective thread (kautuka).
Having performed the worship of the door, the archway, the water-pots, and so forth, according to the prescribed rite.

The supreme preceptor should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the Blessed Lord Hari, who is equal to Śrī, Bhūmi, Vīra, and Lakṣmī, accompanied by the recitation of mantras. Having offered edible foods and other delicacies, he should cause them to be distributed to the devotees in due order.
Having had the artisan fashion a pure armor and having consecrated it with sprinkling,
O Lotus-born One, the Preceptor should then apply the armor to the image with the waters of nine jars and the five products of the cow, as previously described.
Having adorned [the image] with garments and other ornaments, one should worship it up until the point of bringing it forward;
then, having brought it to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should place it upon the lion-throne (siṃhaviṣṭara). One should apply the Śakti to the Root-mantra and pray to the imperishable Hari.
"This consecration with the Jyeṣṭhā stars has been performed by me for your pleasure.
Whatever may have been done incorrectly therein, you ought to forgive that.
Having thus informed the Lord of Lakṣmī, one should perform the daily worship of Hari.
Listen, O virtuous lady, I shall describe the festival of Hari’s sleep;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the festival of sleep,
which brings me joy and bestows happiness upon all the worlds.
I delight either in the front part of the inner sanctum or within the inner chamber itself—
[a place] bound above by golden chains,
provided with cotton mattresses and coverlets, and variegated with the nine precious gems.
It was bound with nets of pearls, perfumed with fragrant substances,
covered with a canopy of fine linen, and adorned with flower garlands;
it was also filled with burning lamps fed with scented oils or ghee.
"I delight in that which is adorned by four excellent, non-extinguishing lamps.
Having thus prepared the bed, one should sprinkle it with meritorious water.
During the festival of the swing, however, the deities are worshipped within the swing itself.
The best of preceptors should also worship those deities even at the time of the ritual sleep;
when the onset of night has begun, he should worship the Lord until the conclusion of the procession.
Then, standing before the Mūla-mantra deity with palms joined in reverence, the teacher—
"O Blessed One, this time for yogic sleep has arrived. Therefore, remain present within this image until the time of your rising.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods, [he moved him] from the root [pedestal] to the couch.
In the absence of a physical image, one should invoke [the deity] upon the *kūrca* grass mat and pray to Hari.
Having bathed [the deity] with nine jars, one should worship the four locations. One should then unite the Lord, who resides within the fire-mandala and the jar, with the image.
One should sprinkle the form intended for sleep with the water from the great pitcher (mahākumbha).
Then, one should worship the deities beginning with Mūla, ending with Havis,
having laid down the Lord together with Śrī and Bhūmi upon a couch.
One should worship those two tufts on the image that is devoid of Śrī and Bhūmi,
having made a formal resolve for four months or indeed for four fortnights;
[one should worship] the God of gods while He is situated upon the couch every day with the articles required for His rest.
The wise one should worship with ritual substances, with a mind bowed in devotion. At that time, he should not perform the daily, occasional, or optional rites, nor the festival;
however, even at that time, the preceptor should perform the festival of Kṛṣṇa’s birth.

There is no other time for it; therefore, one should perform it at that very moment. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the festival—beginning with the morning and including special sacrifices and other rites—should be commenced.
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should perform the end of the god’s night;
if he should perform the auspicious ceremony of the reclining for four fortnights—
or, O Rame, if he should perform the festival and the reclining for three fortnights.
Then there would be no shifting [of the seasons], nor the rising [of the sun] in the month of Kārttika.
At that time, however, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight at the break of dawn,
those dwelling in Puṣkara-dvīpa reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Some sing with divine Dravidian verses accompanied by melody, rhythm, and tone; others please him with Sāman chants.
And the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, awaken him with the Vedāntas.
O you who are born from nectar, I am pleased by that which is performed by my devotees. When I am satisfied, the entire world becomes satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
For my pleasure during that festival, the preceptor [should be honored] by the sacrificer.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, for the welfare of the world, one should fast and perform worship together with devotees and followers of the Bhāgavata.
Indeed, Mārgaśīrṣa is proclaimed to be the rising of the gods.

The month of Kārttika preceding that is proclaimed as the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla). Having performed the observances such as ritual bathing during the hour of Brahmā together with the devotees of the Lord, whoever praises the god Hari, the bestower of all fruits, during that time— || 40.38–39 ||
"O Rame, even one joined with great sins shall attain liberation;
I shall explain that method, so listen, O lotus-born one!
Having entered the temple of the Lord, the Guru, together with those learned in the four Vedas..."
Having praised the one who reclines upon the serpent with *ekāyana* verses,
one should awaken Vāsudeva with songs, dances, and various musical instruments.
Then the preceptor should transfer the Śakti from the bed into the *dhruva* image.

One should show a mirror, a full water-pot, an elephant, the back of a cow, the face of a horse, and a maiden beautiful in all her limbs. Having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should offer milk and white sugar.
One should offer curd-rice and then perform the lustration rite (nīrājana).
Having performed the daily worship up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa), one should pray to Hari:
"The hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, await your vision."
The Gandharvas dance with Apsarases in the dancing hall,
and the best of the twice-born praise you with the Vedas of Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman.
To show them favor, establish your presence within this image.
Having thus invoked the Lord of Gods, one should lead him to the pavilion called Nṛtta.
Having established the lotus-eyed God there, one should worship him with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites,
and thereafter present the four kinds of food and edibles.
The preceptor, an expert in the Pāñcarātra, summoned a reciter of the Purāṇas;
through that reciter, [he explained] the fruits of service to the Enemy of the Daityas,
as well as the fruits that bring suffering to those who have committed transgressions.
Having had it recited, O lotus-eyed one, one should satisfy him with wealth;
having offered various kinds of food and edibles, one should cause them to be given to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having brought the deity to the temple, one should install the Śakti at its base.
"O Viṣṇu, O Acyuta, please accept this worship known as the festival of rising, performed for your delight, just as it has been executed.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should dismiss the festive procession.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter of the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The fortieth chapter:
O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall describe the great festival of Kṛṣṇa’s birth.
The asterism, lunar day, weekday, conjunction,
and also the division; the fortnight, month, and year in which Acyuta descended—
at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages, in an auspicious year and at an auspicious time.
In the month of Siṃha, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, conjoined with the Rohiṇī nakṣatra,
during the Harṣa-kaulava karaṇa, on the auspicious day of Wednesday;
when Mercury had entered Virgo, Venus was in the ascendant, and Jupiter was present as well.
When Saturn is situated in Capricorn, in Taurus, or in Libra;
when Rāhu is situated in Leo and Ketu is situated in Capricorn;
and when the Moon is in Taurus and the Sun is in Leo.
At midnight, when the ascendant was Taurus, Hari, the benefactor of all the world,
was born as Kṛṣṇa to Vasudeva and Devakī in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
At that very time, Janārdana specifically manifested in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, he is to be worshipped by the initiated Bhāṭṭācārya.
I shall explain that procedure: at evening, the best of teachers, having bathed and performed the rites such as the counting [of breaths], should enter the inner sanctum.
Having performed the daily worship and other rites, one should then pray to the primary image:
"O Lord who wields the conch, discus, mace, and Śārṅga bow; O wielder of the quiver and sword;
O Vāsudeva, source of the universe, cause of its creation, preservation, and end! (41.9)

O Hari, you who in former times descended assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa— O best of gods, this is indeed the time for that festival of yours known as Jayantī; desiring to perform that festival, I entreat you.
"O Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, for the pleasure of Your devotees, O God, remain present within this form of Kṛṣṇa for a long time until the conclusion of the worship.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should invoke the power into Kṛṣṇa.
Having placed that image of Kṛṣṇa upon a vehicle on the ground in front of the palace,
and having then established the beautiful image of Kṛṣṇa upon a gem-encrusted lion-throne prepared within a pavilion, one should perform the worship of the gateway.
In front of Kṛṣṇa, one should prepare a seat of grain upon the ground;
having placed the jars according to rule and having duly installed the sacrificial fire,
one should place the image of Kṛṣṇa in the central jar and the Sudarśana discus in the water-vessel.
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the pitchers starting from the east;
and in the corners starting from the southeast, O Rame, one should worship Puruṣa and the others,
having fashioned the mandala of the discus and lotus upon the altar according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa in the pericarp and Keśava and the others in the twelve petals as well, having invoked them in due order starting from the east.
One should worship the host of attendant deities in the maṇḍala as before.
Having worshipped the image of Kṛṣṇa seated upon his throne, preceded by the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other rites,
one should bathe him with water for the arghya, pādya, and so forth, using the bathing-seat.
Having bathed Kṛṣṇa according to the rules with twenty-five jars...
Having brought him to the seat of ornaments and having adorned the lotus-eyed Lord with his crown and other decorations,
he then led the God, the Lord of Lakṣmī, to the dining mat provided with various kinds of food and drink.
Having offered a fourfold heap of food consisting of *śaṣkulī* cakes mixed with fruit, the preceptor should thereafter place the seat toward the fire. Then,
having invoked Kṛṣṇa into its center and performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Then, one should offer oblations of clarified butter from the beginning—starting with the seat and so forth—up to the end of the food;

thereafter, one should offer the four kinds of food, such as the eatables (*bhakṣya*) and others, into the blazing fire. Having performed seven oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should then perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
The preceptor, having performed the offering of the oblation to the form of Kṛṣṇa,
should especially perform the offering of the *arghya*, which bestows all fruits.
On the ground before Kṛṣṇa, he should smear it with flour in the shape of a lotus.
It is endowed with eight petals and possesses a broad pericarp in the center;
having invoked Kṛṣṇa within that, one should [invoke] Vasudeva, Devakī, and then Nandagopa, in sequence upon the eight petals.

O Goddess, one should worship Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, Balabhadra, Niśākara, and Subhadra, as well as the attendants of the Lotus-born One. Taking a conch shell filled with cow’s milk in both hands, [one should offer it].
Standing on the ground with his knees bent, or remaining standing, the most excellent of gurus should present the *arghya* offering to Kṛṣṇa, who has descended for the welfare of the world.
He was born for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa and for the removal of the burden of the earth.
"For the sake of the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas and for the protection of Dharma,
for the destruction of the Kauravas and for the slaying of the Daityas— O Hari, together with Devakī, accept this *arghya* offered by me. (41.31–32)
The sacrificer should likewise offer the respectful water (arghya) to the Lord of the World.
Then, he should place Kṛṣṇa, who resides within the center of a flour-lotus, into the image.
Thereafter, [he should place Him] upon a jeweled swing adorned with flowers and other offerings.
Hanging with golden chains and resplendent with tiny bells,
it was covered with a canopy of fine linen and adorned with nets of pearls;
it was perfumed with saffron, musk, and sandalwood.
I delight in that place which is perfumed on all sides with fragrant substances and incense,
covered with a linen spread and even with a mattress of cotton. Having prepared it thus, the preceptor should then cause the remainder to be invoked into it.
Having laid Kṛṣṇa down, one should then remove the black-wool cloth and the painting.
O Lotus-born One, one should please Kṛṣṇa with songs of the swing and with dances and instrumental music;
and the best of Vaiṣṇavas should sing other Vaiṣṇava hymns.

Brahmins learned in the Pañcarātra, being well-prepared, should recite hymns composed by him before the God, as well as all other auspicious prayers. Then, having worshipped him with the arghya offering and other rites, accompanied by the waving of lights (nīrājana), [he should proceed].
Then, having offered the madhuparka, as well as fresh butter and sugar,
cow’s milk mixed with white sugar, flattened rice (pṛthuka),
and various kinds of foods cooked with cow’s ghee.
Having offered the eight kinds of foods, combined with sugar and other ingredients,
to the God of gods, one should then perform the rite of lustration (nīrājana).
One should present betel leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.

Having performed the recitation (japa) according to his capacity in the presence of the Blessed One, the Guru should unite the Deity— who resides within the water-pot (kumbha), the mandala, and the fire— with the [central] image,
as well as with the door-arches, the pots, and likewise with the pedestal (pīṭha) of Hari.

Then, one should divide the offered food, edibles, and so forth into four parts. The preceptor himself should take one portion, while the other three portions should be caused to be taken by the attendants— the *mūrtipās*, the Vaiṣṇavas, and others.
Then, having led the eternal Kṛṣṇa-form into the inner sanctum,
one should withdraw the Śakti from that image and unite it with the root [mantra].
Thereafter, the Guru, with palms joined in reverence, should bow down to the Lord of Gods.
"O Yellow-Robed One, O Embodiment of the Universe, today they celebrated your Jayanti festival;
I performed the rites there according to the scriptures, yet whether I deviated from the scriptural path or not, I was not capable of knowing that lapse from the scriptural way. (41.48)
"O God, you ought to forgive my transgression, for I am your devotee.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should complete the remaining worship.
For those seeking liberation who are free from desire, however, the breaking of the fast occurs at the conclusion of the festival.
For those who desire fruits such as sons and so forth, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) must indeed take place at dawn.
Then, at daybreak, the preceptor (ācārya), having performed his bath and completed his daily rites,
shall enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and awaken the Lord, O Rame.
Whether ending with the fire-oblation, the festival, or the presentation [of the deity], the Guru,
having completed the daily worship, should then, desiring to perform the festival for the Deity,
hold the vessel containing the words of invocation with both hands.
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, you who bring joy to all the worlds, O Lord of Śrī, be present within this image for the sake of the festival of the swing.
Having thus entreated the Lord of gods, the Teacher of the World, regarding the ritual image, [he spoke].
Having invoked and brought the Lord of Gods from there to the dance pavilion,
the supreme preceptor then worshipped the imperishable Hari, placed him upon a vehicle,
and adorned him with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
In front of the gopura, there was a pavilion provided with four pillars,
enriched with variegated cloths and canopies, and adorned with fruits and sprouts;
in its center hung a jar of milk placed atop a vessel of curd.
One should construct pavilions joined with turmeric water.
In this manner, one should construct many pavilions everywhere along the pathways;
then, one should lead the Lord of the Gods of gods throughout all the pathways.
Preceded by the sounds of musical instruments, dance, song, and the chanting of the Vedas, as well as other auspicious instruments, one should lead [the image] in front of the pavilion.
Then, having given a staff to the cowherd boys, one should employ them.
Those dear to Hari would strike the vessels on the scales with sticks;
and from those struck vessels, the boys would drink the curds and milk,
eat the butter, and even smear themselves with the curds.
With machines, they should sprinkle water mixed with turmeric everywhere;
in this manner, the cowherd boys should act throughout all the pathways. And the cowherd girls should throw balls of fresh butter upon the body of Kṛṣṇa.
Having thus circumambulated Lord Hari in all directions along the processional paths, the preceptor should then lead the deity back inside the temple; there,
in front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), he should worship the deity with offerings such as the arghya water.
Then, having displayed the lamp within the jar, one should lead it into the inner sanctum;
having joined the Śakti to the base, one should then cause the Lord Hari to rest.
"O God, that which has been performed by me is remembered as the festival of the scales (Śikyotsava)."
"O Mādhava, you ought to forgive what has been offered out of ignorance.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should worship at the edge of the bed.
By worshipping in this manner on the Jayantī day, one shall obtain all desires.
"In this regard, O lotus-eyed one, there is a certain distinction which I shall tell you:
when defects such as *viddha* (pierced) occur, the festival is divided in many ways.
[If] the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) or the Rohiṇī nakṣatra is full and conjoined with a Wednesday..."
When that [day] falls on a Tuesday with the ascendant being Taurus and Jupiter having risen,
the worship of Hari in his form as Kṛṣṇa on that day is indeed considered supreme. However,
when it is joined with Wednesday, it is proclaimed as middling.
When Rohiṇī is complete on the eighth day, or when it is joined with even a fraction of the eighth,
and likewise when the eighth is complete and joined with a fraction of Rohiṇī— on that lunar day,
worship should be performed, which destroys great sins.
The eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) joined with even a fraction of Kṛttikā or a fraction of the seventh (saptamī) must not be accepted; for worship performed on such a day is fruitless.
It may be devoid of the eighth day, or it may even be devoid of Rohiṇī.

One should perform the festival on each lunar mansion (tārakā) as well as on each lunar day (tithi). Worship performed on the eighth lunar day when it is joined with even a fraction of Kṛttikā, or joined with a fraction of the seventh, or with Rohiṇī, shall be fruitless.
Having thus observed all this, whoever worships me, O Rāme,
shall experience even the highest yogic states here, and in the end,
he rejoices in my world together with the hosts of eternal sages.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The forty-second chapter:
"In every year, on the eighteenth day of the month of Kaṭaka, I rejoice in Rame."
One should perform the festival of the Gaṅgā’s emergence for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
(42.1) Out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, in the midst of Mahābali’s sacrifice, I assumed the form of a dwarf and begged for three paces of land. (42.2)
Bali, being pleased with me, granted [this boon], and from that point I began to grow;
with one foot upon the earth and the second upon the station of Brahmā,
I passed beyond and shattered the wall of the great cosmic egg from within its hollow.
The water that had entered within flowed out in the form of a river.
Then Brahmā, declaring that water from my foot to be the Gaṅgā,
worshipped her as she descended below with perfumes and other offerings.

Having reached the peak of Kailāsa, the Lord of Pārvatī, recognizing that Gaṅgā as having originated from my feet, worshipped her according to the prescribed rites and bore her upon his head for the removal of his own sins.
Then she was released upon the earth, and at that moment she divided into seven streams,
bearing the names Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī.
From that time forward, the gods, sages, and likewise the brahmins worship the auspicious sevenfold form with devotion on that day.
Therefore, that festival should be observed; I shall now describe its procedure to you.
On the eighteenth day, O Goddess, at the time of sunset, the Guru should pray:
"O Lord whose lotus feet are sacred pilgrimage sites, O Trivikrama, benefactor of the world!
For the purification of the rivers, O God, grant Your presence within this image. (42.10–42.11)
Having thus made this request and having invoked [the deity], one should perform the ritual adornment upon the vehicle.
Having brought it to the riverbank, one should place the Lord Acyuta upon a lion-throne situated there and worship him with water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other offerings.
In front of the deity, one should prepare a pedestal for grain.
Having sprinkled nine new jars— equipped with lids and adorned with all ornaments—
with water from a *puṇyāha* ceremony and then filled them with water.
Having meditated upon the yoga-pīṭha in the central jar, one should worship Gaṅgā:
"O Gaṅgā, born from the foot of Viṣṇu, destroyer of all sins!
O Goddess, for the purification of rivers, please be present in this jar."
Thus, having invoked from the lotus-feet of the Lord, one should worship with the arghya and other offerings.

O daughter of Bhṛgu, having invoked Indra and the others into the subsidiary jars and Sudarśana into the water-pot (karaka), and having worshipped them, one should sprinkle [the area] with the holy-day waters.
Having purified the river, he joined the Gaṅgā—born from the foot of Viṣṇu and held in a jar—to it; then, having worshipped her with garments, flowers, fruits, and other offerings, [he spoke:
"O you who arose from the lotus-foot of Trivikrama and are served by the gods!"
"Release all those who stand in this river and have bathed from their sins.
Having thus entreated Indra and the other gods, the preceptor should cause them to emerge from the water-pot (kumbha).
Having brought the deity to the temple, he should install the Śakti at its base.
"O Lord of the World, on this eighteenth day, I have performed this festival; please accept it out of a desire to do what is pleasing to your devotee.
Having thus informed the Lord of Lakṣmī, O Rame, one should worship him at the edge of the bed.
Now I shall explain, O Lakṣmī, regarding the omission of worship that occurs during daily, occasional, and other rites, whether through ignorance or even intentionally;
for such an omission, a substitute known as the *pavitrāropa* (the offering of the sacred thread) must be performed.

From the beginning of Āṣāḍha until the end of Kārttika, the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to Viṣṇu wards off all defects; it grants pleasure to Viṣṇu and bestows liberation upon men. During the months previously mentioned, in the bright fortnight when the nectar of immortality arises, [one should perform this rite].
On the first, third, or fifth lunar day;
or on the eleventh, the tenth, or even the thirteenth;
or on the twelfth or the full moon, under a lunar mansion presided over by Yama.
Under Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, or Makha (Pūrvaphalgunī),
or under Citrā, Śravaṇa, Revatī, or the Aśvinī stars;
or under the lunar mansion of whichever month it may be, even if it is devoid of the full moon.
O Goddess, having determined one of these [times], the preceptor should perform the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) with every effort during those periods and hold a festival. Indeed,
that time is to be known as the Vaiṣṇava time for the festival of atonement.
Whether it was fashioned by a maiden, a brahmin woman, or even an elderly woman;
or by one in the first stage of life, or even by one in the second stage of life;
or whether it was made from a collection of threads, or produced from linen cloth—|| 42.30 ||
Having taken what was obtained and thoroughly washed it with water,
one should dry the triple-stranded collection of threads in the sun; then,
having dyed them with turmeric and with insect-derived and elemental pigments.
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion the ornament for Hari using equal threads—
either one thousand and eight, or half that number, or even a quarter— with knots joined as desired from the neck down to the feet.
O beloved of the vital breath, the *pavitra* is to be known as a garland of forest flowers (34).
Its knots, O fair-faced one, resemble the *bījapūra*, the mango, the *āmalaka*, and the conch shell; they are like pearls and like the *badarī* fruit (35).
A sacred thread (*pavitra*) endowed with five colors and provided with five staffs (*yaṣṭi*) should be known as the most excellent;
one provided with three staffs is declared to be middling, while that with a single staff is inferior.
According to his means, the best of teachers should fashion one [mark] among these three:

the *vanamālā* (forest garland) is said to extend to the knees, the *kaustubha* to the navel, and the *śrīvatsa* to the region of the chest; that which is called the *kirīṭa* (crown) is situated on the head.
The purifier for the goddesses, Śrī and the others, is known as Padma;
the purifier for the other gods is said to be Sudarśana.
The purifier for the door-arches and the water-pots is known as Śaṅkha.
The measurement for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) shall be according to the [standard] pit-measure; that same measure applies to the altars (vedīs).
For the celestial chariots (vimānas), pedestals, and vehicles, the purificatory rite (pavitraka) is of their respective dimensions;
the same applies to the vessels for light and incense, as well as to the fans and parasols.
The measurement for the chowrie, the bell, the sandals, and the flagstaff should be the same; in this manner, one should have these made for others as well.
For the teachers, the ascetics, and the twice-born, [the measurements] should possess the proper characteristics.
For others, the *pavitra* should reach as far as the navel; for humans, it should be only as high as the breast. This *pavitra* is designated as a "wheel" (*cakra*).
Thus the teacher, or even a craftsman, should fashion the *pavitra*.
Immediately thereafter, one should have it performed according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures;
one should prepare a sacrificial hall provided with doors and archways,
equipped with either four fire-pits or a single fire-pit.
Shining with sacrificial altars and the like, adorned with plantain pillars,
and beautified on all sides by canopies of *darbha* grass garlands and other ornaments—
such is the pavilion endowed with these characteristics that the best of preceptors [should construct]. (42.46–42.47)
Having sprinkled it with water from the Puṇyāha ceremony and then indeed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and having drenched it with scented water, one should fumigate it in every direction.
Having adorned it with lime powder, one should scatter white mustard seeds upon the ground.
On the ninth day, or even on the seventh or the fifth,
having determined the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) of Viṣṇu, one should perform the festival of atonement (*prāyaścitta*).
On the day before the commencement of the festival, the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipa*), [should proceed].
As an auxiliary rite for the sacrifice to the Blessed One, one should bathe preceded by shaving;
one should wear clean garments, sectarian marks (puṇḍra), and sacred threads.
"Beginning tomorrow, I shall perform the Pāvitri worship of Hari."
"You all must also come, devoted to the five times. Having thus entreated them and received their permission,
the Guru, accompanied by the commander of the army, should proceed to the temple of the Blessed One.

Having placed a tray of betel leaves, areca nuts, and other offerings in the presence of the deity, and having worshipped it with water for the guest (arghya) and other articles, one should offer the fruits and other items.
Having prostrated before the Lord, the preceptor stands with palms joined in reverence.
O Supreme Person, whose nature consists of the Vedas beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and who possesses the six divine qualities!
O All-pervading Lord, that which you have described as the pacification of the omission of ritual acts—
the rite known as the *pavitrāropaṇa*— is now being performed by me today.
"O Lord of Gods, O Wielder of the Mace, grant permission to the Lord of the Army.
Having thus petitioned Hari and having received his permission,
he then worshipped the Lord of Sūtravatī according to the prescribed rites.
Taking up a bundle of *darbha* grass, the Guru should pray to the Lord of the Army:

"O Lord of the Army, whose two feet are served by those with elephant faces and others; you have indeed been commanded by the God for the sake of accomplishing the purification and the *aṅkura* ritual. (42.58–59)
"Come with me and the Vaiṣṇavas to collect the clay.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, he should hold darbha grass in his hand.
Then, at the time of evening, he should perform the collection of the clay.
Then, at night, one should worship the *pālikā* vessels and so forth according to the prescribed rite.
Among them, some are suitable for [casting] images, others are for the fire-altar (*āgneya*), others are suitable for wheels, and likewise there are those for human [statues]. (42.61–42.62)
O lotus-eyed one, he should place [the offerings] individually in separate vessels;
then, he should have the attendants take those vessels in their hands.
This should be done amidst the chanting of the Vedas, the sounding of musical instruments, and the waving of yak-tail fans and other such items.
Having circumambulated the sacred abode, one should consecrate the purifiers (pavitra),
either in front of the deity or in the fire-chamber,
upon a mound of rice grains, husked rice, and sesame seeds.
Having stacked the bowls one above the other and placed them upon this [stand],

and having filled the bowl with fragrant substances such as yellow pigment (rocanā), aloe-wood (agaru), musk (kastūrī), and saffron (kuṅkuma), one should invoke the Goddess Śrī into it and worship her.
Having taken fragrant substances, one should employ them in the purificatory rites. Covering the beautiful water-pot with new cloths,
one should invoke [the deity] into it, worship it, and by means of that, effect protection.
There, together with the practitioners, he should pass the night in vigil;
at dawn, having performed his ablutions and observances, the preceptor, with a serene mind,
enters the temple of the Blessed One and first performs the daily worship.
Then, having invoked [the deity] from the root-mantra into the ritual image (karmabimba), one should perform the consecration.
One should adorn the deity with new garments and other ornaments.
Then, having entered the sacrificial hall, the preceptor (deśika) shall remove the coverings.
Taking up the purificatory vessels together with Vaiṣṇava ascetics,
and having circumambulated the temple, he should place them in the presence of the deity.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the Puṇyāha rite, it becomes pure through drying and other such means.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the best of gurus [praised] the Lord, the Root:
"O Acyuta, you are eternally satisfied by enjoyments consisting of your own bliss.
O All-pervading One, [this is for] you who have descended for the welfare of the world in the form of an image."
"O Teacher of the World, for the sake of completing the year-long rites of service,
I now perform this worship preceded by the binding of the protective thread.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, accept it out of a desire for the welfare of the world."
Having thus informed the Lord of Devas, one should sequentially bind the protective thread with a subtle *pavitra* upon the primary image and the others. Then,
taking the head-*pavitra* and placing it in another vessel—
There, having meditated upon and worshipped according to the prescribed rite the Lord of Yoga-postures, [he prays:
"O Viṣṇu, Sovereign of the Crown, Vāsudeva, O Ocean of Compassion!
Abide here in this head-ornament together with your retinue."
Thus, having invoked [me] from the root-mantra into the Siddha-lingas and others that are divine,
as well as into the Sālagrāma stone, which is divine and self-manifested— my beloved— I abide eternally within these; therefore, they are the most excellent on earth.
In the rites for the Siddhas and others, during the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and also during the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa),
the most excellent of teachers should perform worship after invoking them from those very [deities].
