Therefore, having invoked them and displayed the appropriate mudrās, one should worship with the arghya and other offerings.
In this manner, one should perform the worship of all the purifiers according to the prescribed rite.
One should pray to the Śrīvatsa and other marks upon the purifiers in their proper order:
"Obeisance to Lakṣmī, who is established in the Śrīvatsa and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns."

O Sun, presiding over the Kaustubha gem, establish your presence in this purifier that adorns the chest of Hari; it has been fashioned by me as a sacred thread reaching to the belly of the Enemy of Mura. (42.84)
O Moon, you who are like a pearl,
having attained your presence in this pure object known as a necklace, bring about the pleasure of the Blessed One.
O Tulasī, you who are dear to the Blessed One and beautify his entire body— [42.85–86]

"O beloved of Hari, reside at your ease within the sacred thread of the forest garland; O Ramā, dwell in the midst of the lotus among the sacred threads of Śrī and the others. Grant your presence for the welfare of the worlds."
O Sudarśana, you who possess a thousand spokes, always maintain your presence even in the ornaments of the gods who attend upon your celestial chariot;
O beloved of Hari, remain likewise in the door-arches, the water-pots, and all sacred objects.
"O Pāñcajanya, you of great sound, be present now;
O Vajrin, take up your residence among the sanctifiers of men.
In this manner, one should worship each respective deity upon its corresponding sacred object.
Then, holding a handful of flowers, he should pray to the imperishable Hari:
"O Lord of the World, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess in my services performed throughout the year, I adorn your limbs with these purifiers."
"O Lord of Ramā, accept today this worship being performed by me;
O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, accept it along with Śrī and the other goddesses for the sake of purification.
Having thus prayed to the God with the *gāyatrī* mantra preceded by Viṣṇu, [he continued].
One should wear the purifiers (pavitra) starting from the head down to the feet.
Likewise, the Guru should place the purifiers upon the images of the deities and others,
and similarly for the goddesses such as Śrī, while reciting their respective mantras.
O lady of pure smiles, one should adorn all their limbs with purifying substances,
and one should encircle the inner sanctum with threads of turmeric.
[One should likewise decorate] everything from the base of the womb up to the sacrificial altar, situated within the door-surroundings.
Thereafter, one should adorn the clay images with purificatory items;
following that, one should decorate the water-pot, the mandala, the sacrificial pit, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial hall.
Likewise, one should ornament all the vessels for worship and the vehicles.
[Having first established the fire, one should perform the worship of the door and so forth.
Then, having performed the worship of the water-jar (kumbha), the Guru should worship the lotus of the wheel (cakrābja).
Afterwards, one should worship the deity in the fire, and immediately thereafter, the image (bimba).
Listen to this number of offerings for the God in four locations:
either one thousand one hundred, or six hundred and seventy,
or else one should perform three hundred and sixty.
From the day of the ritual bath (avabhṛtha) until the final day of the festival,
the Guru should divide the aforementioned worship equally over those days and perform it for the sake of attaining greater presence (sāṃnidhya).
One should worship Hari in the pitcher and the mandala in the morning and at midday.
At night, there should be worship in the fires; this is the rule provided there is the means for it.
Or, one may perform [the worship] with only the image, using three hundred and sixty [offerings].
For others, the placement of the pitcher, the wheel, the lotus, and the fire should be performed day by day;
one should perform worship at these two times: at midnight and at midday.
Having reached the sacrificial hall, one should perform the installation of the pitcher.
One should prepare the yoga-pīṭhikā upon the great kumbha and the upakumbhas.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the Puṇyāha vessel, one should worship the door and the archway (toraṇa).
Having invoked the Śakti from the root-image (mūlabera) into the great kumbha, one should worship her.
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the pitchers located in the directions starting with the east;
in the corners starting with the southeast, Puruṣa and the others are to be worshipped.
And Sudarśana is to be worshipped in the water-pot (karaka) at the hand of the primary image (mūlabera).
Having invoked and worshipped [the deities] in the twelve-petaled lotus of the wheel-maṇḍala,
one should invoke and worship Keśava and the others on the petals;
and in the square and other fire-pits (kuṇḍas), one should sacrifice to Vāsudeva and the others.
Having performed the daily worship every day according to the rules,
and while the Vedas and Vaiṣṇava hymns are being recited, the best of teachers,
having duly made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), should perform the sacrifice to the Lord.
When evening had arrived,

having placed the image of the sacrifice upon a vehicle together with the discus-marked [Viṣṇu], he established the Lord of Sacrifice upon a pedestal near the lotus-disc, by the side of the fire-sanctuary.

Having brought Hari onto the auspicious throne, the initiated officiating priests (ṛtvij) should then worship him, situated within the fire of the pitcher-maṇḍala, according to the scriptures. The most excellent Guru should worship the ritual image (karmārcā) and the sacrificial icon (makhabimba).
At the time of worship, those learned in the Vedas and likewise those known as Drāviḍas should recite the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas in order, starting from the east.
Then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation, he should cause it to be distributed to the devotees in due sequence.
Then, having placed the ritual image upon a vehicle with great festivity,
and having circumambulated the temple, one should display the jar-lamp.
Having brought it into the inner sanctum, one should establish the Lord upon a seat.
Until the worship by means of mental resolve (saṃkalpa-pūjā) is completed, one should not remove the garments, ornaments,
or even the sacred threads (pavitra) from the deity;
one should not take down the primary image (mūlabimba), nor should one dismiss the protective cord (kautuka).
On the day of completion, in the morning, having placed the Lord Hari upon a vehicle along with the ritual bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha), and having circumambulated the streets,
one should bring him to the riverbank and perform the purificatory concluding bath (avabhṛtha).
Then, having summoned the deity and established him upon a seat in the sacrificial hall,
one should place the *pālikā* on a foot-stool and join the deities there;
one should worship the deity with sprouts upon a lotus-seat while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*.
Having brought [the image] to the bathing pavilion, one should bathe the ritual image with twenty-five jars according to the rite, using the water from the sacred sites (*tīrtha*). Then,
having released the pitchers situated at the door and the archway in their proper order, [one should proceed].
One should join that which resides in the mandala and that which resides in the fire into the great pitcher (mahākumbha).
The preceptor should lead the great pitcher inside along with the image (bimba),
and having placed it in front of the primary image (mūlabera), he should stand facing it.
One should unite the Śakti residing in the Bimba-kumbha with the primary image (mūlārcā).
Then, one should sprinkle the Lord with the water from the great kumbha while reciting the Nṛsūkta. After offering the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis), one should then pray to Hari.
"O you who are consecrated to the rescue of those ignorant in the ocean of saṃsāra!
Accept this worship performed by me for the sake of completing the year-long service; do so out of a desire for the welfare of your devotee."
I am not independent; I perform nothing that is beneficial except as it is ordained.
Rather, impelled by you, I do everything myself like a servant.
Therefore, whatever has been done through the omission of duties or otherwise must be forgiven in its entirety.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, he should then offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
The best of preceptors should then release the protective thread (rakṣābandha) for everyone and cause all the sacred threads (pavitra) to be given to the devotees, O Rame.
The best of preceptors should perform the night worship according to the scriptures.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Pavitraka Festival," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Forty-three: Lakṣmī—
O dweller in the heart-lotus of yogis, you who are perfected through the six qualities!

Devotees worship you, the all-pervading Lord in the form of an image, within the dwellings of cities and other places; yet forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) only rarely offer salutations. O Hari, if you truly desire to see them, let the proper time for that be told.
The Blessed One said: "O Kamalā, I tell you that it is now the time for my worship in my abode;
it is indeed the day of Jupiter in the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya."
On the ninth day, intending to go on a hunting expedition on the tenth day,
he should take his horse for riding along with the sounds of musical instruments and other such things,
and taking his weapons as well, he should go to a river or a lake.
Having cleansed the vehicle and adorned it with cloths and other ornaments,
and having circumambulated the temple, he should lead it to the abode of the Lotus-born One;
on the tenth day, having first performed the daily worship of the God of gods.
The supreme guru should pray to the Lord for the sake of the festival:
"O You whose lotus feet are worshipped by yogis, O You who are consecrated to the protection of devotees!
O Teacher of the World, I desire to undertake a pilgrimage as a hunt for You."
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, requested by me, please be present within this image known as karma.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Lakṣmī, one should meditate upon Him within the ritual image (karmārcā).
Then, having performed the binding of protection according to the rules, one should install Hari.
Having worshipped [the Lord] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) as the final offering.
Then, having mounted the horse upon the Lord of Gods and adorned him with ornaments—
decorated with all garments and garlands suitable for the hunt— [one should proceed].
Accompanied by devoted Bhāgavatas equipped with the requisites for the journey, and having led [the image] into the great forest with his servants clad in armor and bearing weapons,
he offered it there to those forest-dwellers who were constantly intent on meditation.
The preceptor should offer other roots, tubers, and fruits to the Lord;
having caused a hunt to be conducted near a fire-tree,
he should lead [the Lord] to a beautiful water-shed and establish the Lord of the World there.
Having sprinkled the base of the Vahni tree with water from the *puṇyāha* rite,
and having placed the weapons there, the preceptor should then worship them with their respective mantras;
with the root mantra, he should take a leaf of the *śamī* tree.
One should place that [weapon] upon the head of the deity for the sake of victory over all beings;
then, having grasped the arrows and the bow, one should employ them in the four directions, on the ground, and above,
using the Astra-mantra and also the Ṛk verse beginning with "dhanvanā gāḥ."
Then one should worship the God of gods with various offerings:
roots, tubers, fruits, and the like, presented with devotion by forest-dwellers, ascetics, and others, as well as various garlands of flowers. (43.17–43.18)
Having offered it to the God of gods, he should present betel-leaf;
and when evening has arrived, having yoked the horse once again,
[he should proceed] with various lamps, musical instruments, and the recitation of the Vedas.
Having caused [the image] to perform circumambulations through all the streets, O fair-faced one,
and having brought it to the end of its residence, one should display the jar-lamp.
For the sake of pacifying the exhaustion of the deity, one should bathe it with nine jars.
Having fixed the *śakti* at the base, one should then pray to the imperishable Hari:
"O Lord, whatever has been performed by me today for your festival on the tenth day—
if there be anything deficient or excessive in that worship of your devotee, may it be forgiven."
Having thus made this request to the Lord of Gods, one should then worship Him according to the prescribed rites.
O Goddess, I shall now describe another festival that bestows nourishment,
grants heaven to all, and provides liberation to the Vaiṣṇavas.
"O Goddess, in former times there was a Dānava named Naraka, the son of the Earth.
These subjects were previously tormented by him, and they came to me for refuge. Thereupon, O Goddess, I slew Naraka, the lord of the Dānavas."
Having attained a divine body and having praised me, he spoke these words:
"O Puṇyaśloka, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O first-born of the Lotus-seated One!
I entreat you, bowing before you, O lover of devotees, O doer of good."
"I am satisfied that I have been slain by you, O Dānava, for this is very difficult to attain.
By your grace, I shall dwell in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
However, let all the subjects who were previously oppressed now rejoice."
Indeed, they should celebrate a festival in the temples and in their homes under the name of the Man.
They should perform anointing, bathing, and giving of gifts, as well as wearing new garments;
and for the sake of the deity, they should offer the four kinds of food, such as sweets, rice with molasses, and so forth.
Having thus made this earnest request, "Let them announce [it]," he departed for heaven.
Then, O one born from the water, he bestowed his blessing upon both gods and men on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja, at the rising of the moon.
The preceptor should bathe the deity with the remaining oil;
he should first apply it to his own head, and thereafter apply it to the devotees.
This oil, having touched the limbs of the Lord and being consecrated by mantras, [is to be used].
They should carry it on their heads and not smear it upon their bodies;
he who, out of delusion, smears it on his limbs shall go to the Raurava hell.
Then the Guru, having bathed according to the previously mentioned method, [should enter] the presence of the Deity.
Having entered and performed the daily worship up to the conclusion of the fire-offering (homa),
[he prayed: "O Narakan-taka, O Lord of the Śārṅga-bow, for the sake of your festival on the fourteenth day,
O Lord of Ramā, please be present out of compassion within this ritual image."

Having thus made this request and invoked the Śakti from the root [mantra], the supreme Guru, having placed the Lord of Gods upon the vehicle, should lead him to the assembly pavilion. Having worshipped him with incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as the fourfold offerings beginning with jaggery-rice (guḍānna), [he should proceed].
One should offer edible foods and the like, as well as betel for refreshing the mouth.
One should clothe the imperishable Hari in unwashed garments;
O lotus-born one, listen as I describe the procedure for that.
In front of the deity, one should prepare a pedestal of grain; there,
golden pairs of garments, as well as others made of silk,
[should be placed] upon a golden vessel adorned with a coconut fruit and betel leaf.
Having placed [the image] upon a pedestal of grain and sprinkled it with water from the *puṇyāha* rite,
one should then invoke the Moon into those garments and worship him;
or [one may worship him] on an elephant or another excellent vehicle, or upon the head of an attendant.

Having placed [the items] together with the parasol, musical instruments, and so forth, the supreme preceptor should circumambulate the temple and, having entered the inner sanctum (garbha-maṇḍira), should install [the deity] in due order upon the primary image (mūlārcā) and the two divine [images]. 43.43-43.44ab.

One should clothe the images, such as the *karmabimba* and others, in new garments. Then, having offered various kinds of food, both solid and soft, one should cause them to be distributed among the devotees.
Having performed this, one should lead the Lord of Gods into the inner sanctum (*garbhamandira*).
One should employ the power residing in the ritual image within the primary icon.
O Viṣṇu, this festival on the fourteenth day has indeed been performed by me with devotion. Whatever has been omitted here, whether through knowledge or ignorance, [may it be forgiven].
"O Mādhava, you ought to forgive all that, for he is my devotee.
Having thus made this request, one should complete the remainder of the midday worship.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Festival of Naraka-Caturdaśī," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Forty-four.
Formerly, a devotee of mine named Mahābali, the best of the Dānavas, having conquered all the gods, became the sovereign of the three worlds. 44.1
Indeed, being unable to conquer him, the gods sought refuge with me;
for the sake of protecting those who had come for shelter, even without slaying the lord of the asuras,
I shall surely defeat that asura, the thorn of the gods, through a stratagem.
Having thus resolved in my mind, I assumed the form of a dwarf.
While he was performing a sacrifice dedicated solely to me, I approached the sacrificial enclosure;
having gone there, I asked for three steps of ground for the sake of asceticism.
Then, O beloved, he gave me the earth by means of an invisible form;
having taken hold of the earth with one foot and the sky with the other,
I asked Bali again about his merit and the intermediate space.
"But where will you place the third step, O observer of noble vows?
Having heard these words of mine, Bali spoke joyfully:
"To make my word true, place your foot upon my head."
"For the sake of favoring my devotee, having done so and led him to Rasātala,
I shall cause that Asura to exercise the burden of sovereignty there.
While he was thus entreating me at that time, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, [spoke].
"O Lord, I have provided satisfaction for you in the form of fire.
However, I did not offer pleasure [to you], for it became an obstacle to the continuity of the sacrifice.
Therefore, on this day, in dwellings and houses upon the earth—"
Having offered oblations into the fire, they should light lamps with that very fire;
from that time forward, O one born of the ocean, people on earth have performed this according to my command. I shall now describe the festival for the satisfaction of the fire; listen.
If, at sunrise, the fourteenth day is conjoined with a lunar digit (kalā) and the full moon is unpenetrated;
and when the fourteenth day is with Bharaṇī and the full moon is with Kṛttikā— if these two should be thus penetrated, one must not perform the festival of Viṣṇu.
When those two— the lunar mansion and the lunar day— are defiled by a transit or an eclipse,
one should perform the rite on a pure day, having abandoned both the mansion and the lunar day.
If the full moon day alone is defiled by an eclipse, [one should act accordingly].
Having avoided eight *nāḍikās* both before and after [midday],
one should then perform the auspicious festival of the lamp-offering for the satisfaction of the fire.
The preceptor, having risen in the morning and completed the daily worship, [should proceed].
Beginning from the interior of the palace up to the outermost circle of attendants,
one should discard the old clay lamp-bowls all around.
Furthermore, one should clean the vessels made of gold and other materials with sugar and similar substances.
First, one should cleanse the temple and other structures with water in the center;
then, having adorned them with lime powder, one should scatter unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as canopies, arches, plantain pillars, and betel-nut trees.
O Lotus-born One, one should adorn [the shrine] with coconut fruits and flagstaffs;
one should incense everything everywhere with the fragrances of sandalwood, agallochum, and musk.
Then, after thoroughly washing the vessels for the new lamps, [one should proceed].
In those vessels made of gold and other materials,
one should place wicks fashioned from threads or made from pieces of new cloth;
and within them, O Rāma, one should fill them with clarified butter or sesame oil.
Having prepared a pedestal with cow dung on the walls of the enclosure, in the pavilion, and at the gate-towers, one should place the lamp vessels.
In front of the primary image, one should arrange a pedestal of grain.

Then, the preceptor should place a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, brass, or even clay— either square or round— in the center of that [space]. He should then arrange eight [vessels] all around that central vessel.
One should fill the central vessel with an āḍhaka of cow’s ghee,
and likewise fill the eight surrounding vessels with cow’s ghee as appropriate.
In the central vessel, one should place a wick facing upwards in the middle.
One should arrange the vessels in this very same manner for others as well.
All the vessels should be sprinkled with meritorious water.
Then, when the afternoon has arrived, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), [should proceed].
Having reached the root temple, one should pray to the Supreme Acyuta:
"O Lord of Great Renown, O Great Yogin whose form is served by the virtuous,
O Lord of the Earth, be present within this image for the sake of the Festival of Lights."
Having thus prayed and performed worship, the Guru should bind the protective thread (kautuka).
Then, he himself should bind the protective thread on his own right hand.
If there is a single image, he should bathe it; however, if there are many images, he should bathe the principal one (mūla).
Having consecrated the image of the deity with the nine jars, one should worship it;
O lotus-eyed one, one should worship [the deity] with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *prāpaṇa*.
Then, having invoked the deity into the vessel at the stage of invocation, the preceptor—
The attendants should likewise lead the Lord and the lamp-vessels [to the fire-pit].
Then, having reached the perpetual fire-pit, one should kindle the fire;
having invoked Śrīśa, who resides within the vessel, one should worship Him in the fire, O Rame.
One should again offer oblations of cakes mixed with jaggery, parched grain, and other such items.
When the time of evening has arrived, the lighting of lamps is prescribed.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god as having emerged from the lotus-face of Viṣṇu.
Having lit lamps and placed them before the eyes upon the heads of the messengers,
and having again directed Vāsudeva, who had been invoked, toward the vessel,
one should perform a circumambulation of the sacred abode accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments.
Having entered the inner sanctum, one should join with the Lord at his root;
and having placed the lamp-vessels upon a pedestal of grain in front,
[one should offer] the Arghya and other gifts to the God of gods, as well as cakes and sacrificial offerings.
Likewise, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like, parched grain (lāja), and betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
Having worshipped the lamps with the fire-mantra (vahnimantra) and the weapon-mantra (astramantra), the preceptor (deśika) should then himself offer cakes (apūpa) and other edible foods.
Then, having taken up a lamp-vessel with the Netra-mantra or a Vedic verse,
and having shown the lamp to Hari with the words "May you shine forth," the Guru himself should place lamps in the hands of the attendants.
And they were at all the gates, in the pavilions and enclosures,
at all the city portals, on the banks of the lotus ponds,
likewise in the temple of Śrī, in the garden, and in the temples of the devotees' images.
The best of the twice-born should light lamps with wicks already placed within them;
then, having mounted Hari upon a vehicle accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi,
they should proceed amidst the chanting of the Vedas, the sounding of musical instruments, and a hundred lamps.
One should bring [the image] outside through the gate together with the requisites for the procession.
In front of the gate, there should be a pillar made of khadira or sandalwood, one hundred tālas high, or half of that, or half of that again. || 44.45–46 ||
One should procure a straight pillar made of *sāla*, *tāla*, or coconut wood;

one should divide the pillar into four parts and place one part in the excavated ground, making it firm. O Lotus-born One, having placed [the base], one should fashion a pedestal upon the top of the pillar.
One should fashion it either circular or square,
with a width of one cubit, O beloved, using cloths sprinkled with clarified butter, or new cloths treated with oil,
or with bundles of palm leaves, or according to one's means.
The wise one, having sprinkled the pillar with water from the *puṇyāha* rite,
should first place a lamp facing the temple in the center of the pedestal.
Then, taking shallow bowls (*śarāva*), he should place them in its eastern and other directions.

Having taken wicks from them, one should light them in their respective directions for the sake of pacifying the fire and for the increase of the king’s kingdom. One should then cut the base of the pillar and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord.
One should gratify with wealth the servants appointed to their respective tasks;
then, having circumambulated the temple and caused the deity to enter within,
one should display the lamp in the water-pot and apply the Śakti at the base.
Having cooked fresh *āḍhaka* rice mixed with sugar and cow’s ghee along with milk, and having offered it to the God, he should then pray:
"Previously, a festival was performed by me at the request of Bali. (44.54–55)
"O Treasure of Compassion, please forgive this lapse committed through ignorance.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should worship at the edge of the bed.
Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Festival of the Fire-Lamp" in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
Chapter Forty-three.
Chapter Forty-five: I shall describe the ritual for the swing festival (ḍolotsava); listen, O Paṅkajamālinī!
The period beginning with the month of Tulā and ending with the month of Kumbha is declared to be the primary time.
O Rame, one should perform [the rite] for seven days, five days, or three days,
either during the bright fortnight or during the three days beginning with the tenth day of the dark fortnight.
On the seventh lunar day, or on the full moon, or under the asterism of Mārgaśīrṣa, or Śravaṇa, or Rohiṇī, or Citrā, or Phalgunī, or Puṣya;
or even on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti)— having determined this, O Rāma, let us perform the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
One should construct a pavilion in the first and subsequent enclosures;
it should be provided with thirty-two pillars, or half that number. One may fashion the pavilion either out of stone or out of wood.
One should beautifully decorate the pavilion with pearl necklaces, mirrors, plantain pillars, flower garlands, coconut fruits, and the like;
with wreaths of areca nut clusters, and with archways made of mango leaves and other materials.
It was adorned with various beautiful canopies, banners, and variegated umbrellas;
the ground within the pavilion should be smeared with cow-dung water and lamps filled with ghee and resplendent with golden handles.
One should purify it with waters flowing from the snowy mountains and with scented waters;
having adorned it with powders of various colors, with lime, with flowers, and even with unbroken grains of rice, one should fashion a most beautiful [image] in its center.
O Rame, [build for me] a pavilion made of gold, silver, copper, bronze, or wood,
provided with four pillars, resembling a celestial chariot,
equipped with golden chains, and resplendent with various jewels.
Having thus prepared a swing that is either square or rectangular, then on the following day,
the lotus-born one, having performed the ritual observances such as bathing, entered the temple.
Having performed the daily worship and other rites, one should fetch earth in the evening.
One should offer the sprouts at night according to the very path taught by the Teacher.
Then, in the morning, the practitioners, having bathed and undergone the shaving of the head, [should proceed].
All of them, wearing clean garments and having performed the five-fold prostration (pañcāṅga-bhūṣaṇa),
entered the temple of the Blessed One; and having completed the daily worship,
they petitioned the Blessed One for the success of the swing festival (ḍolotsava).
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa, for the sake of the increase of the king and the kingdom,
O Lord of the World, be present within this image for the purpose of the swing festival.
Having thus made this request and having invoked [the deity], one should worship the imperishable God.
The Guru should perform the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) for the fixed image, the portable image, and so forth;
thereafter, he should perform the consecration of the swing (ḍolā-pratiṣṭhā) according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
He should sprinkle the swing with "auspicious-day" waters (puṇyāha-salila), preceded by the recitation of mantras.
In the center of the swing, one should worship Ādiśeṣa; and in the four feet, in due order, one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
Furthermore, one should worship the array beginning with Satya and ending with Garuḍa upon the pillars of the swing, in their respective order.
Having invoked Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya,
the preceptor should worship Hari in his Virāṭ form upon the pillar and in the celestial chariot (vimāna).
He should worship the four Vedas in the chains and Sāvitrī on the banner.
One should worship the Gāyatrī on the banners and the Vyāhṛtis under the parasol. Having invoked Soma in the canopy, one should likewise worship the vowels (svaras) in the arches;
or else, one may worship Ananta or Garuḍa upon all of them.

Having placed the Great Jar (mahākumbha) in the grain-jar (dhānyakumbha), as well as the eight subsidiary jars (upakumbha), I delight in the central jar, Virāja, surrounding it. Having invoked the deities beginning with the feet, or Indra and the others, in their proper order.
Having invoked and worshipped the deities of the swing individually within the water-pots (kumbhas),
O Rame, one should invoke them into the fire and offer one hundred and eight oblations;
or twenty-eight, or eight, oblations of sesame, clarified butter, and sacrificial wood.
Having invoked Vāsudeva in the pericarp of the lotus on the disc,
and likewise Keśava and the others upon the petals, and having worshipped them immediately thereafter,
one should worship the swing as well and offer milk-rice (pāyasānna).
One should offer oblations to Indra and others, as well as to Kumuda and others, in the eastern and other directions respectively.
When the time of evening has arrived, having placed Hari upon an auspicious throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi, one should adorn him with garlands and other ornaments.
Having led the deity clockwise around the temple to the accompaniment of all musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas,
one should present the lamp within the vessel to the God.
One should then place the God upon the swing at an auspicious hour and a favorable moment.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present the sacrificial food (*haviḥ-anna*).
Having performed worship at the four locations, one should cast the *bali* offering consisting of white water-lilies (*kumuda*) and so forth.
After presenting the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites, one should then perform the *nīrājana* ceremony.
One should worship the Lord there with ornaments, seats, and enjoyments; then,
having taken hold of the swing and the ropes, the initiated ones and those guardians of the forms (mūrtipās),
who have mastered the Vedas, should sway it very slowly at that time.
They should satisfy the Lord of the World with the Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
and all those born of the lineage of the Blessed One should [offer] water mixed with camphor and musk for the sake of quelling fatigue, using the Mahopaniṣad and other scriptures. (45.34–35)
Then, offering [the offerings] at intervals, one should cleanse the face with a cloth;
one should also offer betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.
Then, there should be songs by courtesans, blended with the sounds of lutes and flutes.
And with various dances, they should also gratify the Supreme God.
Afterwards, the most excellent Guru should cause food and other offerings to be given to the devotees;
having led the Deity into the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), he should unite the Śakti with the Mūla-mantra.
And one should propitiate [the deity] at the end of the bed until the final ablution (avabhṛtha) in this manner;
one should always perform a festival for the Lotus-born (Aja) at the time of evening.
Beginning from the day of the festival, morning and evening, according to the rule—
One should perform worship at the four locations and cause the offering of oblations (bali) to be made.
One should also perform the worship of the sprouts and the worship of the door and so forth.
The preceptor should perform the rites, beginning with the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), according to the scriptures.
Having offered the primary oblation, one should recite this verse:
"O Lord of the World, this swing festival has been performed by me for your pleasure. Whatever transgression may have occurred therein, O Lord of the Universe," [one should confess].
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, all this [transgression] of yours, a servant, must be forgiven.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should perform the daily worship.
Whoever performs this festival for the Lord of the World, O Lotus-born One, [attains great merit].
Released from the fetters of *saṃsāra*, having attained liberation, he rejoices.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Swing Festival" (*Ḍolotsava*), in the glorious *Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā*.
The Forty-sixth Chapter.
Furthermore, O Goddess, I shall describe the worship during the month of Dhanus, which bestows prosperity, long life, nourishment, and liberation, O Rame. 46.1
O Goddess, from the time the sun is situated in Sagittarius until its entry into Capricorn,
one should worship the Blessed Janārdana at dawn during those days according to the rules, and perform the ritual sprinkling for the sake of his bath.
Having brought the seat of ornaments, one should please the imperishable Hari with hymns accompanied by devotional verses, as well as other praises, dances, and songs;
[one should offer] mung-bean rice with ghee, milk, and spices such as black pepper.

Every day at dawn, one should offer to the Lord food accompanied by side-dishes, sugar, and plantain fruit; it should be endowed with fragrant juices and combined with items to be licked, sucked, and so forth. || 46.5 ||
The fruit of twelve years of worship is obtained in a single day.
(46.6) One should undertake the festival of the glorious study during Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa;
one should commence it on the first day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa. (46.7)
Then, on the eleventh day, one should begin again starting from the tenth;
this shall last for ten days until the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
O Kamalā, such is the procedure for that festival which bestows liberation upon devotees.
Whether it be in the first enclosure, or even in the second enclosure,
or in the third enclosure, or wherever else it might be,
it should be imagined as being in the east, with a mountain rising up to the clouds.
It was beautifully adorned with coconuts, various fruits such as betel nuts,
canopies, rows of lamps, and images;
it was a place fit for the gods, gandharvas, and daityas to move about in comfort.
One should thus construct an excellent pavilion endowed with these characteristics.
Śrī said: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, served by Brahmā, Rudra, and the others!"
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, which is preeminent, worship is performed at the time of dawn. Why is offerings such as mung-bean rice presented at that time?
Why is the festival a bestower of liberation? And why is the pavilion so lofty?
"I wish to hear this in detail, O Blessed One, you who are compassionate toward your devotees. The Blessed Lord said:
"O beloved, you have forgotten the events of the past; I shall cause them to be remembered by you."

O Goddess, in the past, at the time of dissolution, I slept upon a banyan leaf and took delight there, assuming the form of a child; at that time, you were situated upon my chest. From the lotus of my navel, Brahmā was born through my volition.
As he recited from his mouths the four Vedas in accordance with the scriptures,
pride arose in the omniscient Creator of the world, and he did not remember me.
From my ears were born two Asuras who became thorns to the worlds.
They began to slay Brahmā, and he wept like an ordinary man;
then, seeing me lying upon the waters, the four-faced one offered praise.
Thereupon, having understood and seen them, I spoke to those two foremost of Dānavas.
"Choose a boon from me," they both said immediately.
"Choose a boon from me, O Lord of Gods; we shall grant you that which is difficult to obtain.
Having heard these words of theirs, I then spoke with a smile:
"You two Daityas have been slain by me; you shall return to your natural state.
Thus addressed, the two Asuras said to me: "For one month we shall fight with you, and having met our death at your hands, we shall attain our desired perfection. (46.22)
Having thus resolved, O slender-waisted one, I then engaged in hand-to-hand combat for one month with those two who were eager for battle;
having slain them, they attained divinity, bearing the discus and the lotus.

"O Enemy of the Daityas, O Lotus-eyed One, even after knowing Your true nature and having offered salutations with palms joined, we have attained Your own form; for us there shall be no rebirth again,
nor shall there ever be dwelling in Your world."
Thus entreated by them, I indeed caused those two Daityas, who were in my own form,
to pass through the northern gate at the rising of the moon on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Cāpa, and led them along that path.
In the auspicious Śrīvaikuṇṭha, situated above Satyaloka,
which is composed of pure sattva and eternally frequented by hosts of wise sages;
[therein], seated in the center of a jeweled pavilion and adorned with a gem-studded couch.
I see myself standing upon the couch of Śeṣa, adorned by the jewels on his hoods,
being praised by the wise with the Ṛgveda and other scriptures as their sole path,
and attended by my own forms bearing weapons such as the conch and the discus.
He was attended by Vinatā’s son with palms joined in reverence,
as well as by Viṣvaksena, other attendants such as Kumuda,
and Jayā and the others, who, upon seeing me, were filled with wonder in their innermost hearts.
Having beheld my supreme form, their bodies bristling with horripilation, those two best of asuras praised me with various hymns and said:
"O Supreme Soul, O Supreme Brahman, O Higher than the highest, O Lord of the universe! (46.32–33)
O Jñānānanda, embodiment of knowledge, whose form is all-knowing and inconceivable;
O eternal bliss, formless one, savior from the ocean of saṃsāra!
Those dwelling in worlds such as Satyaloka have never perceived your true nature.

People in this world, subject to the power of saṃsāra, do not know [this]. Through thousands of millions upon millions of births and through compassion, you two have reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra; we have gone to you for refuge.
"O large-eyed one, we two pray; make our prayer fruitful!
Since we have reached your abode, O Lord of Śrī, after having been separated from you, even Brahmā and the other gods possess no jewel-palace equal to yours. (46.37)
Having fashioned an image of you, one should perform the Ekādaśī festival.
Then, O Hari, those people who behold you, those who bow down to you, and those who enter by way of the northern gate— [they shall attain the goal]. 46.38–46.39

"Having reached this Vaikuṇṭha, may you two rejoice like the eternal sages. Hearing those words of theirs, I, who am subject to my devotees, then said: "Indeed, this festival is being performed by me for the sake of your satisfaction."

From that time forward, I indeed took delight in all the worlds; having thus established such a festival, especially on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), people enter into liberation. Therefore, it is called the Festival of Liberation (Mokṣotsava).
"O lotus-eyed one, I shall tell you the cause for the prosperity of this water-distribution hall:
it was indeed first requested by the two Daityas;
moreover, they both attained liberation from it, and therefore we serve it."
Having thus resolved, the Daityas and Rākṣasas, desiring liberation,
gathered together day after day and bowed down to that most exalted one.
For their easy access, a water-shed (prapā) was constructed there, equally lofty.

The month of Mārgaśīrṣa is remembered as the morning time for the deities; indeed, this morning time is declared by the great ones to be characterized by *sattva*. Worship performed during that time of approach is considered to be of the nature of *sattva*.
They declare that food made of mung beans and food made of jaggery are of the nature of sattva.
At that time, one should satisfy Vāsudeva with sattvic food during the two previously mentioned festivals, according to their respective divisions of earlier and later.
O beloved, listen to the procedure for what must be performed in the morning and evening:
on the day before the commencement of the festival, the preceptor should offer the ritual germination (aṅkura).
Having performed the daily worship in the morning, he should pray to the Lord of Kamalā.
"O glorious one, wearer of yellow garments, whose neck is adorned by the Kaustubha gem!
46.50 Bring your presence into this image for the sake of sacrifice and sacred study.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods and having projected the power from the root-mantra, 46.51.
One should tie an auspicious thread around the base and so forth, as well as upon oneself;
then, having placed the Lord of Gods upon a vehicle and led him in circumambulation of the temple,
one should bring the Lord of Gods to the great pavilion upon a golden seat.
Then one should place the images of the devotees facing the deity.
Having worshipped the deity and offered foodstuffs and other items,
and having worshipped the images of the devotees, one should offer those same items to them.

The preceptor, having worshipped Vāsudeva according to the rules in the afternoon, should cause the four kinds of food, including edibles and the like, to be offered with a concentrated mind to the Vaiṣṇavas who recite the verses and to those who partake in the meal. (46.55)
One should offer betel-leaf together with mouth-perfume.
Having offered food and other items to the clay images of the devotees, O beloved of my life,
one should place the Lord of Gods upon the vehicle accompanied by dance, song, and other performances.
Having caused the Lord of Gods to enter within, one should join him at the root of the Śakti.

Having performed this for ten days, one should join the all-pervading Lord, who resides in the four locations, at the root; then, standing with palms joined in reverence, one should offer a prayer to the God.
"O Lord of the World, this festival of study was indeed performed by me for your pleasure. For that which was devoid of the scriptures due to delusion, please forgive me, O Treasure of Compassion.
Now, O you who were born from the Ocean of Milk, hear the procedure for the festival of liberation."
When the time of evening had arrived on the tenth day, he should pray to Hari,
who reclines upon the waters of the dissolution-ocean and is served by Madhu and Kaiṭabha:
"I shall begin to perform the festival requested by those two."
"Grant me permission, O Lord of Gods, O Ornament of the Abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission, the preceptor should perform all the rites, beginning with the collection of clay, according to the path of the scriptures.
"O Slayer of Daityas, O Lord of the World, having completed my daily worship at dawn on the eleventh day, I desire to perform the festival of liberation for you;
come to this body of action."
Having thus informed the Lord of Devas regarding the ritual procedure for the image, the preceptor,
having invoked [the deity] and worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings, should lead the protective cord (*pratisara*) into the image; then,
having placed the deity upon the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*), he should proceed with hymns of praise.
Having brought the northern door facing the panel,
the Guru should worship the Lord with water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings in order to pacify the deity's fatigue;
having praised the Lord with the Ṛgveda and other hymns, he should also worship the door-panel.
When the sound of all the Vedas and all musical instruments resounds outside the door,
and when he has been praised with verses and hymns by the wise,
the preceptor should open the door and lead Hari out by that path.
Then those who behold the God and pass through that gateway—
even if they be perpetrators of great sins— become partakers of liberation.
Then, having led the God to the great water-shed, [he places him] upon the lion-throne.
Having established them and honored them in due order with offerings such as water for the hands and feet,
one should bring each of the devotees' images before Hari,
and place fragrant garlands and *tulasī* upon the head of the devotee.
Having set down his sandals upon the ground, he should seat the devotees;
with the songs they sing, he who is compassionate toward his devotees should find satisfaction.
Then, having propitiated the deity, he should present a lamp made of flour.
One should offer various kinds of foods, both solid and soft, as well as diverse fruits (46.74).
Having offered betel-leaf, one should then perform the *nīrājana* rite for Hari.
Having brought Hari inside and established him in the root-mantra, one should pray to Hari (46.75).
"O you who are kind to your devotees, today I shall perform for you the festival of liberation.
O Hari, you have undergone great exertion; you ought to forgive it.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the preceptor should worship at the edge of the bed.

Beginning from the twelfth day, one should perform the rite in this manner during the evening. Having performed this for nine days, on the tenth day the preceptor, having brought the sacred site to the location, should perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) for Viṣṇu.
Having brought the deity to the pavilion, one should establish him upon the lion-throne;
as before, one should perform the rites for the images of the devotees, such as the drawing of boundaries and so forth.
Then, having projected the Śakti from the fire-mandala and the water-pot into the image—
Then, having led [the deity] into the inner sanctum, one should install the Śakti at the base.
Having determined the time of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), O Goddess, one should perform the great festival of Hari’s concluding bath (avabhṛtha) according to the prescribed rites.
From the first day of Mārgaśīrṣa for twenty days,
having performed the two previously mentioned festivals,
one should thereafter conduct the great festival beginning with the hoisting of the banner.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Festival of Liberation," in the venerable Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā;
[followed by] the forty-seventh chapter.

"O beloved, honored by the world, dwelling in the temple of a blooming lotus, today I have learned of your conduct in a former kalpa. O auspicious lady, I speak of this festival out of affection; it was indeed a quarrel between you."
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk is a very great island called Śvetadvīpa.
In its center is a mountain named Trikūṭa, frequented by gods and Gandharvas;
near it is a clear lake inhabited by large makaras.
The lake was fifty yojanas in extent and filled with fish and turtles;
it was frequented by royal swans, mallikākṣa birds, water-fowl, and kāraṇḍava ducks,
and was covered with thousand-petaled and hundred-petaled lotuses.
Filled with water, it was beautified by blue lotuses and white lilies;
that lake was surrounded on all sides by various kinds of trees, such as sandalwood, syandana, nīpa, sāla, tāla, and tamālaka.
And the wind always blows with coolness, fragrance, and gentleness;
such was the lake situated there, O Goddess, when it was afflicted by the summer season.
Then the leader of herds of intoxicated elephants and female elephants [arrived].
Afflicted by the heat, he entered that lake quickly to drink water.
Taking up cool water, he drank it with his lotus leaf;
at that moment, a crocodile seized his foot.
Therefore, being unable to release him, he proclaimed loudly in this manner:
"Salutation to that Great Splendor, the cause of the world, the root, upon whom this universe is supported and in whom it is dissolved. (47.10)
Thus they cried out; then the gods, headed by Druhiṇa, did not come.
Then, having mounted Garuḍa and disregarding you indeed, he approached with speed the vicinity of that crocodile of cruel deeds.
Having severed the head of the Naga king with my discus, I protected him;
the excellent crocodile was slain by me, and the elephant was also set free.
Released from their curse, they attained divinity and bowed down before me.
Having granted them residence in my own realm, I returned once more to Vaikuṇṭha.
At that time, I was indeed barred at the very gate by you;
O blessed lady, I spoke the reason, yet you did not listen to my words.

Then those two, having approached and saluted your feet, recounted the events concerning the lake; thereafter, you placed me upon the coils of the serpent as I desired. (47.16) Then I was laid down by you upon the body of the Naga.
"O lady of beautiful hips, that festival must especially be observed for my worship; O lotus-eyed one, I shall tell you its manner. Śrī said:

"O Lord who is kind to your devotees, you must indeed perform this festival as well. O Hari, wherever your devotees reside, they are unable to perform service; O Lord of the World, their entry into the temple is forbidden."

O Lord Keśava, in order to grant them a vision of You through both scripture and physical ailments, and for the sake of fulfilling the desires of the devotees situated in every street, You indeed mount the palanquin in the form of an image.
"Reveal yourself as bliss that destroys all sins;
liberate those bitten by the crocodiles of saṃsāra, like a lordly elephant.
The Blessed One said:
O Lakṣmī, O lady of virtuous vows, for the sake of your pleasure I shall likewise speak thus:
O lotus-born one, beginning from the month of Makara until the end of the month of Mīna,
one should celebrate the festival of love on days starting with Friday.
Before the break of dawn, having performed his daily obligatory rites and other duties,
he should then enter the temple and complete the internal daily worship,
[saying]: "O Lord, O Lotus-eyed One, you who are consecrated to the protection of your devotees!"
O Hari, O Mādhava, for the sake of your beloved Lakṣmī and out of affection for you both,
I wish to celebrate a festival of quarrel today.
For that purpose, O ocean of mercy, please manifest your presence within the two images.
Having thus informed the Lord of Lakṣmī regarding the primary rite and the preparatory ceremony,
one should invoke Him, worship Him with the *arghya* offering and other rites, and present offerings such as rice cooked with mung beans.
Then, having placed [the image] upon a palanquin, one should carry it in procession through the streets in due order.

When the time of evening had arrived, having placed him somewhere in a pavilion at a distance from his dwelling for the sake of relieving his fatigue, he then offered water for the feet and other honors to Hari,
and immediately thereafter presented various kinds of food.
Having placed the Lord Hari upon a vehicle, adorned him with perfumes and other offerings,
and accompanied by musical instruments, songs on the lute and so forth, and many dances; [he saw him] with lips stained by chewing betel, and attended by a multitude of courtesans.
The Goddess should cause him to enter the inner chamber, yet she should refuse him.
After refusing him thus three or four times, the Guru [should say]:
"O Lakṣmī, today the Blessed One, out of a desire to protect his devotees..."
"O Lotus-born one, you ought not to think otherwise that I have gone outside";
having thus entreated her, the god should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for the goddess.
Then, having performed the night worship, he should cause the two of them to be seated upon the bed.
Having worshipped Mādhava with enjoyments and the various articles for the bed, and having awakened Him in the morning,
the Guru should then apply the Śakti to the base (of the image) and offer this prayer:
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, remover of the elephants' distress, today let there be a festival of love for You."
"Whatever slight disrespect has been shown, that should be forgiven, O Treasure of Compassion.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Lakṣmī, one should then commence the worship.
"Indeed, innumerable incarnations have been made by me together with you."
O lady of pure smiles, I shall now tell you their principal [incarnations].
At each respective time, during the worship of those [forms], men should offer adoration;
according to the manner of their propitiation, I bestow upon them what they desire.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra,
on a Monday conjoined with the asterism Punarvasu, and likewise under the *abhijit* yoga while the moon was in Cancer, Pradyumna indeed took birth in the solar dynasty in the form of Rāma.
At that time, the preceptor should honor Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, Sītā, Bharata, and Añjaneya,
during the dark fortnight of that month when it is joined with the constellation Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā.
On the thirteenth lunar day, during the morning of Jupiter’s day, the Lord, the husband of Ramā,
the Blessed One who has arisen from a portion of Vāsudeva, assumes the form of a boar. At that time, one should worship that Lord Hari together with the Earth.
Restrained, the preceptor should satisfy [the deity] with edible offerings such as powdered mustā.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, on a Saturday,
during the conjunction with the Citrā nakṣatra, in the evening, [he should worship] Narakesarin.

One should worship him who is born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is intent on the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa, who is accompanied by Lakṣmī, and who is subject to his devotees, for the sake of attaining all perfections. O Rame, on that second [tithi] of the bright fortnight, when it is conjoined with the Kṛttikā [nakṣatra], [one should worship].

On the day of the Sun, at dawn, Bala was born from a portion of Pradyumna. On that same day, in the evening, during the afternoon, the Guru himself should worship that powerful Lord who is accompanied by Revatī and holds a plow in his hand.

In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the twelfth day, he assumed the form of a tortoise and, requested by the best of the gods for the purpose of churning the ocean, he bore the weight [of Mount Mandara].
Indeed, in ancient times, born from a portion of Vāsudeva, he likewise supported the mountain during the extraction of the nectar of immortality.
One should worship that Hari with devotion, the bestower of nectar upon his devotees.
On the third lunar day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the moon is in the Uttarā-phalgunī asterism and Jupiter is present,
Kalkī shall again establish the Kṛta Yuga by burning away the wicked.
He was born from a portion of Aniruddha; one should worship him early in the morning.
On the twelfth day of that lunar fortnight, conjoined with the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, on a Sunday, he assumed the form of Vāmana at the very break of dawn.
On that day, when dawn has broken, the wise man should worship Vāmana; in the evening, he should gratify Hari by assuming his Traivikrama form for the sake of subduing Bali, the son of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the dark fortnight under the asterism Puṣya,
on the second lunar day and a Saturday, the birth of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, occurred; Rāma, born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, bore an axe as his weapon.
O King, one should worship Hari at evening with the *avadahana* hymn.
In a former kalpa, on the first day of the Creator’s [creation], a Dānava named Durjaya Soma entered the ocean while carrying away the Veda. (47.55–56)
Then, O blessed lady, desiring the welfare of the Creator, I assumed the form of a fish, entered the waters to rescue the Vedas and slay him;
having taken up the Vedas and slain him, I restored them once more to the Ordainer.

At the beginning of the Yuga, one should worship the God born from the lotus in the form of a fish. Hereafter, O Lotus-born One, I shall now describe to you the sequence of the six sacrifices known as *adhvara* belonging to Vāsudeva, the Creator.

A sixfold festival is prescribed for Viṣṇu on the day of his manifestation (the Rohiṇī nakṣatra), as well as on the new moon, the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, the eleventh lunar day, and at the sun's passage into a new sign. Wherever there is no festival for Viṣṇu on the Śravaṇa day in a sacred temple, [that place is deficient].
O Rame, every month there shall be a festival known as Pañcaparvotsava. Formerly, having performed the daily worship of Hari with prayers,
one would invoke Śakti and place the Lord of Gods upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
One should especially adorn [the deity] with flowers, ornaments, garlands, and so forth;
having honored [him] with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), and having presented edible foods and other offerings,
one should [serve] the requisites for the procession, such as umbrellas, chowries, fans, and the like.
And with the sounds of all musical instruments, one should cause Hari to circumambulate the enclosure wall (64).
For the sake of pacifying the exhaustion of the Lord, having worshipped Him at intervals in the pavilions with water for the guest-offering and other honors, as well as various kinds of foods (65).
Having offered green gram mixed with sugar as well as coconut water,
one should present betel leaf and other mouth-fresheners.
Then, one should lead [the deity] to the front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), facing the primary image (mūlārcā).
One should install the deity in the pavilion and worship him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Then, having displayed the lamp within the jar and offered various kinds of edible foods,
one should lead him into the womb [of the altar] and unite him with the Śakti at the root.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Festival of the Five Parvans," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
[The forty-eighth chapter.]
Listen to me, O Kamalā, for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom:
[I shall describe] a festival for all people that grants the desired success of the gods.
Even when there is an invasion by a foreign army, or when one is oppressed by enemies—
On the ground of Mahāmārikā, amidst the destruction of all people,
when the world is afflicted by great portents and the like, or by malevolent planets and so forth,
one should then worship the earth and perform the Kalhāra festival.
The king obtains the earth, and likewise his enemies are slain;
diseases perish, and he attains exceeding happiness.
The subjects on earth attain exceedingly long lives.
I shall describe that festival which bestows prosperity upon all embodied beings:
either in Vasanta, the king of seasons, or likewise in Sharad, O Rama;
or in the month of Jyeṣṭha, or Śrāvaṇa, or Puṣya, or even Phālguna.
On the fifth or twelfth day of the waxing fortnight, or even on the two preceding days,
as well as under Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, or Aśvinī, or under the three Uttarās,
the wise man should act when the lunar day and the asterism are favorable to the sacrificer.
The best of preceptors, being requested by the patron,
should perform the sacrifice to the Lord with white water-lilies for the sake of pacifying calamities in the region;
having dug earth measuring one cubit in depth in every street within the city.
Having carried away the excavated earth outside, one should fill those [holes] with sandy soil, level them, and then sprinkle them with water and *kuśa* grass. Subsequently,
one should gradually smear the walls of the village houses with lime.

It should be adorned with archways, garlands of banners, and flags. Likewise, one should fumigate it on all sides with excellent incenses made from the resins of sandalwood, agallochum, and musk, and perfume all the streets.
Prior to the commencement of the festival, on the ninth day, the seventh day, the third day, or immediately, for the sake of accomplishing the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*),
the preceptor, having performed the daily worship and other rites, should pray to Hari.
"O Lord of the Earth, O Lord of the World, O Lord of Gods, I shall perform for you a festival of white water-lilies; it behoves you to grant permission for this.
Having thus informed the enemy of the Daityas, he should proceed to collect the clay.
Having completed all the rites accompanied by every auspicious rite,
one should go to the grove of the God on the bank of a pond of white water-lilies (kalhāra),
where there is a pavilion with eight pillars, or even one with four pillars, situated to the west.
Having constructed a water-shed, one should fashion a raised altar in its center (48.17).
Having applied a coating of cow dung, one should decorate it with lime powder;
having sprinkled it with water from the "Auspicious Day" rite, one should arrange a pedestal upon it (48.18).
One should place, in successive order, five *bhāras* of *śāli* rice, half that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*),
and half that amount of sesame seeds on top.
Having drawn a lotus in its center, one should place a water-pot (*kumbha*) filled with scented water in the middle of it.
One should place eight jars and likewise a water-pot (karaka) all around.
Having first performed the worship of the doors, one should worship Vaiśvānara in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
Goddess Mahī in the central jar, and Sudarśana in the water-pot.
Having invoked the eight Śaktis into the small jars with mantras, one should worship them; then,
having offered milk-rice, one should cast the bali-offering for Kumuda and the others,
preceded by conchs, cymbals, trumpets, and the like, along with dance and song.
With the mantra "bhūmir bhūmnā," the preceptor, together with the Vaiṣṇavas,
should take fresh white water-lilies from the pond and place them in a collection of golden vessels, O Rame.
Having performed the rites beginning with the fire-offering, the most excellent of instructors should place a vessel of white lotus flowers on the ground in front of the jar;
then he should pray to the goddess Earth, the bestower of wealth.

"O Goddess, one should worship the Lord with lotus flowers from your hand for the sake of pacifying the defects of the kingdom and for your own pleasure, O Earth. Having thus prayed, the best of preceptors [took] that [flower] from her hand which was placed in the water-pot.
Having meditated on the divine flowers that have emerged, one should contemplate them;
with five hundred flowers, one should fashion a garland for the primary image (mūlabera).
O Rame, with one hundred and eight flowers, one should indeed [fashion a garland] for the action-image (karmabimba).
One should make a garland for Śrī and Bhūmi with half of that [number]; this is the best garland for Śrī and Bhūmi.
For the sacrificial worship and so forth, one should make a garland with twenty-five [strings], and for the sacrificial pit, the mandala, and the jars, one should fashion it with fifty.
One should have various garlands made according to the specific form [of the deity],
place them in a golden vessel, and set it upon the head of an attendant;
then, amidst the sounding of musical instruments, one should perform a circumambulation of the village.
Then, having brought [the deity] to the pavilion and placed it upon the ground in front of the water-pot (kumbha),
the most excellent teacher should then dismiss the Goddess and the Śaktis, releasing them from their positions at the door-arches and the water-pot.
One should bring [the image] to the temple as before with musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas;
one should place a vessel of flowers before the primary image (mūlabera). Having worshipped the lotus-eyed Lord, O Rame, one should pray to Acyuta.
"O Lord of the Earth, O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, come for the sake of completing the Kalhāra festival! O Lord, please complete this festival today in this ritual image.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should gradually tie the auspicious thread (kautuka).
Having sprinkled [the garlands] with water from the Puṇyāha ceremony, one should worship Śrī within the garlands:
"O Yellow-Robed One, Lord of the World, adorned with the forest-garland and other ornaments!
I request you to be adorned by me with garlands of white water-lilies."
"O God, O Teacher of the World, please accept the prayer of your devotee.
Having thus prayed to Puruṣottama with garlands of white water-lilies,
one should adorn the primary image (mūlabera), as well as the ritual images and others, in due order.
Having performed worship at the four locations with *kalhāra* flowers, the wise man should place the Lord of Gods upon a vehicle and, having previously prepared a garden,
establish the God within a pavilion adorned with *kalhāra* flowers.
Having propitiated [the deity], one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other edible foods.
One should take the portion for the preceptor (*ācārya*) and also cause it to be given to the devotees.
Having placed the deity upon the pedestal, one should perform the circumambulation of the processional path.
Then, having led [the deity] into the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should unite the Śakti with the Root [Mantra].
Having thus performed the festival for seven days, or five, or even three days as prescribed, the Guru should perform the ritual bath of purification (avabhṛtha).
One should join the Śakti, who resides within the fire of the pitcher-maṇḍala, to the root. Then,
having released the protective bond, the wise one should cause the ground situated at the water-shed in the garden to be raised up, and thereafter inform the Deity.
"O Lord, that festival known as the Kalhāra-utsava which was performed by me—
whatever error occurred therein through negligence, you should forgive all of that.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should perform the night-worship.
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the supreme festival of Vīra-lakṣmī.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kanyā, even if it is but a single digit,
and provided it is not pierced by the ninth day, one should perform the festival of Vīra-lakṣmī."
One should determine the nine nights according to that day;
the Guru should perform the rites for the offering of sprouts and so forth as previously described.
Every day, at both times [morning and evening], one should perform the worship of the four locations and other rituals.
When evening has arrived, having placed the goddess Śrī upon a golden palanquin and having adorned her most exquisitely,
one should lead her in a circumambulation of the temple with all the requisites for the procession.
Having thus performed the festival, he then [honored] the Goddess in the assembly hall,
which was beautifully adorned with coconuts, betel nuts and various other fruits, canopies, rows of lamps, and sacred images.
Having placed [the deity] upon a golden pedestal and worshipped him in due order with enjoyments arising from the decorated seat, one should pray while on a dining mat;
one should then offer the four kinds of food, including various edibles and flattened rice.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with camphor and having offered betel leaves and other items,
one should cause the offered foodstuffs to be presented to the preceptor and the others.
Having thus celebrated the festival, one should lead the Goddess back inside the temple.

Having thus performed the ninety-nine [offerings], the supreme preceptor, having sprinkled [the image] with water from the jar during that night, should present offerings of jaggery, rice, and other foods. That tenth day which extends into the evening is known as Vijayā.

Even if it is joined with the remainder of the ninth [lunar day], that [time] should indeed be accepted by the best of Vaiṣṇavas. When the twilight has slightly passed and the stars have just begun to appear,
this is the time called Vijaya, which grants success in all rites and goals.
Therefore, for men, the tenth day joined with the evening twilight bestows security.
At that time, the festival of mounting the horse was proclaimed by me;
when the festival of the glory of heroes had arrived on that day, the best of preceptors [proceeded].
For the welfare of the world, one should perform the festival of Śrī and other rites at dawn;
or, for three days, one should celebrate the festival of the image alone, beginning with the spring festival.
At the conclusion of the festival, one should worship the Lord with Śrī upon a single seat.
On Friday, one should perform a festival for the Goddess month after month.
Thus, O beautiful lady, there are many kinds of festivals;
I have described these to you according to their importance, among which [you may choose] whichever one you prefer.
To him who performs [this] with devotion, I, being pleased, grant prosperity, long life,
the increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and even most exalted knowledge;
and at the end, I bestow my own world, and he shall attain the station of Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Festival of the Kalhāra," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā. Chapter Forty-Nine:
Now, the Procedure for Expiation (Prāyaścittavidhi).
Śrī said: O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, omniscient one, best among speakers;
regarding the rites previously mentioned, beginning with the plowing and ending with the festivals— [49.1]
If there is ever a defect or even a breakage of the image of the deity, or if the worship is omitted, or if it is touched by those other than the worshippers;
or if it is worshipped by one lacking the qualities of an Ācārya, or in places such as children's quarters; || 49.2 ||
Or when a Caṇḍāla or similar person enters [the ritual space], or during rites such as consecrations (pratiṣṭhā),
if the duty has not been performed, or if it has been performed otherwise than prescribed— tell me, is there some expiation (prāyaścitta) that should be made? (49.3–49.4)
The Blessed Lord said:

All activities, such as plowing and so forth, must be performed according to the injunctions prescribed in the scriptures; for if there is anything deficient or contrary in what is scriptural, [the result will be flawed]. (49.5)

Indeed, the expiation shall be according to each specific requirement. In the construction of a temple, one should first choose a preceptor who is born into the lineage mentioned by me and who has been initiated through traditional succession.
The patron should request such a guru— one who has been consecrated even in the lotus of the wheel (*cakrābja*),
who knows the true principles of the *Pāñcarātra*, who is aged, devoted, and dear to Hari— to perform the plowing and other preliminary rites. (49.7–49.8)
If such a preceptor did not perform the plowing and other preliminary tasks,
or if another person performed them— including the gathering of stones—
as well as the laying of the foundation stone and the head-stone (mūrdheṣṭaka-śilā); || 49.9 ||
The arrangement [of the mandala] devoid of mantra, as well as the arrangement of the womb (garbhanyāsa),
was previously taught by me at the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) for the initiated guru;
having chosen him, one should perform those various rites appropriate for that specific occasion.
Having performed the consecration in due order, one should then begin [the ritual].

Even in the absence of activities such as agriculture, those rites should be performed with mantras and fire-offerings (homa). Having completed the subsequent consecration, the wise practitioner should indeed commence [the main practice].
Otherwise, there would be the destruction of the patron, the original image, the temple, the king, and the kingdom; therefore, one should perform [the installation] according to the rules,
having first performed the placement of jewels and so forth, for the primary image upon the pedestal.
One should install [the deity] together with the mantra according to one's capacity and according to the prescribed rule;
otherwise, O lotus-eyed one, the presence of the deity will not occur.
Having installed [the deity] in some manner, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.

In rites such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), whether for a water-shed (*prapā*) or a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the arches (*toraṇa*), the banners (*dhvaja*), the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, the jars (*ghaṭa*), and even the *karakas*— if these exceed or fall short of the prescribed measurements— [the rite is flawed]. (49.16–49.17)

O Rame, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) for the pacification of the previously mentioned defects, using sacrificial pits, the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), and likewise fuel-sticks (samidh). One should also recite the eight-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times.
Furthermore, those earthen objects employed for other purposes— such as water-pots and the like,
sacrificial pits, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, *darbha* grass, and enclosing sticks—
as well as cloths marked with divine symbols, banners, and door-arches; || 49.19–49.20 ||
O Rame, one should never use wooden vessels that have been used for the remnants of oblations in rites such as the installation of deities;
if one should take them up out of delusion, one must perform that rite again.
One should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
First, one should offer sprouts after the collection of earth;
even if it has been left undone, or if it has been done, or if it has been eaten by mice and other such creatures.
Or it may be red in color, or perhaps it does not arise at all, O Rame; or the bowls, jars, and small vessels have been placed upside down,
or they have fallen from their proper place, or they are broken, even though consecrated with mantras.
If the consecrations with mantras are lacking, or if the fire-oblations and other rites have not been performed;
or if [the vessels] are tainted by defects such as blood and are indeed devoid of mantras—
then, after purifying the vessels, one should again offer the sprouts.

Having removed the vessels that have fallen from their places and having set them back down in those very spots, one should sow seeds within them. The preceptor should then perform ten thousand recitations of the root mantra and a rite of pacification.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, in rites such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), even when the jars have been set out, [if a jar] is broken, fallen, or cracked,
or if it has been touched by those who are unfit to touch [the deity] within that mandala; || 49.28–29 ||
Having invoked another jar endowed with the proper characteristics and having placed it in that location,
the best of preceptors should invoke the goddess Rāmā from the mandala as before and perform the worship.
Even if [the vessel] has been defiled by ants or touched by those who have fallen [from their caste] and the like,
the knower of the scriptures, having invoked the deity into the jar and having had the altar purified by artisans, should spread rice grains of various colors upon it.
First, one should draw a lotus within a wheel and sprinkle it with meritorious water.
Having invoked the deity from the jar, the preceptor should worship him as before.
After reciting the twelve-syllable mantra ten thousand times, he should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
Having constructed water-stalls, altars, sacrificial pits, archways, and banners,
the preceptor should indeed begin the rite;
for if he should begin the rite without having performed these preliminary acts, all of it will be fruitless.
Having performed those respective rites, the wise one should again commence the ritual;
he should place the eight auspicious symbols in the spaces between the jars.
He should also deposit images within the jars, preceded by the recitation of mantras.

If one should perform [the rite] without having first completed it, one should proceed according to the previously stated rule. If the lamp of one who has not attained nirvāṇa should go out, one should light it again;
having offered ten thousand oblations with the Netra-mantra, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).

If the fire has been consecrated in a pit, on the ground, or on a hearth, and then becomes extinguished; or if it is touched by those who are untouchable, or if oblations of buffalo-ghee and other substances have been offered;
or if, at the beginning of a rite, the installation of the fire is performed through delusion in a manner contrary to the rules—[these are all grounds for re-consecration].
Having re-established the fire according to the method prescribed by the Sage,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter with a thousand recitations of the root mantra.
Thereafter, one should perform the pacifying homa and provide a meal for a hundred Brahmins.
If the fire is not well-kindled when the oblation is offered, one should perform the homa again;
this applies to occasional rites, rites for specific desires, and rituals such as expiatory ceremonies (prāyaścitta).
In such cases, the subsidiary homa should be performed in another sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Or one may perform [the rite] in a worldly fire for Vāstveśa and Kṣetrapāla.
If one performs it in the principal fire, one should again prepare the fire,
as well as the fuel-sticks, the enclosing sticks, the *darbha* grasses, the ritual brooms (*kūrca*), and the sacrificial oblations.
