If even a single item among the vessels such as the *ājyasthālī*, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
or among the substances such as sesame seeds and clarified butter, is lost,
then the entire oblation becomes useless; therefore, one should collect all of them.

In all fire-offering rites, one must not omit sesame seeds or clarified butter. For an oblation performed devoid of these two, no atonement is prescribed. Indeed, while such rites as consecrations and others are being performed, [one should proceed] with joy.
If, by chance, a fifth person should enter, or one who has committed a mortal sin,
or one afflicted with leprosy, or one lacking a limb, or one censured due to impurity from a corpse, or a woman in her menses should enter the hall, [the best of teachers should act accordingly].
Having renounced all objects such as the water-jars and so forth as they were before,
and having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) and smeared them with cow-dung,
one should sprinkle them with the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) water and re-establish the jars and other items.
Furthermore, one should perform all the rites from the beginning in their proper sequence.
If fire should burn the hall, one should construct the pavilion again,
perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*), and carry out the ritual as before.
O Goddess, the most excellent lord should feed a thousand Brāhmaṇas;
[he should recite] the Nṛsūkta consisting of twelve syllables ten thousand times and sixteen times.
First, there should be the consecration of the fire; by that, peace shall come to pass.

One should perform the worship and the fire-oblation (homa) for the Lord of the Site (Vāstvīśa) and the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapa). If one fails to do so out of delusion, that ritual act will become fruitless.
The immersion in water, as well as the opening of the eyes, are constituent parts of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The laying down [of the deity], the consecration, and the placement of mantras;
the fire-offering for the withdrawal of the principles preceded by the placement of the six limbs;
and the daily worship of the door, the worship of the jar, and the worship of the banner.
The worship of the wheel and the lotus, as well as the fire-oblation at the two times,
the sowing of seeds, the worship of the pitcher, and likewise the recitation of the Vedas—
if any one of these is absent, the entire rite is rendered fruitless.
Having performed those rites,
one should perform the re-installation again [if the image] has been touched by uninitiated Brahmins and others, by those born of inverse unions (pratiloma),
by those in a state of impurity, by outcasts (patita), or by those suffering from leprosy or epilepsy. || 49.58–49.59 ||

If one has been touched by dogs, donkeys, and the like, or by those who have turned away from their daily duties, or by Tuluṣkas and others beginning with the fifth caste, or if one has conversed with a woman in her courses;
or if one is wet with blood, has perspiring limbs, or is likewise filled with anger— (49.60)
One who is devoted to another's wife, a thief of others' property, mute, deaf, or even lame, one devoid of sacred mantras,
one who neglects the rites of twilight and other duties, and one who is always intent on reviling others; || 49.61-62 ||
If a distressed reciter of prayers indeed performs worship of Hari,
he should bathe the Lord with twenty-five jars for the pacification of that fault;
likewise, peace is attained by reciting the root mantra a thousand times.
Having offered the oblation and brought the *saṃpāta* [remnants], he should place it upon the head of the deity.
Then the preeminent teacher should perform the worship in due order,
beginning with the ritual immersion bath, followed by the washing of the feet and the sipping of water (*ācamana*).

O daughter of Bhṛgu, [one should perform] the sprinkling with holy waters, the placement of mantras, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the internal sacrifice (hṛdyāga), the conceptualization of the seat (pīṭhakalpana), the removal of used offerings (nirmālya) and so forth, and the purification of the site.
Then one should worship the deity Bimbaśuddhi in due order.
Even if one performs the worship without any one of these [preliminary rites],
that worship should be known as fruitless, even if it is performed according to the rules for each respective rite.
Furthermore, one should perform worship again for the pacification of that fault;
one should perform the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times.
One should also arrange the collection of substances prescribed in the scriptures within the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings.
Having placed [the offerings] down, worship should be performed to Hari or to Tulasī.
In the absence of those, however, that worship and its ritual response are fruitless;
one should then recite the root mantra a hundred times and [offer] water accompanied by the ritual substances.
One should worship [the deity] born from the Ocean of Milk with offerings such as the *arghya* and other rites.
If, in the midst of the worship, the lamp should suddenly go out, the most excellent Guru,
having relit that lamp, should recite the Netra-mantra one hundred times.
With oils produced from the limbs of living beings, as well as with the clarified butter of goats, camels, and others; likewise with oils derived from *madhūka*, *heraṇḍa*, and *puṃnāga* fruits,
and with wicks made from pieces of cloth used by men.
If the Guru performs the worship after having lit [the lamps] while I am sporting,
the presence of the God will not be attained; therefore, to pacify that fault,
one should cleanse the lamp-vessels and light them again with cow's ghee.
One should first bathe the deity with twenty-five jars;
having performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should then commence the worship again.
If even a single service among the offerings, such as incense and the rest, has not been performed, [the rite must be redone].
O Goddess, for the pacification of that fault, the worshipper should recite the Netra-mantra one hundred and eight times;
furthermore, for the pleasure of the Blessed One, he should perform that rite again.
At the time of the inner worship, however, he should close the door.
During the worship in the outer pavilion in the presence of the great multitude,
the wise practitioner should perform the worship of the deity without any covering at all; however,
in other instances, a covering is always required when offering food and other such items.
Regarding vehicles and the like, there is no fault in using ornaments; otherwise, a great defect would arise.
Indeed, the consecration of the deity within the temple is a great matter;
one should not perform the consecration in a place outside the temple.
If one should perform these in reverse order, the Guru should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.
[He should also prepare] an incense burner, a lamp stand, vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings,
a vessel for the *nīrājana* rite, as well as an umbrella, a bell, and chowries.
If the banner or other [objects] should fall, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If a breach occurs in any of these,
one should repair it again and purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
From the time of the consecration until the time of worship, whatever is performed—
the sounding of bells, the recitation of the Vedas, as well as the triple symphony (tauryatrika) and so forth—
one should perform each of these daily during the time of worship for that which has arisen from water.
If the worship of Hari is deficient in the sounding of bells and other instruments,
one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra ten thousand times to pacify that fault.
Furthermore, the preceptor should perform worship with those [instruments] again for the pleasure of the Lord.
If the worship of Kamalā is performed at one time, two times, or indeed all three times of day— due to the absence of prepared materials and so forth—
it should be done immediately following each respective time with the aforementioned times, substances, and other requirements. (49.88–49.89)

One should perform worship for the sake of pacifying faults and carry out a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma). Thus, when there is a deficiency of one day, one should bathe Hari with nine jars and have a propitiatory fire-sacrifice performed using materials appropriate for that day.
One should worship the imperishable Lord Hari with double the quantity of materials.
If [the rite] has not been performed by the end of the fortnight, beginning from the second day,
one should bathe the Lord with eighty-one jars, accompanied by a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).
Having prepared double the amount of materials, one should perform worship in the proper sequence; furthermore, one should feed Brahmins for as many days as the number of days [the rite lasts].
When one month has passed, I indeed take pleasure in that which is devoid of worship.
Having consecrated the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
and having performed a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the twice-born and fed a thousand of them,
he should worship in due order with double the usual materials.
If worship has been neglected during the year, one should therefore perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
If the worship of a human [liṅga] has not been performed for up to three years,
the most excellent preceptor (deśikottama), having installed it according to the scriptures, should worship it.
In self-manifested divine [shrines], the omission of worship is not a fault.
Just as I am self-manifested in the world of Vaikuṇṭha, so it is here;
O beloved, who indeed is my constant worshipper here?
In the same way, because of his presence there, the omission of worship does not constitute a fault;
for even among the divine beings, he was established by the gods themselves from the very beginning.
And from that time on, the gods have come regularly and constantly in succession.
Invisible to humans, they worship the Lord of Ramā.
Therefore, there is no loss of worship for those images;
nevertheless, O beloved, this is so regarding those that are self-manifested and others in the world of humans.
If one who knows the true meaning of the Pāñcarātra does not perform worship due to mutual conflict, lack of proper characteristics, or anger,
it is only for the sake of pleasing ignorant men. (49.102)
One should perform the thousand-spoked worship with one hundred and eight jars;
having first performed the consecration and then completed the rite of peace.
O Rame, one should indeed invoke the deity only after performing the worship of the seat (pīṭha). If one should invoke the deity without having performed the sacrifice to the seat,
that worship is to be known as fruitless, and there is no presence of the deity.
Having recited twelve thousand syllables for the pacification of this fault according to the scriptures, one should perform the worship of the sacred seat (*pīṭhapūjā*).
Any worship performed in rituals, images, and so forth, which is done without the invocation (*āvāhana*), [is ineffective].
That worship should be known as fruitless; one should invoke [the deity] again and worship.
Whether it be the *layayāga* or the *bhogayāga*, even if it is devoid of ritual action, or lacking mantras and mudrās, or performed in a reversed manner. (49.107–108)
To be liberated from these faults, one should recite the root mantra a thousand times;
then the wise practitioner should perform those [rites] again according to the scriptures,
for the deities stationed at the doors as well as those dwelling in the enclosures.
If their worship was previously deficient, the best of priests should perform a hundred recitations of each respective mantra and then perform the worship according to the mantras;
or, even if the worship was performed out of order, he should perform that which was prescribed before.
One should first worship the primary image (mūlabimba) at the conclusion of the lustration rite (nīrājanā);
thereafter, the worship of the ritual images (karmādibimba) and others should proceed in sequence according to the mantras.
Or, O Rame, one may worship them simultaneously, even without having first worshipped the primary image.
Or the best of gurus may perform the worship in reverse order;
O Goddess, for the pacification of that fault, he should recite the root mantra a thousand times.
He should then perform worship again with the mantras as prescribed for the primary image and other objects.
At the conclusion of the seat of ornaments, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) of Hari;
if one fails to do so out of delusion, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times.
Thereafter, the preceptor should duly perform the ritual of lustration.
If it has been seen by those who are uninitiated, by women in their courses and the like, or by those born of inverse unions;
or if it has been seen by outcasts, dogs, jackals, and the like, or by mice and such; or if it has been smelled by flies and frequented by ants. || 49.116–117 ||
If food is touched by worms, hair, or nails; or if it is placed in a broken vessel; or if it is excessively hot or excessively cold; or if it is devoid of condiments;
or if it has not been consecrated with mantras; or if it was prepared for someone else—[it is unfit].
One should not offer to Hari that which is mixed with husks, stones, or fragments of rock,
nor that which is devoid of jaggery-rice. One should bathe Hari with forty-nine jars [of water].
The most excellent guru should perform oblations one thousand times with the root mantra;
having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), he should again carry out the worship.
[From the self-manifested [deities] down to mortals, the worship and the ritual response are equal.]
Then one should offer pure food accompanied by various side dishes. (49.122) If there are broken grains, disease will arise; if there are husks, poverty will occur;
through worms, there will be the loss of sons; and through hair, the destruction of the wife. (49.123)
Death is certain through stones; quarrels arise from ashes;
affliction by fire occurs through charcoal; and defeat in battle results from broken pieces.
Thus, O Goddess, such faults arise from failing to observe the patron.

Therefore, fearing those defects, the sacrificer, remaining vigilant day after day from morning until the end of the night, should oversee his affairs. [If food brought for the purpose of offering should fall in the middle...]

One should throw food and other items from the kitchen into ponds and similar bodies of water; then, having sprinkled the kitchen with meritorious waters, one should have it recited. [49.127] Except for the cooking house, that which has been consecrated by anyone other than the initiated [is not to be used].
O daughter of Bhṛgu, even abundant food that has not been consecrated with mantras, or that has been touched by honey and the like, or even by those who are unworthy,
should be purified with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and then subjected to the rites of drying and so forth.
Then one should offer the food and other items; however, if they are few, one should not act in this manner.
[If the worship of Bhogalakṣmī and Vīralakṣmī is to be performed simultaneously, one should first perform the worship of Bhogalakṣmī, and thereafter that of Vīralakṣmī.]
At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer all the seeds, the *mātrādāna*,
and the *gulānna* to the deity along with special sacrifices.
However, if the *mātrādāna* is lacking, one should perform a *śānti-homa*.
Then, having offered those [oblations] one by one and prostrated, he should ask for forgiveness.
Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the worship— whether ending with the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) or even with the festival—
if the priest has not performed the offering at midday, [he must do so].
The preceptor should perform the oblation twice over, together with the night-oblation;
and the preceptor should likewise perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with double the amount of materials.
This applies if the oblation has not been performed for a period ranging from one day up to a month.
One who is most skilled in mantras should bathe Hari with forty-nine jars,
and at that time, he should perform oblations with twice as many materials. If the fire-oblation is not performed from one month until the end of the year, [the rite is incomplete].
Having consecrated the deity with eighty-one jars of cow’s ghee,
one should then perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) by offering oblations (*juhuyāt*) a thousand times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
O beautiful lady, this should be done with double the usual quantity of materials and with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Thus, even after a year, if one should delight for up to three years,
one should worship an image fashioned by a human being simply after sprinkling it with water.
Now, the specific rule regarding when the *bali* offering is omitted is stated as follows.
If the sacrificial materials have been brought forward and the deity has descended [into them],
then the best of preceptors, having first invoked the deity into his heart from those materials and immediately thereafter taking up other pure materials, [should proceed].
Having invoked the deity from the heart-mantra into that [liṅga], one should offer oblations in the cardinal directions.
To pacify that defect, one should consecrate the deity with milk alone.
One should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and recite the root-mantra one hundred times.
When the image has fallen from its vehicle, or has been touched by those who have fallen and so forth,
one should consecrate the *baliberam* with nine jars and perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), while reciting the root mantra one thousand times.
In the event of the loss of rhythmic clapping, dancing, or singing, or the extinguishing of the lamps,
the most excellent Guru should, for the sake of pacifying each respective defect at that specific time,
recite the root mantra one thousand times and then restore those respective elements.

After the offering of the *bali*, the Guru should invoke the supreme deity from the root [mantra] during the festival and its auspicious rites; having mounted him upon a vehicle, he should conduct the festival,
or he may perform merely the worship at both times.
But this was not done, O Goddess, for the pacification of that fault;
rather, having recited twelve thousand repetitions of the twelve-syllable mantra, one should perform the rite of propitiation (śānti).
[And by means of heat, great winds, dust, and raindrops...]
If one should touch the image of the Blessed One, one should bathe it with nine jars;
having performed a festival in the evening, one should carry out the night worship.
If, however, the death of twice-born men should occur within the village or elsewhere, [one should perform these rites].
As long as the corpse remains within the center of the village, O beloved,
so long does the impurity (āśauca) persist for the village and its inhabitants, and they should not perform worship during that time.
Once the deceased has departed from the village, one should perform the rites for the pacification of the site (vāstu-śānti) and other ceremonies.
The Guru should begin the worship; he should not perform it before that.
However, if death should occur immediately after the worship has commenced, he should complete that undertaken worship in brief.
Once the deceased has departed from the village and the purification of the village has been performed,
the most excellent of instructors should then perform the worship according to the prescribed rules.
Furthermore, if death should occur among women, Śūdras, or children, [the same procedure applies].
There shall be no impurity for villages and the like when the Ocean of Milk arises.
Within a distance of eleven bows from where a Śūdra, a woman, or a corpse has defiled the site,
the Guru should first remove [the impurity] to the outside and thereafter commence the worship.
"The calculation of the number of bows (dhanus) should be performed from the second door along the path of the village; one should not calculate it transversely.
If there is a corpse present, one should perform worship in the lotus-abode (kamalālaya)."
One should offer food prepared at that time to Hari,
or [one may] bathe the Lord with eighty-one jars according to the mantras.
Having performed the rite of pacification (śānti), the preceptor should then conduct the worship in the prescribed manner.
O Goddess, the Vaikhānasa Ṛṣi, who emerged from the nail of Brahmā,
will perform austerities at Gaṅgādvāra on a delightful peak of the Himavat;
he will compose a scripture equal to the Pāñcarātra for the purpose of my worship.
His disciples, headed by Bhṛgu and others— those bulls among sages—
having studied the scripture named Vaikhānasa proclaimed by the Vaikhānasa sages,
[constructed] images such as vimānas and temples as prescribed in that scripture.
Having established them by means of that scripture, they shall indeed worship them in Rame;
thus shall the Śaiva and other scriptures exist upon the earth,
along with the mortals who worship them and have been initiated according to those scriptures.
This scripture should never be touched by those initiated into other systems, by those of other lineages,
or even by newly initiated ones who have not received initiation into this [tradition], nor by those who have been initiated elsewhere. (49.164–165)
If they should touch the Lord of Gods, one should bathe him with twenty-five jars and then perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) as well as a fire-oblation (*homa*).
[Whether he be uninitiated, or even a worshipper born of a lineage other than that of the officiant.]
Whether he be an initiated renunciant, or even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya;
or whether he be an uninitiated Brāhmaṇa, one afflicted with leprosy, consumption, or mute; or one who is one-eyed, deficient in a limb, or even born of an inverse (pratiloma) union. || 49.167–168 ||
Whether it be a woman, one who has not been initiated, a *kuṇḍa*, or even a *golaka*—if such a person should touch Hari, O Goddess, the Guru should consecrate him with nine jars.
Having sprinkled him, he should mutter the root mantra; having muttered it a thousand times, [the rite is complete].
And one should perform a *śāntihoma* (propitiatory fire-offering) for the removal of that fault.
Whether it be a Caṇḍāla or a Pulkasa, or one who is attached to another's wife, or one of unknown birth, a bandit, an outcaste, or one defiled by birth— [one should offer for them].
O Lotus-born One, if a barbarian should enter within or touch the image or the vessels contained therein, one must perform purification according to the prescribed rule;
and having completed the rite for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśānti*) according to the procedure taught in the *Pāñcarātra*, [one may proceed].

As soon as that deity has entered, the Guru should bathe it with eighty-one jars [of water], O Rame, if the previously mentioned [deities] touch Hari. Thereafter, he should perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) according to the path seen in the scriptures.
Whosoever among these may have experienced death within the womb, or who has touched the corpse of the image— for the sake of pacifying such defects—
the consecration established according to the scriptures and likewise the opening of the eyes [should be performed].
The most excellent of teachers should perform the ritual without the preliminary immersion in water (jalādhivāsa).

[The wise one should perform it only during the restoration of a ruined temple or its consecration. When [the site] has been touched by or defiled by the corpses of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, || 49.176–177 ||
Having consecrated the deity with clarified butter, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
If [the deity] is touched by the corpses of a Śūdra or those born in the direct order of castes, or if it is defiled,
the preceptor shall perform the previously mentioned rite of a thousandfold propitiation.
If the primary image (mūlārcā) has been made of cloth, or of various paintings, or even of clay,
the best of preceptors should discard it and install another in its place, performing the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) according to the scriptures.
Everywhere the lord should feed a thousand Brahmins;
likewise the Bhaṭṭācāryas, the practitioners, and the attendants. They should sit upon their seats, eat, and lie down according to the prescribed rule.
If those authorized for the rite should perform it, no fault shall arise at all.
(49.182) If others should perform it, one should smear the ground with cow-dung and water; the preceptor should sprinkle the temple of the deity with water consecrated on an auspicious day. (49.183)
O Rame, previously, if any man whatsoever entered or died within these first five [houses],
he would leave behind the fire situated there, even that which was in the hearth or on the cooking range.
In every place, one should perform a smearing with cow dung and a sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
as well as with the waters of the auspicious day (puṇyāha), preceded by the Vāstu-homa and other rites; then, having consecrated that hall and the fire according to the rules, [one should proceed].
Having performed the visualization, one should then cause the fire-oblation (homa) and the cooking to be done;
O Goddess, starting from the first enclosure up to the flagstaff (dhvajastambha). When the Caṇḍālas and others have departed, one should [worship] Hari with nine pitchers.
If anyone there has died, one should bathe the deity with one hundred and eight jars and perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma),
beginning from the flagstaff and ending at the enclosure of the street.
But if the first enclosure or other areas have been defiled by excrement, urine, or the like,
once those previously mentioned [impurities] have entered, one should sprinkle them with water for the sake of auspiciousness;
then, having removed them from there at that very moment, one should perform cleaning, smearing with plaster, and so forth.
Having purified the ground, one should subsequently sprinkle it with meritorious waters.
One should bathe the Lord of Gods in the inner sanctum with nine jars;
[this applies] in the first enclosure and so forth, or wherever there is a rampart wall.
Having carried out the deceased person by a way other than the main gate, the supreme preceptor should then perform the expiation according to the previously mentioned rule.
[If death occurs] by means of a donkey, a dog, a jackal, and so forth, or by a monkey or a boar...
Whether it be a crow, or even a cock, or a vulture, or indeed a hawk; or a monitor lizard, or even a chameleon, or a royal rat;
[along with] a cat, a snake, a frog, a cricket, and so forth—chameleons and the rest.
One should touch [the image] with twenty-five jars and bathe Hari;
there is no fault of touching the image caused by ants and the like.
Whether these [ants] die inside the inner sanctum or merely touch it, [there is no harm].
Having consecrated the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
one should then perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and carry out the thousand-fold worship.
This should be done for the deities in the first enclosure and likewise for those within all seven ramparts.

O Goddess, in the case of the procreation of the castes, or if women other than those of the first five [classes] give birth, then the procedure there shall be as if it were a miscarriage. Even in the case of the procreation of deer or birds, it shall be treated like a death.
In all cases, there should be a smearing with cow dung, as well as a meal for Brahmins;
likewise, one should perform sprinkling with meritorious waters and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A wise person should thus perform the propitiation of the Blessed Lord Hari.
This has been stated regarding images established by humans;

however, I truly delight in images that are self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*) and so forth, whether made of clay or other materials, even when faults have arisen in them, provided they have been consecrated according to the ritual rules. (49.202)
Having performed the thousand-fold propitiation, one should perform the daily worship. Thus,
having observed the faults and virtues appropriate to each respective time, the preceptor,
after first performing the expiation, should perform the daily worship.
Having performed the worship at night, the offering of the bali, the festival according to the rules,
and also the worship during each half-watch, one then rejoices from the root-mantra. Then the Guru, having invoked [the deity] into the worship of the bed, performs the worship.
Having offered food beginning with rice, one should then have [the image] lie down upon an auspicious bed.
(49.206) [When the image for the specific rite is present there, one must not perform a transposition of the various specific rites. (49.207)
If the image used for worship and other rites during various rituals is inferior,
the most excellent of gurus should perform the complete worship within the ritual icon (karmārcā).
O auspicious lady, he should perform this daily, accompanied by song and dance.
This festival must certainly be performed for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom;
if one should fail to do so out of delusion, the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) will turn her face away from the Lord.
Having bathed the deity in the morning with honey, milk, and ghee, the preceptor [should proceed].
One should offer all items, such as milk-rice and the like, in double portions.

[If news of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtāśauca) is heard at the commencement of the worship, the wise man should observe the period of impurity; he should rejoice according to the rule at the conclusion of the worship.]
In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or optional, as well as during festivals,
ritual bathing, atonement, consecration, and sprinkling, the best of preceptors and the officiating priests should perform the binding of the protective thread preceded by shaving and bathing.
O Goddess, having indeed completed all the various tasks, they should perform them in the proper sequence.
If, out of delusion, one should perform a festival or other rites without having bound [the deity],
then one should perform a *śānti* oblation and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having tied the protective amulet (pratisara) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, O Rame, one should first perform that rite; otherwise, what has been done is as if undone.
This same rule shall apply to the images of the primary deities (mūla-bimba) and the others.

During great festivals and other celebrations, the hand of the Guru and that of the Teacher of the Gods (the deity) must be joined. However, if the mark or the sacred thread (kautuka) is lost or broken,
the Guru, having tied another thread, should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
In rites such as the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and others, the Guru must have his protective thread (pratisara) firmly bound.
If he is ill, then his son or a disciple who has been initiated himself,
having bathed and performed the shaving of the head with the permission of that Guru, [should proceed].
Having tied the thread, one should then complete the remainder of the ritual from that point onward.
If the guru dies in the interim, and his disciple belongs to another lineage (*gotra*),
he should then perform a protection rite for the deity with twenty-five jars.
Having bathed [the image] and performed the *śānti* oblation, the preceptor should carry out the ritual;
for him who proceeds while binding the protective auspicious thread (*maṅgalasūtra*),
there is neither impurity from death nor impurity from birth in that which is born of water.
There is indeed only the requirement for a bath, though there is some distinction regarding the officiating priests;
furthermore, impurity should occur even in the midst of a ritual if one who is "connected by self" has died.
Father, mother, eldest son, and wife are recorded as being those connected by self. (49.223)
In that case, the preceptor, having initiated another for that task, should assign him to it.

(49.224) In rites such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), if the best of gurus who has been initiated should meet his death while his only son remains [uninitiated], [the son shall take his place]. (49.225)
Having donned protective amulets and wearing sandals, he went to the cremation ground;
having performed the ritual according to the rules up to the collection of the bones,
he bathed and returned to his own abode with sixteen jars.
Having been consecrated by those who know the mantras, he should then perform the rites for the deity.

(49.227) Having completed the rites for the deity according to the rules at the conclusion of the festival, he should observe the period of impurity for ten nights as prescribed in the section on ritual acts. (49.228)
The best of preceptors should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), the śrāddha rite, and the sapindana ceremony, or else that which is prescribed in the Pañcarātra.
At the conclusion of the festival, he should worship that deity with one hundred and eight jars.
The most excellent teacher should perform the ritual bath and the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma).
One who has been initiated should avoid the food of the dead, the food of Śūdras, the use of oil,
sexual intercourse, and likewise quarreling.
If one should perform [the rite] out of delusion, one should first bathe the deity with twenty-five jars and perform the thousand-fold worship (sahasrārādhana).
Having first bathed in a great river, the initiated one [should consume] the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The preceptor should perform the recitation of the twelve-thousand-syllable mantra for one day,
observe a fast, and then touch the deity;
O Goddess, the initiate, having bound the ritual bracelet, remains in a single sanctuary.
In the initiation within the inner *ālaya*, one should not tie a bracelet;
for if the binding of protection has been performed with reference to a single rite,
the best of teachers may perform all rites by means of that alone.
If one should bind [the hair] out of delusion, he must perform that rite again. [The following persons may do so:
one initiated for a sacrifice, one whose parents are deceased, the husband of a woman who has become impure, the performer of a śrāddha, and one initiated while his wife is pregnant. (49.236–237)
One should not tie the bracelet, as such conduct is censured.
O Lotus-born One, if the rite of a single *kuṇḍa* is performed during festivals and the like,
one should tie the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) upon the preceptor alone, excluding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

One may perform festivals and other rites for a single day even without the protective thread (rakṣāsūtra). Likewise, one may perform the festival of the clay image (bhaktabimba) and so forth, as well as the immediate consecration (saṃprokṣaṇa).
However, in the case of a rite dedicated to a single ancestor (ekoddiṣṭa), it remains [obligatory] for a year; but in the case of a specific occasion (nimitta), it lasts for eight months.
In the case of a rite for the ancestors (pitṛvarṇa), one should abandon it for six months; in the Vaiśvadeva rite, for three months;
and in the case of a rite for Viṣṇu (viṣṇuvarṇa) or an auspicious ceremony (kautukakarman), for two months.
Even if he is an initiated priest (dīkṣita), the officiant (pūjaka) must abstain from eating after performing the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.

O Goddess, after ten days, one should perform an immersion in a great sacred ford (mahātīrtha) and a recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra three thousand times for the sake of purification. If, out of delusion, one should touch the Blessed One without having performed this, [one must purify oneself].
One should bathe the deity with thirty jars for the pacification of faults;
one should perform a thousandfold worship for the complete pacification of that fault.
If the eater of the śrāddha food should worship the Lord of Gods on that day, [the fault is removed].

And upon entering the inner sanctum, one should bathe [the image] with nine jars. If one hears of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), death-impurity (*mṛta-aśauca*), or [pollution] regarding Viṣṇu or his temple and so forth, one should quickly come from outside with speed to the temple.
A mortal should observe the period of impurity, as should a woman in her menses;
otherwise, one should bathe with twenty-five jars [of water].
If Śūdra property is taken, or if one eats food that is tainted by faults, [one must likewise purify oneself].
Or even through lust, greed, and the like, if one sits on a lower seat for a month,
or if the mind of the initiated person should subsequently become afflicted with remorse,
[he should approach] eight or six pure Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas.
Having selected the officiating priests (*adhvaryu*), and having placed a single jar within a load of rice,
he should first invoke Vāsudeva, the embodiment of the Vedas, into that jar. Then,
he should worship the Vedas— either all four, two, or even just one.
If he were to be consecrated with the water consecrated by that mantra, having heard it from the mouth of a priest, he would be most dear to me;
I await his worship, wondering when he might become such as that.
If one has once employed a pillar or a cloth inscribed with the *pakṣi* [mantra],
one must not use it again, even if one should employ it once more;
having abandoned that, O Lord of Gods, [one should proceed] with twenty-five jars.

Having bathed [the image], one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and recite the eight-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times. [This applies] when the image, the cloth, or the pedestal and so forth are burned during cremation and similar rites. || 49.254–255 ||
If the Sudarśana [image] is burnt by fire, one should bathe it with nine jars;
likewise, if the banner, the canopy, the parasol, or the coverings and so forth are burnt, having properly reconstructed them, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offerings and other rites.
If the flagstaff has been smeared with fire or the cloth [is defiled], one should abandon it;
having installed another in its place for the removal of that fault,
the wise person should perform the ritual from the beginning according to the scripture.

O fair-faced one, O Goddess, if the jar has been carried by a bird, or if it is broken or even fallen, or if the jar has been touched by those who are untouchable, or if the pillar [is defiled], or if the cloth is spoiled,
one should perform the previously mentioned rite.
If that very [image] which contained [the deity] has been defiled, one should invoke the imperishable Viṣṇu into another [image] and install him there in his purity;
then, having again invoked him into that [original image], the best of teachers should worship him.

Having installed the Lord of Birds (Vihagendra), one should perform worship at the two times [morning and evening] until the concluding bath of the festival; however, O Lotus-born One, one need not perform it at those times. On the following day, one should perform the worship with double the quantity of materials.
If worship has been performed in this manner even during these nine days,
one should again raise the banner and conduct the festival;
O Goddess, for the pacification of that fault, one should worship the God according to the previously mentioned method.
Having performed the ritual bathing, the best of preceptors should perform the *śānti*-oblation;
having first worshipped the drum and other instruments, he should then summon the gods.
The wise one should perform the installation of the drum and other instruments according to the scriptures.
If one performs the installation or the worship out of order,
or if the sprinkling with "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) waters has not been performed,
then the supreme preceptor, having recited the root mantra a thousand times, [should proceed].
Having established them as they truly are, one should thereafter sprinkle them with meritorious water.
Having invoked the deities into them, one should worship them, beginning with the *arghya* offering.
Then, having struck [the vessel], one should summon all the deities.
O Goddess, if one should summon the gods without having performed the striking [of the drum], then,
after bathing the god Hari with sixteen jars for the sake of peace,
one should thereafter strike the bherī-drum and summon even the gods.
In the event of a split in the leather or a split in the drumstick, one should perform a pacifying fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
The Guru should repeat the recitation of the Gārutmata mantra one hundred times.
Furthermore, having brought another [drum], the Guru should strike it in the prescribed manner.
In the streets and at each respective quarter, he should summon with hymns the gods together with their followers and attendants, each joined with their particular vehicles;
likewise, from the gates to the end of the roads, he should do so everywhere during the offerings of oblations.
O Goddess, one should offer oblations at the two times of day accompanied by the triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music),
providing the materials for the offering every single day.
However, if even one deity has been forgotten, one should recite their hundred names.
To him who has been forgotten, O Goddess, one should give an offering of food along with water.
O Beloved, if the offering of food has not been performed at its proper time,
one should first perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), pronouncing the names of the deities in their proper order.
Having recited each [mantra] one hundred times, the supreme preceptor should perform the invocation for them at another time with double the offering (*bali*),
even in the event of great rain and the like, or solely due to bandits.
O Goddess, even if the festival is obstructed, one should offer the bali-oblation with water.
Even if the offering of the bali is obstructed, O Rāma, on the following day,
having bathed the deity with sixteen jars and performed the rite of pacification (śānti), [one should proceed].
One should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and the festival together with the preceding rites,
O Goddess, for four or five days; likewise, even if the festival is interrupted,
one should offer the victim to the Lord of Gods, Hari, with eighty-one jars.
Having performed the ritual bathing, the peace-offering oblation (*śāntihoma*), and likewise the *bali* offering,
and having celebrated the festival that had been exceeded,
one should then perform the festival for the deity on that day if the auspicious occasion has been obstructed.
Having consecrated the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
and having first performed the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and the bali-oblation for that same number of days,
one should perform the festival on that day according to the prescribed count.
One should perform the offering of the *bali*; by that, the fault is pacified.
(49.284) If the *bali* is omitted on the day of commencement or the day of departure, or if one does not offer abundant food to Hari, O Rame, [the fault remains]. (49.285)
To pacify those defects, the most excellent of preceptors should consecrate the deity with one hundred and eight jars; then, having performed the rite of peace (*śānti*),
he should offer the oblation of strength (*bali*) and present the great sacrificial food (*mahāhavis*) in due order.
In that manner one should commence the festival; one should not perform it before that.

(49.287) "Whether with lack of devotion or with great devotion, or by whatever means I may delight, if I were to scatter flowers and other offerings upon the body of the God or upon His vehicle," (49.288)
If the crown, ornaments, weapons, or other [attributes] fall, or even if there is shaking,
one should bathe the deity according to the prescribed ritual with nine jars.
Or, if the image of the deity seated upon a vehicle should fall...

Having brought [the image] to the pavilion, O Goddess, and having consecrated it with one hundred and eight jars according to the scriptures, and having completed the *śānti*-oblation and performed the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*),
one should carry out the remainder of the festival.
O Rāmā, if damage should occur to the fallen image,
one should invoke the Śakti into the base and stabilize the body of Hari;
then, having performed the re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should proceed with the hoisting of the banner.
The best of teachers should perform the festival in due order.
(49.293) If the sandals of the God and Goddess are touched by those other than the worshiper, one should bathe the sandals with five jars, even if they have fallen. (49.294)
If death should occur in the village during the time of the festival of a deity,
the wise man should first have the corpse removed, and after completing the ritual for the pacification of the site (vāstuśānti),
he should then perform the offering of oblations (balidāna) and the festival.
But at the time of wandering through the streets, if death should occur on the street,
one should abandon the area outside as a place for the deceased and continue the wandering of the streets;
otherwise, if a festival is arranged, it should be done according to the lowest of the low paths.
Having bathed the deity according to the prescribed rites, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
If death should occur on the street at the time of the chariot festival,
one should subsequently carry out the funeral procession for that corpse, even if it is without offerings, and then perform the festival.
When a village has been burnt by fire and afflicted by a great whirlwind,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances and perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
Having bathed the deity with nine jars, one should conduct a festival.
If, out of delusion, one performs the festival for nine days or other such occasions with either too few or too many [days], then for the pacification of that fault,
one should bathe the deity with thirty water-pots while reciting the *Śānti* hymn.
One should perform the festival as before, preceded by the hoisting of the banner.
(49.302) [In all festivals and similar occasions, one should act in this very manner. Whether it be a village, a town, or a monastery anywhere at all. (49.303)
While the deity is stationed there, I delight in the offerings and festivals;
one should perform these within the inner enclosure and not carry them out externally.
If, however, one should perform them outside, then one should worship Hari with thirty water-pots.

Having bathed [the deity] according to the rules, one should perform the rites up to the edge of the enclosure wall (prākāra). O Goddess, if the Tuluṣkas, Pātitas, and others reside in the streets of the village and so forth, then one should cast the offering (bali) upon the enclosure walls.
If the hoisting of the banner is obstructed by some human fault or by fate—
whether due to drought, by bandits, or by the invasion of a foreign army—
and if the great festival is thus hindered for one, two, or three days, O auspicious lady, [the following should be performed].
Having consecrated the deity with eighty-one jars according to the prescribed rite,
the best of preceptors should discard the previous sprouts, perform the offering of new sprouts once more,
and carry out all the rites beginning with the hoisting of the banner.
In this way, if the festival is interrupted until the end of the day of the *tīrtha*, O Rama,
one should consecrate the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*), and provide a meal for a thousand Brahmins.
Having performed the rite again on the day of the *tīrtha*, preceded by the offering of *aṅkura* (germinating seeds),
when the prescribed month has passed, and likewise under the appropriate lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and lunar day (*tithi*),
if it should occur within the year following the festival; || 49.311–49.312 ||
If, within a year, one has not performed the ritual bathing of the Lord of the Gods with one hundred and eight jars,
one should then perform the festival for the deity whose festival has been omitted.
When a festival such as the spring festival has been omitted, the ritual bathing— whether inferior or superior— must be performed.
Having performed [the rites], one should then carry out the festival in which the [usual] celebrations are suspended, or do so within that month.
One who knows the true meaning of the scriptures should perform the festival of hoisting the banner and other such rites.
However, when the chariot festival has commenced, if the wheel is broken or the axle snaps, [one must act accordingly].
O Goddess, if the rope is severed, or if the crest-pitcher falls, or if the charioteer [falls],
one should perform the rites as before; having sprinkled the chariot with auspicious waters (puṇyāha),
one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) at the end of the procession and provide a feast for the Brahmins.
I indeed take delight upon the chariot for those who are unfit to ascend it.
Having removed them and sprinkled the chariot with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and auspicious mantras (puṇyāha),
one should consecrate it at the end of the procession with nine jars.
When a portion of his chariot has been burnt, I shall tell you the propitiatory rite for it:
at that time, having bathed the deity with the five products of the cow and with auspicious waters,
one should perform the consecration with one hundred and eight jars at the conclusion of the procession.
The most excellent preceptor should perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*) and ten thousand recitations of the root mantra, and he should feed a thousand Brahmins.
When the chariot is greatly scorched, he should lower Hari from the chariot.
Having placed the deity upon the bird-king (Garuḍa), one should lead him to the abode of the Lotus-born (Brahmā).
The Lord of Gods might fall either with the speed of a chariot or together with his chariot.
Having brought the deity to the sanctuary, one should sprinkle it with water preceded by rites for peace.
If death occurs by the wheel [of a chariot] at the time of its turning,
or if the corpse of a deer or a human should be brought out beforehand,
one should dig up the ground touched by the corpse and deposit other earth [in its place].
The most excellent preceptor should sprinkle the ground with auspicious substances, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and water; and having also caused the chariot to be circumambulated,
at the conclusion of the procession, he should bathe the Lord of the Gods with one hundred and eight jars.
Then, having performed the consecration, one should carry out the sprinkling as prescribed by the scriptures.
[And one should perform it, O Goddess, feed [the guests], and the Guru should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.
If, during one, two, or three days, he does not move from his own place, [then success is certain]. 49.326–327.
Or if the mounting of the chariot is obstructed for some days,
O Goddess, one should somehow cause the chariot to be paraded for the removal of the fault.
[If one should cause the great chariot to be paraded through the streets for one month.]

At the conclusion of the procession, one should perform the consecration of Hari, the Lord Vāsudeva, with eighty-one jars, as well as a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and the recitation of the *Mūla-mantra* one thousand times; furthermore,
one should feed a thousand Brahmins.
Having performed the festival annually,

if the mounting of the chariot has not been performed in a particular year, then the preceptor who knows the mantras should subsequently worship each of the supreme deities stationed upon the chariot.
Having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) with one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*),
and having consecrated the chariot with sprinkling water,
the preceptor, the teacher, should then duly place the Lord of Gods upon the chariot.
If there is an omission of the festive rites such as the powder-throwing (cūrṇa) that constitute parts of the great festival,
one should bathe the deity with twelve jars for the sake of pacifying each respective omission,
perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), and then conduct the festival.

One should perform the festival by day during the day, and that festival [should continue] until the end of the night. One should perform the festival in reverse order and carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
This applies to the festivals for the self-manifested deities and others, as well as for the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrthāvabhṛtha).

One may perform [the rite] even at night, but one should not have it performed by a human being. If one performs it at night, then the best of preceptors, having bathed the deity with nine jars, should perform the *śānti* oblation.
If the pilgrimage is obstructed, one should lower the bird-bannered flag (khagadhvaja) and perform the festival again, preceded by the hoisting of the flag. However,
if the sprinkling with the water-pot (kumbhaprokṣaṇa) was omitted, one should [reconsecrate] Hari with thirty jars.
Having performed the ritual bathing, the *śānti*-oblation, and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), one should perform them again; O Goddess,
for as many days as the Lord of Gods remains on the road in the chariot,
one should resolve upon the nine-day festival beginning with the oblations.
Then, one should perform the flower sacrifice on the middle day for the sake of nourishment;
for one seeking growth, in the forenoon; for one seeking merit, at midday;
for one seeking the destruction of enemies, at night; and for all forms of pacification, during the counting [of the ritual].

One should perform that festival with freshly blossomed, five-colored, and fragrant flowers, but not with those that are stale or otherwise decayed. If, out of delusion, one should worship Hari with nine jars...
Having bathed the Lord of the gods, one should again perform the flower sacrifice (puṣpayāga).
At night, having planted the bird-bannered [flag] for the flower sacrifice,
and having offered the bali-oblation to those established in the Vīthi and other Vāstu sites, one should dismiss them.
If the banner should be destroyed at that time, one should raise the banner again;
having performed the worship of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and a thousand-fold *homa* sacrifice in His name,
one should then reinstall Vainateya according to the prescribed rite.
Only after performing the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and other rites should one cause the deity to enter within.
At the conclusion of the great festival, the ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed with eighty-one jars;
if, out of delusion, one does not perform it then, it may be done on the following day.
One should perform the bath with the previously mentioned jars and carry out the rite of pacification according to the rules.
During an eclipse festival, whether on the bathing platform or in a vehicle,
one should perform a minor worship accompanied by sugar, even without the sacrificial oblation (havis).
One should offer sesame powder, mung bean leaves, or flattened rice.
When a great festival is underway, one should perform the festival for the eclipse and so forth;
if one fails to do so out of delusion, [one must act] for the pacification of that fault.
One should perform a bath with twelve jars and recite the *astra-mantra* ten thousand times;
both before and after the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
one should perform the daily worship after bypassing two *nāḍikās*.

"In great festivals and other celebrations, one should avoid [the time] for two muhūrtas. (49.354) Thus, many such faults may arise in a great festival; however, the relative importance or insignificance of the task depends on the requirements of place and time. (49.355)
One should perform expiation through fire-offerings in the festival fires;
one should always perform the five-fold festival and the monthly festival.
If, out of delusion, one does not perform them, then for the pacification of that fault—
With nine water-pots, one should perform the rite for the pacification of that fault;
on the following day, one should offer great food to Hari.
This applies likewise during great festivals and other celebrations, as well as during the festivals of the Goddess and so forth.
The most excellent guru should not perform the festival of the five parvans and so forth; however,
when the festivals of the five parvans and the like, as well as the festival of Kāvya’s day, have arrived,
he should then set aside the festival of Kāvya’s day and perform the five parvans and the rest.
O beloved, if festivals such as the Kṛṣṇotsava are obstructed,
then during the same lunar mansion or lunar day of the following month,
one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) by consecrating the deity with thirty water-jars.
Having performed one thousand recitations of the root mantra, one should celebrate a festival;
even if the festival beginning with Kṛttikā should be prohibited,
the wise man should have that festival conducted according to the procedure prescribed for the Kṛṣṇa festival.
When the time for the Pavitra festival has indeed passed,
the best of preceptors who knows the mantras should perform that festival after consecrating the deity with one hundred and eight [offerings] for the sake of peace.
O lotus-eyed one, if the purifier (pavitra) should be deficient or excessive in number or length,
one should recite the weapon-mantra ten thousand times.
If it has been touched by [impurities] such as those from the reverse order [of the alphabet] or eaten by mice and the like, [one must perform this recitation].
Whether it be unrefined by mantras, or even adorned in reverse order,
thus adorned with impure purificatory rites and wearing yellow garments—
having abandoned that [image], one should [bathe] the Lord of Gods with one hundred and eight jars.
Having bathed [the deity], one should perform the *śānti* oblation immediately thereafter;

having produced a pure and sacred thread (*pavitra*), one should adorn the imperishable Hari. Regarding the worship during the *pavitrāropaṇa*, the number [of offerings] should be performed day by day.
Even in the worship of the four locations, whatever number is prescribed by the scriptures—
if even a single number is omitted, the entire worship becomes fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of Hari without omitting any number.
If there should be an omission in the worship, one should perform the festival again.
O beautiful one, if the pilgrimage to Pāvitrika-tīrtha has not been performed,
one should consecrate the deity with one hundred and eight water-pots.
Furthermore, having performed a festival, one should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).
[If it has been performed by those other than the officiating priest in the festival hall of the deity—
such as sitting upon seats, reclining, eating, and so forth.]
Having sprinkled that place with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti).
During the Cāturmāsya period, one should perform the festival of the Lord’s reclining;
at that time, one should also perform the daily worship of the four stations.

In the event of the omission of a syllable or its transposition, one should likewise perform ten thousand recitations of the root mantra and a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of that fault.
O Rame, previously, for the purpose of performing expiatory rites and the like, the ritual bath with a water-pot (ghaṭasnāna) was performed.
If that [consecration] of Hari were to take place, it should be preceded by the offering of a sprout (*aṅkura*).
Without performing the rites for the sprout, one must not tie the *kautuka* thread;
otherwise, there would be a penance for him consisting of ten thousand recitations of the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having recited the *mantra* and performed the fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*) preceded by the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*),
and having also bound the protective amulet (*pratisara*), one should bathe the Lord Acyuta.
O beloved, if one does not perform the rites beginning with the consecration bath (*snāna*) after making the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), [the following should be done].
Having first performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra ten thousand times.
[First performing the auspicious rites for the sprouts, one should then bathe the imperishable Hari.
However, where the four locations are absent, one should not perform the offering of the sprouts.
One should perform the protective thread ceremony, the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the festival of the Bimba image.
Those beginning with the fifth [class] should touch the jars consecrated with mantras, or they should remain close to them;
one should avoid those jars [otherwise].

Having purified that place with the five products of the cow and other substances according to the mantra, O Rame, one should then install jars endowed with the proper characteristics and measurements, and worship the deities within them.
Or indeed one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times,
or even eight times, the reciter of mantras should chant their names, O Lotus-born One; if he bathes them with a jar drawn up in due order.
The Guru should offer oblations one hundred times with the twelve-syllable mantra at the beginning and end of the first enclosure,
and during the entry of the Caṇḍālas and others; likewise,
he should perform the ritual bath upon the omission of worship and so forth, using the *karmabimba*.
"O Rame, for the entry of the bathing image, the ritual bath is prescribed outside the first enclosure [if] there are Caṇḍālas, those in a state of birth-impurity, or menstruating women. Śrī said:
“O Blessed One, let the procedure for immediate sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) be told to me.
The Blessed One said:
“O Anapāyinī, listen to the rite for immediate sprinkling.”
Having placed a great jar and a beautiful water-pot upon a heap of grain in a pavilion smeared with cow dung,
one should sprinkle them with holy water and then perform the rite of the flower-sprout.
There is no worship of the *upakumbha*, nor the worship of the door, nor the worship of that jar.
One should worship the Supreme Self in the *kumbha* according to the path previously described.
And one should worship the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*) in the *karaka*, or first in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or even upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having established the divine fire, one should worship the deity therein.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra one hundred and eight times using sacrificial fuel and other materials;
having performed the pacifying homa for each [deity], one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having bound the auspicious thread according to the rules, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and other sounds,
he should take the consecrated jar and, having led it clockwise around the temple,
place it upon a pedestal of grain in front of the deity.
Having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) as before, one should offer molasses-rice and other such foods.
Therefore, with every effort, one should quickly perform the rite for pacification (śānti) using the clarified butter (ājya) of goats,
sheep, buffaloes, and that produced from other animals.
Likewise, O Goddess, with curd and milk, as well as with clarified butter that is more than a month old;
with curds mixed with milk, or with impure honey;
with unstrained waters, and even with those that have stood overnight—(these are forbidden).
If the Lord of Gods has been bathed with water from wells touched by Caṇḍālas and others, or with water from ponds,
or with foul-smelling water that has come into contact with corpses— whether it be a small amount or a great quantity of water—
one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) once again.
One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and recite the twelve-syllable mantra ten thousand times;
one seeking liberation should always do so, while one desiring dharma and wealth should do so at midday.
One seeking the destruction of enemies should do so in the forenoon, and for royal affairs, in the afternoon.
At the end of the day, one who desires all enjoyments should always [partake] for the sake of expiation of the waters of great rivers,
as well as the water of a dam,
water consecrated by *sālagrāma* stones, and the water of the *puṣkara* [lake]. (49.401–49.402)
For those [substances] placed in the water-pitchers, by means of consecrations (*adhivāsa*) and worship performed with mantras,
there is no fault of being stale, because the deities have been consecrated therein.
(49.403) [It is] indeed a whirlpool, not a non-whirlpool, but rather a recurring whirlpool.

Sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is said to be of three kinds, according to their respective times. First, when the deity has been installed in the primary image (mūlabera) from the child’s house (bālagṛha), that should be known as the "revolving" (āvarta) [sprinkling], [performed] by Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, and others.
If the worship performed there is deficient at the end of the year,
it is declared to be "non-returning" (*anāvarta*) in rites such as the restoration of the dilapidated (*jīrṇoddhāra*).
Having meditated on Hari from the base in the *bāla* [form], one should contemplate the Lord (*vibhu*) immediately after the reconnection.
Re-establishing [the deity] at the base is called "returning.
One should perform the sprinkling according to the rule, in accordance with the respective times,
for those images and the temple due to the passage of time.
If a deficiency should arise, its rectification is now described.
O lotus-eyed one, the limbs of the previously mentioned images are of two kinds here, according to the distinction between primary and secondary. 49.409
The eyes, head, ears, nose, speech, bow, rows of teeth, the heart, as well as the organ of generation and the fingers—
these are the primary limbs, while the others are secondary.
There, the images are made of gold and silver,
as well as those produced from metals such as copper, and likewise those made of stone; indeed,
they also arise from cloth, clay, and various other materials.
If a defect should arise in self-manifested images, in those perfected by sages, or in the body of Hari—
whether in a primary limb or a secondary member—
one must certainly perform a restoration, even using materials such as cloth.
One should not perform the renunciation of all elements oneself, nor [use] self-manifested [materials] and the like;
even the primary component among the various metals such as gold should be split apart.
Having joined them together with their respective substances, one should then perform the consecration (prokṣaṇa).
An image made of stone or produced from wood may indeed be incomplete;
however, one should somehow provide it with limbs using gold plates and the like.
For images made of painting, clay, or cloth, one should employ their respective materials.
The preceptor, while indeed worshipping images that are self-manifested and so forth,
may have them installed by artisans even without constructing a new temple for them.
If it is not possible to install [the image] even in the case of those that are self-manifested and so forth, [then he should proceed otherwise].
Having installed an image of Bāla and having invoked Keśava into it,

one should fashion the image from the respective metals, with the corresponding forms and endowed with the respective characteristics; however, one should not make it of another form or with other characteristics.
Even if a Turuṣka, a Caṇḍāla, or one born of an inverse union (pratiloma) should touch the images, the pavilion, and so forth, O Rame,
one should nevertheless invoke that power into the image in the house of the child and perform the worship as before.
Having had [the image] made and having installed it, one should worship it in due order.
However, an expert most knowledgeable in the scriptures should not fashion a child-image for those icons that have been stolen by thieves or swept away by rivers or even the ocean.
If the [necessary] power is lacking, the Guru should have an image fashioned; having constructed an unsurpassed temple that is free from all defects,
the preceptor should install it according to the scriptures and perform worship there.

But when there is a breakage of a limb in the ritual implements and so forth, the supreme guru, having invoked that power into the primary image (*mūlakautuka*), should sprinkle it while establishing each respective part;
this applies likewise to the statue, its pedestal, the temple, and the inner sanctum.
This fourfold form of the God of gods is equal;
there should be equanimity toward them, and peace and meditative absorption (samādhi) should be the same.
Whether it be made of gold or other metals, or even of human form, wood, or stone—
O lady of beautiful countenance, one may somehow fashion an image made of clay, cloth, or even various metals such as gold, O Rame; however,
if it is in no way possible to provide [the materials], then the Guru [should act].
Having reflected upon those images, one should fashion new ones;
however, the metal that has been discarded from the old image may be employed in the new one.
Whether it be old or new, if one fashions [the image] within the span of a month, [it shall be auspicious].
Having invoked the power (śakti) into the jar, the supreme teacher should worship it.
After a month, a year, or even longer than that,
having installed the image of the Child (Bālabimba), he should pray to Hari within it.

"One should perform the daily rites (*nitya*), occasional rites (*naimittika*), rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), the purification rites (*pavitra*) and festivals (*utsava*), and so forth, upon the image of the child (*bālabimba*); however, one should never perform ritual acts (*karman*) and the like upon it.
"O Lotus-born One, if the time for the invocation has passed,"
Furthermore, the supreme guru should again make a formal supplication before that image,

O lady of excellent complexion, even if the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) cannot be achieved with images made of stone and the like, whether the image be small or large, or even one made of human form.
Or, having dug in the ground, one should cast it into deep water.
When the image of Hari is being fashioned, the goddesses are to be fashioned along with him;
if the goddesses were not previously fashioned during the creation of the Garuḍa-bannered Lord, [they must now be made].

Furthermore, at the time of re-consecration, one should create [the deities] and sprinkle them with water. Whether it be a single image that was previously installed or even many images, they should remain exactly as they were during the restoration of a dilapidated shrine; one should not perform any alteration.
Furthermore, the distinction between the beds and other furnishings should likewise be maintained at the time of re-creation.
If the pedestal of the self-manifested and other images should become broken,
one should abandon the broken pedestal and fashion another.
If any part of the pedestal should break, one should bind it with iron bands.
O Rame, if the image of Vajra falls or is burnt by fire,
provided there is no defect in the image itself, one should simply perform the consecration again.
If a limb should be broken, one should indeed begin the consecration after repairing it;
O Goddess, if this should occur even in the case of self-manifested [images] and others,
one should repair the broken limb, sprinkle it with water, and then worship it.

Whether it be a human-made image or one that is self-manifested, if there is a joining together or a disjunction [of parts], then after performing the joining, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must be performed; no other rite should take its place. If it is a new [image], one should cause the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the entire statue to be performed.

The restoration of ruined temples, pavilions, and the like is described here. When a portion of a temple built by humans has collapsed, such as the falling of a pinnacle (*kumbha*), the deities residing in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) [are disturbed].

Then, having invoked [the deity] onto the pedestal of the primary image, the Guru, while performing the worship of the primary icon, should join it to the inner sanctum (garbhamandira). Once the connection with the temple structure (vimāna) has been made, he should join the Lord of Ramā together with His celestial abode.
One should sprinkle [the deity] according to the scriptures, excluding the rite of opening the eyes.

When the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) is completely broken, one should arrange a place for the Child (*bālasthāna*). Having invoked the Root [deity] therein, one should invoke all the deities upon that pedestal (*pīṭha*).
The supreme preceptor, having invoked them while they reside in the celestial chariot (vimāna), should perform their worship.
Having constructed the chariot according to the scriptures— either as previously described or otherwise— if the image is broken, he should fashion a house for the child (bālagṛha) as before.
Having established merely the image, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) therein.
Likewise, O Rame, for pavilions, halls, and indeed kitchens,
it is praised to perform the concentration (*samādhāna*) after having invoked the deities elsewhere.

Whether it be a temple previously constructed of wood or even of brick, one should have it renovated using bricks or stone in the case of a restoration of what has decayed. This is the procedure for the restoration of human-made structures and the like.

This is the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated temple in a shrine that is self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*) or of similar nature; however, if only a single part of the temple has collapsed, one should perform a repair.
Furthermore, one should not invoke the deity residing there into the original *kautuka* image.
When the celestial chariot (vimāna) is broken on all sides, or when the pedestal of the primary image is damaged,
one should perform the invocation and worship using the original bricks and other materials,
and then join it together by combining them with new stones and other materials.

Whatever material the celestial mansion (vimāna) previously consisted of— whether stone or another substance— it should be fashioned in that very same way, possessing its characteristic marks or being a replica thereof;
likewise for the image, the celestial mansion, the furnace, and the pavilion.
Or one should likewise arrange it at the gate-tower or the hall when they have become dilapidated.
(49.458) [O Lotus-born One, after the sprinkling of the deity and the temple, one should perform the festival at night and likewise the ceremonial bath on the following day. (49.459)
O Lotus-born One, if it is in any way impossible to join the self-manifested root [pillar] with the temple of the Lord,
then one should construct a small chamber for the child [image] therein, invoke the deity, and bind it [to the foundation].
Whether it be an ancient temple or an image that has been restored,
O beloved, one should consecrate the deity with one hundred and eight jars and sprinkle it according to the scriptures, provided it is a new [construction].

Whether it be self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) or human-made, one should perform the rite of installation for both according to the prescribed rule; there is no difference between them whatsoever. For this is the case for all deities, who possess forms such as the various cosmic arrays (sarvavyūha).
[Of Viṣvaksena, Gaṇeśa, and the Garuḍas who guard the gates,
who have been installed at the gate-towers and other locations in the form of majestic manifestations—
] due to the extraordinary presence of those who are worshipped day by day, [49.464–49.465].
The rite for restoring what has decayed should be performed for those born of great power when there is doubt regarding ritual action due to mutual contradictions;
this may be done by means of a sign, a written note, a command, or the word of the Great-souled Ones.
Having ascertained [the time] by means of a dream or a sign, one should perform the worship of the deity (49.467).
Then one should carry out the worship and other rites so that no transgression occurs;
the preceptor must be perfected in mantra, while the artisans must be perfected in their craft (49.468).
A donor who is fully endowed with wealth is the cause for attaining proximity to the gods;
yet if these [qualities] are applied in reverse order, the three families will certainly perish.
For those ignorant of the ocean of saṃsāra, who have come under the bonds of karma...
Because it was requested by you for the benefit of all the worlds,
this most divine scripture has been proclaimed by me to you;
it establishes Vāsudeva as the root of the universe in the primary sense.
That scripture, known as the Mūlaveda, is also proclaimed by the wise;
O Rame, depending on the differences among its students, this scripture shall become threefold:
the Sāttvata, the Pauṣkara, and the Jayākhya.
Then these divine *saṃhitās* shall be proclaimed by the wise;
thereafter, the *sāttvika* and other *saṃhitās* will come into being.
Therefore, with every effort, I delight in the restoration of what is decayed and similar tasks.
One should not create another characteristic (lakṣaṇa), nor likewise another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
nor indeed another substance (dravya), nor likewise another Bhaṭṭācārya.
One should not compose another tantra, nor should one perform another ritual action (kriyā).
The scriptures, mantras, rituals, and so forth, as well as the images and the temple,
and the noble preceptor— just as they were previously accepted,
so too for as long as time permits, they must be honored and not otherwise.
If this is performed in a contrary manner, the king and the kingdom perish;
therefore, one should diligently perform the installation according to the original procedure.
Consequently, those who have perfected their selves should not practice a confusion of established doctrines.
Or even due to disturbances in the kingdom, or because a guru cannot be found, I delight [in this practice].
When human beings lack worship, as do Rākṣasas and Asuras,
then one should indeed perform excellent worship according to the path taught in the scriptures.

But where worship and the like are performed by way of the *tāmasa* path, even there, worship and the like performed by way of the *rājasa* path alone shall be the bestower of success. Where worship and the like are performed constantly by way of the *rājasa* path...
