Even there, worship and other rites performed with a *sāttvika* disposition always bestow auspiciousness.
Where worship and other rites are constantly conducted with a *sāttvika* disposition,
there the divine worship and other rites always grant security to human beings.
Wherever worship and other rites for the Lord are performed by means of the divine path,
there worship and other rites performed by the most divine [means] alone bestow enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not act contrary to this.
One should perform the worship of the self-manifested [liṅga] and others with the most divine [substance].
When the disintegration of the limbs of the image and so forth, or of the temple and so forth,
occurs, the preceptor, afflicted by remorse, should first draw the wheel of letters (varṇacakra).
Having worshipped that according to the rules, until the deity arises as before, one should observe the vow of celibacy;
therefore, having extracted one's own mantra, one should always practice it with a concentrated mind at dawn.
One should perform the recitation (japa) ten thousand times and offer two thousand oblations (homa).
One should perform worship at the four locations and also feed the Brahmins;
or those endowed with self-restraint should recite the Vedas, or even a single Veda.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Detailed Exposition of Expiation," in the illustrious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
The fiftieth chapter [begins]: Śrī.
"How is the wheel of phonemes (varṇacakra) to be drawn, and what is the fruit of the extraction of phonemes?
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Lotus-born one, to the primordial method of the path of phonemes."
By the thorough knowledge of which the practitioner attains my own nature—
that supreme state which is imperishable, free from the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower,
whose form is light that never sets, and which is the undivided essence of the word "I."
That primordial power residing therein is always impelled;
it is of the nature of light that never sets, devoid of the distinction between the known and the knower.
That single power, when its one portion is agitated, exists in the form of phonemes (varṇas). || 50.3–50.4 ||
Indeed, by its own power and in the form of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman),
it has arisen from the Supreme Lord himself for the liberation of living beings.
Know that to be the unmanifest syllable (avyaktākṣara), like a sweet sound produced by a lute and a throat.
For the sake of stability, he indeed assumes a manifold nature of distinct phonemes; yet,
by way of the subtle nature of the phonemes, he possesses the phonemes of the continuous stream of the current—
especially for one who is liberated from the sheaths of the five paths and is established in me.
Through my grace, he attains the state of direct experience, O beloved;
for the collection of my fourfold nature should be understood by oneself as beneficial.
By means of the yoga of origin and dissolution, it is characterized by the resonance of the form of light.
The letter *sa* ends with *a*, and the letter *ha* likewise ends with *a*.
In the *prabhava* [cycle], the letter *ha* is at the end of the twelve;
in the *akāra-svapyaya* [cycle], both of these are equally at the end of the twelve, consisting of fourfold nature.
In this assembly of the array of phonemes (varṇavyūha), that which is to be known is to be understood through the meditative absorption of gnosis (jñānasamādhi):
rest, emergence, pervasion, manifestation, and the sovereign Vāsudeva.
Here, each one above [the others] should be known as a form (mūrti), and indeed it is exactly thus.
In brief, this is joined with a fourfold sequence preceded by rest.
One should contemplate the Lord Vāsudeva, the eternal, as the rest;
for indeed, the principles beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa come to rest here in dissolution.
Then one should meditate on the god Saṃkarṣaṇa as the letter *ā*, the rising [syllable].
For he, the Self of all, is himself the first to arise and the creator of all.
One should contemplate that god Pradyumna, who pervades [all], as the letter *i*.
By means of that [Aniruddha], who is the self of action, the world consisting of the three Vedas is obtained in its various forms.
One should meditate upon that Ikāra as Aniruddha in his manifest form;
for within it, all powers such as the creation of the world and so forth are manifested.
For it is indeed established in this very way, arranged like a staff;
consisting of four forms up to the letter *sa*, it is joined with my fourfold self.
During the contemplation of the source, one should remember the letter *ha* located at the end of the twelve.
One should contemplate Vāsudeva, who consists of the syllable *sa*, as the state of rest;
one should remember Saṃkarṣaṇa, ending with the syllable *sa*, as the emergence at the time of dissolution. Thus, through the letter *ā*, one should meditate upon the divine fourfold nature.
The twelve-fold group of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) is characterized as internal;
having ascended this which serves as a staircase, one enters that which is beyond the *dvādaśānta*.
This is the first method shown for the path of the phonemes (*varṇamārga*).
The subtle [power] consists of the fourfold reality, has the nature of light, and is supreme; it is composed of that [light].
The intermediate [power] has already been described; hear from me its specific distinction.
Of that which was previously described as preceded by concentration (*dhāraṇā*), there are four born from my own nature.
The power of the one known as *va*, who is *niruddha*, is named *rāga*;
she is the Great Lakṣmī called *māyā*, whose other name is *la*.
She is remembered as the Great Speech (*mahāvāṇī*) of the one known as *vidyā*, whose designation is *repha*.
The notion of wind is Mahākālī, and the power of action (kriyāśakti) is known as Ya. The three forms beginning with Brahmā, their respective wives, and those who are their attendants—
all that, both manifest and subtle, resides within the first part of the letter A.
In the middle [portion], the immutable Puruṣa, the enjoyer, is established in the supreme part;
every transmigrating Puruṣa is established in the final part.
This middle method of the path of the letters has been shown to you.
Now, O Lotus-born One, I shall describe the final mode (rīti).
The final mode is Vaikharī, which distinguishes between effort and place of articulation;
it certainly becomes manifest in the utterance of distinct speech.
This Mātṛkā, augmented by the power of Viṣṇu, becomes the guide to the respective right paths for living beings bound to bodies;
therein, fivefold powers are proclaimed to be like those of Viṣṇu himself.
Those who preside over the *mātṛkā* which is a garland of phonemes—
Vāsudeva and the other *vyūhas*, the ten and two beginning with Keśava,
and Śrī— [attain this].
"O Hari, how could they extract the phonemes without a distinction of designations?
Therefore, first explain the designation, the distinction, and the power.
The Blessed One said:
The Udgītha is the beginning of the meters, and likewise the Praṇava is the deliverer (tāraka).
The all-pervading Oṃkāra is declared to be the sheath of Brahman, known by the name Tāra.
It consists of the letter A, which is immeasurable, pervasive, and designated as Dhṛṣṭa.
The letter Ā is known as the Primordial God (Ādideva), Bliss (Ānanda), and the Concealer (Gopana).
The letter I is this one named Rāma, the three-eyed Lord who binds with Māyā.
The letter Ī is indeed the Five Dots (Pañcavindu), the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and the Mind-born (Manobhava).
The letter *u* is known as Bhuvana, and its arising is remembered as Uddāma.
The letter *ū* is Ūrja, the Lord of the World, the Universal Form, and the one dwelling in the cave of the heart.
The letter *ṛ* is named Viṣṭara, the Bestower of Happiness, and the Leader of the World.
The letter *ṛ* shall be named Pīṭha, as well as Yogināgapati; the letter *ḷ* is Viśvamūrti, Maheśa, and Chinnasaṃśaya. The letter *ḹ* is Bhūtabhavya, Devadatta, and Virāṭ.
The letter *e* is Sāttvata, three-cornered, the source of the world, and formless.
The letter *ai* is Vīrasena; he is known as Damana and Godhana.
The letter *o* is Bhūṣaṇa, Bhūti, Otadeva, and Vikramin.
The syllable *au* is declared to be the medicine (*auṣadha*), the triple Veda (*trayī*), Viśvāvasu, and Hari;
the syllable *aṃ* is Kapilākṣa, and Vyoman is remembered as Pītāmbara.
The syllable *aḥ* is Sarvavit and Sāṃkhya, while the Visarga is likewise the creator of emanation (*sṛṣṭikṛt*).
The letter *ka* is Kamala, Brahmā, the bearer of the conch, and likewise Prakṛti.
The letter *kha* is Kharvadeva, the bearer of the discus, and he whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
The letter *ga* is Padmapāṇi, the destroyer of disease, and the wielder of the mace.
The letter *gha* is the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the sun that possesses heat and radiance;
the letter *ṅa* is Ekadaṃṣṭra, Vakratuṇḍa, and the bearer of the sword.
The letter *ca* is Cañcala, the moon, the one with earrings, and the dispeller of darkness.
The letter *cha* is the destroyer of deceit, the wielder of the mace, the slayer of rebirth, and the Guru.
(50.44) The letter *ja* is the destroyer of birth, the conqueror of anger, and the Eternal One.
The letter *jha* is the essence of the Sāmaveda, golden-hued, and known as Jhaṣa. (50.45)
The letter *ña* is white as the moon, holds a noose in his hand, and is the best of the Bhrigus;
the letter *ṭa* gladdens the heart, holds a shield, and is the supreme mountain-dweller.
The letter *ṭha* possesses the Kaustubha gem, is a pillar of wisdom, wields a lance, and is remembered as the unbearable one.
The letter *ḍa* is Puṇḍarīkākṣa, the wielder of the mace (*mausala*), whose valor is unbroken.
The letter *ḍha* is Puṣpabhadra, Vṛṣakarmā, and Pratardana.
The letter *ṇa* is Vanamālī, the Teacher, and the protector of Vaikuṇṭha.
The letter *ta* is marked by the *tāla* gesture; he is remembered as Vairāja and Sragdhara.
The letter *tha* is the restrainer of all, the archer, and the protector of the world.
The letter *da* is the subduer, the self-controlled, Atri, and the destroyer of Tripura.
The letter *dha* is the giver of wealth, meritorious, auspicious, and the destroyer of delusion.
The letter *na* is Bhadrapāṇi, as well as Rodhana and Nandaka.
The letter *pa* is Padmanetra, pure, and facing west.
Pha is Phullanayana, Śikhaṇḍin, and Śvetavāhana;
Ba is Nimiṣa, Hrasva, Matimān, and Kālanemijit.
Bha is to be known as Jñeyasiddhi, Subhadra, and Sūkṣmadarśana.
The letter *ma* is Mount Mandara, Time, and the lover of the *mādhavī* and *pāṭala* flowers.
The letter *ya* is the seed-syllable of Vāyu, the Subtle One, Śaṅkha, and the Four States of Existence.
The letter *ra* is Fire, the Great Flame, the Soul of the Universe, and the Eternal Burner.
The letter *la* is called Vibudha, while *ma* is Māhendra and Dhaneśvara;
the letter *va* is Amṛtāsāra, Varuṇa, and Sudhākara.
The letter *śa* is Śubhada, Lakṣmī, Śrīvatsa, and Kakubha.
The letter *ṣa* is the wrathful one, the stake, and the sun in the form of fire.
The letter *sa*, however, is nectar, the satisfied one, and Soma with twelve aspects.
The letter *ha* is the supreme self and the vital breath; may truth reside in the throat.
The letter *kṣa* is Nṛsiṃha; the final letter is remembered as Brahmaṇya.
The letter *ḷ* is Duṇḍubha, Bharga, Viṣkambha, Vimala, and Tanu.
Hereafter, I shall also declare the deities and the Śaktis.

Vāsudeva and the other four, along with the two beginning with Keśava— these sixteen deities, O Rame, are the presiding lords of the vowels. Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are known as the powers (śaktis) of the [four] manifestations (vyūhas).
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śakti, Vibhūti,
Icchā, Prīti, Rati, Māyā, Dhī, and Mahimā—
these are proclaimed as the powers (śaktis) of Keśava and the other [deities]. 50.61.
Listen, my dear, as I speak of the deities presiding over the letters beginning with *ka*:
Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātmā, Madhusūdana, Kapila—the presiding deity of knowledge—Viśvarūpa, and Vihangama. (50.62–50.63)
The Boar-souled one, the Mare-headed one, Dharma, the Lord of Speech,
the God who reclines upon the single ocean, Kūrma the supporter of the netherworld,
Varāha, Narasiṃha, and likewise the Stealer of the Nectar.
The Lord of Śrī, possessed of a divine body, whose nature is lovely, and who holds the stream of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, and the one who carried away the Pārijāta tree;
the Lord of the worlds, peaceful in soul, Dattātreya, the great master.
Then the Blessed One, lying upon the *nyagrodha* tree, was embodied as Ekaśṛṅga;
then the Lord in the form of Vāmana, the all-pervading Trivikrama;
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, the supreme.
Rāma, who wields the flaming axe, and the other Rāma, the wielder of the bow;
the Lord Kalki, the knower of the Vedas, and the Master who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla)—these and four other gods, beginning with Rāma, are indeed [the incarnations]. (50.68–69)
These two, consisting of the syllable *raṃ*, belong to the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya [spirants].
[The goddesses are] Dhīḥ, Tārā, Vāruṇī, Śakti, Padmā, and likewise the other Vidyā;
Sāṃkhyā, Viśvā, Khagā, Bhūḥ, Gauḥ, Lakṣmī, and Vāgīśvarī.
Amṛtā, Dhāriṇī, Chāyā, Nārasiṃhī, and likewise Sudhā;
Śrī, Kīrti, Viśvanāmā, Satyā, Kānti, Saroruhā; Māyā, Padmāsanā, Kharvā, Vikrānti, and Nīrasambhavā. || 50.71–50.72 ||
Nārāyaṇī, Hariprīti, Gāndhārī, Kāśyapī, Vaidehī, Vedavidyā, Padminī, and Nāgayāyinī—
these goddesses should be known as your portions, the powers beginning with 'Ka'.
In this way, all the gods, goddesses, and Mothers attend upon her.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Deities of the Castes and Other Matters," in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Chapter Fifty-one:
O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe to you the nature of the four types of mantras—bīja, piṇḍa, and so forth—as they have been proclaimed. 51.1
This manifestation of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma), endowed with twelve rays, characterized by consciousness,
and consisting of six qualities, has a fourfold division:
in some places it is the seed (bīja), in some the aggregate (piṇḍa), in some the name (saṃjñā), and in some the word (pada).

The fourth state, deep sleep, dreaming, and waking are, in sequence, the seed-syllables and so forth. O lotus-eyed one, a seed-syllable should be understood as having either one vowel, two vowels, or many vowels, consisting of a pair of both vowels and consonants.
In between, there is an iron ball joined with its own essence in certain places;
these are the designations for the various objects to be expressed, conjoined with the word "namaḥ" and the syllable "oṃ.
They are characterized by the connection of action and agent, as well as praise and address.
The mantra is said to be the essence of the state, endowed with various higher knowledges (*abhijñā*).
This fourfold mantra, complete within the self of the deity,
bestows the desired accomplishment through its connection with that fourfold nature.

Having understood, according to reality, both the field (*kṣetra*) and the nature of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña-bhāva*) in relation to the mantras, O Lotus-seated One, the wise practitioner should employ the mantras. (51.8) Śrī—
"O Lord, tell me of the field (*kṣetra*) and the true nature of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) regarding mantras,
so that by understanding which they shall not be deluded and shall attain accomplishment (*siddhi*) without delay.
The Blessed One said:
"The seed is the life-force of those possessing seeds; the rest is proclaimed as the field.
Having understood this, they are not deluded and shall attain perfection before long.
O Lotus-dweller, I shall now explain all of that in detail."
The seed is the life-force of those things that possess seeds, and the remainder is declared to be the field (kṣetra).
For those things that are seedless, the seed is said to be the beginning, and the other is proclaimed as the field.
Furthermore, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is said to belong to both seeds and physical bodies.
Furthermore, the remaining field is indicated as being devoid of the letter *a*.
The first vowel-mora (*mātrā*) would be the individual soul (*jīva*), while the second and subsequent ones would be the body.
In the case of a single mora, it would be the soul; the characteristic of the element earth is the formative impression (*saṃskāra*).
When it is being uttered, it is the field; when it is without sound, it is the body (piṇḍaka). The first is designated as the living soul (jīva), while the remainder they declare to be the field.
Thus has the true nature of the field and the knower of the field been demonstrated to you.
Those mantras whose *piṇḍa* or *bīja* occurs at the beginning, middle, and end— either in all three or in any one of them— are effective for all times. However,
in the absence of a *bīja* for mantras, one should take the first syllable as the *bīja*.
Afterwards, the entire mantra is said to be joined with the *anusvāra*.
Having thus understood the method of the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), whoever practices it,
the mantras sport with that person who is colored by passion.

When the person whose senses are restrained stands within the gaze of the Teacher, situated upon the fourteen-fold path of Prakṛti in the world of manifestation, and upon the path of the restless Prakṛti beginning with deep sleep, excluding the fourth state (turya); || 51.19 ||
The mantras, with faces brightened by grace, having drawn [the soul] out from the path of the worlds (bhuvana) and the path of the levels (pada), generate dispassion at every step;
they lead it gradually through the stages of the principles (tattva), the digits (kalā), the phonemes (varṇa), and the words (pada).
Having attained even a slight degree of serenity, with all bonds completely shaken off,
they reach the abode of Śrī Viṣṇu and rejoice like the eternal sages (nityasūris).
Thus has the sequence of worship been proclaimed in the scriptures.
One who has conquered the senses and subdued anger, who is proficient in the Yoga scriptures, who is devoted to daily rites and other duties, who is free from greed and delusion,
and who delights in serving the guru as well as in the worship of the Blessed Lord.
Being himself wise, a Brahmin,

and the foremost knower of the Vedas, he was first of all a Vaiṣṇava, having received [initiation] from a guru who was a knower of the Pañcarātra, devoted to the five daily observances (pañcakāla), perfected in mantra, and a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having studied and mastered the path of phonemes, the deities, and the seed-syllables of the mantras, O Goddess— [in a place] that is pure,
free from thorns, smeared with cow dung, and perfumed with incense (51.26–51.27).
Having sprinkled [the ground] with the five products of the cow and smeared it with sandalwood and other unguents,
the practitioner of mantra should first worship his own chosen deity upon a spot of earth, perfuming it with incense, lamps, flowers, perfumes, and so forth.
Then, having spread out clay there, scented with perfumes, incense, and so forth,
one should prepare a very level pedestal for the *mātṛkās*, either square or circular, measuring two cubits or even one cubit, and then spread that [clay] over it.
She who is but one, yet possesses diverse colors, the goddess who has sixteen forms, is the manifest mother of mantras— your very body composed of mantra.
A practitioner of mantra may spread [the grid] either in the shape of a lotus or in the shape of a wheel.
One should draw the form of a wheel for a male and a lotus for a female,
respectively. Having sprinkled it, the wheel should be fashioned, adorned with sixteen spokes, complete with a hub and a rim, and marked with lines of sandalwood powder.

In the center of that [mandala], the vowels are placed at the beginning of the meters; likewise, the *sparśa* consonants are in the region of the navel, and the *ya*-class consonants are in the region of the rim. When the letters have been thus arranged according to the twelve-syllable vidyā—
Or else, O Goddess, one should worship according to the sequence with the Śrī-mantra. Then, in the center of its pericarp, one should contemplate the Mother of Letters (Mātṛkā),
the goddess who is without beginning or end and whose nature is the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
The goddess Padminī, who holds a noose and a goad, wears a garland of lotuses;

she is gracious, possesses the luster of the interior of a lotus, and is the sole sustenance for all the worlds. Her limbs are fashioned with perfect color, and she is adorned with ornaments of various hues.
One should know that the Praṇava is the body of Śabdabrahman; it is remembered as the head.
One should know that *a* and *ā* are the eyebrows, *i* and *ī* are both eyes, *u* and *ū* are the ears, *ṛ* and *ṝ* are the nose, and *ḷ* and *ḹ* are the cheeks. (51.38–39)
One should know that *e* and *ai* are the two lips; *o* and *au* are the rows of teeth; *aṃ* is the tongue; *aḥ* is the utterance; one should remember the *ka*-group as the hands;
the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups as the feet; and the wise one should remember *pa* and *pha* as the sides.
The syllable *ba* shines in the rear and the front parts; one should contemplate the syllable *ma* as the navel.
One should know that *ya* and *ra* are the vital breath and warmth; the wise know *laṃ* to be the necklace (*hāra*).
One should remember the syllable *va* as the waist-band, and *śa* and *ṣa* as being in the throat.
One should know the letter *sa* to be the heart; one should remember the *ha* situated within the heart.

One should know the radiance spreading forth to be the letter *kṣa*, blazing like lightning. One should know the stage located at the tip of the nose, and one should remember that which is called *ya* in the heart.
The *jihvāmūlīya* is said to have its place at the root of this tongue;
the *upadhmānīya* is declared to have its place between the two lips.
Thus, with lotuses composed of these phonemes, she is garlanded from the throat down to the tips of her feet.

Recalling the forest garland, the mantra-mother, and the deity of the mantra, one should worship her with water for honor, water for the feet, and other offerings, saying: "Oṃ, salutation to the Mother of Mantras!
Accept this water for honor," and so on, in due order with various enjoyments.
Then, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, prostrating on the ground with the eight limbs, he said:
"O lotus-eyed one, beloved of Padmanābha, Mother of all!
Explain the supreme mantra and the accomplishment that follows it."
Having thus prayed with a restrained mind, the practitioner of mantra should himself perform the ritual placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*).
Meditating upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, he should extract the desired mantra.
In this regard, there is a certain distinction; listen as I explain it to you.

For whichever caste (varṇa) there is a corresponding asterism (nakṣatra) and zodiac sign (rāśi), [the first letter of that caste's name] is determined by its initial vowel; however, the two castes beginning with the letter 'A'—the Āryas and the Vaśyayujas—are traditionally held to have Aśvinī as their asterism.
For the letter 'I', Bharaṇī and the three following stars, Kṛttikā, are assigned. (51.50–51)
The four [syllables] beginning with *ṛ* belong to Rohiṇī; then there is one for Mṛgaśiras;
Raudra likewise consists of only one; two are considered to belong to Punarvasu;
or else two belong to Pauṣṇa; or, according to another opinion, the first and last [of these two] are so considered.
Among the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā, the first two are Puṣya, the next two are Āśleṣā, and then Makhā (Punarvasu).
One is said to be Aryaman; a pair is called Bhargadaivata (Phalgunī);
a pair is Sāvitra (Hasta); and two are Indrādhidaivata (Citrā).
One [digit] for Viśākhā, two for Anurādhā (Maitra), and immediately after that three for Jyeṣṭhā (Aindra);
one for Mūla, three for Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and one for Uttarāṣāḍhā; and one alone is considered for Abhijit.
Two stars belong to Vaiṣṇava, while Śraviṣṭhā and Śata-tāraka each consist of one; Śādivarṇa consists of only one star, Aja Ekapād consists of three,
and Ahirbudhnya consists of three stars— such are the stars among the asterisms.
In the beginning, the four [letters] are Aries; likewise, the vowels are Taurus.
Similarly, the pair [of consonants] is Gemini, Cancer, and the King of Beasts (Siṃha).
The remaining two are the letters from Śa onwards, while Kanyā is the first letter after Ka, which is Libra.
The cavarga is said by the wise to be Scorpio and Sagittarius;
the ṭavarga is Capricorn and Aquarius; the tavarga is Pisces; the pavarga belongs to the final sign, as do the letters from ya onwards.
Whichever asterism corresponds to the first syllable of the practitioner's mantra— || 51.59–60 ||
One should examine the union and non-union of those two, as in the case of a man and a woman.
Having drawn a four-square grid upon the ground, one should place the letters beginning with 'A' therein.
Whichever square contains the syllable of the practitioner's name, [that is the result].
If the first letter of the mantra should be situated in that very [element], it is "accomplished" (siddha); however, one should know that in the second it is "to be accomplished" (sādhya).
In the fourth [element], it is certainly the reverse of "accomplished."
If [the syllable] is *siddha*, that which is *siddha* is achieved through recitation and other means; if it is *sādhya*, that which is *sādhya* is achieved;
and if it is *susiddha*, it certainly leads to great fruit as soon as it is mastered.
However, if it belongs to an enemy, there will be ill fortune, and if it is a corrupt letter, it brings destruction to the student.
Having examined the signs, one should test for compatibility;
then the practitioner, endowed with all the observances, should accomplish the mantra.
However, regarding the four root-mantras, one need not examine their compatibility.
The Tāra mantra, the eight-syllabled mantra, and the twelve-syllabled mantra—these two [along with the others] are the authorized recipients of these four mantras.
O lotus-eyed one, all [of them] become [liberated]; there is no enmity among them.
Mantras are considered to be of three types according to their gender: feminine, masculine, and neuter.
Mantras characterized by *saṃstyāna* (cessation) end in *svāhā*, while those that are neuter end in *namaḥ*.
The remaining ones are masculine mantras; such are the modes of mantra.

For the rites of eradication, subjugation, inciting enmity, and minor magical acts, feminine mantras are recommended; for the accomplishment of such tasks, masculine mantras should be used. Mantras ending in *phaṭ* are praised for purposes such as causing death and for warding off disturbances caused by spirits and the like.

Those ending in *huṃ* are praised, while those ending in *vauṣaṭ* are likewise used for nourishing and for the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha. Those ending in the dative case are praised, and those ending in *oṃ* are used for all accomplishments.
It is the reflection of all sentient beings and a protection from the ocean of saṃsāra;
because it joins together reflection and protection, it is called "mantra" by the wise.
Alternatively, it is known as "mantra" for the reason that it must be kept secret.
This word ending in the suffix -raḥ is masculine in both worldly usage and the Veda.
However, in the technical treatise (śāstra), the rule for the anusvāra is applied to the root *mantr*.
By means of the mantra the deity is established, and by the mantra alone is he dismissed.
The wise know that among all forms of knowledge, the knowledge of mantra is the supreme;
everything pertaining to this world and the next is accomplished through mantra alone.
Just as a seer (ṛṣi) is so called because of his vision of the metrical feet within the syllables of a mantra.

They say that the vision is of the fruit, and not again the vision of the mantra. The deities, when propitiated by means of the mantra according to the procedure taught in the chapter on Yoga, bestow the fruit of the mantra for one who is free from all desires.
Devoted to bathing at the three junctions of the day, one should recite the unsurpassed mantra.
What was prescribed for the Kṛta age should be doubled in the Tretā;
it is said to be tripled in the Dvāpara, and the mantra should be quadrupled in the Kali age.
By practicing thus, one attains the fruit through the grace of the guru.
Alternatively, one should mutter another twelve-syllable mantra a hundred thousand times,
and having prepared a fire-chamber for the oblation, one should offer half of that number as oblations into the fire.
O Goddess, with clay from a sacred site (yonimṛd), [one should construct] a pit that is either circular or square;
for a thousand oblations, it should be one cubit, with each corner measuring one cubit.
For a hundred thousand (niyuta) oblations, the pit is two cubits, and likewise for a million (prayuta), it is three cubits.
For the *śaṅku-homa*, [the sacrificial pit] is four cubits; for the *mahāśaṅku*, however, it is six cubits.
For the *vṛnda-homa*, it is seven cubits, and for the *mahāvṛnda*, it is eight cubits.
For rites involving oblations exceeding these, [the size] should follow those respective numbers.
One should fashion the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be twenty-four cubits in extent.
Where there is wood, that is the ear; where there is smoke, that is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there is ash, that is the head.

Where the *darbha* grasses are properly situated, there the hair is said to be located. Where the fire blazes, O Rame, that is indeed its tongue. If the *homa* offering is made on the head of the fire, there is sin; if it is made on the hair, there is poverty.
The destruction of the eyes occurs, O blessed lady, when it is on the ears;

the arising of disease when on the nose; mental affliction when on the tongue; and the granting of all perfections when placed within a well-adorned vessel made of forest-grown wood, gemstone, or iron. (51.88)
Having established the fire and performed the Vaiṣṇava oblation with primary offerings,
one should then arrange a yogic seat for Hari in the midst of the fire.
Having invoked him there, one should pray for the presence of the Lord until the conclusion of the oblation.
Whatever mantra the practitioner of mantra recites,
uttering that very mantra while meditating on the deity with the mind and pronouncing [the name] in the dative case,
he should offer oblations with "svāhā" at the beginning and end, remaining concentrated according to the rule.
One should perform the *homa* every day and guard the fire without weariness. One should not burn the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) or the *darbha* grass spread according to the rule.
I am pleased with the practitioner who recites the mantra following this prescribed path.
Indeed, even dreams that bestow the attainment of mantras may occur;
[dreams of] the preceptor, the image of the Goddess, and the ritual implements;
[or of] a Brahmin, a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata), a king, an umbrella, chowries, and elephants.
A lion-throne, a full water-pot, cows, a maiden, and wealth for a bride;
a lamp, a conch, as well as a vehicle, the *śrīvatsa* mark, sandalwood, white cloth, garlands and ornaments, and likewise a white umbrella. (51.95–96)

If one undertakes a journey oneself, facing either north or east, [one may encounter] jewels, musical instruments such as the kāhala, honey and clarified butter, the acquisition of land, and the sight of a great river or the ocean. (51.97)
He beheld the celestial chariot of Viṣṇu, the blazing moon and sun,
the stars and the planets, the moonlight and the sphere of Dhruva,
the resonance of the Vedas, the radiant fire, and also the Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
The sacrificial ladles, the *sruk* and *sruva*, various kinds of food offerings,

and the manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*) of mantras previously mentioned— these, O Goddess, indicate success for the practitioner; whereas the sight of one with a shaven head indicates failure for the reciter.
Wearing blue flowers and red flowers upon his head,
he himself bears a shaven head and likewise mounts a donkey;
he embraces widows while being reviled by the most wicked men born of inverse unions.
"Anointing with oil, drinking oil, and traveling toward the southern direction—
observing such things as these in a dream, one should perform a rite of pacification.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Vision of Auspicious and Inauspicious Dreams" in the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
Fifty-second Chapter:
I shall speak before the practitioner of those [births] that bring about prosperity.
In the sky, he hears the hosts of gods [proclaiming] the sound of the rims of chariots and the beating of drums; he converses with the Siddhas regarding his own welfare and finds delight;
and he beholds celestial chariots and the speech of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
And at the time of the fire offering, the seven-flamed fire is seen with three crests,
resembling pure crystal and adorned with a clockwise curl.
There is the perception of a divine fragrance, and the sight of parasols and banners.
In the rite of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the Guru should observe these signs.
The practitioner should indeed report them to the Guru and to no one else.
At the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (homa), the wise man should feed at least twelve Vaiṣṇavas.
Until the perfection of the mantra is attained, one should worship Hari,
who has been fashioned from wood or other materials and possesses a form according to one's desire.
Day by day, one should recite the mantra while offering oblations and satisfying [the deity] with food.
Those mantras which are devoid of the power of the seed-syllable (bīja) and the limbs (aṅga) are indeed useless.
Therefore, one should contemplate [the mantra] as possessing the limbs, joined with the seed-syllable, and joined with the power;
the pervasive Mandara is proclaimed to be its seed-syllable.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having extracted that immeasurable and thus-arisen [seed-syllable] joined with *pāṭala* and *priya*, should extract the supreme mantra.
Brahmā is its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the goddess Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (*chandas*).
Vāsudeva is the one to be propitiated; the field is the color white-complexioned.
The deity is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the powers are Lakṣmī and Śrī as well as Māyā. One should thus deposit this [mantra] upon these six locations on the body. || 52.10–52.11 ||
Thus, when the mantra has been applied in sequence and rendered complete with its ancillaries, it should be placed upon the body, the palm of the hand, and indeed in all twelve locations.
The placement (nyāsa) is like that of the twelve-syllable mantra; the Praṇava is the color of crystal.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) ends with *namaḥ* or *svāhā*, even in the case of recitation, worship, and oblations.
There is no mantra higher than the *praṇava*; everything is established within the *praṇava*.
O Rame, the practitioner of mantra attains his desired object through the recitation of the *praṇava*.
O Lotus-born One, I shall declare the extraction of the twelve-syllable mantra:
*praṇava*, *bhadrapāṇi*, *draṣṭṛ*, and likewise *mandara*;
*otadevam*, *jñeyasiddhi*, *vāsudeva*, and *vāruṇī*.
Aprameya, Vāmana, Lakṣmī, Vairāja, and Sāttvata;
Sudhākara, Gopana, Soma, and Bhuvana;
Dānta, Tryaśra, Vāmana, and Gopana joined with the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Having grasped even the Seer from the midst of the circle of the Mother-letters (mātṛkācakra),
one should recite each syllable one hundred thousand times, established in the observance,
[meditating upon] Vāsudeva, the bull-like god, who is the mass of supreme bliss.
One should meditate upon Him who resembles pure crystal, the primordial deity of all gods,
two-armed and endowed with the six qualities, for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
O lotus-eyed Goddess, hear now this eight-syllable mantra.
Taking the beginning of the *chandas* [mantras], one should worship Vyāpaka, Pāṭalapriya, Bhadrapāṇi, Vāsudeva, and Mādhavī, whose deity is water;
as well as Rodhana, Gopana, Mahājvāla, and Gopana.

Śaṅkha, the one named Vyāpaka, and Vanamālin—O Rame, Ādideva shall bring forth the pervasive seed-syllable of Vāyu. One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of this mantra in the same manner as that of the twelve [syllables]. || 52.22–52.23 ||
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī; Antaryāmin is remembered as the sage.
The deity is Nārāyaṇa himself; he is declared to be the presiding divinity and the sacred field (kṣetra).
The supreme ether is the intellect (buddhi); the principle is likewise the white syllable.
"O Goddess, for every single syllable there exists a seer; I shall tell them to you:
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra whose wealth is asceticism, Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, and lastly Atri, who was born from a jar."
The Vedic meters beginning with the Gāyatrī, as well as those ending in the Virāj;
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Agni, and Varuṇa (the lord of waters);
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa—these are the deities corresponding to each syllable.
Space is the supreme field because it is the ultimate limit of the imperishable.
O Lotus-born One, there are seven worlds beginning with Satya; in reverse order, these are the seven planes for the seven imperishables, ending with the earth.
Earth, fire, wind, space, the sun, heaven, and then the moon;
the constellations and likewise the zodiac signs—these are the principles (tattvas) in their proper order.
O beloved, I shall now explain the etymological interpretation (nirukta) of this mantra for you.
The root *avi* ending in *kvip* is traditionally recorded as having the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and functioning as an agentive derivation (*kartṛ-sādhana*).
Following this, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭ*, the vocalization (*prasāraṇa*) of the letter *v*,
the application of the rule for the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) with the prefix, and finally, the absence of *guṇa* at the end is prescribed.
Because it pervades all that is both internal and external, it is so called;
since the root *ava* has the sense of "protecting," this is stated with the suffix *-man*.
When the guna quality is applied to both the letter *v* and the penultimate vowel, [the form *avyaya* arises].
By the rule *pṛṣodarādi*, the elision of the nasal (*an*) in *manaśca* is declared.
(52.34) Hari indeed protects his devotees from sins by the mere act of remembrance;
because he protects this world from the ocean of saṃsāra, he is called the Protector (*Trātṛ*). (52.35)
Therefore, the god Nārāyaṇa is said to be the meaning of the syllable *praṇava*;
he alone is the god who is saluted, the one supreme refuge of them all.
At the beginning of creation, the god Nara is the supreme creator of the waters.
Therefore, the waters (*nārāḥ*) are called his path (*ayanam*).
And for the sake of that deity, he is named Nārāyaṇa;
for the waters (*nārāḥ*) are the path (*ayana*), the abode of the Person (*puruṣa*), the enemy of Madhu.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the base word; from that comes the name "Vāsasa. Having thus received this mantra directly from the mouth of the Guru, one who is intent on serving the Guru shall accomplish all mantras.
Having propitiated Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion and with a mind focused on no other,
he, being composed, meditated upon this God within the mandala of the discus and lotus—
four-armed, with noble limbs, and attended by his weapons such as the discus.
Resembling a dark rain cloud, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
wearing yellow garments, gentle, adorned with a forest garland,
and embellished with shimmering bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and the Kaustubha gem.
Seated upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi—
having thus meditated on Hari, the minister should be intent on the recitation of the mantra.
The minister should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times, and perform libations half that number.
One should offer half of that into the fire; from that, one shall attain success.
When the King of Mantras is fully mastered, any other mantra will also attain success. O Rame, if this mantra remains unaccomplished, no other will become successful.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should mutter the root mantra;
Hari is the giver of the four aims of human life, there is no doubt about this—
[especially] for one who desires to bring [him] under control here without worshiping another deity.
Hari abandons that mortal; others should abandon him in every way. O Goddess, he falls from both [worlds] and does not attain success.
Furthermore, if a man desires a mantra for the accomplishment of his goals, [he must act accordingly].
One who desires wealth, having drawn an auspicious maṇḍala, should worship Hari with sesame seeds,
bilva fruits, nimba leaves, flowers, rice grains, campaka, nandyāvarta, mallikā, mālatī, and karavīra.
One should offer oblations with *yūthikā* flowers, each counted by the hundreds;
O Rame, the practitioner of mantra should perform these oblations for seven days with this mantra.
By the power of this mantra, one obtains inexhaustible wealth.
Having ground together saffron, sandalwood, nutmeg, yellow pigment, lac, camphor,
and musk with water from that very powder,
one who is single-minded should draw the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) on the ground for seven nights.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having presented boiled rice mixed with jaggery (*gulodana*),
one should then step upon the heart of the Giver of Wealth (*Dhanada*) with one's feet and recite the King of Mantras ten thousand or even a million times, having conquered the senses.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the best of mantra-knowers should, at the conclusion of that,
behold Kubera before him and bestow inexhaustible wealth;
likewise, having drawn the Bhadra-maṇḍala near an anthill.

One should worship the deity as before; finally, upon the ground of an anthill, one should offer a *nāgabali* consisting of ground flour mixed with coconut water and milk. Then, [one should proceed] to the site of the anthill.
Having washed that spade, one should consecrate it during the night.
Having worshipped the deity in a mandala or a svastika with a thousand oblations,
the practitioner, being composed, should dig into an anthill with the spade.
One obtains an inexhaustible treasure and various kinds of jewels;
or else, having performed a sacrifice for seven days within an auspicious maṇḍala,
and having offered one hundred thousand oblations and provided a feast for the brahmins.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa as his own self, the best of practitioners,
beholding the pure surface of the earth in a place outside the agrahāra,
shall have many treasures manifest before his very eyes, O Rame.
Or, by means of this mantra, the knower of mantras whose eyes are marked with collyrium obtains a treasure; he acquires it, of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, O auspicious lady, one should perform a sacrifice dear to Hari within the maṇḍala.
Having fastened the sacrificial wood to the shoulder of the bull, one should then pull the plough upon it;
thus the surface of the earth becomes purified, and from the furrows (sītās) one obtains jewels and gold—
priceless and great, obtained through grace and difficult even for the gods to attain.
Having prepared the processed mercury and having again recited the mantra over it a hundred thousand or ten million times—
or as many times as one is capable— with a concentrated mind,
everything will turn into gold by the mere touch of that liquid.
O Lotus-born One, there is no doubt that even a stone or a clod of earth, when heated by fire,
becomes gold when combined with medicinal herbs and mercury and brought into contact with iron. || 52.67–52.68 ||
One who desires a daughter should worship the God whose banner is Garuḍa day by day, offering a thousand oblations of ripe fruits, flowers, and parched grain; at the conclusion of that rite,
he obtains his desired daughter without hesitation.
O lotus-eyed one, listen as I describe the yantra that brings subjugation:
one should draw an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark using yellow pigment (rocanā) and other substances,
combined with sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, camphor, and musk.
With a golden needle, one should draw with these fragrant substances in due order a wheel possessing eight spokes, complete with a hub and rim, and endowed with flames;
one should inscribe the syllables in the eight locations upon the eight-petalled lotus.
One should clearly write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the central square while proceeding clockwise;
then, right there, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) followed by the syllable *oṃ*.
After that, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* within the circle of the navel and in the eight directions.
The syllable *hrīṃ* in the circle of the navel is the syllable for subjugation;
likewise, in all directions, one should include the word "vaśam" (subjugate).
Having invoked the Lord of Gods therein and worshipped him, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra.
Then one should offer one thousand and eight oblations;
thereafter, everything becomes subject to him who wears the pill. Alternatively, [one may offer] dust from the feet mixed with red sandalwood.
Having assumed a human form or a female form as desired,
and having fashioned an image [of himself], he should project his own self into it and meditate upon Hari.
He should strike the base [of the image] with jewels produced from the Mare’s Mouth (haya-māraja).
Every day there should be a recitation of the mantra one thousand and eight times.
At the end of seven days, through this recitation, even a woman or a man will become submissive,
as will even a king or his queen, though situated at a great distance.
Afflicted by desire, her eyes unsteady with intoxication, she presents herself—
whether through the fulfillment of her own purpose or by means of desired riches—
to please the practitioner through the recitation of the mantra as prescribed.
Or, having drawn a wheel as before inside the skull of a dead woman with a substance such as yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and having written the name of the desired woman in its center,
one should then [place] that skull in the fire.
Having heated [the vessel], one should recite the mantra for seven days according to the previously stated number;
then that woman, even if she is far away, will obtain whatever is desired. Now listen, O lotus-eyed one, to the method for bringing the classes of Yakṣas under control.

Dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree, the practitioner of mantra, having worshipped the deity there upon a mandala of a lotus and wheel, should offer oblations with fuel-sticks from the banyan tree ten times every day; thus, when seven days have been completed, [the rite is perfected].
Having first drawn a yakṣa or a yakṣī on a banyan tree with saffron and other pigments, one should personally perform all those rites facing it.
On the seventh night, remaining at the banyan tree like one terrified, as [the deity] becomes enraged; 52.87.
The best of those who know mantras should burn guggulu incense mixed with clarified butter.
Rising up facing a banyan tree, he will directly perceive either the Yakṣī or the Yakṣa; he may then ask that one for his supreme desire.
The Yakṣī and the Yakṣa grant [their powers] to the practitioner as is appropriate.
Now listen also to the means for accomplishing the netherworld (pātāla), O you who were born from the Ocean of Milk!
Having performed the rites such as worship at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa) as previously described, [one should proceed].
Near the entrance of the subterranean chamber (biladvāra), one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times.

With single-minded concentration, the best of practitioners should perform ten thousand oblations (homa) for each of the following: milk-tree wood, śamī wood, dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and clarified butter.
The long-eyed maiden, afflicted by desire, emerged from that cave herself, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand,
taking her minister with her to her own palaces as she pleased.
She rejoices in various divine enjoyments that transcend the human realm.
O lotus-eyed one, this is called the subjugation of the Naga maidens.
One should cause a sacrificial pavilion to be constructed beside the entrance to Pātāla.
One should fashion a lotus-wheel there, provided with banners and arches and adorned with water-pots at the doors; one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa therein,
perform sacrifice as before, and carry out the fire-oblation according to the previously stated number.
Restraining one's diet and with undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
At that very moment, the daughters of the lord of nāgas,
overcome by passion and surrounded by thousands, will appear before the practitioner.
Accompanied by other maidens equal to herself, she brought the minister under her control; having taken him to that supreme city of the Naga realm,
she entered and captivated the minister with various enjoyments.
Having drunk the elixir (*rasāyana*),
he sports with women until the dissolution of all beings, his appearance equal to that of a god.
Listen, O Rame, as I describe to you the marvelous method for attaining the sword (*khaḍgasādhana*).
The practitioner, having ground his own bodily blood mixed with charcoal from a cremation ground,
should draw an auspicious sword four tālas in length.
Standing at the base of that [sword] in a cremation ground, the wise one should mutter the mantra while touching its root.
At midnight, in a desolate place, it emits flames;
O fair-faced one, by its flames the ten directions shine,
and various kinds of beings become causes of fear.

Fearless and motionless, thus composed in meditation, one should recite the mantra while firmly grasping the sword with the hand as it flashes. Reciting the mantra, one goes through the sky to where the Vidyādharas and others dwell.
By the power of these [mantras], that king becomes a knower of mantras;
he is a conqueror of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and daityas—how much more so of mortals?
With sword in hand and constantly reciting the mantra, he goes to heaven.

There too, one obtains all enjoyments together with throngs of apsarases. Having quickly taken up a sword and made it invisible with leaves produced from the *pippala* tree, one should perform a million recitations.
O Rame, one should offer ten thousand oblations with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and seeds.
Having inscribed [the mantra] upon a sword with rājāvarta stone mixed with human blood, elephant ichor, and yellow bile, one should worship Hari with them.
In that [rite], having touched the sword according to the previously mentioned path, the recitation is prescribed;
with one thousand and eight repetitions, there arises the occurrence of heat and so forth.
In heat, the accomplishment is inferior; in the production of smoke, it is middling.
When the supreme fire has been seen, he himself, bearing a sword,
shall subsequently traverse the desired worlds and obtain abundant enjoyments.
And the knower of mantras should write the mantra upon a conch shell with water mixed with yellow orpiment.
One should recite that mantra while touching [the fire] until the appearance of flames.
From the midst of that, O Rāma, a maiden arises as a bestower of boons,
holding a rosary, a medicinal pill, a forehead mark, collyrium, and sandals.
That maiden gives to the minister everything that causes wonder: divine medicine, mercury, and *rasāñjana* kept in a skull-cup;
while the minister recites the mantra with a rosary, even without the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*).
One obtains all desired pleasures; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having placed a pill in one's mouth, one may fearlessly seize a serpent.
For the serpent does not bite him, and even if bitten, he is not harmed.

For him who bears the *tilaka*, whatever creature— be it a man, a woman, a deer, or the like— the practitioner of mantra remembers, that being shall quickly stand before him, O Rāme. By applying collyrium to his eyes, he shall become invisible even to gods and asuras.
The minister, wearing the two sandals, may walk upon water or even fire as if upon the ground; no fear arises from them.
Whatever other region he remembers while standing there, he indeed reaches it in an instant.

By drinking the divine elixir, every disease is destroyed. (52.121) If metals, stones, and other substances are smeared with this mercury, they all turn into gold; and if it is consumed, one attains youthfulness. (52.122)
The mantra-practitioner who displays the net of Indra (indrajāla) should draw an illusion upon the ground:
[the goddess] Kṛṣṇā, four-armed, gentle, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful in every limb; having worshipped her with the mantra, he should then recite it.
The practitioner of mantra, composed in meditation, should recite the mantra ten thousand times or a hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of that, the Goddess becomes perfected; she [manifests] a great fourfold army, a wondrous force both in the sky and on the earth with weapons raised.
Having been quickly propitiated with the mantra, she who grants all desires will show even the entire three worlds to the practitioner. Furthermore,
the manifestation of the pill is described as arising from the lotus-born [Goddess].
Having ground together realgar, kuṣṭha, yellow orpiment, saffron, gorocanā,
and cakrāṅga with the three sweet substances (madhūtrika),
one should form a pill and place it in the center of a wheel and lotus.
Or one should worship the imperishable Hari on the night of the eleventh day;
having worshipped him on the twelfth day, one should recite the mantra according to the prescribed order.
Then, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) in the fire with ghee a thousand times.
This perfected pill shall indeed accomplish everything for the practitioner.
Having placed a stone in a skull, one should hurl it at the head of an enemy;
he will be driven away or die, along with his lineage and his circle of friends.
O Goddess, I shall describe the rite for accomplishing a *vetāla*, which is very difficult to attain:
one should immediately seize a dead youth— either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya— who is free from wounds, and place him in an empty house.
Having washed away all impurities and placed [the corpse] upon the lotus of the wheel,
one should step upon its heart with the foot and abide in meditation;
reciting the mantra day and night, at midnight the corpse trembles.
Fearless, one should strike the body with consecrated white mustard seeds;
that trembling body then rises up and stands before [the practitioner], saying with palms joined in reverence, "What shall I do? (52.135).
And he bestows upon the mantra-practitioner other things difficult to obtain, such as a sword;
likewise, a divine sword-hilt, a medicinal herb, an elixir (*rasāyana*), a pill, sandals, and perfected mercury contained within a bamboo tube. (52.136–137)
Foot-ointment, a rosary, or whatever else is difficult for men to obtain;
by means of foot-ointment, the practitioner gains the power of traveling through the sky and other realms.
With a sword, the certain slaying of enemies who are like lions occurs.
Great diseases are pacified merely by using divine medicinal herbs.
Having first prepared a mandala on a piece of ground free from thorns,
one should place twenty-five jars endowed with all auspicious characteristics.

One should arrange the door-pitchers in the four directions and the archways, filled with substances such as ghee according to the Droṇa-mantra, and provided with threads, kuśa grass, lids, and cloths.
One should consecrate each and every jar with the mantra alone;
with the eight-syllable mantra, recited at least one hundred and eight times for each,
using water from the night, sandalwood paste, and white dūrvā sprouts.
On the inner surface of a birch-bark leaf, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
outside the lotus, an eight-spoked wheel provided with a hub and rim.
One should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the region of the pericarp and the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center.

One should write the eight syllables on the eight petals at the navel and the consonant-syllable (sparśākṣara) [in the center]. Furthermore, one should place the letters beginning with *ya* in the area of the rim, and the vowels in the eight spokes;
[one should also place] the Sun (Bhāskara), conjoined with Mahāmāyā and Agni, as the crest upon the staff.
Having thus [drawn the lines] on the rim in the cardinal and intermediate directions, O Lotus-born One, one should wrap it continuously with a white thread; then,
one should place a pill into a jar situated in the midst of a *droṇa* measure of rice.
Having brought down the Lord from his heart onto the mandala of the wheel and lotus,
one should worship the god Nārāyaṇa within them with devotion, using white garments, white flowers, and likewise white sandalwood.
One should offer rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with curd and milk;
[one should meditate upon] Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Śrī, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred moons, situated within the orb of the full moon.
Having meditated, the mantra-practitioner, with palms joined in reverence, should pray for that which bestows all goals:
"Grant me supreme peace, which destroys all defects. [He should offer] curd, milk, ghee, and rice into the northern round pitcher. || 52.151–52.152 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for seven days with guggulu resin, honey, and seeds,

using the previously mentioned number of oblations; one should then bathe those afflicted by disease with water from ritual jars while reciting the root mantra and meditating upon the Lord who grants all.
Resembling the nectar of the full moon and trickling with the essence of ambrosia,
O Lotus-born One, one should take that pill from his lotus-feet and, having raised up the one afflicted by disease from all sides, place it upon his head.
All diseases, such as epilepsy and others, depart by means of the mantra. Then,
having taken a vessel made of clay, or one of bell-metal, or even one of wood,
and having placed therein nectar mixed with curd and clarified butter;
One should offer cooked rice as an oblation to the spirits at the foot of the sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa).
Afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them wealth and other gifts.
When this is done, all defects and diseases, beginning with leprosy, [are cured].
Even without the administration of medicines, diseases are pacified by the power of my mind;
in this way, O Rāmā, the eight-syllable mantra bestows manifold fruits.
What more need be said? Whatever the practitioner desires, that he receives.

Having renounced all desires, he who gratifies Nārāyaṇa through recitation, fire-oblations, worship, and other rites, goes to the supreme state. Those who worship the embodied forms such as Nṛsiṃha with their respective mantras [attain the same].
I grant them even those desires that are difficult for the immortals to obtain;
having first extracted the *praṇava* (Om), and after that the *vahnijāyā* (Svāhā),
[one should place] the Moon (*sudhākara*), the one named Rāma, and the Sun (*bhāskara*) equal to Kūrma.
One should extract "A-pra-meyam," "Vā-manam," and ending with "Sā-tva-tāntam";
one should recite this for one year and shall obtain all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*).
One should extract "A-pra-meyam," "Man-dara-m," and ending with "Sā-tva-tāntam."
Kamala together with Mahendra, followed by Māyā and Bandhumat;
then Sarvadāhaka, Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Mandara;
[and] Nyagrodhaśāyin together with Satya, Māyā, and Mandara.
Having first established the seed-syllable, the mantra endowed with great flames,

and the Nṛsiṃha-herb at the proper time, the best of mantra-knowers should take it up; he should recite it one hundred thousand times, O Rame, and there shall be the destruction of enemies and the destruction of diseases.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, as well as Soma the Pervasive,
Vaidehī, Vāsudeva accompanied by Mahājvālā,
Nārāyaṇa, Kīrtimant, and Mālā the Pervasive.
Accompanied by the ending *huṃ phaṭ*, it destroys all enemies,
pacifies all diseases, and turns back piśācas and other malevolent spirits.
One should recite it one hundred thousand times per syllable, and one will attain the presence of the deity.
O Goddess, this Nārasiṃha mantra wards off all diseases,
destroys all enemies, and annihilates Brahma-rākṣasas;
it is one that has conquered anger, is all-pervading, subtle, and indeed omnipresent.
Again, having grasped that very [mantra] along with Bhadrapāṇi, Mādhava, Gāndhārī, and the one known as Rāma— [the mantra] which is equal to the sky and Mount Mandara,
reaching the throat, and whose end is immeasurable— they know this to be the aggregate of mantras (mantrapiṇḍa).
Having first extracted the word *klīṃ*, as well as *madana*, *gopana*, *śāntātmāna*, *bhūṣaṇa*, *dānta*, and *vyāpaka*;
[and] *nyagrodhaśāyin*, *kīrti*, ending with *lakṣmī*, and *śaṅkha*.

One should mutter this collection of mantras; Nṛsiṃha will attain pleasure. When the mantra is mastered, the practitioner undoubtedly attains all perfections. Having first extracted the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, as well as Brahmā, the bestower of happiness.

One should mutter the seed-syllable of Vāyu, ending with the pervasive [syllable], together with the protector of Vaikuṇṭha, Krodhana, and Gopana, O Rame; this causes the expansion of progeny. O Goddess, I shall now speak another unsurpassed mantra of Rāma.
Having first extracted the *praṇava*, one should write the fire (*anala*) in its center.
One should recite the single-syllable mantra consisting of the sky-syllable (*vyomākṣa*) and the primordial deity (*ādideva*).
Brahmā is the sage (*muni*), the *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chanda*), and Rāma is its presiding deity (*devatā*).
One should fashion the limbs of Hari, whose nature is fire, joined with a long crescent moon;
endowed with the seed-syllables, powers, and so forth, one should employ it for the desired purpose.
[Seated] upon a lotus throne on a mandāra platform by the bank of the Sarayū river...

Having meditated upon Rāma— dark-complexioned, seated in the vīrāsana posture, adorned with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), with that same hand resting upon his left knee, and attended by Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā— the wise practitioner should recite the mantra.
Meditating on the Supreme Self for one hundred thousand suns with undistracted mind,
the attainment of a kingdom, the destruction of enemies, and [the success of] ministers become certain.
One should remember Vahni, Kīrti, Mandara, the Seer, and Dhīpada.

This two-syllabled mantra of Rāma bestows all desired fruits. Having first extracted the seed-syllable *aṃ* and then remembering the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should [place] Fire, Bliss, and Time, followed by Concealment and the seed-syllable of Wind.
Having extracted [the mantra] ending with Vāsudeva, one should meditate upon this five-colored *anuṣṭubh*.

Viśvāmitra is declared its seer (*ṛṣi*), *paṅkti* its meter (*chandas*), and Rāmabhadra its deity (*devatā*). The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power-syllable (*śakti*) are the first letter and so forth, respectively.
One should place [the syllables] a hundred times at the center of the eyebrows, the heart, the navel, the two thighs, and the two feet.
One should know the six-limbed [protection] as before by means of the letters of the mantra, and the weapon-mantra (astramantra) by means of the root-mantra.
In the middle, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree in a forest, is a seat of flowering creepers.
He was watching the Lord, who had his arrow aimed at the corner of his eye by Lakṣmaṇa, while being fanned by Jānaki;
he was dark-complexioned, with a head adorned by a mass of matted locks, and surrounded by hosts of sages.
Having meditated thus, one who desires victory should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables.
One attains all perfections and the destruction of enemies occurs.
The six-syllabled mantra is of six kinds and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
It consists of each individual syllable of the fifty *mātṛkā* mantras;
it is manifold, beginning with Lakṣmī, Vāk, Manmatha, and Tārā.
Each single mantra of Śrī, Rāma, and Manmatha is preceded and followed by seed-syllables (*bīja*).
It may consist of four syllables or six syllables, granting all that is desired.
This six-syllable mantra is said to have one hundred and twenty-eight variations, ending either with *svāhā*, *huṃ phaṭ*, or *namaḥ*.
Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
Agastya, and Śiva— these are declared to be the sages in this sequence. The metre is known as Gāyatrī, and Rāmabhadra is its presiding deity.

Alternatively, for one whose seed-syllable is *kāma* (the letter *ka*) and so forth, [one should perform] the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels, or with the ends of the mantra, at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), between the eyebrows, in the heart, the navel, the thighs, and the feet— just as the sage Viśvāmitra did for Manu.
Beautiful like a dark rain cloud, endowed with the Jñānamudrā,
seated in the Vīrāsana posture with one arm resting upon the knee,
adorned with all ornaments, and possessing a lotus-face with a gentle smile.

Having meditated upon Rāmabhadra in one's heart—who, after conquering Rāvaṇa along with his hosts, brought about the protection of the three worlds—one should recite the mantra one million times. Then, [the mantra is]: "To the son of Daśaratha" (dāśarathāya), followed by the word "vidmahe. (52.199–200)
Having extracted "Sītāpadaṃ," followed by "vallabhāyai," then "dhīmahi," and then "tanno rāmaś cāpi pracodayāt"—
this Gāyatrī, beginning with "Tārā" and so forth, bestows the goals of human existence.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the section on the extraction of mantras within the glorious Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā.
In the fifty-third chapter:
While Govinda was speaking thus, the lotus-like Śrī addressed him.
O Govinda, lotus-eyed one, ancient Supreme Person;
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the world, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Master of the universe, you who are capable of delivering [beings] across the ocean of saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross and shoreless. || 53.1–53.2 ||
O Pradyumna, the fortunate and glorious one; O Aniruddha, the unconquered;
O Nārāyaṇa, embodiment of compassion, salutations to you, the inner ruler of all! (53.3) For all these living beings are indeed submerged in the ocean of afflictions.
Among the aforementioned actions, is there any action whatsoever that is easy to perform?
O Hari, is there nothing among all the Vedas or all the scriptures [that provides such]?
O Lord of the World, why do you not protect all these people who are suffering?
The Blessed One said:
"O Goddess, born from the heart of a lotus, seated upon a lotus throne, many means have been devised for their deliverance. (53.6)
O Rame, ritual action, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, sacrifices such as the Vājapeya,
the attainment of power through mantras, worship of the gods, pilgrimages to sacred fords, and so forth—
I bestow such fruit upon them in accordance with their actions. Śrī said: "In this world, a father indeed instructs his sons in virtuous deeds."
"You set all these subjects to work in blameless tasks.
The Blessed One said:
"O daughter of the Ocean of Milk, Lakṣmī, everything is established in my mind."
"Even though you already know me, you wish to test me further.
I have devised the means and the pitfalls according to the scriptures;
the means were previously set forth, while the others are considered forbidden."
For the purpose of avoiding misfortune, I have declared the penances:
the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, the Kṛcchra, and likewise the Sāṃtapana;
as well as bathing at sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā with the permission of the virtuous.
By performing any one of these, one is liberated from great sin.
Being liberated, one attains heaven and rejoices with the inhabitants of heaven;
if his merit should be exhausted, he will fall back to earth.

Some actions accomplish what is harmful, some accomplish what is beneficial, and there is also the avoidance of harm; this is the threefold nature of actions, which is taught according to the scriptures. I delight in that which consists of expiation. Thus is the threefold classification of actions prescribed by the treatises.
A wise person, knowing the true principles of the scriptures, having abandoned both the means and the avoidance known as expiation and having resorted to the Vedic way of life,
should take refuge in me by reciting this mantra.
O sinless one, I shall explain to you that six-limbed means for that [attainment]:
the resolve for favorability, the avoidance of unfavorability, the conviction that "He will protect me," and likewise the choice of Him as protector. (53.18)

In the wretchedness of self-surrender, there is a sixfold taking of refuge. Having thus come to me for refuge, one who is pure, devoted to good deeds, and free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue may cross the ocean of saṃsāra. || 53.19–53.20 ||
Free from undertaking, free from hope, without possessiveness, and without egoism; devoted to the sciences, established in Sāṃkhya, and grounded in austerity—
he who is intent on the means [of liberation] does not merit even a ten-millionth part of that [merit].
Śrī said: "You ought to explain the meanings of the words 'favorability' and so forth with respect to Hari.
The Blessed One replied:
In this context, "conformity to all" is said to mean being agreeable;

likewise, "contrariety" refers to the avoidance [of harm] toward living beings. Abandonment consists of the casting off of pride born from learning, character, and the like, as well as of miserliness.
Due to the incompleteness of the necessary factors, the incapacity for actions,
the failure to establish eligibility, and the exhaustion of place, time, and quality,
as well as because of the abundance of obstacles, the means do not succeed at all.
Thus, that loss of pride is called wretchedness and meanness;

it arises from the easy accessibility of power, from the eternal union with compassion, and from the relationship between the Lord and those to be ruled, which has existed from time immemorial. (53.26)

O Goddess, that firm conviction which thinks, "He will not protect those who are favorable," would be a misplaced trust that destroys all merit. Even though He is compassionate, clearly capable, and the Lord of embodied beings, [one might still doubt Him]. (53.27–53.28)
The thought "one should not protect [me] unless requested" is the prayer for that;
likewise, the entreaty for protection is the request, "May you be my protector.
Through that, while being protected by him, there is no separation from ownership over the fruit.
Indeed, the surrender of oneself is said to culminate in the offering to Keśava.
Nyāsa, which is synonymous with nikṣepa, is endowed with five limbs;
it is called saṃnyāsa, tyāga, and also śaraṇāgati.
This fourth means has been taught to you as one that yields swift results;
the three previous means may be unpleasant.
However, there is a turning away from these means through both conformity and its opposite.
Even through wretchedness, the cessation of [other] means is spoken of here.
The devising of protective means arises from the confidence that "He will protect me. What is called the "choosing of the Protector" is the communication of one's own intention.

For even though he is omniscient, the soul of the universe, and ever compassionate, because the course of saṃsāra continues its own momentum, he awaits the expectation of protection [from others]. Indeed,
the relinquishing of the burden of "self" and "mine" is called the surrender of the self.
Violence, theft, and so forth have been shown by the scriptures to be obstacles;
[while the performance of rituals, Sāṃkhya, and so forth have been shown by the scriptures to be means].
One who abandons both obstacles and means, having resorted to the middle way, [is liberated].
Having resolved, "He will protect [us]," one should entrust each to their respective domain;
one should awaken the Lord of the God of Gods, the Protector, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Then, the best of those who know mantras should extract the mantra from the wheel of syllables.
[The mantra consists of: Sarvadāhakasaṃyukta, Śrīvatsa, and Manobhava;
Mandara, Vyāpaka, Dvitva, Bhadrapāṇi, and Gopana;
Mahājvāla, Ādideva, and thereafter the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
The Seer, Dharaṇī, Lakṣmī, Candra, and Vyāpaka;
likewise Nyagrodhaśāyin, Lakṣmī, Vanamālī, and Auṣadhi;
Śrīvatsa, Vyāpaka, Kharva, Aprameya, and Dhāriṇī.
Vāsudeva, accompanied by Mahājvālā, facing west;
the lotus-eyed beholder, together with Lakṣmī and the conch;
and Madana Sāttvata, accompanied by Sarvadāhaka.
Śubhada, Pañcabindu, Kāla, Vyāpaka,
Vairāja, Sāttvata, Kīrti, Ādideva, Mahānala, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāyubīja, Aprameya, and Dhāriṇī.
One should extract the syllable Ānanda (Ā) and the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Ya), ending with the Pervasive One (Ha).
Then, having joined it with the wife of Fire (Svāhā) and reciting "Namaḥ" at the end,
one who knows the true meaning of the mantra should become composed in mind regarding this pair.
Whether with concentration or preceded by you, one should take refuge in me through the eight-syllabled, the twelve-syllabled, or the four-syllabled *praṇava*;
or even if devoid of a mantra, provided he avoids other deities.
Having taken refuge in me alone, one attains the eternal state.
For this meaning of the scripture, once performed, delivers a person;
yet it is lost through this lack of steadfastness when joined with means and obstacles.
In the event of falling into the abyss of the lower realms, one should immediately perform an expiation;
for in this matter, the expiation is simply taking refuge once again.
Indeed, even when adopting various means as a remedy, this alone is the way.
For the non-confusion of the dharmas, for the protection of the family,
for the gathering of the worlds, and for the establishment of boundaries,
a wise person should not transgress the customary conduct even in thought.
For just as a king’s favorite, disregarding even that river— which was made by the king for the benefit of the world, beautiful, and productive of abundant crops—
might leap over it and mount a stake; || 53.53 ||
Thus, a mortal who transgresses the boundary established by me is no longer dear to me, even if he was previously beloved, because he has overstepped my command. Therefore,
a wise person should mentally avoid grasping at [the notion of] it being a mere means.
Relying thus upon this fourth refuge as his means,
having transcended all affliction, he enters the stainless state.
Relying on the middle way, which is free from both the unfavorable and the favorable, he abides therein.
This taking of refuge is supreme; it carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
This is the refuge for those who lack knowledge, this very thing for those who possess discernment;
this is the further shore for those desiring to cross over, and this is the infinity for those who long for it.
But in the event of an occasion for expiation arising from the occurrence of all manner of sins,
O slender-waisted one, if she should seek refuge with me along with you, then,
having thinned away all her sin, she will undoubtedly come to me alone.
But if one is devoted to skillful means (upāya), having enjoyed superhuman pleasures,
he eventually attains detachment and enters my state.
Therefore, both those free from desire and those with desire [should practice] for the sake of their own perfection.
My mantra-formed body is to be constantly worshipped by men;
likewise, especially at the time of worship when Hari is being adored,
the best of teachers should display the mudrā for the delight of the Blessed One.

That which is called *mudrā* belongs to the *piśācas*, the *asuras*, and the *rakṣasas*. Because it causes joy (*muda*) to flow away (*drāvayati*), it is therefore proclaimed as *mudrā*. Some are formed with one hand, and some with both hands.
These should be employed at their respective times for the sake of achieving the presence of the deity.
Although consciousness indeed resides in the fingers, O Rame,
nevertheless the mantra is the presiding authority here and bestows its fruit.
Covering her ears with both hands while pronouncing the name and lineage [of the teacher], and grasping his feet in reverse order— if she does this when she is beloved,
this is the gesture of salutation (abhivādana-mudrā) which she should employ toward teachers and others.
Having cast oneself upon the surface of the earth with both hands, the head, the feet, as well as the mind, the intellect, and the ego,
one should touch the ground with all eight limbs; this is the *namaskṛti-mudrā*.

With the heart and the head, the hands joined in a hollowed añjali gesture directed upward—this is to be known as the salutation preceded by prostration; it quickly propitiates the gods. Extending the index finger while forming a fist at the crown of the head [is another].
One should whirl the index finger; that is the mudrā of the fire-rampart (*vahniprākāra*).
One should display it at the time of self-protection and in the face of great terror.
The yoga-mudrā consists of the left palm placed near the navel.
Having turned that [left hand] upward, one should likewise place the right [hand] over it.
Having placed the left as before and the right facing downward,
if this is performed, it is called the *yogasaṃpuṭa* mudrā.
The joining of the tips of the index finger and the thumb is the *tattvamudrā*.
It should be displayed by the Guru during the placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*), as well as during mental worship and at the time of offering the *arghya* and other oblations to Hari.
Having placed the thumb between the ring finger and the middle finger,
and having formed a fist at the heart, this is the Heart-Seal (hṛdayamudrikā) placement.
Then, having bound that fist below, it is joined with the tip of the index finger.
One should touch the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) with the thumb; this is the head-mudrā (śīrṣamudrikā).

If one places the fist with the thumb pointing upward upon the crest-lock (śikhā), that is declared to be the crest-lock mudrā (śikhāmudrā); if that same mudrā is turned face-downward, [it is another].
When [the gaze] is fixed between the eyebrows, it is celebrated as the Netramudrā.
Having placed the two thumbs very firmly inside the fists of both hands,
if the placement at the base is firm, it should be done in reverse.
That mudrā is called the Armor (Kavaca); having recited the mantra, one should display it.
Having formed a fist with the three fingers beginning with the little finger, one should perform the snapping of the index finger and thumb of the right hand in the eight directions as well.
If one performs a circumambulation of the head, that constitutes the *astramudrā*.
Having formed the hands into a bud-like shape (*mukulita*), one should place them upon the head with the mantra;
