this is to be known as the *kirīṭamudrā*. Now hear about the one called *śrīvatsa*.
Having joined the wrists, one should bring the two thumbs together;
one should extend the remaining fingers like branches and place them upon the right thigh.
Those learned in the scriptures call this very gesture the *padmamudrā*.
One should employ [this mudrā] as the seat for the goddesses Śrī and the others within the lotus. Having inserted the thumbs and the little fingers of both hands inside,
one should join the tips of the remaining fingers together with one another.
One should place this Kaustubha-mudrā on the left side of the chest;
with the two thumbs excluded, one should extend the fingers straight along the sides of the thighs.
One should let the hands hang down from the neck; they know this as the Vanamālā-mudrā.

Having extended the fingers and joined the two hands together with each other, one should perform a rotation to the left and right; this is the mudrā called Cakra. One should also apply it at the base of the right arm for the purpose of protection.
First, one should grasp the left thumb with the right fist;
then one should extend the other fingers and conceal the fist with them.
One should join the tip of the right index finger with the thumb.
O Goddess, one should place this conch mudrā upon the left arm.
Having joined the two hands at the elbows and so forth, the wise practitioner should extend the pair of middle fingers and join the others, forming fists.
O Goddess, one should display this *gadā*-mudrā with the left hand,
and with the other [right] hand, one should likewise display the *padma*-mudrā according to the prescribed rule. One should join the backs of both hands together and [join] the little fingers.
One should bind the two index fingers like a beak with their tips pointing downward;
the thumbs should be like feet and the other fingers like wings, which one should move. This is the mudrā of Vainateya; one should apply it at the base of the thighs.
Having extended all the fingers of both hands immediately thereafter,
one should move them slightly while contracting them like the heads of serpents.
O Goddess, this is the Śeṣa-mudrā for the hands, feet, and face.
But for purification, there is the employment of the deity Paramātman.
Having contracted the three fingers beginning with the little finger and joining them with the thumb, one should then apply the index finger; this is the mudrā of Viṣvaksena.
One should likewise show it at the tips of the feet and employ it for the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
First on the palm of the left hand, then on the right hand,
and again on the palm of the left, one should perform a striking with the fingers.
This mudrā, known as the *tālatraya*, is used for opening doors and similar tasks;
the most excellent guru should also display it at the time of placing the ritual vessel.
One should join the two middle fingers of both hands against the backs of the palms.
One should contract the thumb with the thumb and the little finger with the little finger; all the other fingers should be extended.
This mudrā, known as Kāmadhenū, always effects complete purification.
Having formed the añjali with both hands, slightly opened and clearly manifested—this mudrā is to be employed for invocation. Now hear, O Bhārgavī, regarding the rite of installation:
having turned the two hands downward, [one should join] the two ring fingers with the two thumbs.
"O Goddess, this is the application for cleansing and installation.
Having formed a fist with the right hand, one should display it with the thumb pointing upward. O Goddess, this is the *pratimā* mudrā; one should employ it at the time of worship."
Having turned the right hand upward with the fingers slightly bent,
one should again display this *svāgatā* [mudrā] with the word "Welcome.
Having placed the two hands joined together, with the two thumbs [pressed against each other], || 53.105–53.106 ||
One should rub one’s respective little fingers; this is the *saṃnidhi-mudrā*.
Having placed the pair of elbows upon the navel of both hands, and having joined the wrists, one should then slightly open them.
She should slightly move [the hands] and display them in prayer. O lotus-eyed one, she should make the *añjali* gesture with the fingers slightly opened;
this is the *sāṃmukhya-mudrā*, used for bringing Hari face to face.
I shall now describe the *kumbha-mudrā*: if, at the time of bathing, the most excellent Guru should display his joined palms (*añjali*) with the face turned downwards;
and if he should join the tips of the five fingers together, it is the *grāsa-mudrikā*.
In the offering to the God and the Goddess, one should remember this [mudrā] for the others:
then the wise person should join the thumb with the middle and ring fingers, having lengthened the pair of little and index fingers.
One should display this [mudrā] for grains, flowers, fruits, and so forth during this homa;
however, at the time of offering the bali, one should employ the puṣṭi-mudrā.
This consists of the two thumbs and the index, middle, and little fingers of both hands.

One should touch the other branches and display them by extending [the fingers]. This is to be known as the *japamudrā*, used when performing recitation (*japa*) over water. Having entwined the tips of the index finger and the ring finger with one another— || 53.114–115 ||

Having formed the two thumbs like a staff, one should gradually make a fist; this mudrā of the little fingers and the others is for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*). Furthermore, O beautiful lady, offer flowers and *tulasī* according to the prescribed rule.

Having bathed, wearing clean garments, and observing silence, one should purify one’s hands and feet while reciting the root mantra or the twelve-syllable mantra. O Rame, one should gather [leaves] from various creepers and trees within one's own garden.
Having placed [the offerings] in vessels made of bamboo, and having covered them,
he should go to his home; then, on a pure spot covered with leaves,
having set them down again and purified them, he should worship Hari with those flowers.
In the morning, a pair of lotuses and three blue lilies are recommended;
at midday, the mādhavī, two *ketakī*s,
*mālatī*, *campaka*, *puṃnāga*, and *suraparṇikā*.
The *nandyāvarta*, the white flower, the *karavīra*, and the *padmaka*;
the pure *mandāra* and that which has the luster of the *pāṭala*;
the *vicakila* at evening, and both kinds of *mallikā*.
One should worship Hari with *vakula*, *jāti* flowers, and those produced in the forest; likewise with *jātī*, *mallikā*, *hrībera*, *tamāla*, and the three types of *damanaka*.
The two *tulasī* plants— the white and the black— as well as the *kevalā* and the *kṣapakā*,
with these one should worship at all times and likewise offer them reverence.
Water-born flowers such as the lotus and others become stale after three days.
There is no fault of being stale in the worship of camphor and the like; with these,
such as lotuses and so forth, the practitioner should perform the worship and adoration of the Blessed One while reciting the name of the Blessed One one hundred and eight times.
One should perform worship at his feet; for him, heaven shall be certain.
He who performs or causes to be performed the worship of Hari with the Thousand Names shall obtain all desires in the world of mortals and a full lifespan.
Having experienced prosperity through sons, grandsons, and so forth, one then rejoices;
having attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, one delights like an eternal sage (*sūri*).
Worship with *tulasī* leaves is equal to worship with hundreds of thousands of flowers.
One should prepare its site with one hundred and eight [lotuses], O Lotus-born One;
having attained the station of Vaikuṇṭha, he rejoices together with his followers.
Or, whoever [provides] a garden, a pond, or a field for the purpose of worship...
He indeed gives [this merit] in the world of Malla and shall dwell there eternally.
Therefore, having fully considered the scripture dear to the Blessed One,
as well as the place, time, and qualification, a devoted person should perform worship.
"Haris himself is the giver of its fruit, which is auspicious both in this world and the next.
Thus did the nectar of the scriptures, drinkable by the ears and bestowing liberation upon listeners, issue forth from the lotus-mouth of Vāsudeva.

"O Sage, I have heard the Pāñcarātra for the welfare of the world. Sent by Hari, I have instructed you in its most subtle meaning. [I am] Vedaśiras of the Bhāradvāja lineage, born of the Kauṇḍinya family. (53.135–136)

Kavaṣa, however, was of Vasiṣṭha lineage yet named Bhārgava, and he belonged to the family of Viśvāmitra; these four great sages— Marīci and the others— were knowers of the dharma of seeking refuge and were thinkers on the two [principles].
"O Sage, four supreme sages born from the conch, the bow, the discus, and the mace— those who have emerged from the weapons such as the discus and others,
initiated by the Blessed One— will come to you."

Having instructed them in this, come to Vaikuṇṭha, which is served by the sun-like sages; for the pleasure of the Lord, may you rejoice like the eternal sages. (53.140) [Even one who is born into the lineage of your circle of disciples, though foolish, if he is initiated...]
He alone is worthy of propitiation, pure, and a great knower of Brahman.
No other Bhāgavatas are [fit] for the worship of us two;
even if other initiated brāhmaṇas perform supreme adoration, [it is not accepted].
"Through delusion, great harm will come to kingdoms and nations;
therefore, with every effort, this must be carried out by those born of your lineage of disciples.
Thus was he instructed by Śrī, [and this work] is known as the *Śrīpraśna*.
I have taught this Pāñcarātra scripture to you.
This scripture was obtained by me after practicing austerities for a long time;
therefore, it must never be given to one who is not a devotee or who lacks faith.
O lords of sages, this should not be spoken to one who is envious or to one who is merely ritualistic;
rather, it should be told to the virtuous, to devotees of Viṣṇu, and to those who observe the five daily rites (pañcakāla).
O wise ones, it should be told to those who are constantly fearful of saṃsāra and who possess deep faith.
And you, in turn, should instruct [them] regarding the fields of merit and so forth;
having prepared a representation of the Blessed One in accordance with the scriptures,
and having propitiated the Blessed One, you shall before long attain your own desired goal.
"In performing sacrifices for your own sake or for the sake of others, you are the primary authorities.
And those Brahmins who belong to your lineage shall also be consecrated according to the prescribed rites;
they too shall become authorities for their own sake and for the sake of others."
Vedaśiras said:
